innovation.killer_doubt: Subthreshold sip is exponential in Vt: at ~80 mV/dec, +/-6-sigma Vt (~+/-250 mV) spreads sipped charge >1,000x; the self-limiting fix needs an amplifier per ~3 cells.
innovation.decisive_experiment: SPICE Monte Carlo with foundry Vt statistics, then a 28 nm MPW of 0.2 fF local nodes on short bitlines: measure sipped-charge spread over 1e5 cells and cell droop after 16 reads. ~$120k.
innovation.prior_art: Fine-grained activation (Udipi, ISCA 2010; FGDRAM, MICRO 2017); non-destructive 2T0C gain cells (imec, Kioxia); study N-04 [training knowledge].

title: Factory seconds: sell test-reject DRAM dies as AI-grade memory
idea: Outlet stores sell slightly flawed 'seconds'. DRAM makers take dies that fail JEDEC retention or defect screens but run at about 1% raw BER under relaxed refresh, and bin them into an 'AI-grade' SKU: CXL modules with a page-level LDPC controller, sold for error-tolerant data such as KV, activations and low bit-planes.

physics.key_insight: A relaxed-BER SKU with system ECC sells bits that are scrapped today. It is also the market vehicle for ECC-paid cells: raw BER 1e-4 already halves capacitor height (C0 N-62).
physics.killer_doubt: Reject-die failures are clustered (rows, columns, banks, periphery), not iid, and makers already sell eTT/UTT grades. Net new supply may be only ~2-5% of bits.
physics.decisive_experiment: Buy ~1,000 UTT/eTT DDR4/DDR5 dies and map BER against refresh and temperature with DRAM Bender (FPGA). Measure clustering. Run cross-die LDPC plus refetch for KV and weights (~$250k).
physics.prior_art: eTT/UTT gray-market DRAM grades; Flikker (ASPLOS 2011); EDEN (MICRO 2019); HRM Par+R (DSN 2014, via search snippet). A formal AI-grade SKU: none found.

innovation.key_insight: A relaxed-spec 'AI-grade' SKU behind a long-codeword CXL controller turns retention-failing dies and marginal process windows into bits. AI tensors are read in multi-KB blocks, which amortizes page-level LDPC.
innovation.killer_doubt: Mature-node rejects are a few % and already resold (Micron SpecTek). Ramp fallout (HBM, 1c) is mostly stack, TSV or hard defects; added supply likely 2-8%, not 5-15%.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Buy 200 DDR5 reject or downbinned dies (or run standard DIMMs hot at 10-50x tREFI) and map error clustering on an FPGA tester. Then measure the BER and burst profile that a 4 KB LDPC with interleaving clears.
innovation.prior_art: Micron SpecTek downgraded parts; ArchShield (ISCA 2013); X-PPR recycled-DRAM CXL repair (2025). In-study twin: R21 I-01312 (ADVANCE) and R26 I-05038. Fold into I-01312.

title: CDN edge caching: weak memory tier holds only clean data
idea: Adapted from CDNs, which can lose a cached object because the origin always has a copy: the OS places only clean, file-backed pages (page cache, read-only model files, container images) on a pool of cheap low-grade DRAM with detection-only codes, and any detected error simply invalidates the page and refetches it from SSD.

physics.key_insight: Clean file-backed data has a free backup, so a weak tier needs only detection; Linux already drops and re-reads clean page-cache pages on an uncorrectable error.
physics.killer_doubt: In VM clouds the host sees guest page cache as anonymous, dirty memory. Clean, host-visible pages may be only ~10-20% of DRAM, capping savings at a few percent.
physics.decisive_experiment: Measure host-visible clean-page residency on 1,000 container and VM hosts, then run a CXL tier of second-life DIMMs with CRC detection and 4x relaxed refresh under Linux tiering; count refetches and p99 latency.
physics.prior_art: Luo et al. DSN 2014 heterogeneous-reliability memory (parity plus recovery of clean pages from disk); Flikker (ASPLOS 2011); Linux memory_failure clean-page recovery.

innovation.key_insight: Clean, file-backed pages have an authoritative copy elsewhere, so detection plus refetch can replace correction for a large share of server memory.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already published and partly shipped (HRM, Linux hwpoison). Above ~1e-7 BER nearly every 64 B line refetches from SSD at ~50-100 us; below it, it is ordinary tiering.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None beyond R17 I-02525's DRAM-Bender study of clustered versus diffuse faults in reject dies; fold the clean-page policy into the I-01312 CXL controller. ~$0 incremental.
innovation.prior_art: Heterogeneous-Reliability Memory (Luo et al., DSN 2014); Linux hwpoison clean-page drop; in-study R17 I-02525 and R28 I-10427 (both DROP).

title: Generated embeddings: replace terabyte tables with tiny hash-fed networks
idea: Po: the table is stored inside a brain. Recommender embedding tables are replaced by a multi-hash encoder feeding a small MLP that generates each ID's embedding on the fly, with only the hottest ~1% of IDs cached explicitly.

physics.key_insight: The capacity bound favours it: tail IDs with few interactions carry little learned information, so a generator covers them while explicit rows for the hottest ~1% keep memorisation.
physics.killer_doubt: Production tables already ship pruned and int4 (~4-8x). A light DHE decoder costs ~0.7 uJ per lookup, ~50x a 128 B fetch (~15 nJ). Production NE loss is unmeasured.
physics.decisive_experiment: Train DLRM on Criteo-1TB with four tables: full, int4 plus pruning, the CAFE hot/hash hybrid and a DHE hybrid. Report NE against bytes and FLOPs per lookup. Pass: >=5x smaller than int4-pruned at <0.02% NE loss (<$50k).
physics.prior_art: DHE (Kang et al., KDD 2021); TT-Rec (MLSys 2021); ROBE (MLSys 2022); CAFE hot/hashed hybrid (SIGMOD 2024); QR embeddings (KDD 2020). From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Recommender embedding tables are TB-scale. Computing rows from multi-hash codes through a small MLP, and caching only the hot ~1% exactly, could cut them 10-100x.
innovation.killer_doubt: This is published DHE plus hybrid caching. Each lookup becomes ~1-10 MFLOP instead of a ~256 B read, multiplying inference compute 10-100x, so production keeps quantized, hashed tables.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On MLPerf DLRM-DCNv2 / Criteo-1TB, compare hybrid DHE with int4 rows plus Unified Embedding: AUC, FLOPs per sample, p99 latency and DRAM. About $50k of GPU time.
innovation.prior_art: Deep Hash Embedding (Kang et al., KDD 2021); MP-Rec hybrid table/DHE (Gupta et al., 2023); Google Unified Embedding (NeurIPS 2023); TT-Rec; R28 I-00749 (DROP).

title: Astronomy CCD correlated double sampling enables 20 mV memory links
idea: Astronomical CCDs read single electrons by correlated double sampling, subtracting a reset sample from the signal sample. Put clocked CDS receivers on interposer/TSV links so offsets and low-frequency noise cancel, allowing 20-30 mV swings driven from a dedicated switched-capacitor 0.1 V rail.

physics.key_insight: Auto-zero/CDS removes comparator offset, the real floor of low-swing links. With E ≈ C·Vswing·Vrail, mm-wire charging falls ~50x. kTC noise on 100 fF is only ~0.2 mV.
physics.killer_doubt: Wire CV² is a minority of the ~2.5 pJ/bit interposer path (1 pF x 0.4 V² ≈ 0.16 pJ). Clocking, PHY and receivers (~30-100 fJ) remain: ~1.5-2x, not 10x.
physics.decisive_experiment: 22/28 nm MPW test chip (~$350k) with 64 CDS low-swing lanes on 3-5 mm interposer-like lines and a switched-capacitor 0.1 V rail. Measure pJ/bit and BER <1e-15 at 4-8 Gb/s against a 0.4 V reference.
physics.prior_art: NVIDIA ground-referenced signaling (~0.54 pJ/bit, 2013). Low-swing on-chip interconnects (Ho/Horowitz). SRAM bitline sensing at 50-100 mV with offset cancellation.

innovation.key_insight: CDS dynamically cancels receiver offset and 1/f drift, allowing ~30 mV swings. It is better aimed at DRAM's on-die global data lines, the dominant HBM energy term.
innovation.killer_doubt: The PHY is only ~0.5-1 of HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit, and ground-referenced or capacitive low-swing links already reach ~0.3-0.5 pJ/b. The reset phase halves per-lane throughput.
innovation.decisive_experiment: 28 nm MPW: a 1 mm interposer-class line with a CDS receiver at 30 mV versus a calibrated StrongARM baseline. Measure extrapolated BER and fJ/bit at 4-8 Gb/s across temperature. About $150k.
innovation.prior_art: NVIDIA ground-referenced signaling (2013); capacitively driven low-swing interconnects (Ho, Horowitz); offset-calibrated sense amplifiers; double-sampling comparators.

title: Via-ROM weight chiplet: frozen weights need no DRAM
idea: Eliminate DRAM, its writes and its refresh for deployed model weights: encode weights in a single custom via-mask layer of a mature-node ROM die (one via = one bit) hybrid-bonded under the compute die; the data survives power loss by construction.

physics.key_insight: For frozen weights, writes and refresh are pure waste. Read-only bits over hybrid bonds give ~0.1 pJ/bit and fab EUV-free in the U.S.
physics.killer_doubt: A 28 nm via-ROM bit is ~0.03-0.06 um2 vs ~0.001 um2 per DRAM cell (30-60x less dense). A 4-bit 70B model needs ~11,000 mm2; ~2.5 GB fits under one die.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Cost-model the multi-bit ROM-CIM density needed to beat $20/GB DRAM at the bandwidth-per-area of a bonded stack, against Taalas-class hardwired logic (desk study, <$20k).
physics.prior_art: Taalas HC1 hardwires an 8B model on N6 (2026, prior knowledge). ROM-based compute-in-memory literature (2022-25). Classic mask-ROM.

innovation.key_insight: Frozen weights need zero write endurance, so they can leave DRAM for surplus mature-node mask ROM. A 3-8B on-device model in ROM frees ~4-8 GB of LPDDR per AI phone.
innovation.killer_doubt: Model churn: phones live ~4 years while base models change yearly. And 28 nm NAND-ROM (~0.005 um2/bit) is ~2x DRAM area per bit, so expect cost parity, not 5x cheaper.
innovation.decisive_experiment: 40/28 nm MPW: a 16-64 Mb via-programmed NAND-ROM macro holding a quantized model slice, measuring density, read pJ/bit and page bandwidth. Add an accuracy study of LoRA on a ROM base across model generations. About $400k.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1 (N6, weights in mask-ROM metal/via layers; AMD acquiring) (via search snippet); Hidden-ROM and YOLoC ROM-CiM (2022); SanDisk/SK hynix HBF.

title: Token-sweep restore: inference reads replace refresh, shortening capacitors
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: in LLM-inference memory every weight row is activated once per decode step (~10-16 ms) and each activation restores the cell, so the controller disables refresh and guarantees the sweep period; if serving pauses beyond the bound it drops the weights and reloads them from flash, keeping refresh power exactly zero.

physics.key_insight: Dense-model decode sweeps every weight row each ~10-30 ms, so an inference-only HBM could specify a 16 ms retention window and skip refresh almost for free.
physics.killer_doubt: Above 85 C HBM already refreshes every 32 ms, so the Cs gain is ~2x, not 4x. Sense signal (Cs/C_BL) also sets Cs, so shorter capacitors need new sensing.
physics.decisive_experiment: Capture row-activation traces from vLLM on dense and MoE models at batch 1-256 to find the worst unswept interval. Pair them with retention-tail and sense-margin models of a 2x-shorter capacitor. ~$80k.
physics.prior_art: Smart Refresh (MICRO 2007) skips refresh on recently accessed rows; RANA (ISCA 2018) drops eDRAM refresh when data lifetime is below retention (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: LLM decode activates every weight row each ~10-50 ms step, restoring cells for free. Weight-only DRAM can delete refresh and be binned or designed to a 16 ms retention spec.
innovation.killer_doubt: Cs is sized mainly by the Cs/Cbl sense ratio, not leak-down, so a 4x shorter window saves perhaps 1.2-1.5x in Cs, not 3x; refresh costs only ~5-20% of bandwidth.
innovation.decisive_experiment: With DRAM Bender/SoftMC on DDR5 and HBM parts at 85-95 C, disable refresh under a weight-sweep pattern at 16-64 ms; map failing rows and the retention-yield gain over the 64 ms spec. Under $100k.
innovation.prior_art: Smart Refresh (Ghosh and Lee, MICRO 2007) skips refresh for recently activated rows; RANA (ISCA 2018) uses DNN data lifetimes to cut eDRAM refresh.

title: Top-k KV from in-memory scoring of MSB-plane sketches
idea: Keys are quantised per channel to INT8 (KIVI-style) and stored as bit planes. The 4 MSB planes live in a PIM-capable tier (HBM-PIM or LPDDR5X-PIM). The low planes and V live in a cheaper capacity tier (LPDDR or CXL DRAM). Each decode step broadcasts the query to bank-level units, which compute approximate q.k scores from the MSB planes with bit-serial adds at the sense-amp stripe or the existing PIM MAC units, and return only scores (2 B per token per KV head). The GPU picks the top-k tokens (k ~ 1-4k) and fetches their full K and V. Nothing is stored twice: the sketch is the high planes of the real data.

physics.key_insight: Scoring on the MSB planes of the real INT8 keys avoids storing a duplicate sketch. KV capacity splits between a PIM tier and a cheaper tier.
physics.killer_doubt: KIVI 2-bit KV already gives ~8x capacity in one tier. Fetching the top 2k tokens (~160 KB each, 70B GQA) is ~0.33 GB per sequence-step: ~5 ms over CXL.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into the I-09070 dossier: trace-driven 128k-context decode simulation (Ramulator plus an AttAcc model) of MSB-plane top-k on UPMEM or LPDDR5X-PIM, compared on tokens/s/$ with ShadowKV and KIVI-2bit.
physics.prior_art: ShadowKV, Quest and InfiniGen top-k KV; SpAtten MSB-first fetch; AttAcc, HBM-PIM, AiM; R11 ADVANCE I-09070; R28 DROP I-03037. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Split keys by bit significance and the sketch is the real data's MSB planes: PIM scores tokens in place, the GPU fetches only top-k, full KV moves to cheaper tiers.
innovation.killer_doubt: GPU-side quantized or low-rank key sketches (ShadowKV, Quest, SparQ) already save ~5-7x KV without PIM. PIM availability, and whether 4-bit-key top-k recall reaches ~95%, are undecided.
innovation.decisive_experiment: GPU emulation at 128k tokens on RULER/LongBench with Llama-3.1-8B. Compare top-k recall and accuracy of 4-MSB-plane key scores against full keys and ShadowKV, then model PIM timing from LPDDR5X-PIM specs. ~$60k.
innovation.prior_art: Quest, SparQ, InfiniGen, ShadowKV [training knowledge]; StarC PIM selective-token access and hybrid-bonded near-memory top-k (prior logs); KIVI; Samsung LPDDR5X-PIM.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM holding year-frozen foundation model weights
idea: A standard base die, built on a DRAM-periphery or mature logic process, adds one contact/via mask that encodes a frozen model's weights as present or absent vias. Each bit takes about 2-4 F^2 and needs no capacitor and no refresh. The dies stack HBM-style beside the accelerator, and each new model release costs just that one mask. The time-scale insight: weights stay unchanged for 6-18 months, so they need no rewritable cells.

physics.key_insight: Frozen weights need no endurance or refresh. Workaround: a capacitor-less DRAM array whose storage-node contact is the programming via, giving DRAM density, non-destructive read and no read disturb.
physics.killer_doubt: HBF claims 8-16x HBM capacity at similar cost; a single-level 6F2 ROM saves only ~20-30% of DRAM wafer cost (no capacitor), so it loses ~5x on $/bit.
physics.decisive_experiment: Run an accelerated read-disturb test on commercial 3D TLC and SLC-mode NAND (~1e4 reads/s per block) to find HBF's rewrite interval at 20-50 weight reads/s. Add a step-count cost model of capacitor-less DRAM-array ROM. ~$80k.
physics.prior_art: Taalas HC1 mask-ROM weights on TSMC N6 (via search snippet, earlier logs); Sandisk/SK hynix HBF OCP spec 2026; contact/via mask ROM; sibling ideas I-00502, I-04289.

innovation.key_insight: Frozen weights need no endurance or refresh, and one via mask on a generic base array is the cheapest per-model customisation of storage.
innovation.killer_doubt: HBF claims 8-16x HBM capacity at similar cost (via search snippet), against ~3x cheaper for via-ROM, so HBF wins ~3-5x on $/GB and is rewritable; models churn every 3-6 months.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Sizing only: a $/GB and latency model of a 28 nm via-ROM base-die stack versus HBF for MoE random-expert access, using the published HBF spec. ~$20k.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1 mask-ROM weights on N6, AMD acquiring (via R16 snippet); SanDisk/SK hynix HBF OCP spec (Aug 2026); YOLoC ROM-CiM; R16 family I-02186/I-01226.

title: Unified charge-debt counter for retention and row hammer
idea: Each row carries one counter that accumulates time weighted by temperature plus neighbor activations weighted by coupling. A row is refreshed when its debt crosses a threshold, so one mechanism handles both retention and hammer.

physics.key_insight: Any refresh relaxation needs hammer protection decoupled from REF commands; one per-row debt that resets on any restore is the natural way to unify them.
physics.killer_doubt: By the 85 C tail model, 4x interval leaves ~1.5% of rows weak, 8x ~11%. PRAC already counts per-row ACTs; additivity of hammer and leakage loss is unmeasured.
physics.decisive_experiment: DRAM-Bender on 20 DDR4/DDR5 dies (~$150k): measure HCfirst versus time since victim refresh (0-100% of retention) at 50 and 85 C; the debt model holds if HCfirst falls linearly with elapsed fraction.
physics.prior_art: JEDEC DDR5 PRAC per-row activation counters; RAIDR retention bins; RowPress shows aggressor on-time matters, so ACT counts alone are incomplete.

innovation.key_insight: Hammer charge loss and leakage loss add in the same storage node, so one per-row deadline is the physically correct trigger. A leaky analog replica would track temperature for free.
innovation.killer_doubt: Without per-row retention profiles the time term is identical for every row: normal refresh plus PRAC. Profiles hit VRT, and refresh is only 16-33% of idle power.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Ramulator study driven by DRAM Bender per-row retention and hammer-coupling maps from 10 DDR5 chips (~$100k). Pass if debt-triggered refresh cuts refresh operations >=4x at equal UE rate, including VRT.
innovation.prior_art: JEDEC DDR5 PRAC per-row counters; RAIDR retention bins; Micron analog accumulator patents; Self-Managing DRAM (2022); this study's I-05623 analog integrator (R22).

title: Eliminate the 64-ms retention spec: ephemeral sub-femtofarad cells for transient tensors
idea: Eliminate the assumption that every bit must survive 64 ms: build a memory class whose storage node is a planar ~0.5 fF capacitor with no pillar and ~100 us retention, used only for AI activations, KV-cache spill and gradients that are overwritten within microseconds; the controller tags allocations by lifetime and never refreshes them.

physics.key_insight: A matched-lifetime tier is the logical end of refresh-free design; at ~100 us a planar 0.5 fF node needs only ~1 pA leakage, trivially met.
physics.killer_doubt: Little's law: capacity <= bandwidth x lifetime. At HBM3E's ~1.2 TB/s per stack, 100 us holds ~120 MB, SRAM-scale and already on-die (H100 has 50 MB L2).
physics.decisive_experiment: Trace an LLM inference and a training step on GPU; count bytes whose write-to-last-read interval is under 100 us yet spill off-chip; kill if <5% of DRAM traffic. ~$20k.
physics.prior_art: RANA (ISCA 2018), gain-cell eDRAM for DNN accelerators, refresh-free eDRAM buffers; review I-04810 dropped the same class.

innovation.key_insight: Once N-04 sensing fixes the signal, retention binds. ~1 fF with a Si access device gives ~27 ms, matching HBM's 18-29 ms full sweep: access becomes refresh, pillar ~5x shorter.
innovation.killer_doubt: Planar 0.5 fF needs ~7,000 nm2 (8x the cell), so a ~240 nm stub is needed. At 95 C the tail halves to ~13 ms, below sweep; +25 ns tRCD.
innovation.decisive_experiment: (1) Profile lifetime and access-period histograms from production LLM inference and training traces (~$50k). (2) On FPGA DDR5/HBM, cut refresh 4x and run decode with access-certified rows, counting errors at 85-95 C. Pair with N-04's 1 fF MPW.
innovation.prior_art: RANA (ISCA 2018), ZEM (2021), CAMEL eDRAM co-design (2023) (via search snippet); triage N-64 lease and N-04 sensing. No capacitor-shrink co-design found (search summary).

title: One optical copy of weights broadcast to a hundred accelerators
idea: First principles: read-only weights need O(1) storage, not O(N) copies, if broadcast bandwidth exists. Keep one model copy in a central memory node and stream it in layer order through a passive 1:128 optical splitter tree to accelerators running in lockstep; each holds only a few-layer SRAM ring buffer.

physics.key_insight: Read-only weights need one copy. A passive splitter tree amortizes the transmitter, and a central node can hold weights in cheap LPDDR instead of N copies in HBM.
physics.killer_doubt: Each receiver needs the full weight-read rate: 70 GB per 30 ms is ~19 Tb/s, ~$1.9k at $0.1/Gbps, versus ~$1.0-1.75k HBM saved. 1:128 split loses 21 dB.
physics.decisive_experiment: Build a 1:32 PLC splitter testbed fed by a 16-wavelength x 100G DWDM source and an EDFA booster. Measure BER and power margin at every port. Add a cost model for 10-20 Tb/s receive-only SiPh chiplets. ~$400k.
physics.prior_art: Cerebras weight streaming (MemoryX/SwarmX broadcast, electrical); Celestial AI photonic memory fabric (prior knowledge). Passive optical weight broadcast to accelerators: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Read-only weights need O(1) copies. A passive splitter tree can feed many decode-only replicas in lockstep, leaving each accelerator's HBM for KV.
innovation.killer_doubt: Each leaf must ingest weights at HBM rate (~2-8 TB/s, while NICs give ~0.1 TB/s). Rack-scale sharding already keeps weights at only ~5-10% of an NVL72's ~20 TB of HBM.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fleet model of HBM freed versus replica size (HGX-8 to NVL72) and model size. Plus an FPGA bench: a 1:32 splitter, 100G PAM4 lanes, two boards decoding a small model in lockstep; measure BER and utilization. ~$300k.
innovation.prior_art: Fiber Memory preprint (arXiv 2607.08407): splitter-tapped fiber weight broadcast to pods (via search snippet); Cerebras MemoryX/SwarmX weight streaming; Phase B N-80.

title: Substitute die-to-wafer bonding with micro-transfer-printed DRAM tiles on compute
idea: Release 0.5-1 mm2 DRAM tiles from their wafer by undercutting a sacrificial layer, pick thousands at once with an elastomer stamp, and print them directly over compute tiles on the processor wafer, followed by planarization and a via step for um-scale connections.

physics.key_insight: Stamps place thousands of thin tiles per cycle with no hybrid-bond aligner. Lithographic vias at ~10 um pitch still give ~1e4 links/mm2 at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit.
physics.killer_doubt: DRAM over hot logic: retention halves per ~10 C, so 105 C junctions mean ~4x the refresh of 85 C. DRAM wafers lack a release layer and need carrier laser-debond.
physics.decisive_experiment: Thin a commercial DRAM wafer to ~10 um on a laser-release carrier and transfer-print 1 mm2 tiles onto a dummy logic wafer. Planarize, add vias, then measure print yield, placement and retention-tail shift. ~$600k.
physics.prior_art: X-Celeprint/X-FAB uTP foundry for III-V, GaN and photonics, <1 um misalignment and up to 99% yield (via search snippet); no DRAM-on-logic uTP found.

innovation.key_insight: Stamps place thousands of thin DRAM tiles per cycle over compute, avoiding die-to-wafer bonder throughput, with old-fab tiles at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit.
innovation.killer_doubt: Commodity DRAM wafers lack a release layer. Print placement is ~+/-1.5 um, forcing >=5-10 um via pitch, while SoIC/SeDRAM hybrid bonding already runs <=9 um in production.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Thin 20 old-node DRAM dies to ~10 um on release tape and print them onto a heater-equipped logic test wafer with adaptive-patterned vias. Measure placement error, via yield, pJ/bit and 85-95 C retention. ~$300k.
innovation.prior_art: X-Celeprint/Rogers micro-transfer printing; Deca adaptive patterning; SeDRAM (IEDM 2020) and TSMC SoIC hybrid bonding; in-study I-02653 (DROP).

title: Vertical oxide CCD string: transistor-less 3D charge-shift memory
idea: Etch one high-aspect-ratio hole through 128-256 alternating W/Mo and SiO2 word planes (the same module as 3D NAND), and line it with a thin gate oxide and an ALD IGZO/IGO channel. Clock planes in 4 phases (2 gates per bit): each bit is a packet of ~1,000-5,000 electrons in an accumulation well. Si CCDs lose stored charge to thermal generation (dark current); wide-gap IGZO generates essentially no carriers, so packets hold, limited only by inter-well barriers and gate leakage. Reading shifts packets out of the top of the string into a charge-transfer sense amp (B1-04) on bonded periphery, and data recirculates to the bottom: a delay-line memory with 32-64-bit strings and thousands of parallel holes per line access. Planes are segmented into small blocks to keep plane RC at ~1 ns per phase.

physics.key_insight: Charge shifted through an oxide channel wears only the gate dielectric, and NAND-like tiers need no per-bit transistor or capacitor: the largest deposition-only density lever.
physics.killer_doubt: imec's IGZO CCD reaches CTE >98%, but 128 transfers need >=0.9999 (0.98^128 keeps 7.5%). At imec's >4 MHz, a 64-stage shift takes ~16 us: buffer-class, not DRAM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into the I-10793 dossier: university planar 4-phase IGZO CCD lines of 128-256 gates, measuring per-transfer CTE against clock (4-100 MHz) and dark fill at 85 C. Go if >=0.9999 at >=20 MHz.
physics.prior_art: imec IEDM 2024 planar and IMW 2026 vertical IGZO CCDs (via search snippet, logged R16); 1970s Si CCD memories. Same card as R16 ADVANCE I-10793.

innovation.key_insight: Deposition-only charge-shift strings remove the per-bit transistor, capacitor and EUV, and wide-gap oxide channels hold packets with no dark current: block-access density at 3D NAND cost.
innovation.killer_doubt: Bit 64 needs ~128 gate transfers, so at imec's CTE of 98% (if per transfer) only ~7% survives. DRAM-class needs >=0.9999, clocked ~100x faster than imec's 4-6 MHz.
innovation.decisive_experiment: 32-64-plane vertical IGZO CCD pillars through imec IIAP or a university fab. Measure per-transfer CTE against clock (5-200 MHz) and temperature, and packet loss after 128 transfers. ~$600k.
innovation.prior_art: imec IGZO CCD: planar 142-bit (IEDM 2024, CTE >98%) and vertical 3D CCD (IMW 2026) for CXL buffer (prior logs). Same family as N-08/I-05275.

title: Chilled-DIMM certification grade with 256 ms refresh
idea: Worse: run DRAM at 85-95 C, where leakage doubles every ~10 C. Flip: create a 'cold-loop' grade: modules on datacenter liquid cold plates held at 25-35 C are binned and certified for 256 ms refresh, and dies that fail the hot spec but pass cold are sold into this grade.

physics.key_insight: Liquid-cooled AI racks hold DIMMs 50-60 C below spec. Retention roughly doubles per ~10 C, so a cold-certified grade has ~30x headroom for a 4-8x refresh stretch.
physics.killer_doubt: Tail cells are GIDL or trap-assisted, with weak temperature activation and VRT. An 8x longer window lets ~5.3M activations hit a row versus ~0.7M. Rescued dies may be <2%.
physics.decisive_experiment: Profile 500 DDR5 dies, including hot-retention rejects, on DRAM Bender at 30, 50 and 85 C; extract tail activation energy, VRT rate and hammer threshold at 256 ms; compute cold-grade yield. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: LPDDR temperature-compensated refresh via MR4; RAIDR (ISCA 2012) and AVATAR multi-rate refresh; vendor ETT/downgrade die sales.

innovation.key_insight: Liquid-cooled AI racks hold DIMMs near 30-40 C, where retention is several-fold longer, so a cold-certified grade could absorb hot-fail dies and relax refresh.
innovation.killer_doubt: Refresh is ~10-20% of power and bandwidth, so 4x less saves ~8-15%. LPDDR already scales tREFI with temperature via MR4; tail activation ~0.3-0.6 eV caps gain.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Thermal-chuck retention-tail maps of 100 hot-test-reject and 100 passing DDR5 dies at 30, 55 and 85 C on an FPGA tester, with 4 weeks of VRT tracking. Count dies passing 256 ms at 35 C. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: LPDDR4/5 MR4 temperature-based refresh multipliers; DDR 2x refresh above 85 C; Liu ISCA 2013; in-study R19 I-11539 and I-11080 (DROP) [training knowledge].

title: Potluck cookbook: open-source, silicon-proven DRAM periphery IP commons
idea: A potluck works because everyone shares recipes. Fund an open-source library of DRAM periphery blocks (sense amps with offset calibration, row-hammer trackers, pumps, LPDDR/DDR5 PHYs) with silicon-proven layouts on U.S. 28/22 nm processes, so startups and foundries can build memory dies without decades of trade-secret circuit know-how.

physics.key_insight: Silicon-proven open SA-offset calibration, pumps and hammer trackers on US 22/28 nm would lower entry cost for bonded-periphery or BEOL oxide-cell entrants.
physics.killer_doubt: The moat is process and yield learning (~1e-9 bit-fail tails), not circuits. Logic-wafer SAs apply only to bonded or BEOL-cell dies. The $500M to $50-100M saving is unsupported.
physics.decisive_experiment: Tape out an offset-calibrated SA bank against MIM-cap bitline loads, a VPP pump and a PRAC-style counter on a US 22/28 nm MPW. Publish measured offset sigma and pump efficiency. ~$600k.
physics.prior_art: OpenRAM (SRAM); OpenGCRAM (Stanford 2025, gain cell); LiteDRAM (controller and PHY). No open on-die DRAM periphery library found.

innovation.key_insight: Silicon-proven open sense-amp, pump and hammer-tracker blocks only matter once periphery moves to a logic wafer; then they cut an entrant's design cost.
innovation.killer_doubt: Entry barriers are cell process, yield learning and capex, not circuit IP: a ~$50-100M design saving against a $15B+ fab. DRAM-side periphery lives in the DRAM process.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-04714: open-source that tape-out's 28 nm periphery die (offset-calibrated sense amps, decoders, hammer tracker) and measure reuse by two outside teams. Adds ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: OpenRAM (UCSC); LiteDRAM and DRAM Bender (controller side); commercial DDR5/LPDDR5 PHYs (Synopsys, Cadence, Rambus); similar I-04102 dropped.

title: RISC-V-style royalty-free DRAM patent pool and periphery generator
idea: Like RISC-V plus the MPEG-LA patent pool, a foundation assembles expired 6F2/8F2 cell, sense-amp and DLL patents with donated ones into a royalty-free pool and ships an open-source periphery compiler that generates JEDEC-compliant row/column logic for a given process.

physics.key_insight: An open periphery generator plus a pooled, documented expired-patent base lowers design and legal entry cost for allied DRAM entrants; demo is software only.
physics.killer_doubt: The binding barrier is fab capital (~$15B) and process yield know-how, not IP. DRAM periphery is pitch-matched full-custom, and the big 3 are unlikely to donate live patents.
physics.decisive_experiment: $300k: extend OpenRAM to generate an open-bitline DRAM row/column periphery for one open PDK; tape out a 1 Mb 1T1C-emulation test array on MPW; survey 5 would-be entrants on whether IP blocks them.
physics.prior_art: OpenRAM (SRAM compiler); RISC-V and MPEG-LA pool models; CXMT acquired the Qimonda patent base for freedom to operate.

innovation.key_insight: An open, process-parameterized DRAM periphery generator (sense amps, decoders, pumps) would cut design entry cost for new array technologies, especially oxide and gain-cell entrants.
innovation.killer_doubt: Incumbents will not donate live patents and pre-2006 ones are already free; DRAM periphery is analog and process-specific, and 0 open DRAM PDKs exist to generate against.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Extend OpenRAM to generate a 1T1C/2T0C array with sense amps and charge pumps on SKY130 or GF180, tape out on a free MPW shuttle, and measure yield and timing against predictions.
innovation.prior_art: OpenRAM (UCSC) open SRAM compiler; RISC-V and MPEG-LA pool models; commercial memory compilers (Synopsys, Arm); Open Invention Network defensive pooling.

title: Train models with KV-dropout so memory starvation is harmless
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: inject random KV eviction (drop 30-70% of past tokens' KV, biased toward older ones) as a regularizer during pre- and post-training, turning the harm of missing context into learned robustness so inference can evict aggressively with negligible quality loss.

physics.key_insight: Eviction robustness can be trained in. Models never shown missing context collapse under H2O-style eviction, while trained ones should degrade gracefully.
physics.killer_doubt: Evicted information is gone, so needle recall falls roughly with the drop rate. MLA (~93% KV cut), DMC (4-8x) and Gemma-3 local:global (~5x) already beat the claimed 2-4x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Continue pretraining a 1B model on ~20B tokens with 30-70% stochastic eviction (~$60k of GPU time). Compare against DMC at equal KV budget on RULER and LongBench.
physics.prior_art: DMC (NVIDIA 2024); MLA (DeepSeek-V2); DuoAttention; Gemma-3 local/global layers; H2O, SnapKV, TOVA eviction. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Training under stochastic eviction could teach models to carry facts forward redundantly. Random Attention (2026) shows reasoning traces already tolerate random eviction, and the fragile part is the prompt.
innovation.killer_doubt: MLA, GQA and DMC already cut KV 4-14x architecturally, and no training recovers an evicted needle. The residual gain over the 2026 state of the art may be <1.5x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Continue pretraining a 1B model on 2-5B tokens with 30-70% biased stochastic eviction. Compare RULER and needle retrieval at 2-4x smaller KV budgets against SnapKV and Random Attention on the untouched model. About $50-100k of compute.
innovation.prior_art: DMC (Nawrot et al., ICML 2024) trained KV compression; Locret retaining heads; DeepSeek MLA and NSA; Random Attention inference-time eviction (arXiv 2609.03430, via search snippet).

title: Genome-assembler succinct structures with rank/select engines in controller
idea: From genome assemblers that squeeze terabyte de Bruijn graphs into succinct bitvectors: add hardware rank/select and Elias-Fano decode units to the memory controller so pointer-heavy structures (graphs, tries, inverted indexes, B-tree internals) are stored near entropy size yet traversed in one or two memory accesses per hop.

physics.key_insight: Pointer-heavy structures do carry 5-20x overhead over their information content, and succinct layouts (LOUDS, Elias-Fano) reach near-entropy size.
physics.killer_doubt: Software already gets the memory saving; popcnt/pdep rank/select take ~10 ns. Each hop costs 2-3 dependent ~100 ns misses; a controller engine saves only the ~40 ns on-chip round trip.
physics.decisive_experiment: Profile SDSL-lite rank/select and Elias-Fano traversal on graph, trie and inverted-index workloads. Model in gem5 a controller-side engine that removes the on-chip round trip. Advance only if speedup >2x (<$30k).
physics.prior_art: SDSL-lite; Succinct (NSDI 2015); near-memory FM-index accelerators (GenStore, MEDAL); SpZip (ISCA 2021). From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Rank/select and Elias-Fano units in the controller could fold the 2-3 dependent accesses of a succinct traversal into one memory round trip, so near-entropy layouts work for general pointer data.
innovation.killer_doubt: Software select with BMI2 pdep/tzcnt already takes ~10-30 ns, and real indexes and graphs are already compressed (Lucene PFOR, delta CSR), so extra saving is ~1.5-2x, not 3-10x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Build a CXL FPGA card with rank/select and Elias-Fano engines. Run succinct trie, graph and inverted-index traversal against BMI2 host software and compressed-CSR baselines, measuring ns per hop and bytes per edge. About $200k.
innovation.prior_art: SDSL/sux succinct libraries, FM-index FPGA accelerators, SpZip. Same mechanism as R34 I-05348 (HOLD) [training knowledge].

title: Via-programmed ROM for frozen model weights frees DRAM
idea: Combine mask-ROM economics with AI inference: weights frozen for a product's life are encoded in one via layer (1-2F2 per bit, multi-level via resistance for 2 bits) on a die whose other masks are shared, so only the via mask changes per model, written by e-beam or DUV. The weights never need refresh, never wear out, and stop occupying HBM.

physics.key_insight: Frozen weights need neither refresh nor endurance, so a write-once store can legitimately offload them from HBM: a real demand-side lever.
physics.killer_doubt: Mature-node ROM at ~0.03 um2/bit costs ~$10-20/GB to make, 7-14x DRAM's $1.48; selector-free 1-2F2 crosspoints have sneak paths; models churn every 3-6 months.
physics.decisive_experiment: Cost model plus one shuttle: a 28 nm via-ROM macro with 2-level via resistance; measure density, read energy and level margin over 1e6 bits; compare cost per GB with HBF NAND. ~$150k.
physics.prior_art: Via and contact mask ROM (decades); Taalas hardwired-model inference chips; SanDisk/SK hynix High Bandwidth Flash serves read-mostly weights and stays updatable.

innovation.key_insight: Frozen weights need zero endurance and fill ~50-60% of HBM in MoE serving (est.). Mature-node ROM with one via mask per model could free that. Merge into the I-02186 dossier.
innovation.killer_doubt: SanDisk/SK hynix High Bandwidth Flash targets the same read-mostly weights with rewritable NAND ~10-30x denser than ROM. Model churn of 3-6 months strands mask sets.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fleet economics model (~$100k): weight share of HBM by serving configuration, mask cost per model lifetime, and ROM versus HBF $/GB. Plus a 28/40 nm MPW testing 2-bit multi-level via resistance.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1 hardwired Llama 8B (2026; AMD acquisition reported, per R16 log); SanDisk/SK hynix HBF (2025) [training knowledge].

title: Secondary-market DDR4 reborn in CXL memory expansion boxes
idea: Box: reclaimed DDR4 DIMMs x standard x standard x CXL controller with per-rank ECC remap and aging-aware refresh x refurbished chassis x refurbishment line. DDR4 from decommissioned servers is tested, graded and re-hosted behind CXL controllers that hide its latency for tier-2 data.

physics.key_insight: A refurbishment line grades retired DDR4 into retention and hammer bins, then hosts each bin behind CXL with its own refresh and ECC remap, turning scrap into far memory.
physics.killer_doubt: Supply ceiling: the server DDR4 shipped in 2019-2021 and now retiring is perhaps 6-10% of 2026 bit demand that a third party could capture. Hyperscalers keep theirs (GreenSKU).
physics.decisive_experiment: Buy 1,000 retired DDR4 RDIMMs (~$50k). Profile 85 C retention, HCfirst and failures, and host the best bins behind a commercial CXL card. Census the decommissioned GB/yr outside hyperscalers.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera DDR4 reuse; existing resellers of refurbished DIMMs.

innovation.key_insight: Aging-aware refresh and per-rank ECC remap inside the CXL controller let graded DDR4 bins serve as tier-2 memory without host changes.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-00348. Shipping CXL controllers already do ECC and post-package repair; the DDR4 pool is one-time and shrinks as fleets move to DDR5.
innovation.decisive_experiment: As for I-00348, plus measure how much capacity aging-aware refresh rescues beyond pass/fail retest; kill if under 5%. About $60k.
innovation.prior_art: Marvell Structera X; Meta Vistara; Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); REAPER retention profiling; R16 I-06172 (DROP).

title: Base-array mask ROM with one e-beam-written via layer
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: pre-build generic NOR-ROM wafers (4F2 transistor arrays, DUV plus SAQP, ~25 masks, no capacitor) in bulk; once a model is frozen, program its weights by e-beam direct-writing a single via layer with two via sizes per bit-pair (2 bits/cell), so inference weights live in silicon with zero refresh and zero standby.

physics.key_insight: Frozen weights need no writes or refresh: a DUV-only NOR/via-ROM die (~25 masks, no capacitor, no EUV) at ~800 nm2/bit matches 1b density, with zero read disturb unlike HBF NAND.
physics.killer_doubt: E-beam writing ~2-4e13 vias per wafer takes tens of hours; use a ~$0.3M ArF via mask per model instead. Real doubt: fleet model life under ~12 months strands frozen silicon.
physics.decisive_experiment: 28 nm MPW NOR-ROM macro with via-size 2-bit cells: measure read margin and access time across corners; in parallel, a $/GB model at SAQP F=20 nm versus HBF including read-disturb rewrite budgets.
physics.prior_art: Mask ROM (1970s); YOLoC ROM-CIM (DAC 2022); SanDisk High Bandwidth Flash for weights (2025); Taalas hardwired-model chips (2026). All from memory, unverified.

innovation.key_insight: Frozen weights need no capacitor or refresh; a via-programmed ROM on a generic base array cuts per-model customization to one layer.
innovation.killer_doubt: Taalas HC1 already etches Llama weights into mask ROM on TSMC N6; for capacity, 3D-NAND-based HBF is ~10x denser than 2D ROM and reprogrammable.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Cost model only, no silicon: e-beam write time for ~1e11-1e12 via shots per 300 mm wafer versus a ~$100k DUV via mask amortized over chips per model version.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1 mask-ROM 'recall fabric' (AMD acquisition 2026, via search snippet); via/contact-programmed ROM; SanDisk/SK hynix High Bandwidth Flash for weights.

title: Deep-space LDPC pages: refresh at the 1% retention quantile
idea: CCSDS deep-space links decode reliably near 1e-2 raw BER. Store each 4 KB page as one LDPC codeword (~15% parity, decoder in the HBM base die or CXL controller) and set refresh where 1% of cells have decayed instead of where the last 1e-9 tail cell does; the median retention distribution is far longer than the tail, so the interval grows from 64 ms to ~1-2 s.

physics.key_insight: Refresh need not chase the 1e-9 tail: flipped cells stay flipped under internal refresh, so raw BER stays bounded and a page-level code can absorb it.
physics.killer_doubt: Refresh costs 46 fJ x 15.6/s = 0.72 pJ/bit/s; LDPC decode ~1 pJ/bit per read, so any bit read over ~once per second loses. Weights are read 10-50x/s.
physics.decisive_experiment: Replay FPGA-measured error maps at 1-8 s intervals through hard-decision LDPC and BCH models; compare decode energy times read rate against refresh energy saved, using HBM inference traces (~$100k).
physics.prior_art: Hi-ECC (Wilkerson, ISCA 2010) multi-bit 1 KB codes to stretch eDRAM refresh; our N-63 scrub-as-refresh at BER ~1e-5 with lazy syndrome dominates.

innovation.key_insight: Code against the 1% retention quantile, not the 1e-9 tail. Retention errors are one-way (Z-channel, ~4% parity bound); page-granular AI traffic tolerates codeword reads; line CRC gives a fast path.
innovation.killer_doubt: Decode cost: soft LDPC at ~1e-2 BER is est. ~1-5 pJ/bit and microseconds, against ~0.7 pJ/bit/s of refresh saved; it wins only for pages read less than every ~3 s.
innovation.decisive_experiment: DRAM Bender plus FPGA soft-LDPC (~$150k): age DDR5 rows 0.5-2 s at 85 C across data patterns and fit per-page error tails against Poisson. Pass if 15% parity gives page failure <1e-15.
innovation.prior_art: Hi-ECC (ISCA 2010); SECRET leaky-cell ECC (-87% refresh power); Qimonda per-page refresh US7975170. LDPC for DRAM refresh: none found (via search snippet).

title: CCD memory fixed: vertical bucket-brigade strings feeding one base sense amp
idea: 1970s CCD memory died because serial charge shifting made access slow. Keep its strength, no per-cell contact, but cap strings at 8 vertical tiers. Charge packets in gated wells along a vertical channel are clocked down into one sense amp at the base, the whole string is latched into SRAM in about 20 ns, and it is written back in reverse order. This removes per-tier staircase and bitline contacts.

physics.key_insight: Latch the whole string into SRAM (~20 ns) and write back in reverse (LIFO) order; 8 tiers need only ~16 transfers, so CTE ~0.99 suffices. Fold into I-01064.
physics.killer_doubt: Density collapses: a gate-all-around CCD hole needs ~150 nm hex pitch (0.0195 um2), so 8 bits per hole is 0.0024 um2/bit, ~2x worse than 1b DRAM (0.0011).
physics.decisive_experiment: Desk layout study (~$30k): bits/um2 vs string length for 60-150 nm hole pitch including per-row slits and sense paths; then add the LIFO latch scheme to the I-01064 test chip.
physics.prior_art: 1970s CCD memories (serial latency killed them); LIFO write-back is standard shift-register practice. Vertical CCD memory: none found (via search snippet).

innovation.key_insight: Short 8-16-bit oxide CCD strings latched to SRAM keep DRAM-class latency, with no capacitor, access transistor, EUV or per-tier contact. They tolerate CTE 0.999, which long strings cannot.
innovation.killer_doubt: Clock speed. imec shows >6.25 MHz planar and >4 MHz 3D; a ~20 ns string read needs ~1 GHz phase clocks (24-32 transfers). Trap-limited CTE at GHz is unmeasured.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Planar 16-32-gate IGZO/IGO 4-phase CCD with segmented low-R gates at a university fab (~$300k), RF-probed. Measure CTE versus clock from 10 MHz to 1 GHz, at 25/85 C, with and without fat zero.
innovation.prior_art: imec IGZO CCD (IEDM 2024: 142 bits, >98% CTE, >200 s, >1e10 cycles; IMW 2026 3D) targets CXL buffer, not DRAM latency (via search snippet).

title: Gain-cell NAND string with dual-gate bypassable read transistors
idea: [Box: storage-node gate | dual-gate IGZO 2T0C | series-string current sense | monolithic vertical string | Si | 3D-NAND hole-and-plate deposition] Build 2T0C gain cells along a vertical macaroni string like 3D NAND; each read transistor has a back word-plate that, driven high, forces it on regardless of its stored node, so unselected cells act as pass gates and only the selected cell's storage node modulates string current. Write transistors hang off a second vertical write-bitline in the same hole.

physics.key_insight: The read side works: a 64-cell IGZO series string (~10-15 kOhm/cell, ~0.5-1 uA) swings a 100 fF short bitline 50 mV in ~10 ns, with NAND-style pass-voltage bypass.
physics.killer_doubt: Topology: the outer word plane gates only the outermost layer, so a write transistor between storage node and inner write bitline has no gate; it reverts to a floating-gate cell.
physics.decisive_experiment: Planar first (~$250k, university fab): 16-cell series string of dual-gate IGZO 2T0C, read margin vs pass-gate Vt spread at 85 C; TCAD a gate-able 3D write-path topology before any vertical build.
physics.prior_art: 3D NAND pass-voltage read; stacked and vertical IGZO 2T0C (imec, IME-CAS); Phase B N-43 coaxial 2T0C. NAND-string 2T0C: none found.

innovation.key_insight: A NAND-topology string of 2T0C cells, with back-gate bypass so unselected read FETs act as pass gates, puts no capacitor or per-cell contact in each hole.
innovation.killer_doubt: 64 series IGZO FETs (~50-200 kOhm each) carry ~0.1-0.3 uA: 30-100 ns to develop 100 mV on 100 fF. Also needs two planes per tier and per-cell floating nodes.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Planar series strings of 8/16/32/64 dual-gate IGZO TFTs (~$150k). Measure string current, sense time and read disturb versus N and bypass voltage. TCAD the two-channel vertical hole.
innovation.prior_art: NEO 3D X-DRAM 1T1C/3T0C in a 3D-NAND-like flow (company-reported); IMECAS 4-layer 2T0C (VLSI 2026). No series-string gain cell found.

title: Leakage decay as built-in recency weighting for analog KV caches
idea: Invert 'charge decay is a failure that refresh must undo' -> make decay part of the math. KV-cache and state-space values are stored as un-refreshed analog charge whose leakage time constant is programmed per bank by body bias, so stored magnitude decays exponentially with token age, implementing the recency weighting (decay gates, ALiBi-like bias) models already learn.

physics.key_insight: IGZO gain-cell retention (1e3-3e4 s) matches long-context session spans; droop as soft eviction plus zero-detect reclaim fits decay-gated models with zero refresh.
physics.killer_doubt: Cell retention spreads >=2 decades and halves per ~10 C, so decay is uncontrolled noise, not ALiBi; refresh for 43 GB of KV costs only ~0.25 W.
physics.decisive_experiment: Software: inject lognormal retention spread (sigma 0.5-1 decade) and 2x per 10 C drift into KV caches of an open 8B model; go if long-context loss <1% versus 2-bit KV. ~$30k.
physics.prior_art: RANA retention-aware training (ISCA 2018); StreamingLLM and H2O eviction; RetNet and Mamba decay gates; our B4-06 graceful-forgetting KV holds the core.

innovation.key_insight: KV data has a bounded useful life, so un-refreshed gain cells with in-array attention remove both refresh and HBM KV traffic. Decay-as-recency is a small twist on this.
innovation.killer_doubt: Decaying K/V magnitude is not ALiBi's additive logit bias. Leakage spans >10x across cells and drifts ~7%/C (Ea~0.6 eV), so decay is noise unless trained around.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fine-tune a 125M-1B model (~$50k compute) with per-cell decay drawn from measured gain-cell leakage distributions plus temperature drift. Compare quality with a 2-bit KIVI digital KV baseline at matched bits.
innovation.prior_art: Leroux et al., Nature Comp. Sci. 2025: gain-cell KV store with analog attention and sliding window (via search snippet); RANA (ISCA 2018) data-lifetime eDRAM refresh.

title: Grade-B DRAM exchange selling dies with certified error maps
idea: Box [medium: any | access: any | sense: standard | integration: DIMM or CXL | substrate: bulk | fab: existing fabs]. A broker buys dies that fail JEDEC retention or hammer limits, tests each to a signed per-die error map, and sells them to hyperscalers whose controllers load the map to retire rows and set per-bank refresh.

physics.key_insight: A signed per-die error map lets controllers retire rows and set refresh per bank, turning JEDEC rejects into predictable capacity instead of untested gray-market parts.
physics.killer_doubt: ETT/UTT downgrade markets already absorb most of the 5-15% fallout. The map adds value only if controllers honor it, and DDR5 lacks per-bank refresh-rate control.
physics.decisive_experiment: With one OSAT, map 2,000 rejected dies (retention, hammer, VRT over 7 days), load the maps into an FPGA DDR5/CXL controller, and verify zero UEs over 3 months versus unmapped controls. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: ETT/UTT downgrade die sales; ArchShield fault maps (ISCA 2013); RAIDR multi-rate refresh; DDR5 PPR.

innovation.key_insight: A signed per-die error map lets a CXL controller retire rows and set per-bank refresh, turning JEDEC rejects into a trusted product rather than grey-market parts.
innovation.killer_doubt: Downbins already sell (Micron SpecTek, eTT/UTT). Truly scrapped dies are a few % after redundancy, and host memory controllers cannot load per-die maps; only custom CXL controllers can.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Folded into in-study I-05038: map faults in ~500 UTT/downgraded DDR4/DDR5 parts over temperature and time on an FPGA tester; compute map-recoverable good bits per die and broker price spread. ~$120k.
innovation.prior_art: Micron SpecTek downgraded parts; ArchShield (ISCA 2013); in-study I-01312 (ADVANCE), I-05038 and I-08260 (HOLD) [training knowledge].

title: Compressed-sensing readout makes selector-less crossbars usable
idea: The cheapest possible cell is a two-terminal resistor at a wire crossing with no transistor or selector, but sneak paths forbid single-cell reads. Read a whole 1k x 1k tile with pseudo-random row voltage patterns, measure column currents, and let a decoder in the interface chiplet solve the linear system (with sparse coding and block parity) to recover every bit.

physics.key_insight: With every line driven and columns held at virtual ground, +/-V patterns make an odd-I-V crossbar exactly linear. Sneak paths become decodable, and decoding by tile suits bulk weight streaming.
physics.killer_doubt: IR drop: a 1k-cell 20 nm Cu line (~3 kOhm) sags ~0.75 V at 1 uA/cell on a 0.2 V read; cells need >=10 MOhm. ReRAM endures 1e6-1e10, needs 3e8-7e13.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fabricate 64x64 and 256x256 passive crossbars (ReRAM, plus fixed resistive-via ROM) at a university fab. Drive them with Hadamard patterns from a 256-channel DAC/TIA board. Measure raw BER against size, cell R and spread (~$400k).
physics.prior_art: Zidan et al., multiport closed-form sneak-path readout (IEEE TNANO 2014, via search snippet); Strukov passive 4K crossbars; Cassuto sneak-path coding. Compressed-sensing readout: none found.

innovation.key_insight: With every row and column actively driven, crossbar currents sum linearly, so the read becomes matrix inversion in an interface chiplet rather than a selector problem.
innovation.killer_doubt: IR drop breaks linearity: a 1k-cell 20 nm line is ~2.5 kOhm; ~0.5 mA summed current drops ~0.6 V, above a 0.2 V read bias (estimate). ReRAM endures only ~1e6-1e10.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Build a 128x128 selector-less HfOx crossbar at a university fab; read it with Hadamard patterns and a least-squares decoder; measure bit error rate against array size and line resistance. About $250k.
innovation.prior_art: Imperial/Southampton mCAT multi-port readout with mathematical sneak-current cancellation (via search snippet); one-step row readout (arXiv 1903.01512); Cassuto sneak-path coding [training knowledge].

title: Taffy-pulled wire-in-glass preform sliced into through-glass-via wafers
idea: Stack copper-cored glass capillaries into a preform, draw it down 500x on a fiber tower, re-bundle and redraw (as multicore fiber is made), then slice the rod like salami into 100 um glass discs. Each disc holds millions of 2 um-pitch through-glass vias formed in one draw.

physics.key_insight: Draw-stack-redraw-slice makes ~1e7 vias/cm2 in one thermal process. A fine-pitch, alignment-free z-axis wire slab could forgive registration errors in die-block bonding (I-02164).
physics.killer_doubt: Molten ~1 um Cu cores Rayleigh-break in ~0.1-1 s in the draw neck. Cu/borosilicate CTE (17 vs 3.3 ppm/K) gives ~0.7% cool-down strain. Bundle jitter >0.5 um/cm.
physics.decisive_experiment: At a university fiber tower (~$150k), draw a 3-stage Cu-in-borosilicate preform and a hollow MCP-glass preform to be Cu-plated later. Slice to 100 um. Measure via continuity on 1e5 vias by X-ray CT, plus resistance and positional jitter.
physics.prior_art: Taylor-Ulitovsky glass-coated microwire. Microchannel-plate draw-stack-slice (Photonis, Incom). Iterative-draw nanowire arrays (Bayindir group, 2011). LPKF LIDE laser TGVs. Applied to interposers: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Draw-stack-redraw (microchannel-plate style) makes high-AR Cu via fields in one thermal process; a dense random via field needs no registration, like an anisotropic conductor.
innovation.killer_doubt: Via density is not the memory bottleneck (lateral RDL is). Cu-glass CTE mismatch (~1.3% strain over ~1000 K) debonds cores; molten-Cu cores under 5 um risk Rayleigh breakup.
innovation.decisive_experiment: At a university fiber tower, draw and redraw a Cu-in-borosilicate rod and slice 100 um discs. Map via continuity, resistance and hermeticity after 1000 cycles of -55/125 C. About $150k.
innovation.prior_art: Taylor-Ulitovsky Cu microwire; microchannel-plate and fiber-faceplate draw-stack-redraw; LPKF LIDE laser TGVs; Intel/Absolics glass-core substrates.

title: Nanoimprinted oxide-TFT memory built into glass package substrates
idea: Display fabs process glass at ~$100-300/m^2 versus ~$70,000/m^2 for finished DRAM wafers, a ~300x area-cost gap. Use nanoimprint lithography at 40-50 nm half-pitch on Gen-8 panels to pattern oxide-TFT gain cells, then cut the panel into glass-core package substrates carrying the memory directly under the chiplets.

physics.key_insight: Area cost is the lever: at ~0.05 um2/bit (~50x below DRAM density), IGZO gain cells on glass under $1,000/m2 cost ~$0.9/GB, below DDR5, with negligible refresh.
physics.killer_doubt: At 45 nm, patterning cost scales with area on any substrate: ~8 critical layers at ~$500-900/m2 is ~$5k/m2 (~$4/GB). Glass compaction (~5-20 ppm) defeats ~10 nm overlay.
physics.decisive_experiment: On 150 mm glass coupons, use HP-style self-aligned multilevel imprint (SAIL) to make a 64-kb IGZO 2T0C array at 50-100 nm, which needs no overlay. Measure yield, Vt sigma, 85 C retention and compaction maps. ~$600k.
physics.prior_art: SEL CAAC-IGZO NOSRAM/DOSRAM (on Si); HP SAIL roll-to-roll TFTs; PragmatIC flexible IGZO ICs; NIL wire-grid polarizers on panels (prior knowledge). Panel-scale DRAM: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Glass panels cost ~200x less per m2 than finished DRAM wafers (~$61k/m2), and memory in the package substrate sits millimetres under the chiplets.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 2T oxide gain cell at 45 nm half-pitch is ~0.07 um2 (~1/30 of 1-beta density), which cancels the area-cost gap. No NIL tool overlays ~8 nm across Gen-8 glass.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A desk cost model of a 6-8-layer oxide gain-cell flow on Gen-2/3.5 glass with step-and-repeat NIL. Then imprint two aligned layers on 300 mm glass at a university fab and measure overlay. ~$200k.
innovation.prior_art: SEL CAAC-IGZO DOSRAM/NOSRAM; Intel glass-core substrates; Canon NIL trials at Kioxia; J-FIL wire-grid polarizers on glass; Phase B N-36, N-50.

title: Stacked camera-sensor pixel bonding: per-subarray copper ports to logic
idea: Adapted from the pixel-level Cu-Cu hybrid bonding of stacked smartphone image sensors: the DRAM array wafer bonds face-to-face to a logic wafer so each subarray (mat) has its own ~100-wire vertical port. Global I/O routing and shared periphery go away.

physics.key_insight: Per-mat bonded ports remove the intra-die global data bus (~1/3 of access energy) and periphery from the array wafer. SeDRAM ships the bank-level version, proving the physics.
physics.killer_doubt: DRAM over hot logic at 95-105 C has ~4x tail leakage, pulling refresh to ~16 ms. Each die needs 3M+ bonds at <=1 um pitch, demanding mat-level redundancy.
physics.decisive_experiment: Die-to-wafer hybrid-bond (imec/Leti) a 28 nm logic MPW with per-mat ports to a short-bitline or BEOL-IGZO array. Measure pJ/bit per mat against SeDRAM's 0.88, bond yield, and retention at 105 C. ~$800k.
physics.prior_art: UniIC/XMC SeDRAM: IEDM 2020, 34 GB/s/Gb, 0.88 pJ/b, mass-produced (via search snippet). Samsung periphery-under-cell 4F2 VCT (2028); Kioxia CBA; YMTC Xtacking.

innovation.key_insight: Bonding the array wafer to a logic wafer moves the ~49% periphery off the DRAM die and exposes per-mat parallelism: array efficiency ~0.51 to ~0.75, and far more bandwidth.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipping: UniIC SeDRAM bonds DRAM to logic wafers (34 GB/s/Gb, 0.88 pJ/b; two SoCs in mass production). Samsung PUC is on incumbents' roadmaps. Needs a DRAM line.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Nothing a $1M team can settle. For the venture, model array efficiency and $/bit including the cost of the bonded logic wafer, using SeDRAM-reported data. Under $30k.
innovation.prior_art: UniIC SeDRAM on XMC 3DLink (via search snippet); Tezzaron DiRAM; Samsung periphery-under-cell for 4F2; YMTC Xtacking and Kioxia CBA in NAND.

title: Aviation dissimilar redundancy: cross-vendor ECC words
idea: Adapted from fly-by-wire systems that use dissimilar processors from different vendors so one design flaw cannot fail every channel: each ECC codeword in a module or CXL pool is assembled from dies of at least three different vendors or process lots, so a vendor-specific weakness (a hammer-sensitive layout, a lot-wide retention excursion) can hit only one symbol.

physics.key_insight: Every chip in a rank sees identical activations. Mixing vendors with different hammer thresholds and layouts turns simultaneous multi-chip flips into single-symbol errors that chipkill corrects.
physics.killer_doubt: Mixed ranks run at the slowest timings and the weakest refresh/PRAC behavior. If UEs are mostly single-device and channel faults, decorrelation buys <10% UE reduction.
physics.decisive_experiment: Build homogeneous and three-vendor DDR5 RDIMM ranks on an FPGA controller; run hammer, retention and data-pattern stress at 85 C; compare multi-symbol errors per codeword. ~$150k.
physics.prior_art: Dissimilar redundancy in avionics fly-by-wire; chipkill/SDDC; no memory application found.

innovation.key_insight: Decorrelating vendor- and lot-systematic failure modes across a codeword is the right instinct for qualifying second-source or new U.S. dies.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 10-chip DDR5 codeword from 3-4 vendors still puts 3-4 same-design chips under identical commands; one vendor's hammer weakness exceeds chipkill's 1-symbol correction. Mixed timings run slowest.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Folded into in-study I-04094: build mixed-vendor DDR5 RDIMMs, run TRRespass/U-TRR on an FPGA tester, and count codewords with more than one failing chip versus single-vendor modules. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Chipkill (IBM 1997); vendor-correlated field failures (Facebook 2015; Sridharan 2015); TRRespass/U-TRR; in-study I-04094, same mechanism (DROP).

title: Gen-8.5 display glass replaces 300 mm wafers for capacity memory
idea: Substitute DRAM fabs with idle LCD/OLED backplane lines: use their IGZO TFT process on 2.2x2.5 m glass to build 4-8 stacked layers of relaxed-pitch (~0.8 um) oxide-semiconductor gain-cell arrays, dice into large memory tiles with a bonded small CMOS controller, and sell as CXL far-memory modules.

physics.key_insight: Transistor-written IGZO gain cells keep endurance unlimited; a bonded Si controller replaces slow TFT periphery; depreciated Gen-8.5 lines add EUV-free supply in ~2 years, not 3-5.
physics.killer_doubt: Cost scales per tier: ~$100-150/m2 per IGZO tier at ~16 GB/m2 (F=0.8 um, 12F2) is ~$6-9/GB, 4-6x DDR5 cost; viable only while contract stays >$10/GB.
physics.decisive_experiment: Buy one tier on a Gen-4.5/6 IGZO pilot line (~$500k): 0.8-1 um 2T0C arrays with a bonded Si sense chiplet; measure bit yield, 85 C retention, access time and real $/m2.
physics.prior_art: SEL CAAC-IGZO DOSRAM; Phase B N-36 glass carriers and N-38 panel memory; sibling I-10785 advanced; I-02880 Si-chiplet sensing.

innovation.key_insight: Depreciated Gen-8.5 oxide-TFT lines are EUV-free, helium-light capacity outside DRAM fabs. Transistor-written gain cells need no HAR capacitor, so a slow CXL tier fits their tools.
innovation.killer_doubt: At ~1.5 um (the FPD stepper limit), ~7-10 GB/m2 per tier costs ~$15-25/GB. That matches only today's ~$20/GB contract price; if prices normalize to ~$5/GB, the idea dies.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Do one Gen-6/8.5 partner run at minimum rules: 2T0C test arrays plus n-only IGZO sense amps. Measure cell area, retention at 85 C and Vt sigma, then feed a mask-count cost model (~$300k).
innovation.prior_art: No DRAM-on-display-line product found (R17 search). SEL DOSRAM/NOSRAM on Si; Phase B N-36/N-38; I-10785 ADVANCE and I-03879 DROP in other batches.

title: Vertical CCD strings in a 3D-NAND stack, four phase contacts
idea: Revive 1970s CCD serial memory (Fairchild F464, Intel 2416), which needed no contact or access transistor per bit, as vertical charge-coupled strings: a 3D-NAND-style alternating oxide/gate stack is etched once for channel holes, and every fourth gate layer is tied to the same clock phase so charge packets march up the hole to a sense node at the top. With only four phase lines, the staircase and per-tier contacts disappear.

physics.key_insight: Channel shifting dodges the write-endurance wall. Ganging every fourth tier onto four phase rails removes the staircase: one critical hole mask, ~50 bits/hole, ~2-3x 1b density.
physics.killer_doubt: 2 GHz fails: 50 ganged planes per phase are ~0.35-3.5 nF (6-60 W at 2 GHz). At imec's >4 MHz, a 100-transfer access is ~25 us. CTE needs >=0.9995.
physics.decisive_experiment: On a 16-tier stack of selectively etchable gate materials, prove selective-recess phase contacts with no staircase. Then measure vertical IGZO-liner CTE against clock (1-50 MHz) and temperature (25-85 C). ~$700k.
physics.prior_art: imec IGZO 3D CCD buffer memory (IEDM 2024; 3-word-line 3D demo 2026); our N-08; Fairchild F464 and Intel 2416 CCD memories.

innovation.key_insight: Tying every fourth tier to one clock phase deletes the staircase: four phase contacts serve ~200 tiers from one hole mask, and recirculation doubles as refresh.
innovation.killer_doubt: The far packet needs ~200 transfers: at CTE 0.98 ~2% survives (>=0.99995 needed). 50 ns average implies ~2 GHz against imec's 4-6 MHz; whole blocks shift per access.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fold into the I-08879 test chip (~$250k): add an 8-16-tier phase-tied vertical coupon through a NAND-pilot partner. Measure plane RC, shift energy per bit and per-transfer CTE from 10 MHz to 1 GHz at 85 C.
innovation.prior_art: imec 3D IGZO CCD (IMW 2026, word lines as phase gates); Intel 2416/Fairchild F464 recirculating CCDs; in-study I-02002 (same phase-tying), I-10793.

title: Open-PDK shuttle CMOS plus university BEOL cell post-processing
idea: Combine open-source SKY130/GF180 shuttle chips carrying sense amps, ECC and refresh controllers with university post-processing of capacitor or oxide-TFT arrays on the top-metal pads, giving full-stack reliability testbeds (real arrays plus real ECC) for a few tens of thousands of dollars. Buildable in a university nanofab: low-temperature BEOL steps on diced shuttle die.

physics.key_insight: Real sense amps plus real BEOL oxide arrays for ~$50-150k: the decisive testbed for charge-transfer sensing (N-04), ECC-margin tails (N-62) and multi-level drift maps.
physics.killer_doubt: Die-level litho and planarization on ~10 mm2 diced die. Sky130 top-metal pitch is ~3 um and Al BEOL tops out near 400 C: IGZO anneal <=350 C.
physics.decisive_experiment: One GF180/Sky130 shuttle with 64 sense amps plus pad openings; post-process a 4 kb IGZO 1T1C/2T0C array at <=350 C; measure signal vs Cs and the 85 C retention tail.
physics.prior_art: Shulaker et al. (Nature 2017): CNFET+RRAM on foundry CMOS; Weebit ReRAM in SkyWater 130 nm; imec IGZO 2T0C. Not as a shared open testbed.

innovation.key_insight: Real sense amps, ECC and refresh logic under real BEOL oxide arrays for tens of $k: the shared test vehicle the top triage cells (N-04, N-43, N-62) need.
innovation.killer_doubt: Pad-level coupling adds ~0.1-1 pF per line versus a 35 fF bitline; charge-sense realism needs <=5 um top-metal access on diced die, hard for university CMP.
innovation.decisive_experiment: One open-PDK shuttle with SA/ECC tiles exposing a 5 um-pitch top-metal grid; post-process a 1 kb IGZO 1T1C or 2T0C array at <=350 C; measure sense margin and retention tail. ~$80k.
innovation.prior_art: Stanford/MIT/SkyWater monolithic 3D (DARPA 3DSoC); BEOL IGZO-on-CMOS at imec, Georgia Tech, Purdue; SkyWater S130 ReRAM option.

title: Pollen-tube confined epitaxy grows monocrystalline channels in every tier
idea: A pollen tube grows only inside the style's channel; deposit a cheap 120-pair PECVD oxide/nitride stack as in 3D NAND, strip the nitride through slits to leave tunnels, then grow single-crystal Si into all tunnels at once by template-confined lateral epitaxy seeded from the substrate at each slit base.

physics.key_insight: An ON stack plus nitride strip plus confined lateral epitaxy could give single-crystal tiers with no strained Si/SiGe superlattice, avoiding the germanium chokepoint (6-38% of refined Ge).
physics.killer_doubt: Upper tunnels must seed through a ~6 um epitaxial slit trunk, then grow ~0.5-1 um laterally in ~20 nm tunnels, with unproven defect density. imec already grew 120 Si/SiGe bilayers.
physics.decisive_experiment: On 300 mm coupons, make an 8-pair ON stack with support pillars, strip the nitride, and run slit-seeded selective Si epitaxy at 600-700 C. Count defects by TEM/ECCI and measure lateral growth length per tier. ~$400k.
physics.prior_art: Purdue confined epitaxial lateral overgrowth (CELO, 1990s); IBM template-assisted selective epitaxy (TASE, 2015); imec 120 Si/SiGe bilayers (2025) (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Si thickness set by deposited nitride, not epitaxy, gives SOI-like c-Si tiers at NAND stack cost. Only transistors beside the seed slot need c-Si (~100-200 nm of growth).
innovation.killer_doubt: Precursor starvation and facet/twin defects in ~20 nm-tall tunnels across 100+ tiers; upper tiers seed late from a 6-7 um slot fill. Superlattices may already reach ~120 layers.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Build 8-16 oxide/nitride tiers on Si, cut seed slots, strip the nitride, grow selective Si (DCS/HCl) laterally 100-500 nm; get TEM defect counts per tier plus gated-diode leakage tails at 85 C. ~$500k with an epi partner.
innovation.prior_art: TC Lab patent family: nitride-strip tunnels filled by confined epitaxial overgrowth for stacked thyristors (via search snippet); Purdue CLSEG/CELO; Samsung/imec Si/SiGe superlattice 3D DRAM.

title: Po: shrink the capacitor to amplify — MOS varactor parametric gain
idea: Po: an amplifier with no gain transistor. Sample the bitline differential onto a pair of silicon MOS varactors held in accumulation, then pulse them into depletion so their capacitance falls ~5x while charge is conserved, raising the differential voltage ~5x before the latch.

physics.key_insight: Charge-conserving capacitance collapse gives DC-free, near-noiseless pre-latch voltage gain with no matched transistor in the path: a low-voltage complement to charge-transfer pre-sensing.
physics.killer_doubt: Fixed sense-node parasitics (~1-2 fF) cap gain at ~2-3x unless varactors reach ~10 fF (~0.5 um2 each at 2 nm EOT), versus ~0.2-0.3 um2 for a whole 1b sense amp.
physics.decisive_experiment: 28-65 nm MPW (~$250k): sense amps with 2-10 fF accumulation-mode varactor preamps on 35 fF dummy bitlines; measure net gain, input-referred offset sigma over 10k amps and added latency versus an offset-cancelling baseline.
physics.prior_art: MOS-varactor discrete-time parametric amplifiers in ADC residue stages; DRAM charge-transfer pre-sensing (Phase B N-04). In DRAM sense amps: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Collapsing capacitance at constant charge gives ~5x voltage gain before the latch from silicon and oxide alone, relaxing sense-amp offset without matched gain transistors.
innovation.killer_doubt: Common mode is amplified too: ~0.5 V CM x 5 gain x 2% varactor C-V mismatch is ~50 mV offset, giving back the saving. N-04 charge-transfer presensing already supplies gain.
innovation.decisive_experiment: 28-65 nm MPW: varactor-pair preamps on a 512-cell bitline replica. Measure input-referred offset sigma, kT/C noise and gain spread, compared with charge-transfer presensing (N-04). ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: MOS-varactor discrete-time parametric amplifiers (Ranjbar/Oliaei, JSSC); charge-transfer presensing DRAM; study N-04 [training knowledge].

title: GPU-owned sense amps: array stack bonded straight onto accelerator
idea: Limit: no base die and no DRAM-process periphery. Array-only layers with 8:1 bitline muxes are hybrid-bonded at fine pitch directly onto the accelerator die. Sense amps, decoders and controllers are built in the accelerator's 3 nm logic, at about 1/4 the area of DRAM-process periphery.

physics.key_insight: Sense amps in logic need only ~19 mm2 of N3 for 24 GB at 8:1 muxing, and bonds at ~2 um pitch suffice per subarray. Periphery-off-array is sound.
physics.killer_doubt: An 8:1 mux senses 1 of 8 cells a wordline destroys: serial restore pushes tRC to ~100 ns. At 95-110 C refresh rises 4-8x. Array-only dies are untestable pre-bond.
physics.decisive_experiment: Thermal and refresh model of a 24 GB array die on a 1 kW accelerator, plus a DRAM-process subarray test chip with 8:1 mux timing sequential restore ($300k). Compare against N-40's bonded-SA wafer.
physics.prior_art: Tezzaron DiRAM (sense amps on separate logic layer); triage N-40 MSB-DRAM and N-41 carrier-is-memory; HBM4 foundry logic base dies [training knowledge].

innovation.key_insight: Cell-only wafers with sense amps and decoders in the accelerator's logic make the cell die ~100% array and push interface energy toward ~0.3 pJ/bit. Fits N-41's carrier slot naturally.
innovation.killer_doubt: One bond per column per 512 cells needs ~0.7 um pitch, so wafer-to-wafer only: logic and cell yields multiply (0.6x0.85=0.51), and one layer caps near 45 GB.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Join I-04714's experiment. W2W-bond a 28 nm logic MPW (SAs, sub-array decoders, repair) at 0.7-1 um to an IGZO or MIM cell wafer. Measure sense margin, bond yield and retention at 95-105 C. ~$600k.
innovation.prior_art: US10340261/US10600772: cell chip bonded to logic chip holding SAs and word drivers; US11996389 logic-on-DRAM-cell bond (via search snippet); UniIC SeDRAM; Phase B N-41.

title: Composite: silicon sense chiplets mass-transferred onto glass DRAM panels
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite: large glass panels carry stacked oxide-TFT DRAM tiers, while all precision sensing lives in 50x50 um silicon sense chiplets placed every few millimetres by micro-LED-style mass transfer (millions per hour) and wired by panel redistribution layers; glass does storage, silicon does amplification.

physics.key_insight: Glass panels for transistor-written IGZO gain-cell tiers (endurance unlimited), with sensing moved to mass-transferred Si chiplets, which avoids slow, variable TFT sense amps.
physics.killer_doubt: At ~$100-150/m2 per TFT tier, 32 tiers at F=0.3 um (16F2 cell) is ~$2.4/GB, above DDR5's $1.48. 10x needs F~0.1 um, ~30 nm overlay on glass.
physics.decisive_experiment: On a Gen-2/4.5 display R&D line, stack 4 IGZO 2T0C tiers at 0.5 um. Measure per-tier D0/yield, tier-to-tier overlay after glass compaction, 85 C retention, and read latency through 2 mm RDL bitlines.
physics.prior_art: Phase B N-38 (panel 3D oxide memory) and N-36 (glass carriers); SEL CAAC-IGZO DOSRAM; X-Celeprint micro-transfer printing of Si chiplets.

innovation.key_insight: Glass does storage, silicon does amplification: transferred Si sense chiplets fix TFT sense-amp offset while IGZO 2T0C tiers keep transistor-written, endurance-safe writes on depreciated display lines.
innovation.killer_doubt: Chiplets every 3 mm imply ~1.5 mm bitlines (~300 fF, 60x a 5 fF cell), so TFT preamps are needed anyway; panel steppers resolve ~1.2-1.5 um, not 0.3 um.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On Gen-2 glass, build one IGZO 2T0C tier at 0.5-1 um with TFT 8:1 local mux plus micro-transfer-printed 28 nm sense chiplets. Measure chiplet contact yield, sense margin versus bitline length, and 85 C retention. ~$400k.
innovation.prior_art: Phase B N-38 panel oxide memory and N-36 glass-carried tiers; R27's I-01819 R2R IGZO; SEL/Sharp CAAC-IGZO memory; X-Celeprint micro-transfer printing [training knowledge].

title: Banker's insured deposits: refresh-free banks for data with backups
idea: A banker guards insured deposits lightly because losses are covered. Pages with a valid copy elsewhere (model weights, page cache, read-only datasets) go into banks run with refresh off or at 1-4 s, protected by strong per-line detection codes; a detected error triggers a transparent refetch from flash, CXL or a remote replica instead of a crash.

physics.key_insight: Clean, backed-up pages can trade refresh for detection: Linux already drops and re-reads clean page-cache pages on uncorrectable errors, so slow-refresh banks need little new software.
physics.killer_doubt: At 4 s and 85 C, BER ~9e-4 makes ~64% of 4 KB pages fail SECDED; 1 s works, but TRR rides REF commands, so hammer exposure rises ~16x.
physics.decisive_experiment: DRAM-Bender FPGA on 30 DDR5 dies (~$150k): SECDED-fail rate versus refresh interval (64 ms-4 s, 45-85 C) and HCfirst versus interval; then a kernel patch mapping clean page cache to slow banks.
physics.prior_art: Flikker (ASPLOS 2011) per-bank slow refresh for non-critical data; Smart Refresh skips recently activated rows; Linux hwpoison clean-page recovery.

innovation.key_insight: Clean data with a valid backing copy can treat a decay error as a cache miss, as processors already do with parity-only clean L1 lines. Applied here to refresh policy.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 1-4 s, raw BER ~1e-5-1e-4 fails ~0.5-5% of 64-B lines. Flash refetch at ~80 us adds ~0.4-4 us average latency against ~100 ns DRAM.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On a DRAM Bender FPGA tester, hold refresh off for 1-4 s at 45-85 C and log line-failure rate and repeat-failure persistence (~$80k). If >0.1% of lines fail, refetch alone is dead and needs correction (I-07888).
innovation.prior_art: Flikker (ASPLOS 2011) critical/non-critical refresh split; parity-only clean cache lines refetched from L2 (IBM, Intel); RAIDR; Phase B N-64 lifetime-leased refresh (training knowledge).

title: Vertical CCD strings: 3D NAND geometry clocked as charge-coupled DRAM
idea: Revive 1970s CCD serial memory inside a 3D-NAND-like stack: a vertical gate-all-around oxide-semiconductor or poly channel with 128 wordline tiers is clocked in three phases to shift charge packets up and down, with one sense/regenerate amplifier at the string foot. There is no per-cell contact, capacitor or access transistor, and bidirectional shifting halves average latency.

physics.key_insight: Charge moves through a semiconductor channel, so endurance is unlimited; one sense amp per 128-bit string, no per-bit contact. Family member: one dossier with I-04670/I-01064.
physics.killer_doubt: 128 tiers x 3 phases = 384 transfers: imec planar IGZO CTE >98% keeps 0.98^384 ~4e-4; need >=0.9997. Word-plane RC turns 60-130 ns into ~us.
physics.decisive_experiment: University 16-32-tier vertical GAA CCD, IGZO versus poly-Si channel: CTE versus clock (1-100 MHz) at 25-85 C; kill if CTE <0.9995 at >=10 MHz.
physics.prior_art: imec IGZO CCD buffer memory (IEDM 2024 planar; first vertical 3D CCD 2026, via search snippet, logged R16); 1970s Si CCD memories; Phase B N-08.

innovation.key_insight: A transistor-less, capacitor-less vertical charge-shift string has one sense node per string. Its writes stay in a semiconductor channel, so it avoids the write-endurance wall.
innovation.killer_doubt: 128 tiers in 3 phases hold ~42 packets. At imec's >98% CTE, 0.98^128 leaves 7%. 60-130 ns access needs ~1 GHz clocks against the 4-6 MHz demonstrated.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Build a 16-gate vertical IGZO CCD string in a university fab. Measure per-transfer CTE against clock rate from 1 to 500 MHz at 85 C (~$250k). Stop if CTE is below 0.9995 above 100 MHz.
innovation.prior_art: imec IGZO CCD buffer memory: planar 142-bit (IEDM 2024), vertical (IMW 2026), per earlier stage-2 search logs. Phase B N-08; 1970s CCD memories.

title: Matrix Semiconductor's write-once 3D ROM as a weights tier
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 8-deck antifuse crosspoint (2001) failed because nobody wanted write-once storage. LLM inference does: burn model weights into a stack of antifuse decks over the accelerator's periphery, read in tens of ns. The weights no longer occupy DRAM, which then holds only KV cache and activations.
