physics.key_insight: Antifuse filaments have no read disturb or retention drift, so write-once decks suit weights read ~1e9 times a year; programming 280 Gb takes minutes.
physics.killer_doubt: An 8-deck crosspoint at F=20 nm is ~5 Gb/mm2, ~4x below rewritable 200+-layer NAND (~20 Gb/mm2); models churn every 3-12 months; poly-diode decks exceed 400 C over logic.
physics.decisive_experiment: Spreadsheet first (~$0): $/GB-year of 8-deck antifuse versus pSLC high-bandwidth flash under 6-12-month model churn; only if it wins, a BEOL oxide-diode antifuse test deck.
physics.prior_art: Matrix/SanDisk 3D OTP (2001-05); Sandisk High Bandwidth Flash for weights (2025); Taalas hard-wired model chips; ROM-based compute-in-memory (training knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Inference weights are written rarely. A field-programmable OTP tier in the accelerator BEOL streams them at sub-pJ/bit with no refresh, freeing HBM for KV cache. One SKU serves any model.
innovation.killer_doubt: Rewritable High Bandwidth Flash (SanDisk/SK hynix) targets 8-16x HBM capacity for weights. An 8-deck crosspoint gives ~2.4 Gb/mm2. Models churn every ~3-6 months and strand burned dies.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Build a 2-deck OTS-selector oxide-antifuse crosspoint at <=400 C on a foundry BEOL coupon. Measure program yield, read margin and disturb over 1e12 reads, and model decode tokens/s per dollar against HBF (~$400k).
innovation.prior_art: Matrix Semiconductor/SanDisk 3D OTP (2001-05); Taalas hard-wired-model silicon; SanDisk + SK hynix High Bandwidth Flash for inference weights (training knowledge).

title: Interposer-as-memory: oxide DRAM tiers in the passive interposer
idea: Under 400 C, build four oxide-channel 1T1C DRAM tiers in the BEOL of the large passive silicon interposer that already sits under the GPU and HBM, patterned with ArF at 40 nm. The interposer becomes about 100 GB of near memory directly under the compute die.

physics.key_insight: Interposer BEOL runs cool and idle under GPU and HBM; oxide cells there give sub-pJ/bit micro-bump access with no TSVs. A passive interposer needs I-02936-style periphery.
physics.killer_doubt: Flagship GPUs moved to CoWoS-L (organic RDL plus Si bridges), shrinking the host. Realistic 6F2 1T1C at 40 nm, 50% efficiency: ~50 Mb/mm2 per tier, ~30-40 GB, not 100.
physics.decisive_experiment: Add a one-tier oxide 1T1C/2T0C block to a 65 nm-class interposer shuttle (~$300k); measure retention and yield after TSV, micro-bump and die-attach thermal steps at 85 C.
physics.prior_art: Phase B N-50 (same idea, ALIVE); TSMC eDTC deep-trench capacitors in CoWoS interposers; active base dies (Intel Foveros).

innovation.key_insight: The silicon interposer is ~2,500 mm2 of already-paid silicon directly under the compute die. Memory tiers there could add ~100 GB at sub-pJ/bit with no TSVs.
innovation.killer_doubt: A passive interposer has no transistors for sense amps. Each 40 nm 1T1C tier needs a ~5 fF HAR capacitor. Flagship packages are shifting to CoWoS-L organic interposers.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Build a yield-and-cost model plus one coupon: a 2-tier oxide gain-cell array (not 1T1C) with IGZO periphery on an interposer-class 65 nm BEOL. Measure retention at 95 C under a hot die (~$350k).
innovation.prior_art: Duplicate of Phase B N-50 (gain-cell interposer). CEA-Leti IntAct active interposer; TSMC deep-trench capacitors in CoWoS interposers; no DRAM-tier interposer found (training knowledge).

title: Bit-significance stack: MSB planes on clean dies, LSB planes on cheap dies
idea: Shift the unit of placement from the word to the bit-plane along the stack's vertical axis: sign, exponent and high-mantissa planes go to 4 protected dies, low-order planes go to 8 dies running at 1% BER with no ECC, and the base die re-interleaves planes into words on the fly.

physics.key_insight: Bit-plane placement lets low-significance planes tolerate ~1% BER, so binned-out or weak dies could hold LSB planes and add usable supply.
physics.killer_doubt: Savings are small: on-die ECC is ~6% of bits, refresh 16-33% of idle power. Plane-splitting confines MSB-only fetches to 4 of 12 dies, a third of stack bandwidth.
physics.decisive_experiment: Inject 1e-3 to 1e-2 BER into the low mantissa planes of bf16 and fp8 Llama-class weights and measure perplexity. Add a census of die-sort rejects that would pass at 1% BER. ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: Sparkk (MEMSYS 2014) MSB/LSB refresh split; Flikker (ASPLOS 2011); EDEN (MICRO 2019); Any-Precision LLM bit-plane layout (ICML 2024) (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Placing bit-planes across dies by significance gives AI stacks a use for refresh-relaxed, low-voltage or reject dies, and allows precision-on-demand fetches.
innovation.killer_doubt: With FP8/FP4 only ~25% of bits sit in tolerant low-order planes, not two-thirds, and refresh is ~5-10% of active HBM power. Sparkk did cross-chip significance placement in 2014.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Inject LSB-plane errors (1e-4 to 1e-2 BER, plus row/column fault maps from a few hundred real reject dies) into FP8/BF16 LLM weights and KV, and measure perplexity. ~$80k.
innovation.prior_art: Sparkk (2014) per-chip significance-aware refresh; Flikker (ASPLOS 2011); EDEN approximate DRAM (MICRO 2019); Phase B N-77 bit-plane memory.

title: Lifetime-leased refresh: streamed and dead data are never refreshed
idea: A lease table in the memory controller (or HBM base die) puts each 2 MB region in one of three classes. (i) 'Dead': freed pages, retired KV. (ii) 'Streamed with period <= P': weights and live KV in LLM decode, read every token. (iii) 'Normal'. Class (ii) rows are restored as a side effect of every full activation. A per-region activation timestamp certifies that each row was opened within tREF, and the controller issues a targeted refresh only for rows that miss the deadline. Class (i) rows get no refresh at all. For most of an inference HBM, the all-bank REF command and its tRFC blackout disappear. A further step is an HBM bin specified for 'access-guaranteed' use, with a relaxed retention screen. Dies that fail today's 32 ms retention test become usable for weights.

physics.key_insight: LLM decode activates every weight row each 10-25 ms sweep, inside tREFW, so streamed rows refresh themselves; HBM dies failing the 32 ms screen could be binned for weights.
physics.killer_doubt: Skipping REF also skips in-DRAM TRR row-hammer refresh, so PRAC/RFM is required; per-bank refresh already hides most tRFC, leaving ~5-10% bandwidth. Retention's share of HBM yield loss is unknown.
physics.decisive_experiment: FPGA DDR4/DDR5 tester (DRAM Bender): replay LLM weight-stream traces with REF disabled plus ACT-based targeted refresh at 85 C for 30 days; log errors. Separately quantify dies rejected only by the retention screen.
physics.prior_art: Smart Refresh (Ghosh and Lee, MICRO 2007) skips recently accessed rows; ESKIMO (MICRO 2009) skips unallocated memory; LPDDR PASR. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Dense decode re-activates every weight row each token, so activations already restore it. Per-region activation timestamps could retire blanket REF and its tRFC blackout for streamed HBM regions.
innovation.killer_doubt: MoE decode touches ~5-10% of experts per token, so many weight rows go unread for >32 ms. Dense-model upside is 5-15% bandwidth; retention rejects are a few percent of dies.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Ramulator 2 with real dense and MoE LLM decode traces: histogram row-activation intervals against the 32 ms window and count rows needing targeted refresh. Software only, ~$50k.
innovation.prior_art: Smart Refresh (Ghosh and Lee, MICRO 2007) skips recently activated rows; RANA data-lifetime eDRAM refresh (ISCA 2018); prior batch I-04810 dropped on the same mechanism.

title: Compression-funded ECC: compressible rows earn slow refresh for free
idea: On write, the controller compresses each line: exponent Huffman for float tensors, base-delta-immediate or zero-run for integers and pointers. If the result is <=54 B, it appends 70 parity bits (t=7 BCH over GF(2^10)) in the same 64 B slot and sets a mode bit in the existing ECC/metadata side-band. A per-row counter tracks whether every line in the row is in 'strong' mode; strong rows move to a slow refresh bin (RAIDR-style Bloom filter) and weak rows stay at 64 ms. A line that becomes incompressible demotes its row immediately, the safe direction. Reads run the full decode only when the cheap syndrome is nonzero.

physics.key_insight: Compression frees in-slot room for t=7 BCH at zero capacity cost; at 1e-4 raw BER a ~512-bit codeword fails <1e-15, so compressible rows tolerate 0.5-1 s refresh.
physics.killer_doubt: Inference now stores FP8/FP4 weights and KV, compressing <10-15% against the 15.6% needed to fit 54 B; the BF16-era 44 B figure fails, so fully compressible rows are rare.
physics.decisive_experiment: Dump real HBM contents (FP8/FP4 weights, KV) from vLLM runs and measure the share of 8 KB rows fully <=54 B; FPGA DDR5 BER at 0.5-1 s, 85 C to confirm a <=2e-4 tail.
physics.prior_art: COP compress-and-protect (Palframan et al., ISCA 2015); Hi-ECC 1 s refresh (Wilkerson et al., ISCA 2010); MECC morphable ECC. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Compression slack can pay for strong ECC inside the same 64 B slot, which zeroes the capacity cost of ECC-relaxed refresh or margin for compressible data.
innovation.killer_doubt: BF16 lines compress to ~44 B, but FP8/FP4 weights and KV carry ~6.5-7 bits/byte, leaving under the 10 B needed. One incompressible line pins its 8 KB row fast.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Measure per-line compressibility (<=54 B) of real BF16, FP8 and FP4 weights, KV and activations from vLLM runs, and the share of fully compressible 8 KB rows. Software, ~$30k.
innovation.prior_art: COP compress-and-protect main memory (Palframan, Kim, Lipasti, ISCA 2015); Hi-ECC refresh relaxation (Wilkerson et al., ISCA 2010); RAIDR retention binning (ISCA 2012).

title: Vt-coded in-stack tier decoder: kill the staircase so 3D DRAM lines can be short
idea: 3D NAND reaches each tier's horizontal line through a staircase whose length grows with tier count; DRAM wants short lines (sub-page activation, low RC), and at 64 tiers a ~32 um staircase is longer than a 512-cell line. Instead, route every tier's horizontal line under 2*log2(N) vertical select-gate pillars before it merges into one common vertical contact. In each tier, each select region is permanently depletion-mode (always on) or enhancement-mode according to that tier's binary address, so driving the pillars with an address and its complement opens exactly one tier's path. The code is written per tier during deposition with one coarse (um-scale, i-line) block mask, or, as in Macronix-style LSM for 3D NAND, by programming charge-trap select gates once at test.

physics.key_insight: Binary Vt-coded select pillars address N tiers with 2log2(N) gates instead of an N-step staircase: ~2.7 um rather than ~32 um at 64 tiers, which allows short 3D lines.
physics.killer_doubt: The selected line crosses 12 series ~20 kOhm oxide pass devices: ~240 kOhm x 30 fF ≈ 7 ns per edge. Unselected tiers float without a second coded pull-down path.
physics.decisive_experiment: Build an 8-tier IGZO or poly-Si test stack with 6 coded select pillars plus complementary pull-down pillars. Measure selected-line RC, VPP pass-through loss and unselected-line coupling disturb at 85 C.
physics.prior_art: Macronix VG-NAND layer select by multilevel operation (LSM, ~2011); NMOS depletion-mode ROM decoders; 3D NAND staircase-reduction work. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Binary Vt-coded select regions decode N tiers with 2*log2(N) pillars (12 at 64 tiers), so line ends shrink ~12x and short, sub-page 3D DRAM lines become area-affordable.
innovation.killer_doubt: Each line crosses 12 series oxide select devices (~30 kOhm each, ~0.4 MOhm total). Unselected-tier wordlines float instead of being held at a rail, inviting coupling disturb and leakage.
innovation.decisive_experiment: 8-tier IGZO TFT stack with coded depletion/enhancement select regions (block-mask doping or charge-trap programming). Measure series resistance, line RC, and unselected-line float drift and disturb at 85 C, plus SPICE of 64-tier decode. ~$350k.
innovation.prior_art: Macronix VG-NAND layer selection by programmed select gates (LSM); NMOS depletion/enhancement-coded ROM decoders (1970s-80s) [training knowledge].

title: Delay-line recirculating 3D string refreshes data by circulation
idea: As in mercury delay lines and drums, data in a vertical 3D DRAM string never sits still. The tiers are charge-coupled gates, and charge packets shift one tier per clock past a single regenerating sense amp at the string base, which restores each packet as it passes. No lateral access transistor is needed per tier, and refresh comes free with the circulation.

physics.key_insight: Regenerating each packet once per 64-128-tier pass relaxes CTE to ~0.999-0.9995; writes go through a semiconductor channel, and imec reports >1e10 cycles without wear.
physics.killer_doubt: Capacity tier, not DRAM: at imec's ~4-6 MHz a 64-128-tier pass is ~10-30 us; DRAM tRC (~45 ns) would need GHz word-plane clocks against ~100+ ns plane RC.
physics.decisive_experiment: Planar 3-phase IGZO CCD loop (32-64 stages) with a regenerating amp at the end (university fab, ~$300k): per-transfer CTE at 4-200 MHz, fat zero, 85 C dark charge, error rate after 1e6 recirculations.
physics.prior_art: imec IGZO 3D CCD buffer memory for CXL type-3 (IEDM 2024, IMW 2026); 1970s CCD and delay-line memories; Phase B N-08; I-06518, I-01064.

innovation.key_insight: Looped or bidirectional shifting past one regenerating amp per 64-128-tier string resets transfer loss on every pass with no per-tier access transistor: the 1970s CCD-memory refresh loop moved into oxide.
innovation.killer_doubt: 128 tiers x 3 phases is 384 transfers. imec's >98% CTE keeps ~0.04%, and ≥0.9999 is needed. At the demonstrated ~6 MHz clocks one pass takes ~60 us.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fabricate 16- and 64-tier IGZO vertical CCD strings with a regenerating latch at the base. Measure CTE against clock (1-500 MHz) and bit errors after 1e6 recirculations at 85 C. ~$400k.
innovation.prior_art: Intel 2416 and Fairchild CCD memories (recirculating loops with refresh amplifiers); imec IGZO 3D CCD (IMW 2026) (via search snippet, prior logs). Merge into I-10793.

title: OS lossy heap: applications declare error tolerance per allocation
idea: Inverts 'memory must be bit-exact': a new mmap flag (MAP_LOSSY plus an error bound) sends ML activations, image buffers and analytics sketches to a region where the memory controller applies error-bounded floating-point compression (ZFP/SZ-style) on writeback. Exactness stays the default; lossy bytes are opt-in and typed.

physics.key_insight: ZFP fixed-rate mode yields fixed-size blocks, so a CXL expander can compress lossily at line rate without the indirection tables that burden variable-size compressed memory.
physics.killer_doubt: ML stacks already quantize activations and KV to FP8/INT4 in software; 3-8x on 30-60% of the footprint is only 1.25-2.1x overall.
physics.decisive_experiment: FPGA CXL Type-3 card with fixed-rate ZFP (~$300k): run HPC fields, analytics sketches and FP8 activations through an mmap lossy region; measure effective capacity, added latency and end-task error.
physics.prior_art: AVR in-controller approximate compression (Chalmers, 2019); Flikker; EnerJ; ZeroPoint lossless memory-compression IP; ZFP/SZ hardware cores.

innovation.key_insight: Typed, opt-in lossy allocation keeps exactness the default while letting a controller trade error bounds for capacity on tolerant buffers.
innovation.killer_doubt: The big tolerant data is already compressed in software: AI tensors at 4-8 bits, media as JPEG/HEVC. Controller ZFP adds <=1.5x on the remainder, plus variable-size page management costs.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Capture heap dumps from 5 ML and media servers. Apply ZFP at each app's tolerance to the data that is not already quantized or compressed, and report the net capacity gain ($50k). Stop below 1.3x.
innovation.prior_art: EnerJ approximate types; Flikker; Doppelganger approximate cache (MICRO 2015); AVR approximate value reconstruction (Eldstal-Ahrens and Sourdis); CXL compression expanders.

title: Video-codec P-frames: delta-encoded memory pages against reference pages
idea: Borrowed from MPEG inter-frame coding: a CXL memory-expander controller keeps 'I-pages' as references and stores near-duplicate pages (VM clones, forked workers, fine-tuned weight variants, beam-search KV copies) as XOR/byte-delta 'P-pages' with offset hints, decoded in a ~20 ns pipeline on read. A MinHash similarity index chooses each page's reference at write-back time.

physics.key_insight: Exact dedup misses near-duplicates. bf16 full fine-tunes with ~1e-3 relative weight change leave many weights bit-identical, so lossless XOR deltas against a reference page compress well.
physics.killer_doubt: A P-page read costs two DRAM reads (reference plus delta), and a write to a reference forces its dependents to re-encode. Realistic gain over KSM plus compression: ~1.2-2x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Snapshot memory on 20 multi-tenant and model-serving hosts. Offline, measure capacity after KSM plus zstd, then after MinHash-chosen XOR deltas (<$50k). Advance only if the deltas add >=1.5x.
physics.prior_art: Difference Engine (OSDI 2008), sub-page patching of similar pages; Thesaurus (ASPLOS 2020), LSH-clustered base+delta lines; ZipNN fine-tune XOR deltas. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Near-duplicate pages that exact dedup misses can be stored as base-plus-delta behind a CXL controller, with LSH or MinHash picking the reference at write-back.
innovation.killer_doubt: Every P-page read needs 2 fetches (reference plus delta) plus decode. KSM, CoW KV sharing and BitDelta already capture most of the redundancy, so the marginal gain is likely <1.3x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Snapshot memory of 3 production-like hosts (VM farm, forked workers, multi-variant LLM server). Measure what XOR/byte-delta adds beyond KSM plus zstd, then simulate the 2-fetch latency in a CXL model.
innovation.prior_art: Difference Engine (Gupta et al., OSDI 2008) sub-page patching of similar pages; Thesaurus (ASPLOS 2020) LSH base+diff; KSM; vLLM copy-on-write beam KV.

title: Temporal mipmap KV cache with on-demand full-resolution recall
idea: Attention K/V is stored as a pyramid over token time. The last ~2k tokens stay at full resolution. Older spans are pooled into 8- and 64-token summary vectors that stay in HBM, while their full-resolution copies are parked in flash. When a query puts more than a threshold of attention mass on a summary, the controller fetches that span at full resolution for the next step, like texture mipmapping applied to time.

physics.key_insight: Pyramid summaries in HBM, with full-resolution spans in flash rather than DRAM, make resident KV grow roughly logarithmically with context. HBM is the costliest bit (~3x DDR5 wafer area).
physics.killer_doubt: Flash bandwidth: Llama-3-70B KV is ~320 KB/token, so a 4k-token recall budget is ~1.3 GB per step. At 10% churn per 30 ms step, one sequence needs ~4.5 GB/s.
physics.decisive_experiment: Log attention mass per 64-token span on 128k-1M-context traces (Llama-3-70B; RULER, LongBench), measuring span churn per step and accuracy with one-step-lagged recall. Replay the recall stream on 4 NVMe drives (<$60k).
physics.prior_art: ArkVale (NeurIPS 2024) page summaries plus recall; InfLLM; Quest; ShadowKV; InfiniGen (OSDI 2024); InstInfer in-SSD attention. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Keep KV as a time pyramid: recent tokens at full resolution, older spans pooled into HBM summaries, full copies on flash recalled when attention mass lands on a summary.
innovation.killer_doubt: Flash reads take ~50-100 us per 20-50 ms decode step, and spread attention triggers recalls in every layer and head. KV-retrieval systems already do summary-plus-recall from CPU memory.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fork vLLM with pooled summaries in HBM and full KV on NVMe. On RULER and LongBench at 128k-1M tokens, measure recalls per step, stall time and accuracy against ShadowKV and InfLLM. About $60k.
innovation.prior_art: InfLLM, ArkVale (NeurIPS'24), ShadowKV, RetrievalAttention, Quest, Landmark attention; R11 I-04022 (DROP) [training knowledge].

title: Discarding and recovering: partial-good HBM stacks sold as lower tiers
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: instead of scrapping stacks with one bad tier or weak TSV lanes, fuse out the bad tier or half the lanes in the base die and re-bin the stacks as 8-high or half-width parts for inference cards and edge devices. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)

physics.key_insight: With independent tier failures, ~87% of failed 12-high stacks (75% yield) have one bad die. Sold at 11/12 capacity (like H200's 141/144 GB), that recovers ~+18% bits.
physics.killer_doubt: Many stack rejects are TSV power shorts, base-die faults, warpage or underfill voids that cannot be fused out. If >50% are, the gain falls below ~+7% HBM supply.
physics.decisive_experiment: Through a vendor partnership (~$300k), run failure analysis on ~500 rejected HBM stacks and classify each as tier-fusable or stack-level. Prototype base-die remap firmware and qualify one 11/12-capacity SKU.
physics.prior_art: JEDEC HBM lane repair and spare TSVs. GPU-level harvesting (H100 enables 5 of 6 stacks). Vendor lower bins (prior knowledge). Public tier-fuse re-binning: none found.

innovation.key_insight: HBM stack-ID addressing lets the base die fuse out a failed die group, so 12-high fallout can be salvaged as 8-high or half-width capacity bins.
innovation.killer_doubt: Most HBM loss is TSV and bond failure; known-good-die screening already removes bad dies. Salvage adds perhaps 5-10% supply, within existing vendor binning. Outsiders cannot access fallout.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Using one vendor's fallout data, classify 1,000 failed stacks by failure locus: single die, TSV/bond or base die. A salvageable share above ~30% would justify a fuse-map rebin flow.
innovation.prior_art: Vendor speed and capacity binning plus lane repair; NVIDIA H100 PCIe ships 5 of 6 stacks enabled; partial-good salvage is standard in logic.

title: CCD fused into 3D NAND-style string: vertical shift-register DRAM
idea: Combine a charge-coupled device with a 3D NAND gate stack: 200 tier gate planes wrap one vertical oxide-semiconductor channel, and clocking the gates shifts charge packets held in surface wells toward a floating-diffusion sense node at the top. Each gate is both 'capacitor' and transfer switch, so there is no per-cell capacitor, contact or access transistor.

physics.key_insight: Striping one cache line across 512 strings turns serial shifting into a fixed-latency parallel burst; floating-diffusion gain makes ~0.1 fF (~600 e-) wells enough.
physics.killer_doubt: 200 tiers means up to ~400 transfers per pass: at 3e-3 loss per transfer only 30% survives, and 100-200 ns serial access far exceeds DRAM tRC (~45 ns).
physics.decisive_experiment: Add 400-transfer recirculating loops to the I-01064 planar IGZO CCD chip: measure cumulative loss and pattern-dependent trailing charge, and set the maximum usable string length.
physics.prior_art: Duplicate of Phase B N-08 and I-01064; 3D NAND word-plane stack as host. Vertical CCD memory: none found (via search snippet).

innovation.key_insight: Floating-diffusion gain lets a CCD well hold very little charge (~0.1 fF), so one hole etch serves many bits. Striping a line across 512 strings hides serial latency.
innovation.killer_doubt: 200 bits on 200 gates is impossible: a packet needs 2-4 gates, so it holds 50-100 bits. 600-800 transfers per rotation is ~100 us at imec's demonstrated 6 MHz.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Superseded by the I-08879 CCD speed/CTE test. Only revisit long strings if that test shows CTE >=0.99998 per transfer at >=500 MHz.
innovation.prior_art: imec IGZO CCD memory claims DRAM-beating density at ~50 layers with multibit (IEDM 2024; 3D at IMW 2026) (via search snippet).

title: Po: memory printed like a newspaper — roll-to-roll nanoimprinted oxide cells
idea: Po: memory is printed like a newspaper. Extracted: roll-to-roll nanoimprint 50 nm features onto steel or polyimide foil, with spatial-ALD oxide channels and planar capacitors, making 1T1C arrays on a 1 m web; the slower cells sit behind a small silicon cache.

physics.key_insight: Area cost, not density, sets $/bit: an IGZO 1T1C at ~0.02 um2 (0.7 fF planar) gives ~3-6 TB/m2, so even $300/m2 lands near $0.05-0.1/GB.
physics.killer_doubt: At 50 nm, ~6 aligned layers need ~10-15 nm overlay; polyimide moves 10-20 ppm/K, 100-200 nm per kelvin across 1 cm. Spatial-ALD IGZO Vt sigma at 50 nm is unknown.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into the I-01819 demo: one multilevel SAIL stamp at 50 and 100 nm on steel foil on carrier; measure overlay, killer defects/cm2 and 85 C 1T1C retention. ~$400k.
physics.prior_art: HP Labs SAIL roll-to-roll TFTs; PragmatIC IGZO FlexICs; this study's I-01819 (advanced by two critics) is the same mechanism at 100 nm.

innovation.key_insight: Area-cost arbitrage is real: processed DRAM silicon costs ~$100k/m2 against display-class backplanes at ~$100-300/m2. Oxide 1T1C works with no silicon crystal.
innovation.killer_doubt: Web overlay is microns against ~15 nm needed (20 ppm/K foil: 20 um/K per metre). At realistic >=$1-5k/m2 and 17x lower density, the gain is <=1-6x, not 100x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A ~$400k sheet-level test: one self-aligned multilevel imprint stamp defines a 4 kb IGZO 1T1C array at 100 nm on steel foil. Kill if functional cells are <99.9% or overlay error is >30 nm.
innovation.prior_art: HP Labs SAIL roll-to-roll self-aligned imprint (2000s); U. Michigan roll-to-roll nanoimprint (Guo); PragmatIC FlexIC; Thinfilm printed memory; Holst Centre flexible IGZO [training knowledge].

title: All-oxide CMOS periphery lets memory panels need no silicon chips
idea: Ideal: periphery made from the same cheap film as the cells. Closest: build sense amps, decoders and refresh logic from complementary oxide TFTs (n-ZnSnO with p-SnO or p-Cu2O, all abundant, <=300 C) using bootstrapped dynamic logic to compensate the weak p-FET, so panel memory needs no bonded silicon driver ICs.

physics.key_insight: Panel memory needs on-glass periphery. IGZO gate-driver-on-array already ships n-only bootstrapped decoders, so only the sense amps need new work, and offset cancellation can stand in for a good p-oxide.
physics.killer_doubt: Large-area oxide-TFT Vt sigma of ~20-50 mV gives a 6-sigma sense-amp offset of 120-300 mV against a ~50-100 mV bitline signal. Displays still use silicon column drivers.
physics.decisive_experiment: On a university or Gen-2 oxide TFT line, build 10k offset-compensated n-only latch sense amps plus a bootstrapped decoder at L=0.5-1 um. Measure offset distribution, sense time versus signal, and energy per access. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: IGZO gate-driver-on-array in OLED/LCD panels; SEL CAAC-IGZO NOSRAM/DOSRAM; Phase B B2-08 complementary-oxide sense amps; p-SnO/Cu2O TFT literature.

innovation.key_insight: On-panel oxide decoders and muxes make panel memory addressable without millions of bonded lines; display gate-on-array and IGZO microprocessors show n-only oxide logic already ships.
innovation.killer_doubt: p-type SnO/Cu2O reach only ~1-5 cm2/Vs with poor on/off, and oxide-TFT Vt sigma of ~30-100 mV rivals a ~100 mV bitline signal, forcing offset-cancelled sense amps.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On a university or foundry oxide-TFT line, build n-only auto-zeroed sense amps reading 2T0C gain-cell columns; measure offset, sense time versus bitline C, and energy at 85 C. ~$300k.
innovation.prior_art: Display gate-on-array oxide drivers; PragmatIC Flex-RV IGZO RISC-V (Nature 2024); SnO/Cu2O CMOS inverters (NOVA Lisbon, KAUST); SEL CAAC-IGZO logic.

title: Fettling attention: grind off flip burrs from KV before softmax
idea: Foundry fettling grinds the burrs off sand castings. The KV cache lives in 1%-BER cells as int4, with per-head scales protected. The attention kernel 'fettles' each key and value it loads by clamping it to calibrated per-channel bounds and capping softmax weights (top-k trimmed), so a flip that creates an outlier logit cannot hijack attention.

physics.key_insight: KV is the largest inference memory consumer, and attention averages over many tokens, so moderate iid noise in values is genuinely tolerable.
physics.killer_doubt: An int4 code cannot leave its range, so clamping does nothing. At 1% BER, flip noise is 10x quantization noise (~2.3 effective bits), and capping softmax breaks one-hot retrieval heads.
physics.decisive_experiment: Simulation (<$20k): KIVI int4 KV on Llama-3-8B with 1% injected flips. Compare clamp+cap, ECC on the MSB plane only (flip noise 2.5x quantization noise), and no protection, on RULER and LongBench.
physics.prior_art: Ranger range restriction (2021); EDEN (MICRO 2019); unequal error protection of DNN bit-planes; KIVI/KVQuant 2-4-bit KV. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: KV lives seconds to minutes and can be rebuilt by re-prefill, so it fits low-refresh cells naturally. int4 with protected scales already bounds flip magnitude, and clamping caps the residual.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 1% BER, ~4% of int4 KV elements are corrupted. Clamping adds little beyond int4's own bound; it hinges on unmeasured attention tolerance, and perplexity loss >0.3 kills it.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Run the same fault-injection harness as I-10421 on int4 KV (Llama-8B, RULER and LongBench), with and without clamping and softmax capping, at 1e-3 to 1e-2 BER and with asymmetric decay. Under $30k.
innovation.prior_art: Ranger range restriction (Chen et al., DSN 2021); FT-ClipAct (2020); EDEN (MICRO 2019); KIVI and KVQuant int2-4 KV quantization.

title: Top-k memory: base die filters KV cache before the link
idea: Invert 'memory returns what was asked for': for attention, the host sends the query vector to the HBM base die, which scores keys in low precision across the KV pages beneath it and returns only the top-k keys/values at full precision.

physics.key_insight: Top-k selection can sit next to the KV store. Returning only the selected keys and values at full precision cuts link energy in long-context decode.
physics.killer_doubt: HBM TSV bandwidth roughly equals PHY bandwidth (~1-2 TB/s per stack), so the base die still streams every key. Storage is unchanged; SparQ/Quest save the same on GPU.
physics.decisive_experiment: Measure top-k recall and accuracy against k with 4-bit key scoring on RULER and LongBench. Model base-die versus GPU-side selection energy using HBM4 TSV counts. Software, ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: AttAcc (ASPLOS 2024), NeuPIMs, SK hynix AiM; Quest (ICML 2024), SparQ, InfiniGen (OSDI 2024) do query-aware top-k KV fetch (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Top-k attention lets memory return ~5-10% of KV. Done where internal bandwidth exceeds the link, long-context KV can live in cheaper DRAM, not HBM.
innovation.killer_doubt: The HBM base die sees only TSV bandwidth (about the ~2 TB/s PHY), so base-die scoring saves only PHY energy (~20-30% of 3-4 pJ/bit). In-bank scoring is the real lever.
innovation.decisive_experiment: In Ramulator2+DRAMPower, compare base-die and in-bank MSB-plane-sketch scoring against Quest on unmodified HBM, on RULER-128k: tokens/s, pJ/token and accuracy at k=2-10%. Under $150k.
innovation.prior_art: Quest (ICML 2024), InfiniGen (OSDI 2024), AttAcc (ASPLOS 2024), H2EAL (2025 preprint), IBM StarC; Phase B N-70; R11 I-09070.

title: NAND-style bad-block maps let partially-good DRAM dies ship
idea: Worse: scrap or down-bin any die whose repair fuses run out. Flip: ship DRAM with a host-visible bad-mat table, like NAND bad blocks, and sell a nominal 32 Gb die as 30 Gb usable, with the OS or CXL controller simply never mapping dead mats.

physics.key_insight: Retiring subarrays through host/CXL page tables instead of fuses recovers dies that fail only on redundancy. The bigger prize is HBM stack harvesting (selling 11-of-12-die stacks).
physics.killer_doubt: Fallout is mostly global shorts, IDD and periphery fails, not mat-local. At ~85% yield that recovers ~3-6% more bits, not 10-20%. Dead mats also leak.
physics.decisive_experiment: With one vendor or OSAT, sort fail-bit maps of 10k rejected dies into mat-local vs global, then demo an FPGA CXL controller retiring a die's bad subarray rows. ~$200k.
physics.prior_art: Half-good DRAM (ZX Spectrum 4532 parts, 'audio RAM'); GPU die harvesting; DDR5 PPR/sPPR; Linux page offlining.

innovation.key_insight: In HBM, one bad die or channel after CoWoS bonding scraps a whole GPU package; host-visible channel/bank disable rescues far more value there than DDR die binning.
innovation.killer_doubt: Mature DRAM yields leave only a few % of dies failing after redundancy, not the claimed 10-20%; PPR and OS page offlining already map out small fails.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Buy ~1,000 reject DDR5 components and scrapped HBM stacks; map failure locality on an FPGA tester to measure the share confined to <=2 mats or one pseudo-channel. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: DDR4/5 post-package repair; Linux page offlining (Facebook 2015); partial-good down-bins; H100 ships 5 of 6 HBM sites; X-PPR (via search snippet).

title: Core-Rope ROM for Frozen Model Weights in Mature Fabs
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope memory, where the program was woven into the hardware: frozen foundation-model weights are written into via-programmed multi-level ROM chiplets (one custom via mask per model on a 28-40 nm mature line), read with small-swing sensing and no refresh or row restore, stacked beside the accelerator.

physics.key_insight: No-refresh, no-restore ROM reads at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit from idle mature-node capacity offload static weights from HBM without DRAM wafer starts.
physics.killer_doubt: 2-bit via-ROM at 28 nm is ~50 Mb/mm2 vs 1b DRAM ~440: a 70B 4-bit model needs ~5,600 mm2; via mask ~$100-200k per model version against 3-12 month model churn.
physics.decisive_experiment: 28 nm MPW (~$150k) of a via-programmed 2-bit ROM macro: measure bits/mm2, read pJ/bit and BER, then a model-churn cost model versus HBM $/GB at 2026 prices.
physics.prior_art: Taalas hardwired-model inference chips (recalled, unverified); ROM-based compute-in-memory (e.g., YOLoC, DAC 2022); mask-ROM is textbook.

innovation.key_insight: Static inference weights need no refresh, restore or writes; ROM storage removes endurance and refresh from that share of memory and cuts access energy.
innovation.killer_doubt: Taalas HC1 already puts weights in mask ROM on 6 nm; 28-40 nm via-ROM is ~10-50x less dense than 1b DRAM, so a 4-bit 70B model needs ~7-16 reticle dies.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Lay out a 2-bit via-programmed ROM macro in a 28 nm PDK, extract bit density and pJ/bit, and compare $/GB of weights against DRAM at 4x contract price over a 12-month model life.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1: Llama 3.1 8B weights in mask ROM on TSMC 6 nm, 2026 (via search snippet); academic ROM-based compute-in-memory macros.

title: Ephemeral RAM: leaky poly-Si cells for data that dies young
idea: IFR: the data dies before the bit does. Define an ephemeral memory class with 0.5-2 ms retention made of cheap, leaky poly-Si 2T0C gain cells stacked in NAND-style tiers, and have the accelerator runtime map only activations, gradients and KV blocks with measured lifetimes under a millisecond onto it, so refresh is never issued.

physics.key_insight: If data dies before the bit decays, refresh is never needed: retention can be a per-allocation contract rather than a 6-sigma cell spec.
physics.killer_doubt: Refresh-free capacity is capped at bandwidth x lifetime: 3.35 TB/s x 2 ms ~7 GB/GPU; sub-ms temporaries already stay in SRAM; poly-Si tail ~0.2-5 pA misses ms.
physics.decisive_experiment: Instrument the PyTorch/CUDA allocator on LLM training and serving (~$50k) and histogram HBM bytes by lifetime; go if >30% of capacity-time dies within the retention target. Then switch the cell to IGZO, tuned to 1-10 s.
physics.prior_art: Flikker/RAIDR-style retention-aware refresh; Kioxia/IMECAS 3D IGZO gain cells; lifetime-typed ephemeral memory tier not found.

innovation.key_insight: Data that dies before the cell loses it needs no refresh at all. A runtime that tags allocation lifetimes could run a short-retention tier refresh-free.
innovation.killer_doubt: Accelerator DRAM holds mostly weights and KV cache living seconds to hours; training activations live ~0.1-1 s. Sub-ms data is likely <10% of capacity, already in SRAM.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Instrument HBM allocations in PyTorch training and vLLM inference traces, then histogram lifetimes weighted by capacity and by traffic. Revisit only if >30% of capacity lives <2 ms. Under $50k.
innovation.prior_art: RANA (ISCA 2018): refresh-optimised eDRAM that skips refresh for short-lived CNN data; RAIDR/Flikker refresh relaxation; gain-cell eDRAM (Teman/Giterman); imec IGZO 2T0C.

title: H-free sputtered-Si laser grains as in-stack CMOS and floating-body tiers
idea: Sputter amorphous Si at ~100 C (no PECVD hydrogen) over ~0.5-1 um of SiO2 that carries a lattice of small grain-filter holes, then melt it with an excimer-laser pulse: the mu-Czochralski process grows one location-controlled single-crystal grain (3-7.5 um) from each hole, with electron/hole mobilities of 460-510 / 121-250 cm2/Vs reported by the Delft group. The ~100 ns pulse heats only the top ~0.3 um, so oxide tiers below stay cool. Use the grains for (a) complementary sense amps and decoders inside the stack, without Smart Cut's hydrogen implant (B3-09's main risk), and (b) floating-body capacitor-less 1T cells, which need holes and therefore cannot be made in n-type IGZO, for Ge-free 3D silicon DRAM tiers.

physics.key_insight: Grain-filter excimer crystallization of sputtered Si gives hydrogen-free single-crystal n- and p-FETs inside a stack: the fallback for Smart Cut's implanted hydrogen in I-11545.
physics.killer_doubt: Grains are ~6 um apart with random orientation, so SA pairs must share a grain. Floating-body tiers hold only ~10-100 ms at 85 C and need litho on every tier.
physics.decisive_experiment: On a 4-tier IGZO 1T1C coupon, sputter Si, laser-crystallize it and build in-grain CMOS SA pairs. Measure IGZO Vt and retention shift after laser shots, and pair offset sigma (go: <20 mV shift, <5 mV sigma).
physics.prior_art: TU Delft (Ishihara) mu-Czochralski single-grain TFTs; TSRI/NARL laser-crystallized monolithic 3D; CEA-Leti nanosecond-laser sequential 3D. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Hydrogen-free route to single-crystal-quality p- and n-FETs inside the stack: the fallback that de-risks Smart Cut's implanted hydrogen for in-stack sense amps (I-11545).
innovation.killer_doubt: Delft grains (3-7.5 um) were shown with ~1 um-gate devices. Sense-amp pairs need <=20 mV mismatch at ~0.1 um in twinned grains. Floating-body Z-RAM failed even on crystalline SOI.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Sputter Si over a finished 2-tier IGZO TFT stack (0.7 um SiO2 buffer, grain filters). Laser-crystallize with Delft's tool, then build 0.1-0.25 um n/p FETs and SA pairs. Measure mismatch, Ioff, and underlying IGZO Vt shift. ~$350k.
innovation.prior_art: Delft mu-Czochralski single-grain TFTs, including a 2-layer 3D CMOS inverter and 6T-SRAM (prior logs); CEA-Leti 400 C ns-laser CMOS; Z-RAM floating body [training knowledge].

title: Double-blind inventory clearinghouse to kill DRAM bullwhip hoarding
idea: Po: every warehouse is made of glass. A neutral party collects encrypted inventory and order data from DRAM makers, distributors and top buyers and, via secure multiparty computation, publishes only weekly aggregate true-demand and channel-inventory indices (like JODI for oil).

physics.key_insight: A buyer-only index (hyperscalers, OEMs, distributors) aligns incentives: buyers gain from deflating phantom demand, sellers need not join, and MPC lowers the antitrust exposure of sharing.
physics.killer_doubt: Three makers (~95% share) gain from spikes and carry price-fixing history (2002-06 fines), so they won't join; spikes mostly reflect inelastic demand and 3-5-year fab lead times.
physics.decisive_experiment: Run a 6-month MPC pilot with 10-15 buyers (~$500k): weekly aggregate inventory-weeks and order indices; test whether it predicts contract-price turns and cuts double-ordering against TrendForce baselines.
physics.prior_art: JODI oil data; WSTS monthly aggregates; TrendForce/DRAMeXchange inventory estimates; Boston Women's Workforce Council MPC wage-gap study.

innovation.key_insight: Secure multiparty computation lets rivals publish only aggregate channel inventory, like JODI for oil, to deflate phantom double orders that amplify a ~10-15% gap into a 4x price.
innovation.killer_doubt: Three makers hold ~90% of bits and profit from opacity in a shortage; one abstention blinds the index. DOJ withdrew information-exchange safety zones in 2023.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Use an open MPC library with 5 distributors/ODMs and 3 buyers for 6 months ($400k). Test whether the weekly aggregate index leads contract-price moves better than TrendForce estimates.
innovation.prior_art: JODI oil data; WSTS aggregates; TrendForce/DRAMeXchange estimates; Boston Women's Workforce Council MPC payroll study; Atallah's secure supply-chain protocols.

title: Memory-side top-k gate returns token indices, not keys
idea: Eliminate shipping full key vectors: each HBM pseudo-channel's base-die slice holds a small dot-product unit and comparator tree that scores the query against stored keys inside the stack and returns only the top-k token indices; only those value rows then cross the interface.

physics.key_insight: Custom HBM4E logic base dies are a real vehicle. Top-k there skips the ~2.5 pJ/bit interposer path for key scans with no array change. It is I-09070's fallback mode.
physics.killer_doubt: Base die gets only ~1x external bandwidth through TSVs, so scan time is unchanged. Saving is ~2.5 pJ/bit on INT4 keys, ~5% of per-token memory energy vs GPU-side Quest.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold this into the I-09070 simulation as a base-die variant. Synthesize a 128-d INT4 dot-product plus bitonic top-k at 5 nm and confirm under 3% base-die area (<$50k).
physics.prior_art: SK hynix/Samsung custom HBM4 logic base dies. AttAcc. Near-memory attention literature. Quest/SparQ already get the traffic cut in software.

innovation.key_insight: HBM4 custom logic base dies make in-stack top-k deployable without touching DRAM arrays; only indices and selected values cross the PHY.
innovation.killer_doubt: The base die sees only TSV bandwidth, about equal to the ~2 TB/s PHY, so decode gets no speedup. The gain is PHY/interposer energy, ~20-30% of 3-4 pJ/bit.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Model base-die internal versus PHY bandwidth from HBM4 TSV and channel specs. If internal is at least 2x PHY, synthesize the scorer at N12/N5 in 3-5% of base-die area and simulate decode tokens/s. Under $100k.
innovation.prior_art: AttAcc (ASPLOS 2024) attention on HBM-PIM; Duplex (MICRO 2024) logic-die PIM; HBM4 custom base dies (SK hynix/TSMC, Samsung).

title: Octopus arm ganglia: in-tier decoders built in the same channel film
idea: Octopus arms carry their own ganglia; in a 3D stack, form a small oxide-TFT decoder in each tier from the same channel film and the same slit/hole patterning as the cells, so each tier needs only ~log2(N) shared address lines instead of N individually contacted wordlines.

physics.key_insight: Decoding inside the stack makes contact count grow with log2(N), not N, so line-end area and staircase masks stop scaling with tier count.
physics.killer_doubt: One etch through identical tiers cannot give each tier a unique code, and n-only IGZO decoders (~10-30 cm2/Vs) must swing VPP ~3 V onto long lines.
physics.decisive_experiment: Build an 8-tier IGZO stack in which per-tier deposition (doping or thickness) sets a Vt code. Show 1-of-8 tier select with log2 lines and measure margin at 85 C. ~$400k.
physics.prior_art: Our N-47 Vt-coded in-stack tier decoder (ALIVE) supplies the missing per-tier code; 3D NAND in-channel string/ground select transistors.

innovation.key_insight: Decoding inside each tier makes line-end contacts scale as log2(N), not N. Active local drivers hold unselected lines at a rail, unlike passive Vt-coded series selects.
innovation.killer_doubt: Identical tiers decode identically: unique addresses need per-tier masks, deposition-coded Vt or programming. IGZO drivers at ~10-30 cm2/Vs may make line ends ~3-10x larger.
innovation.decisive_experiment: University fab, ~$250k: a 4-tier IGZO stack with deposition-coded Vt per tier plus same-film NMOS decoders. Measure address margin, Vt spread against 100-200 mV coding steps, and wordline rise time at 3 V.
innovation.prior_art: SanDisk US9240420 in-tier oxide-TFT word line select (via search snippet); US9418743 3D NAND local WL drivers; Macronix layer select; in-study N-47, I-11544.

title: Nanoimprinted via-ROM weight tape laminated onto a readout die
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): frozen model weights are encoded as present or absent conductive vias in a roll-to-roll nanoimprinted passive crossbar (~200 nm pitch, ~25 Tb/m2) with printed Schottky contacts to block sneak paths, laminated face-to-face onto a small silicon sense-amp die that reads whole rows in parallel. Nothing active is printed; only the bit pattern is.

physics.key_insight: Frozen weights need no writes, so read-only via-ROM avoids the write-endurance wall entirely. At 100-200 nm pitch, imprinted decks could cost <$1/GB against $20/GB DRAM, with no EUV.
physics.killer_doubt: On PET, 200 nm overlay across 10 cm needs <1 ppm stability against ~20 ppm/K, a miracle, so assume rigid substrates. 1k x 1k passive arrays need selector on/off >=1e4.
physics.decisive_experiment: On rigid Si or glass, nanoimprint 256x256 via-ROM crossbars at 200 and 100 nm pitch with ALD oxide Schottky selectors. Measure on/off ratio, read margin, via defect rate and row access time. University NIL, ~$400k.
physics.prior_art: Mask/via ROM; Intel/Micron 3D XPoint crossbar-over-CMOS; HP Labs nanoimprint crossbars; hardwired-weight LLM chips (Taalas). Printed or imprinted weight ROM not found.

innovation.key_insight: Frozen weights need only a fixed bit pattern; separating a cheap patterned film from a small sensing die is the right instinct for read-only storage economics.
innovation.killer_doubt: 200 nm pitch is 0.025 Gb/mm2, ~15x below 1b DRAM; face-to-face lamination needs silicon under all ~22,400 mm2 for 70 GB, and 20-70 ppm/K film distortion misaligns 200 nm pads.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Imprint a 1 cm2, 200 nm-pitch via crossbar with printed Schottky contacts on PET; laminate to a test die; measure overlay error across the die, rectification ratio needed at 1k x 1k, and read time. ~$300k.
innovation.prior_art: HP Labs nanoimprinted crossbar memories (mid-2000s) [training knowledge]; Taalas mask-ROM weight chips; silicon via-ROM weights dropped earlier (I-01226, I-04585, I-07639).

title: Vertical charge-coupled strings store 64 bits per pillar without capacitors
idea: A bit is just a charge packet and needs only a potential well, not a capacitor plus transistor. Use NAND-like vertical pillars whose tiered gates clock 3-phase wells that shift packets to one sense amplifier at the pillar top: 192 tiers give 64 bits per pillar at 60 nm pitch.

physics.key_insight: Charge shifted through a semiconductor channel wears only gate dielectrics, dodging the write-endurance wall; one sense amp per 64 bits removes per-cell transistors, capacitors and contacts.
physics.killer_doubt: 192 transfers need CTE >=0.9995 (imec IGZO: >98%); a 64-bit shift at imec's ~4 MHz takes ~48 us; 60 nm pitch is ~2.5x too tight (realistic ~300 nm2/bit).
physics.decisive_experiment: Merge into the I-10793/N-08 dossier: university-fab planar 3-phase IGZO and poly-Si CCD lines of 192 gates; measure CTE versus clock (4-100 MHz) and dark fill at 85 C. Go if >=0.9995 at >=20 MHz.
physics.prior_art: imec IEDM 2024 planar IGZO CCD (CTE >98%) and IMW 2026 vertical 3D IGZO CCD (via search snippet, logged in R16); 1970s Si CCD memories.

innovation.key_insight: Deposition-only charge-shift strings remove the per-bit capacitor, transistor, tungsten contact and EUV; one sense node per 64 bits is a real resource-intensity lever for block-access memory.
innovation.killer_doubt: Bit 64 needs 192 transfers: at imec's CTE 0.98 only ~2% survives; >=0.9995 needed. At ~6 MHz a read takes ~10 us; 60 nm pitch is ~2.5x tighter than NAND.
innovation.decisive_experiment: 32-64-tier vertical IGZO CCD pillars (university fab or imec IIAP): measure CTE per transfer vs clock (1-50 MHz) and temperature, and end-to-end packet loss after 192 transfers. ~$600k.
innovation.prior_art: imec IGZO CCD: planar 142-bit (IEDM 2024, CTE>98%), vertical 3D CCD (IMW 2026) for CXL buffer (via search snippet, prior logs). Merge into I-10793/N-08.

title: Image-sensor pinned-photodiode storage node with a transfer gate
idea: Adapted from the CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode: store the bit as electrons in a fully depleted buried n-well capped by a p+ pinning layer, isolated from every Si/SiO2 interface, and move it to a floating diffusion through a transfer gate. A source follower reads it like a 4T pixel, so ~1-3k electrons suffice instead of ~30k.

physics.key_insight: Pinning moves stored electrons off every Si/SiO2 interface: median dark current ~0.1-5 e-/s at 25-60 C, >1e4x below a 13 fA (8e4 e-/s) tail, with channel-written charge.
physics.killer_doubt: Planar cell is ~0.1-0.2 um2/bit (50-90x 1-beta). A 40 nm vertical well needs ~2-3e18 cm-3 doping at 0.5-1 MV/cm, where tunnelling erases the dark-current advantage.
physics.decisive_experiment: 65-110 nm CIS MPW (~$300k): pinned wells 0.1-0.5 um wide with fill-and-spill electrical write and 25 ns CDS column read; measure transfer lag, write accuracy and dark-current tails at 25-85 C versus width.
physics.prior_art: CIS global-shutter pinned storage nodes; Fossum QIS jots (0.1 e-/s); our N-84 Jot-RAM is the vertical, multi-level version.

innovation.key_insight: Pinning keeps the storage well away from every Si/SiO2 interface, cutting generation current ~1e4x below the 13 fA tail. What carries over is buried-channel storage for CCD strings.
innovation.killer_doubt: Retention is no longer the scarce axis: BEOL-stackable IGZO gain cells already reach aA-class leakage. A planar 3-4T pinned cell is ~0.3-0.5 um2, 200-300x DRAM's 0.0017 um2.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Planar needs no experiment, because the area math kills it. The only open path is N-84's 40 nm vertical well: a ~$30k TCAD check of 2-3e18 cm-3 pinning doping against BTBT onset at 0.5-1 MV/cm.
innovation.prior_art: Global-shutter pinned storage diodes (Sony, onsemi, ST); Teranishi/Fossum pinned photodiode; IGZO gain cells (imec, Kioxia) give aA leakage; Phase B N-84 Jot-RAM (training knowledge).

title: Panel-level 3D oxide memory [SPECULATIVE]
idea: Deposit 64-128 tier stacks on 620x750 mm glass using display-industry PECVD and sputter tools; pattern channel holes by step-and-repeat nanoimprint at ~100 nm features (large-area imprint is proven at 100-200 nm pitch for wire-grid polarizers); one HAR etch per tier group; spatial-ALD oxide channels. Each tile (a few mm) is self-contained, with complementary-oxide local sensing (B2-08), so there is no cross-panel overlay requirement; tiles are diced and bonded to small Si I/O chiplets. This revives ram-venture A1-03 (display-glass memory, killed at 2 um rules) by getting density from tiers rather than pitch.

physics.key_insight: Taking density from tiers rather than pitch lets imprint at F~100 nm on glass reach ~2x 1-beta per area. Self-contained mm-scale tiles avoid panel-scale overlay.
physics.killer_doubt: No panel-size HAR etcher or conformal ALD exists; both are new $100M+ tools. Uncompensated, an 8 um, 200 MPa stack bows 0.7 mm glass ~13 mm over 620 mm.
physics.decisive_experiment: On Gen-2 glass, deposit a stress-compensated 16-tier oxide/W stack, imprint 100 nm holes and etch them. Map bow, hole CD and depth from centre to edge. Go if CD 3-sigma <10%.
physics.prior_art: Phase B N-38; SEL CAAC-IGZO; Canon NIL; large-area wire-grid imprint. Earlier verdicts: I-10785 ADVANCE, I-03879 DROP.

innovation.key_insight: When density comes from tiers rather than pitch, F~100 nm is acceptable, so imprint and display-class litho could in principle replace EUV for 3D oxide memory.
innovation.killer_doubt: 3D memory capital is HAR etch and deposition (roughly half of 3D NAND tool spend), not litho. No panel HAR-etch tool exists; 64-128 tiers (~3-13 um film) warp glass.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Deposit a 32-pair oxide/nitride stack on 370x470 mm Gen-2 glass at a display R&D line. Map bow, stress and imprint-overlay residuals across the panel, then cost-model a panel HAR-etch tool. ~$400k.
innovation.prior_art: Large-glass imprinted wire-grid polarizers at 100-200 nm (prior logs); Kioxia/Canon NIL for NAND. No display-line DRAM found (R17 search).

title: Movable-type memory: one standard storage-element socket, swappable bit physics
idea: Like Gutenberg's interchangeable type in one press, define an open hybrid-bond 'socket': a fixed periphery and sense wafer with a standard 0.5 um-pitch bond pad per sub-array plus fixed voltage, timing and signal windows. Any new storage-element wafer (capacitor, ferroelectric, magnetic) bonds on and is tested with no periphery redesign.

physics.key_insight: Bond density works: each bitline needs one bond anywhere along its ~20 um length (~0.7 um2 per bond), so 0.5-0.8 um hybrid bonds can carry per-bitline sensing.
physics.killer_doubt: One periphery cannot fit all physics: DRAM senses 14-60 mV of charge, MTJs ~10-50 uA at <0.5 V, PCM resets at ~100-200 uA, FeRAM pulses 1.5-3 V plates.
physics.decisive_experiment: Programmable charge/current sense front-end chip at 130-180 nm, die-to-wafer bonded to MIM 1T1C and MTJ coupon arrays at a university hybrid-bond line (~$600k); compare margins with native test chips.
physics.prior_art: YMTC Xtacking and Kioxia CBA bond arrays onto CMOS wafers; 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM plans with bonded periphery (training knowledge); foundry MPW test-chip programs.

innovation.key_insight: Per-bitline bonding fits: one bond anywhere along a ~20 um bitline (~0.8 um2) allows 0.5-0.8 um pitch. A logic-node periphery wafer makes ECC decoders and CCD sense nodes cheap.
innovation.killer_doubt: One periphery cannot serve all physics: charge cells sense 15-60 mV, MTJs need 10-50 uA reads, FeRAM 2-3 V plates. Sub-um hybrid bonding is fab or imec/Leti-only (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Restrict the socket to charge cells: a 180 nm programmable charge-sense periphery die, bonded to MIM 1T1C and IGZO 2T0C coupon arrays at a partner hybrid-bond line (~$600k); compare margins with monolithic test chips.
innovation.prior_art: Kioxia CBA and YMTC Xtacking (array bonded onto CMOS); Samsung/SK hynix bonded-periphery 4F2 VCT DRAM plans; CEA-Leti MAD BEOL memory platform [training knowledge].

title: Matchstick: consume-once reads with decoupled sense amps skip restore
idea: A match is used once: add an isolation gate so the SA latches from a +/-100 mV bitline signal without driving the bitline rail to rail, and add a READ-CONSUME command; for data the host marks read-once (streamed KV cache, network buffers, transpose scratch) the row is left destroyed and marked free, so neither full swing nor restore happens.

physics.key_insight: Skipping restore for data that is never re-read saves the bitline swing, CV^2/2: ~17 fJ per 35 fF pair, ~140 pJ per 1 KB row. tRAS halves for those rows.
physics.killer_doubt: Consumption must cover a whole row (8 KB per rank). KV caches and weights are re-read every token, so read-once traffic is likely <5% of activations.
physics.decisive_experiment: Trace study across LLM serving, networking and analytics: measure the fraction of activations whose entire row is dead after the read. If <10%, stop. ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: IBM destructive-read eDRAM architecture proposals (~2000s, from memory); restore truncation (HPCA 2016); isolated offset-cancelling SAs; Phase B N-64.

innovation.key_insight: Decoupled sense amps can latch a row without developing the bitlines; for data truly dead after one read, the restore swing, the largest activation term, can be skipped.
innovation.killer_doubt: KV cache is re-read every token, not once; for row-aligned streams activation is ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit versus 3-20 pJ/bit I/O, so system energy falls under ~5%.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Instrument LLM training and inference traces for the share of HBM bytes read exactly once and row-aligned; model savings in DRAMPower. Build only if over 30% of bytes and 10% energy. ~$40k.
innovation.prior_art: Destructive-read DRAM with write-back buffers (2000s); restore truncation (HPCA 2016); bitline-isolation sense amps are standard [training knowledge].

title: Transfer-print thin memory membranes, then wire them lithographically
idea: Reverse bond-then-connect: undercut-release memory chiplets into <10 um membranes, pick them with a PDMS stamp onto the logic wafer, planarize with BCB, and pattern vias and copper across both with ordinary lithography, giving a monolithic-like 2-3 um-pitch connection with no bumps.

physics.key_insight: Lithographic vias over transfer-printed thin dies could give hybrid-bond-class 2-3 um pitch without HB tools, CMP flatness or particle-free bonding: a capital-light U.S. path.
physics.killer_doubt: Transfer-print placement is ~+/-1.5 um (3 sigma), too coarse for 2-3 um pitch without per-die adaptive litho. DRAM thinned below 10 um loses gettering, which may shift the retention tail.
physics.decisive_experiment: Grind DRAM test dies to 8-10 um, transfer-print them onto a logic wafer, planarize with BCB, and align 2.5 um vias die by die on a stepper. Measure via-chain yield (1e5), placement error, and retention before and after. ~$350k.
physics.prior_art: X-Celeprint/X Display micro-transfer printing of CMOS chiplets (Rogers lineage); chip-first fan-out with Deca adaptive patterning; Fraunhofer chip-in-polymer (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Micro-transfer printing plus lithographic vias gives bump-free 2-3 um-pitch memory-on-logic with university tools, a prototyping route around wafer-to-wafer hybrid-bonding capital.
innovation.killer_doubt: Hybrid bonding already runs <=10 um pitch in production (SoIC, SeDRAM). ~1-2 um print placement error forces per-die adaptive patterning; bought DRAM dies expose only ~100s of pads.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Print ten thinned (<10 um) test chiplets onto a patterned wafer, planarize with BCB and pattern 2.5 um-pitch vias with per-die alignment. Measure via yield, resistance and thermal-cycle survival. ~$150k at a university fab.
innovation.prior_art: X-Celeprint/Rogers micro-transfer printing of CMOS chiplets; Deca adaptive patterning; chip-first fan-out (InFO); imec micro-transfer printing of III-V on silicon photonics.

title: Magnify tiers 300x: convert idle 3D NAND fabs to gain-cell lines
idea: Reuse 3D NAND tool sets (alternating film stacks, one deep channel-hole etch, staircase contacts) to build 300-500 tier vertical-channel IGZO 2T0C gain cells, with a string-select scheme giving random access per tier and aggressive refresh.

physics.key_insight: Deposition-defined stacking with one hole etch is the only proven route below $0.1/GB, and IGZO gain cells are transistor-written (imec >1e12 cycles), so endurance is not the wall.
physics.killer_doubt: NAND strings are series; random-access 2T0C needs lateral transistor pairs per tier (the 3D DRAM blocker). Even 0.2% per-tier killer defects give 0.998^300 = ~55% block yield.
physics.decisive_experiment: Desk model (~$50k) of $/GB versus tier count from NAND per-tier cost and published IGZO 2T0C footprints; then a 4-8-tier vertical-channel IGZO 2T0C stack at a partner line, measuring per-tier Vt spread and defects.
physics.prior_art: NEO Semiconductor 3D X-DRAM (NAND-like process); IMECAS 4-tier 2T0C (VLSI 2026); Kioxia 8-layer horizontal IGZO (IEDM 2025); Phase B N-43.

innovation.key_insight: Deposition-defined stacking on 3D-NAND tools is the known route to ~10x cheaper bits without EUV. Reusing NAND tool sets turns existing capital into DRAM-class capacity.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 2T0C needs two independently gated devices per bit; a NAND-style series string gives no per-tier random access. Uniform IGZO Vt (σ ≤ 20 mV) across 300+ tiers is unshown.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On a university 8-tier oxide/nitride mold, build vertical-channel IGZO 2T0C cells with string-select access. Measure per-tier random read/write, Vt sigma across tiers, and 85 C retention. ~$500k.
innovation.prior_art: NEO 3D X-DRAM PoC on a 3D-NAND process (May 2026, via search snippet, prior log); Kioxia OS-DRAM; Macronix 3D AND; Samsung/SK hynix 3D DRAM; N-28.

title: Thousand-times-leakier cells tamed by a refresh engine per tile
idea: Inverts 'access transistors must leak <=13 fA': use the cheapest stackable access devices (unannealed sputtered poly-Si or oxide TFTs leaking ~10 pA) so retention is only ~10-100 us, and put a micro-sense-amp under each 4k-cell tile (CMOS-under-array) that refreshes its own tile continuously without touching global bitlines.

physics.key_insight: CMOS-under-array tile sense amps keep refresh traffic off global bitlines, so bandwidth survives even very short retention.
physics.killer_doubt: 10 pA on ~1 fF gives ~20 us retention; ~5 fJ per local refresh is ~2 W/GB versus DDR5 ~12 mW/GB; oxide TFTs are equally cheap and leak <1 aA.
physics.decisive_experiment: No hardware needed: SPICE a 4k-cell tile with 1 fF local bitlines and measured LTPS/IGZO Ioff tails; compute standby W/GB. Kill if >100 mW/GB, which first-order numbers predict.
physics.prior_art: Gain-cell eDRAM with local refresh; CMOS-under-array (Micron CuA); IGZO 2T0C gives the same cheap stacked tiers without leakage.

innovation.key_insight: Re-scoped: a CMOS-under-array sense amp per 4k-cell tile refreshes locally, keeping refresh off global bitlines and bandwidth. Insurance if 3D oxide tiers retain only 1-64 ms hot.
innovation.killer_doubt: As stated (10 pA, ~50 us retention), even 1-5 fJ per local refresh costs 0.17-0.86 W/GB in standby vs ~0.012 W/GB for DDR5; a 1 TB server burns 170-860 W.
innovation.decisive_experiment: SPICE plus a 28 nm MPW tile (metal caps emulating 4k cells, leaky TFT models) to measure fJ/bit per local refresh and tile availability. Pair it with 85-110 C retention maps of stacked IGZO tiers. About $300k.
innovation.prior_art: CMU subarray-level parallelism and refresh-access parallelisation (Kim, Chang); gain-cell eDRAM with us retention (Teman/Giterman); Micron CMOS-under-array in 3D NAND.

title: Vertical charge-coupled columns store packets without access transistors
idea: Deposit a 3D-NAND-like gate stack around a single-crystal or recrystallized channel and clock the gate tiers in three phases to shift charge packets up the column to one sense node at the top, so 128 bits share one transistor and no capacitor.

physics.key_insight: A crystalline channel is the real CTE fix (Si CCDs reach ~0.99999). Workaround: rotate it, horizontal CCDs in epi Si/SiGe 3D-DRAM stacks, vertical gate pillars as shared phases.
physics.killer_doubt: No single-crystal Si fills 128-tier holes; poly-Si grain-boundary generation (~100-1000x bulk) cuts 85 C hold from ~3 s (crystalline, ~120 e-/s/well) to ~3-30 ms.
physics.decisive_experiment: Planar 16-gate surface-channel CCD on SOI vs on laser-crystallized poly-Si at a university fab (~$200k): measure CTE at 0.1-1 GHz clocks and dark generation per well at 85 C.
physics.prior_art: 1970s Si CCD memories; epitaxial Si/SiGe stacks for 3D DRAM (Samsung, imec). Vertical CCD memory: none found (via search snippet).

innovation.key_insight: A buried-well CCD string has no access-transistor tail; only thermal generation drains packets. The insight holds only for a wide-gap channel, not for silicon.
innovation.killer_doubt: Poly or recrystallized Si has grain-boundary generation centres, giving ~1e3-1e5x c-Si dark current and ms-class retention at 85 C (estimate). Single-crystal vertical channels are unmanufacturable.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed separately. The IGZO CCD speed test under I-08879 supersedes it. If Si is still wanted, measure dark current on a laser-recrystallized poly-Si planar CCD at 85 C (~$100k).
innovation.prior_art: imec IGZO CCD memory (IEDM 2024 planar; IMW 2026 3D) chose a wide-gap channel (via search snippet); 1970s Si CCD memories (Intel, Fairchild).

title: Teletext data carousel: broadcast weights to accelerators that store nothing
idea: Borrowed from broadcast TV data carousels that loop content for any receiver to catch: a rack-level weight server streams the model layer by layer in a continuous optical multicast loop from ROM/NAND, and every accelerator computes on each layer as it passes, aligning its batches to the carousel phase.

physics.key_insight: Passive optical splitting delivers one weight stream to N accelerators. Receive-only energy of ~0.5-1 pJ/bit could undercut local HBM reads (~3.5 pJ/bit), making weights a shared broadcast resource.
physics.killer_doubt: Each GPU needs its shard every step: 405 GB/8 GPUs at 20 steps/s is ~1 TB/s ingress. Wide-EP NVL72 serving already holds weights at ~5% of HBM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Simulate layer-locked continuous batching on vLLM traces to measure throughput lost to carousel phase alignment. Build a 1:16 passive-split 4x100G FPGA link demo measuring delivered pJ/bit. ~$400k.
physics.prior_art: Cerebras weight streaming (MemoryX/SwarmX broadcast to CS-2, for training); NVLink SHARP multicast; DSM-CC and teletext data carousels (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: In large-batch decode every replica consumes the identical weight stream, so one copy can be multicast to many accelerators instead of being stored N times.
innovation.killer_doubt: Each receiver still needs full weight bandwidth: 70 GB FP8 at 20 steps/s is 1.4 TB/s (~11 Tb/s) optical input per accelerator. Wide TP/EP already stores weights ~once per rack.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Trace a 72-GPU wide-EP deployment and a DP-replica deployment for duplicated weight GB per rack; emulate the carousel phase-alignment latency with NCCL multicast on 8 GPUs. ~$50k.
innovation.prior_art: Cerebras MemoryX/SwarmX weight streaming; Fiber Memory preprint arXiv 2607.08407 (via R16 snippet); NVLink SHARP multicast; R16 I-00277 dropped, I-05406 HOLD.

title: Eliminate fixed-function reliability: firmware-defined, fleet-learned refresh and ECC subscription
idea: Ship <=400 C BEOL memory modules whose refresh timing, reference levels, ECC codes and remap tables live in updatable controller firmware. The vendor learns drift models from fleet telemetry, pushes updates and sells this as a reliability subscription that raises usable capacity over time.

physics.key_insight: Low-thermal-budget memories drift (IGZO PBTI Vt), so references and refresh learned in the field will be necessary, as NAND read-retry proved.
physics.killer_doubt: The mechanism is already standard (SSD FTL read-retry, updatable CXL controller firmware, DDR5 ECS/PRAC). The subscription is pricing, not a physics or supply gain, and ns-latency rules out FTL-style retries.
physics.decisive_experiment: Not needed as a standalone invention. Fold adaptive-reference firmware into the I-01312 controller prototype and measure drift-tracking gain on IGZO test arrays.
physics.prior_art: NAND SSD FTLs with read-retry and LDPC soft decode; RAIDR/AVATAR adaptive refresh; field-updatable CXL memory controllers.

innovation.key_insight: NAND-style read-retry and drift tables in updatable firmware could let oxide BEOL cells with hydrogen/PBTI Vt drift ship before full characterization.
innovation.killer_doubt: Works only if drift is deterministic and learnable; random telegraph or VRT-like jumps beyond the ~20 mV multi-level budget defeat fleet-learned models.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Stress 64 kb IGZO gain-cell arrays at 85-110 C for 1,000 h; fit a drift model on half the dies and test whether firmware reference tracking holds raw BER <1e-4 on the rest. ~$250k.
innovation.prior_art: NAND read-retry tables and FTL firmware updates (all SSD vendors); Astera Labs COSMOS fleet telemetry for CXL; DDR5 ECS error counters.

title: Eliminate the incumbents' data monopoly: open 1-um access-device PDK across universities
idea: Publish an open process kit for 100 mm wafer access devices (Si, SiC, Ga2O3 variants) runnable in ten U.S. university nanofabs, each running monthly shuttles with standardized retention-tail test structures; pooled data on millions of cells reveal which elimination (junction, oxide, body) shrinks the tail.

physics.key_insight: Retention-tail statistics are the hidden data moat; pooled ppm-scale tail maps across many fabs could rank tail mechanisms, especially for oxide channels.
physics.killer_doubt: 1 um devices miss the nanoscale GIDL/trap-assisted tunnelling fields that set the Si tail, so transfer is doubtful. 1e8 cells/yr reaches only ~5.5 sigma against a 6-sigma at 1e10 need.
physics.decisive_experiment: Pilot with 2-3 NNCI fabs (~$600k): the same IGZO 2T0C retention-tail macro at 1 um and 100 nm Lg, with 1e6 cells each. Test whether the tail shape scales; if it does not, 1 um shuttles are moot.
physics.prior_art: NNCI university nanofab network, Natcast/NSTC prototyping, SkyWater SKY130 open PDK, DoD Microelectronics Commons; no open retention-tail database found.

innovation.key_insight: Retention-tail statistics are locked inside three firms. Standardised test structures shared across U.S. university fabs would let outsiders iterate on access devices, oxide TFTs especially.
innovation.killer_doubt: Tail cells matter at the 1e-6 to 1e-9 quantile of a 1.7e10-cell die. Millions of pooled 1 um cells reach only ~1e-6, with different physics (no GIDL or single-trap tails).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Pilot in two university fabs: run one oxide-TFT test chip carrying 1e5-cell retention arrays twice, and check fab-to-fab tail agreement before scaling up. About $400k.
innovation.prior_art: SkyWater SKY130 open PDK (with Google); NSF NNCI university fabs; CHIPS Act NSTC/Natcast shared facilities. None of these targets access-device leakage tails.

title: Error-Tolerant DRAM grade: JEDEC spec permitting 1% raw cell errors
idea: Inverts 'every bit must work as shipped': a new JEDEC grade allows up to 1% faulty cells, with a boot-time defect map plus stuck-at masking codes for static faults and a rate-0.85 LDPC for random ones in the controller, sold as a cheaper price tier.

physics.key_insight: A capacity-tier spec grade that tolerates a raw fault rate lets the controller pay for weak cells and the retention tail, and ties to the ECC-paid capacitor (N-62).
physics.killer_doubt: At 1% raw, each 64 B block has ~5 bad bits: BCH t>=12 costs >20% parity; LDPC needs ~4 kb codewords, breaking 64 B access. 1e-4 is just N-62.
physics.decisive_experiment: Buy off-spec die (SpecTek-class bins), take fail bitmaps at 85 C, and classify random vs clustered faults; FPGA controller to test 64 B code overhead and latency at 1e-4/1e-3/1e-2 raw.
physics.prior_art: Micron SpecTek sells off-spec DRAM; DDR5 on-die SEC ECC; Flikker/approximate DRAM; Phase B N-62 ECC-paid capacitor.

innovation.key_insight: Mature-node DRAM loses ~10-20% of die (more on ramping nodes like 1c) partly to cell faults that a boot-time fault map plus erasure coding could recover at ~2-5% overhead.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 1% random faults DDR5 on-die SEC leaves ~39% of 136-bit words uncorrectable; the rate-0.85 LDPC needed costs 15% capacity plus decode latency, eating most of a 10-25% gain.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Buy ~500 downgraded/UTT DDR4-DDR5 components from broker channels, map faults over temperature and time on an FPGA tester, classify static vs random vs gross, and compute recoverable good bits per die.
innovation.prior_art: ArchShield (Nair, Kim, Qureshi, ISCA 2013) fault-map tolerance; Micron SpecTek downgraded components; DDR5 on-die ECC and post-package repair; Linux page offlining.

title: Rescue rejected DRAM dies behind a strong-ECC buffer controller
idea: Box: existing dies x existing access x existing SA x ECC buffer chip on module x existing substrate x existing fabs. Buy dies that fail JEDEC bins with <=1% bad bits at scrap prices and package them on modules or CXL cards whose buffer chip runs LDPC plus remapping, sold as a new grade.

physics.key_insight: Strong LDPC behind a CXL buffer tolerates bit-fail densities that fail JEDEC bins, and ~us latency is acceptable in a capacity tier.
physics.killer_doubt: Rejects are mostly gross, periphery, IDD or speed fails, and redundancy already fixes scattered bits. At ~85-90% yield only ~1-3% of bits are recoverable. 1% bad is ~1.6e8 bits, clustered.
physics.decisive_experiment: Buy 1,000 rejected or eTT dies through a broker and map fail bits on an FPGA tester. If fewer than 30% show scattered fails that LDPC corrects at <1% overhead, stop. ~$150k.
physics.prior_art: Micron SpecTek (off-spec component brand); UTT/eTT downgraded-DRAM market; DDR5 PPR; I-07272 (subarray retirement, other batch).

innovation.key_insight: In a 4x price spike, bin-failing dies with sparse bad bits are cheap supply; a CXL buffer with remapping and strong ECC can resell them as a far-memory grade.
innovation.killer_doubt: Most final-test rejects are gross failures (IDD, speed, whole mats), so recovery may add only ~2-5% supply; 1e-2 raw BER needs ~15-20% parity and 4 KB read-modify-write.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Buy ~500 off-bin and broker-scrap DDR4/DDR5 parts; map fail bits with DRAM Bender at 85 C; compute the fraction usable under page remap plus Chipkill, and its $/GB. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Micron SpecTek downgraded parts; X-PPR (CAL 2025) recycled-DDR4 repair in CXL; ArchShield (ISCA 2013); Meta CXL DDR4 reuse.

title: Minify resident chat sessions with typing-indicator KV prefetch
idea: Minify how long an LLM session's KV cache stays in HBM/DRAM: idle sessions are parked compressed in CXL flash. A restore is triggered by early client signals (tab focus, the typing indicator, a cursor in the input box), so the ~1-3 s it takes a human to type hides the reload.

physics.key_insight: Same mechanism as I-08555: client focus/typing events trigger KV restore from flash. Merge into the I-08555 dossier; its 'compressed parking' adds ~1.2-4x (CacheGen-style) on flash bytes.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate. Shared doubt: NAND wear. A 70B node makes ~3 GB/s of new KV, ~280 TB/day if spilled, ~9 drives' worth at 1 DWPD.
physics.decisive_experiment: Folded into I-08555's experiment: one trace-replay study covers both.
physics.prior_art: CachedAttention/AttentionStore (ATC'24) scheduler-hint prefetch, Mooncake, LMCache; client typing signal not found.

innovation.key_insight: Duplicate of I-08555, which states the same typing-indicator KV prefetch more concretely. Merge it there. Its add-on, keeping parked KV compressed, stacks with I-04883.
innovation.killer_doubt: Same as I-08555: ~50 GB/s of aggregate flash restore bandwidth per 200-session node, plus wasted prefetches when a tab gains focus but no message follows.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Covered by the I-08555 experiment. Add a compressed-at-rest arm (FP8/INT4 KV on flash) to measure how restore bandwidth falls against accuracy.
innovation.prior_art: CachedAttention, LMCache, Mooncake (KV offload to SSD); in-batch duplicate I-08555.

title: Proof-of-work logic: speculative-decoding drafts run from junk DRAM
idea: Crypto miners shrug off memory errors because every result is cheaply verified. Host LLM speculative-decoding draft models and their caches on retention-reject or relaxed-refresh DIMMs: the full model's verification pass rejects any token a memory error corrupted, so the only cost is a slightly lower acceptance rate.

physics.key_insight: Speculative decoding's rejection sampling stays exact for whatever draft distribution was actually computed, so draft-side memory errors cost only acceptance rate.
physics.killer_doubt: Draft models are 1-8B parameters (2-16 GB) per accelerator and want HBM bandwidth. That absorbs <<1% of DRAM output, so the impact on the weak-bin market is negligible.
physics.decisive_experiment: Inject bit flips at BER 1e-6 to 1e-4 into a draft model's weights and KV in vLLM, and measure the acceptance-rate loss. About a week of GPU time.
physics.prior_art: EDEN (MICRO 2019) approximate DRAM for DNNs; speculative decoding (Leviathan 2023; Chen 2023). Weak-bin draft hosting: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Speculative decoding's verifier rejects any token a memory error corrupts, so draft models can run on weak or relaxed-refresh DRAM at zero correctness cost.
innovation.killer_doubt: Draft models and their caches are ~1-5% of inference memory and must sit beside the target model in HBM for latency; the weak-bin outlet is tiny.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Inject DRAM-like bit errors into a 1B draft model's weights and KV at BER 1e-9 to 1e-5 in vLLM; measure acceptance-rate loss and throughput. ~$10k.
innovation.prior_art: Speculative decoding (Leviathan 2023, Chen 2023); EDEN approximate DRAM for DNNs (2019). The combination: none found.

title: Mycorrhizal memory sharing: gradient-driven DRAM lending between servers
idea: Servers on a CXL switch fabric run a decentralized 'wood-wide-web' protocol: each node advertises a scalar gradient (free memory minus pressure), and pages flow one hop at a time from surplus to starved neighbours, the way mycorrhizal fungi move sugar from sunlit to shaded trees. There is no global allocator; borrowed pages carry a lease that is recalled when the donor's gradient flips.

physics.key_insight: Diffusion-style local balancing needs no global allocator. A gradient-and-lease protocol is cheap to simulate and could simplify the control plane of multi-switch CXL fabrics.
physics.killer_doubt: Microsoft Pond measured ~7% DRAM saving at 16-socket pools, not 10-15%. Each CXL switch hop adds ~70-100 ns, and multi-hop lease recalls when the gradient flips risk thrashing.
physics.decisive_experiment: Replay Azure and Google cluster traces (~$30k) through a pooling simulator, comparing gradient diffusion with a central allocator at 8-64 sockets. Report stranded DRAM recovered, migration bytes and recall stalls.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft Pond (ASPLOS 2023); Meta TPP (ASPLOS 2023); Cybenko diffusion load balancing (1989); CXL 3.x fabric-manager pooling.

innovation.key_insight: Decentralized, lease-based page lending needs no central pool manager and recalls memory when a donor's pressure rises: wafer-free capacity at 4x prices.
innovation.killer_doubt: Microsoft Pond measured ~7% DRAM savings at 16-socket pools, not 10-15% of supply. On one CXL switch every peer is one hop, so gradient diffusion reduces to a central allocator.
