innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay Azure and Alibaba memory traces through a 32-node simulator comparing gradient diffusion with a central Pond-style allocator; kill if it recovers under 3 points more GB at the p99 SLO. About $30k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft Pond (ASPLOS 2023); Memtrade (SIGMETRICS 2023); Infiniswap (NSDI 2017); diffusion load balancing (Cybenko 1989); CXL pooling appliances.

title: Map-tile mipmapped KV cache: zoom only where needed
idea: Map apps load coarse tiles, then zoom in. Keep pooled summary keys for each 64-token block in HBM and score those blocks first. Full-resolution KV blocks come from CXL or flash only for the highest-scoring tiles.

physics.key_insight: Summary keys in HBM with full KV in a capacity tier has the right shape: it moves KV out of HBM, which uses ~3x the wafer per bit.
physics.killer_doubt: Already published and open-sourced. The tier link is a bound: fetching 2k tokens x ~327 KB over a 64 GB/s CXL x16 link takes ~10 ms per decode step.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Reproduce Quest or ShadowKV with a CXL-tier offload on LongBench/RULER and measure the HBM footprint against tokens/s (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: Quest (ICML 2024), InfLLM, ShadowKV, InfiniGen (OSDI 2024), RetrievalAttention.

innovation.key_insight: Block summary keys in HBM, with full KV in CXL or flash, cut the HBM KV footprint 4-8x at small accuracy cost.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already published as Quest page min/max keys, InfLLM block representatives and ShadowKV landmarks with KV on the CPU. Fetches from CXL/flash (~1-100 us) stall decode unless prefetched.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Nothing new to settle. Reproduce ShadowKV/Quest on RULER-128k with KV on CXL versus HBM to measure the residual HBM fraction and tokens/s.
innovation.prior_art: Quest (ICML 2024), InfLLM (2024), ShadowKV (2024), InfiniGen (OSDI 2024), RetrievalAttention, PQCache.

title: Second-life DRAM: re-certify decommissioned server dies under strong ECC
idea: Worse: shred millions of 3-5 year old DIMMs while new bits cost 4x more. Flip: industrial lines recover modules from retired servers, run deep retention and hammer profiling, and resell them graded into tiers behind controllers with chipkill plus elastic refresh for cold or secondary memory pools.

physics.key_insight: Same core as I-00845. It adds tiered grading and elastic refresh for cold pools, which fits the clean-page weak tier (I-01324).
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-00845. Usable supply is the annual retirement flow (~1/5-1/6 of the installed base at 5-6 year server lives), not the whole installed base.
physics.decisive_experiment: None separate: settled by I-00845's 5,000-DIMM profiling and CXL field pilot.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU DDR4 reuse; ITAD resellers; same as I-00845.

innovation.key_insight: Same mechanism as I-00845, framed as an industrial line: profile, grade and resell retired DIMMs into tiers behind chipkill and elastic refresh.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-00845 and R16 I-00224. Secondary DDR4 prices track the shortage, and a CXL card plus controller adds ~$0.3-0.8/GB, squeezing the margin.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Folded into the I-00224 pilot, plus Q4-2026 bid sheets from three ITAD brokers for 64 GB DDR4 RDIMMs to fix the input cost. ~$10k incremental.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X; ITRenew/Iron Mountain recertified hyperscale hardware.

title: Retired hyperscale DIMMs re-certified with a per-module retention passport
idea: Second-hand DRAM has not won trust because buyers cannot see a module's wear or retention. A test cell measures each retired DIMM's retention tail at temperature and writes a module-specific refresh multiplier and a weak-row list into its SPD. Modules with leakier access transistors then run at 2x refresh instead of being scrapped.

physics.key_insight: Per-module retention profiling turns marginal used DIMMs into usable supply during a ~4x price spike, trading refresh rate for scrap.
physics.killer_doubt: Retired hyperscale DIMMs are mostly DDR4, unusable in DDR5 hosts without CXL; hosts ignore custom SPD refresh fields; refurbished-DIMM resellers already test and resell.
physics.decisive_experiment: Profile 1,000 retired DDR4 RDIMMs at 85 C for retention tail and errors; if <5% need >1x refresh, the passport adds nothing beyond standard refurb testing. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: Refurbished server-DIMM resellers; Microsoft GreenSKU reusing old DDR4 behind CXL (from memory); CMU REAPER/AVATAR retention profiling.

innovation.key_insight: Retention-profiled reuse turns retired DIMMs into supply during a 4x price spike. The trust layer (a measured tail) is the only new part.
innovation.killer_doubt: DDR4 cannot plug into DDR5 platforms, so reuse needs CXL expanders. DDR4 already has hPPR/sPPR row remap and 2x refresh, so the passport adds a few % salvage at most.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Test 1,000 retired DIMMs for retention tails at 45-85 C and 1x/2x refresh. Compute salvage fraction and $/GB against CXL expander cost. About $200k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) reuses DDR4 via CXL; ITAD secondary DIMM market; REAPER/AVATAR retention profiling; DDR4 post-package repair.

title: Bit-plane-major storage with progressive-precision fetch
idea: Rearrange bit order: weights are stored transposed so that each DRAM burst holds the same bit position of 512 different weights. The accelerator fetches the top 4 bit-planes first and fetches lower planes only for layers or tokens whose error estimate needs them.

physics.key_insight: One bit-plane-major copy serves several precisions, making precision a fetch-time knob; most useful for KV-score sketches and batch-1 edge decode.
physics.killer_doubt: Production already stores 4-bit weights, and batched serving fetches the most planes any token needs, so dynamic savings fall to ~1.1-1.3x of decode traffic.
physics.decisive_experiment: Software emulation (~$30k): bit-plane fetch policy on Llama-class decode at batch 1, 32 and 128; measure bytes moved and accuracy against a static 4-bit baseline.
physics.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024); Matryoshka Quantization (2025); Stripes bit-serial accelerator; in-study I-02063 (HOLD), I-05653 and I-09970 (DROP).

innovation.key_insight: A bit-plane-major layout makes precision a fetch-time knob. Its best use is MSB-plane KV scoring (I-02063) and batch-1 edge decode.
innovation.killer_doubt: Production already stores 4-bit weights, and batched decode fetches the most planes any token needs, so realistic savings are ~1.1-1.3x of decode traffic (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Software emulation (~$30k): a plane-fetch policy on Llama-class decode at batch 1/32/128 versus static 4-bit, measuring bytes moved and accuracy.
innovation.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024); Matryoshka Quantization (ICML 2025); Stripes bit-serial accelerator; in-study I-02063 (HOLD), I-05653 and I-09970 (DROP).

title: Landmark keys in DRAM, full KV blocks indexed on flash
idea: Inverts 'attention needs every past token resident': DRAM keeps one landmark key per 64-token block, and the full KV blocks sit on NVMe/CXL flash. Each decode step fetches only the top-k blocks whose landmarks score highest against the query.

physics.key_insight: Block-landmark scoring makes attention sparse enough for full KV to live off-HBM; at 1M tokens a 70B GQA model needs ~330 GB of KV per sequence.
physics.killer_doubt: Fetching 32 blocks x 64 tokens x 320 KB (70B GQA) is 0.67 GB per decode step: ~48 ms on a 14 GB/s SSD, ~200 pJ/bit versus HBM ~3.5.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. To size it, run Quest/InfLLM-style top-k with KV on a 4x Gen5 SSD array versus CPU-DRAM offload at 128k-1M tokens (RULER), reporting tokens/s per sequence, SSD DWPD and J/token. ~$30k.
physics.prior_art: Landmark Attention (2023), Quest (ICML 2024), InfLLM, ShadowKV, RetrievalAttention, InstInfer in-SSD attention, CachedAttention SSD KV store (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: Long-context decode reads only a few KV blocks per step, so per-block summary keys in DRAM can gate fetches and leave most KV on flash.
innovation.killer_doubt: Published since 2023-24. Flash bandwidth is the wall: top-32 64-token blocks x 80 layers is ~650 MB/step for 70B GQA, ~13 GB/s per stream at 20 tok/s (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Sizing only: run a ShadowKV/RetroInfer-style flash tier on Llama-3.1-70B over NVMe RAID; measure streams per SSD and RULER accuracy against block size and top-k. ~$30k.
innovation.prior_art: Landmark Attention (NeurIPS'23), Quest (ICML'24), InfLLM, ShadowKV, RetroInfer, InstInfer in-SSD attention [training knowledge]; R16 I-04022 and I-09974 dropped.

title: Socketed design-for-disassembly DRAM packages for multi-life reuse
idea: Box [standard die | standard | standard | compression-interposer LGA packages on CAMM/CXL boards | n/a | solderless assembly]: standardize DRAM packages that mount without solder and carry an on-package wear/retention log, so dies move from retired boards to new controller generations.

physics.key_insight: An on-package retention and wear log makes die-level reuse traceable; solderless attach matters for soldered LPDDR and CAMM systems.
physics.killer_doubt: DIMMs are already socketed, and a DDR5 die cannot speak DDR6; only a CXL bridge enables cross-generation reuse, which works on whole DIMMs anyway.
physics.decisive_experiment: Signal-integrity test of a compression-LGA DRAM package at 6.4-8.5 Gb/s, plus a cost model of ~16 sockets per module against second-life value.
physics.prior_art: JEDEC CAMM2/LPCAMM2 compression-attach modules (2023); socketed BGA test sockets. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Design for reuse is the right lever: an on-package retention and wear log makes second-life grading cheap and trustworthy.
innovation.killer_doubt: DIMMs are already socketed; the barrier is the DDR4-to-DDR5 protocol mismatch, not solder. Compression sockets add an estimated ~$1-3 per package.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Classify 500 retired DIMMs by failure cause and protocol generation. If solder or board failure is under 10% of losses, kill, and pilot the log as an SPD extension instead. ~$40k.
innovation.prior_art: CAMM2/LPCAMM2 compression-mounted modules; SPD EEPROM on every DIMM; Microsoft GreenSKU DDR4 reuse.

title: Optane's selector drift turned into DRAM retention
idea: In 3D XPoint, the ovonic threshold switch's threshold voltage drifted upward with log-time after each firing, which eroded read margins. Use two back-to-back OTS films as the access device of a crosspoint 1S1C capacitor cell. After each access the threshold drifts up, so the selector's off-state leakage falls as the stored bit ages. Each access or refresh re-fires the selector, which resets its state.

physics.key_insight: Selector drift as a feature is clever: after firing, Vth rises with log-time, so leakage falls as the bit ages, and each refresh resets it.
physics.killer_doubt: OTS off-current near half-bias is ~pA-nA, 1e3-1e6x above the ~1-13 fA retention budget; ~50 mV/decade drift on a ~250 mV/decade slope buys ~10x.
physics.decisive_experiment: 30 nm OTS devices on a 1 fF on-chip MIM: measure node decay from 0.25-1 V hold over 1 us-10 s after firing, at 85 C; go only if leakage <=10 fA at 0.3 V.
physics.prior_art: Intel/Micron 3D XPoint OTS selectors (drift documented); our N-85/N-87 two-terminal-selector 1S1C crosspoint family.

innovation.key_insight: Clever failure-mining: log-time threshold drift makes off-leakage fall as the bit ages, and each access resets it.
innovation.killer_doubt: OTS off-current at ~0.5 V, 20 nm is ~1e-11 to 1e-9 A vs ~8e-15 A needed for 64 ms on 5 fF. Drift buys a few-fold per decade, not 1e4-1e6.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Measure off-current vs time after firing on back-to-back GeSe-class OTS cells with 1-5 fF on-chip capacitors, at 25-85 C, plus cycling. Partner coupons. About $150k.
innovation.prior_art: OTS drift is well characterised in Intel/Micron 3D XPoint selector work. 1S1C selector-DRAM proposals: Phase B N-85, N-87. Drift-as-retention: none found.

title: Retired-server DIMM reclamation business delivering tens-of-cents-per-GB pooled memory
idea: Ideal: memory that already exists and costs nothing. Closest: buy decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs from hyperscaler refresh cycles at scrap-plus prices, auto-test and grade them, and mount them on CXL Type-3 expander cards whose controllers remap weak rows and add stronger ECC, sold as pooled second-tier memory.

physics.key_insight: Cost framing is right: marginal reuse cost is test, card and controller, far below 4x-inflated new DRAM.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-06172; $0.05-0.15/GB is low, since a CXL Type-3 controller card (~$150-300 per 256-512 GB) alone is ~$0.3-1/GB, still ~20x under $20/GB.
physics.decisive_experiment: Folded into I-06172; obtain controller-card BOM quotes and retired-DIMM auction prices to fix the $/GB band.
physics.prior_art: Same as I-06172: GreenSKU, used-DIMM brokers.

innovation.key_insight: The clearest economics framing of the reuse cluster: landed cost is test plus card plus controller, plausibly ~$0.5-1/GB against ~$20/GB contract DDR5.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-00224. The claimed $0.05-0.15/GB leaves out the CXL card (~$0.3-0.8/GB) and the DIMM price, which tracks the shortage. Supply is capped by retirements.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Folded into the I-00224 pilot, plus Q4-2026 bid sheets from three ITAD brokers for 64 GB DDR4 RDIMMs to fix the input price.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X DDR4 reuse; ITRenew/Iron Mountain Sesame decommissioned-hyperscale resale.

title: CXL bridges give retired DDR4 modules a second decade
idea: Scale shift from server to rack: when servers retire after 4-5 years, keep their DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs and seat them in CXL memory-expander cards. The cards use controllers built on existing 28 nm logic lines and serve a far-memory tier at ~150-250 ns.

physics.key_insight: Right scale shift: retire the server, keep the DIMMs, and serve them through a mature-node CXL bridge.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-06172 and already deployed; a 150-250 ns tier suits only cold pages (~20-30% of footprint), capping how much new DDR5 it displaces.
physics.decisive_experiment: Folded into I-06172; measure the cold-page fraction on target workloads to bound displaced DDR5.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) DDR4 behind CXL. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: The plain form of the reuse play: keep DIMMs when servers retire and seat them in CXL expanders built on trailing-node logic.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-00224 and already deployed. Latency of 150-250 ns suits only cold pages, roughly 20-40% of a typical footprint (estimate, TPP-style tiering).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Folded into the I-00224 pilot. Measure the share of pages that tolerate 200 ns under a TPP-style tiering kernel on production-like traces.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X; Meta TPP tiered-memory page placement in Linux.

title: Vacuum-sealed bag: FPGA CXL card compresses memory inline
idea: Stimulus 'vacuum storage bag' (same clothes, a third of the space) -> a 10-person team builds an FPGA CXL memory expander that compresses cache lines inline (LZ4/base-delta hybrid with hardware page metadata), presenting 2-3x more logical capacity than physical DRAM.

physics.key_insight: Inline compression behind CXL multiplies capacity per DRAM die without wafers, and an FPGA demo is cheap.
physics.killer_doubt: It is already commercial. Fleet data show ~20-30% of memory cold at ~3x, a system gain of ~15-25%, not 2-3x, and it adds ~50-100 ns decompression latency.
physics.decisive_experiment: None warranted beyond replaying public far-memory traces through LZ4/base-delta models (~$20k), as for R16 I-08737.
physics.prior_art: ZeroPoint Technologies; Marvell Structera A inline LZ4; OCP Hyperscale CXL Tiered Memory Expander; Google zswap far memory (ASPLOS 2019). From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Inline cache-line compression behind CXL multiplies logical capacity for compressible cold data with no new device, only a controller.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already productized: server data compresses ~1.5-2x on average, and vendors ship or specify it. A $1M FPGA card adds nothing an incumbent lacks.
innovation.decisive_experiment: No novelty experiment needed. If pursued, a trace-driven compressibility study of production AI and database heaps on an existing CXL compression expander. ~$50k.
innovation.prior_art: IBM MXT inline main-memory compression (2001); Marvell Structera A CXL expander with inline LZ4 (2024); ZeroPoint Technologies compression IP.

title: KV cache whose precision decays with token age and attention
idea: Box: approximate × KV manager × 16-token block × age-triggered × format ladder FP16→FP8→INT4→INT2→evict. A background re-quantizer demotes blocks as they age and as their accumulated attention mass stays low, while sink tokens and recently attended blocks stay at full precision.

physics.key_insight: Attention mass concentrates on sinks and recent tokens, so mixed precision beats eviction; ~3-4 bits average is a real 4-5x KV cut.
physics.killer_doubt: Published many times (KIVI, MiKV, ZipCache, H2O, StreamingLLM); past attention mass misses query-dependent retrieval, so demoted needles lose accuracy at INT2.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing beyond the literature is needed; if pursued, run RULER/needle tests at 128k on an open model comparing the age ladder with MiKV/ZipCache at equal bits (<$20k GPU time).
physics.prior_art: KIVI 2-bit KV; MiKV importance-aware mixed precision; ZipCache salient-token quantization; H2O heavy-hitter eviction; StreamingLLM attention sinks.

innovation.key_insight: Making precision follow token age and attention mass matches how attention decays. Duplicate of I-04883/I-00304, which earlier batches dropped.
innovation.killer_doubt: Production KV already ships as FP8/NVFP4 (~4.5 bits with scales), so a 3-4 bit average buys ~1.2-1.5x, not 4-5x. INT2 erodes long-range retrieval.
innovation.decisive_experiment: RULER/needle test at 128k on a 70B model: compare the age-graded ladder against flat NVFP4 KV at equal bytes in ~1 GPU-week. Stop below 1.5x.
innovation.prior_art: KIVI, MiKV, ZipCache, KVQuant, PM-KVQ; NVFP4/FP8 KV caches in vLLM and on Blackwell.

title: Datacenter-wide prefix radix tree deduplicates shared KV across users
idea: IFR: identical context is cached once for the planet. Closest with no materials: a cluster-wide radix tree keyed by token prefixes stores shared KV blocks (system prompts, popular documents, few-shot examples) once per pod, and requests are routed to the pod holding their longest prefix.

physics.key_insight: Shared prefixes (system prompts, documents) are a large share of KV. Storing them once per pod with longest-prefix routing is real demand reduction, and it is already shipping.
physics.killer_doubt: Prior art ships it. The only remaining gain is the cross-pod duplicate share, and moving KV between pods costs ~0.33 MB/token (70B GQA) of network traffic.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Replay a multi-tenant chat trace through a cache-aware SGLang router and a Mooncake-style global pool, and report the HBM-GB-hours that cross-pod dedup saves beyond per-pod caching.
physics.prior_art: SGLang RadixAttention and cache-aware router; Mooncake (Kimi, FAST'25) global KV pool; NVIDIA Dynamo KV-aware routing; llm-d prefix-aware scheduling.

innovation.key_insight: Shared system prompts, documents and few-shot blocks make prefix KV globally redundant; prefix-affinity routing stores each block once per pod and also skips its prefill compute.
innovation.killer_doubt: Shipping in production stacks. Per-pod prefix caching already captures the 30-70% shared share; cross-pod duplication left over is likely only ~1.1-1.3x more (estimate), traded against load imbalance.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None for novelty. Replay an agent-heavy multi-tenant trace through SGLang router or Dynamo with and without a global radix index; measure residual duplicate KV GB and TTFT under hotspot load. ~$15k.
innovation.prior_art: SGLang RadixAttention and cache-aware router (2024); Mooncake global KV pool (FAST'25); NVIDIA Dynamo KV-aware router; llm-d prefix-aware scheduling; Preble [training knowledge].

title: Idle chat sessions keep tokens, not KV caches, until resumed
idea: A KV entry is ~100-500 KB per token but the token that produced it is 2 bytes, and most KV memory belongs to sessions idle between user turns. Evict idle sessions to token IDs only and re-prefill them on return using cheap older-node recompute chiplets, trading FLOPs for bytes.

physics.key_insight: A token is 2 B against ~327 KB of KV per token, and idle sessions dominate KV residency. Tiering idle sessions out of HBM is the right lever.
physics.killer_doubt: Re-prefilling 32k tokens on a 70B model is ~4.6e15 FLOP, ~3 kJ per resume. An NVMe reload of the same ~10 GB costs tens of J, so storing wins.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. On one 8-GPU node (<$10k), measure resume energy and latency for recompute versus an LMCache/Mooncake NVMe reload at 8k-128k context.
physics.prior_art: vLLM recompute preemption, HCache (EuroSys 2025), CachedAttention/AttentionStore (ATC 2024), Mooncake, LMCache.

innovation.key_insight: An idle session needs only its 2-byte tokens. Re-prefilling on resume trades FLOPs for bytes and frees resident KV in proportion to the idle duty cycle.
innovation.killer_doubt: vLLM already offers recompute preemption. Re-prefilling 100k tokens costs seconds of accelerator time, which is why CachedAttention and LMCache spill KV to DRAM or SSD. Old-node chiplets worsen FLOPs/W.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Trace-driven simulation on public multi-turn chat timings: DRAM-GB saved versus added GPU-seconds for recompute, compared with SSD spill. Under $20k.
innovation.prior_art: vLLM recompute preemption; CachedAttention (ATC 2024); HCache (EuroSys 2025) hidden-state restore; Mooncake and LMCache KV tiers.

title: Swap stored embedding rows for IDs hashed through a tiny MLP
idea: Substitute lookup with generation. Recommendation models replace multi-TB ID embedding tables with deep hash embeddings: k hash functions turn each ID into a dense code, a small shared MLP produces the embedding on the fly, and exact rows are kept only for the hottest 1% of IDs.

physics.key_insight: Identical to I-06735: DHE plus exact rows for the hottest 1% of IDs. The hybrid is the right deployable shape.
physics.killer_doubt: A duplicate of I-06735, and the hybrid is already published: CAFE gives hot IDs exclusive rows and hashes the rest. Its gain over int4-pruned tables is unmeasured at production scale.
physics.decisive_experiment: Covered by I-06735's Criteo-1TB comparison; no separate experiment is warranted.
physics.prior_art: DHE (KDD 2021); CAFE (SIGMOD 2024); mixed-dimension embeddings (Ginart et al. 2019). From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Swapping stored ID rows for k-hash codes plus a shared MLP, and keeping exact rows only for the hottest 1%, trades DRAM for compute.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-06735 and published DHE. The hot cache is MP-Rec's hybrid. Compute rises 10-100x per lookup, and production prefers int4 rows plus collision hashing.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Same as I-06735: DHE against quantized and hashed tables on MLPerf DLRM-DCNv2. Measure AUC, FLOPs per sample, latency and DRAM.
innovation.prior_art: Deep Hash Embedding (KDD 2021); MP-Rec (2023); dup of I-06735 [training knowledge].

title: Fixed-rate ZFP codec in the L2 fill path for simulation arrays
idea: Box: lossy random-access compression × L2 fill/evict path × 4×4×4 float block × fixed 8–16 bits per value × HPC fields. Arrays live in DRAM as fixed-rate ZFP blocks; a cache-side codec decompresses on fill and recompresses on eviction, so code sees plain doubles.

physics.key_insight: Same core mechanism as I-09037, with the codec in the L2 fill/evict path. It also saves on-chip fabric bandwidth and is worth carrying as a variant inside the I-09037 dossier.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate. An L2-side codec needs a CPU vendor to change the core uncore, while a CXL device does not. 4^3 blocks also need array strides that physical-line caches never see.
physics.decisive_experiment: Folded into I-09037. Add one cache-simulator arm (gem5 or ZFP cached arrays at an L2-sized cache) to measure the extra bandwidth saved over the controller-side placement.
physics.prior_art: zfp cached compressed arrays (software cache, same fill/evict semantics), FPGA ZFP codecs; hardware L2 ZFP not found.

innovation.key_insight: Duplicate of I-09037. Fold in as its host-side variant: a codec at L2 also cuts DRAM and fabric bandwidth up to ~4x for STREAM-bound stencils, which CXL cannot.
innovation.killer_doubt: Needs a CPU vendor to change the uncore, and a 4^3 block spans 16 half-lines across 4 planes, so caches need array strides. AVR/MemSZ already did LLC-side lossy.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Folded into I-09037. Add one gem5 or zfp-cached-array arm at an L2-sized cache to measure bandwidth saved over the controller/CXL placement on the same three codes.
innovation.prior_art: AVR (ICPP'19) and MemSZ put lossy codecs at the LLC; zfp cached compressed arrays; FPGA ZFP codecs (DE-ZFP, ZFP-V).

title: Compute embeddings from hashes instead of storing terabyte tables
idea: Recommendation embedding tables are terabytes of mostly cold rows hit by random gathers. Replace lookup with deep-hash embedding: k hashes of the ID feed a small on-accelerator MLP that synthesizes the vector, while only the hottest ~1% of IDs stay in an explicit cache.

physics.key_insight: Tail IDs carry little learned information, so a generator plus an explicit cache of the hottest 1% could shrink multi-TB tables 10-100x without new wafers.
physics.killer_doubt: A DHE-class decoder (k=1024, ~1800-wide MLP) costs ~1e7 MACs (~5 uJ) per ID, against ~15 nJ to fetch 128 B. Hundreds of IDs per sample multiply dense compute ~100x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Train DLRM on Criteo-1TB (<$40k) four ways: full table, INT4 plus pruning, CAFE hot/hash, and DHE plus a hot-1% cache. Report NE, resident GB and J/query. Drop if NE loss exceeds 0.1%.
physics.prior_art: Deep Hash Embedding (Kang et al., KDD 2021); TT-Rec (MLSys 2021); CAFE hot-row hybrid (SIGMOD 2024); QR embeddings (KDD 2020).

innovation.key_insight: Trading DRAM for compute suits a memory shortage: hashed IDs into a small MLP, plus exact rows for the hottest ~1%, could cut recommender tables 10-100x.
innovation.killer_doubt: Published DHE and MP-Rec. Each lookup becomes ~1-10 MFLOP instead of a ~256 B read (10-100x more compute); ~0.1% AUC loss matters, so production keeps int4 hashed tables.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Train hybrid DHE against int4 hashed tables on Criteo-1TB at equal AUC; report GB saved per added GFLOP and serving cost at current DRAM and GPU prices. About $40k of compute.
innovation.prior_art: Deep Hash Embedding (KDD 2021); MP-Rec hybrid (2023); TT-Rec (MLSys 2021); Google Unified Embedding; R30 I-06735 (DROP).

title: Bit-exact integer reversible transformers erase the activation stash
idea: Imposed limit: training may store activations for only one layer. Residual blocks use invertible coupling and run in fixed-point integer arithmetic, so the backward pass rebuilds each layer's input exactly, with no floating-point drift, and no activation stack is stored.

physics.key_insight: Bit-exact reversibility makes activation memory independent of depth. With 80-128 layers at long context it removes the dominant term of the training stash for ~1.3-1.5x compute.
physics.killer_doubt: BDIA-transformer (ICML 2025) already reverses bit-exactly without changing the standard architecture. Still open: parity at LLM pretraining scale, plus ~5-15% throughput lost to deterministic kernels.
physics.decisive_experiment: Pretrain BDIA and baseline 1B-7B decoders on ~50B tokens. Compare loss, measured peak HBM, and throughput with deterministic kernels at 32k-128k context. ~$300-600k of GPU time.
physics.prior_art: BDIA-transformer, Zhang/Lewis/Kleijn ICML 2025 (via search snippet); RevNet (2017); Reformer (2020); MacKay et al. fixed-point exact reversible RNNs (NeurIPS 2018).

innovation.key_insight: Fixed-point coupling layers invert bit-exactly, so the backward pass rebuilds each layer input with no drift and activation memory stops growing with depth.
innovation.killer_doubt: The baseline is full checkpointing at the same ~1.33x compute. Its boundary stash for a 405B model at 128k context (TP8 x CP16) is ~4 GB/GPU, under 5% of HBM.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Train a 1B integer-coupling reversible decoder and a standard Llama-1B for 20B tokens; compare loss, and peak HBM against full checkpointing plus CPU offload at 32k-128k context. ~$60k GPU.
innovation.prior_art: RevNet (2017), Reformer (2020), RevViT (CVPR'22); BDIA exact bit-level reversible transformers (2024); Maclaurin et al. 2015 exact fixed-point reversible learning [training knowledge].

title: Dictionary: fleet-trained compression dictionaries pinned per workload
idea: Train zstd-style dictionaries per workload class (JVM heaps, Python objects, embeddings) from fleet samples, ship them signed with the binary, and pin them in the hardware compressor's SRAM so even single 4 KB pages compress against a rich shared context.

physics.key_insight: 4 KB pages compress poorly for lack of context; a shared trained dictionary supplies that context, and pinning it in compressor SRAM makes it free per page.
physics.killer_doubt: Linux zram already accepts zstd dictionaries. Dictionary gain on 4 KB pages is likely ~10-30%, and compressed tiers hold ~20-30% of memory, so net DRAM saved is ~2-8%.
physics.decisive_experiment: Train zstd dictionaries on page samples from JVM, Python and embedding workloads; measure the 4 KB-page ratio with and without a dictionary across a week of drift. Kill if gain <20%. ~$10k.
physics.prior_art: zstd dictionary training (Meta); Linux zram zstd/lz4 dictionary support (~v6.12, from memory); Intel IAA canned Huffman tables; TMO/zswap far memory.

innovation.key_insight: A 4 KB page compresses poorly alone; a shared per-workload trained dictionary supplies the context, plausibly lifting the ratio from 2x to 3x.
innovation.killer_doubt: Linux zram already accepts pre-trained zstd dictionaries. Going from 2x to 3x frees 1/6 of cold-tier bytes, ~3-8% of node DRAM at a 20-50% cold share (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Train per-class zstd dictionaries on 1 week of sampled fleet pages; replay zswap traces for JVM, Python and embedding services; report ratio and decompress latency with and without. ~$30k.
innovation.prior_art: zstd dictionary training; Linux zram algorithm_params pre-trained dictionaries (~6.12); Thesaurus (ASPLOS'20) cluster-base compression [training knowledge].

title: JPEG for the KV cache: DCT along the token axis
idea: Treat each attention head's K and V as an image (tokens x channels), apply a block DCT along the token axis where neighbouring tokens correlate, and quantize with per-head learned quantization tables like JPEG luminance tables; the attention kernel inverse-transforms blocks in SRAM.

physics.key_insight: KV energy concentrates at low frequency along the token axis, so transform coding plus per-head quantization tables can stack on plain quantization. Pre-RoPE keys correlate best.
physics.killer_doubt: FreqKV (ICLR 2026) already applies DCT along the sequence dimension. The baseline is wrong: 2-bit KIVI already gives ~8x versus FP16, so a transform must beat ~2 bits/element.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. To size the residual gain on Llama-3-8B, compare FreqKV plus 2-bit quantization against KIVI-2 at equal bits on LongBench/RULER; continue only if >1.5x smaller at equal accuracy. ~$10k GPU.
physics.prior_art: FreqKV (arXiv 2505.00570, ICLR 2026) DCT along sequence (via search snippet); CacheGen (SIGCOMM 2024) token-delta coding; KIVI, KVQuant pre-RoPE keys (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: The KV cache is a highly correlated tensor, so media-codec transform coding (decorrelate, adaptively quantize, entropy-code) beats per-element quantization for storage.
innovation.killer_doubt: KVTC (ICLR 2026) already does PCA transform, adaptive bit widths and entropy coding at up to 20x (via search snippet), beating the 4-8x claim. RoPE breaks token-axis smoothness of keys.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Add a token-axis DCT (values, pre-RoPE keys) on top of a KVTC-style channel PCA. Measure the extra compression at equal RULER/LongBench accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B; kill if <1.3x. ~$20k.
innovation.prior_art: KVTC, Staniszewski & Lancucki (arXiv 2511.01815, ICLR 2026) (via search snippet); KIVI, KVQuant, GEAR, Palu low-rank KV [training knowledge].

title: Thermally drawn preform ribbons shrink centimeter laminates into nanoscale cells
idea: Ideal: draw memory like optical fiber, kilometers at a time. Closest: stack a cm-scale preform of glass, oxide semiconductor and low-melting metal (Sn-Zn or Al alloy) laminates in a cell cross-section, thermally draw it 1000-10,000x into ribbons whose layers shrink to 10-50 nm, then cut and tile ribbons orthogonally into crossbar or gain-cell tiers.

physics.key_insight: Thermal drawing really is km/hour and litho-free, and draw-down sets layer thickness geometrically; the multimaterial-fiber toolset exists.
physics.killer_doubt: Oxide semiconductors do not flow at glass draw temperatures, and co-drawable glassy chalcogenides leak far above the ~10 fA retention budget. Drawing replaces deposition, which is already cheap, not lithography.
physics.decisive_experiment: University draw tower (~$150k): draw a chalcogenide-semiconductor/glass/metal laminate to 50 nm layers, then cut and contact one stack as a TFT. Measure layer continuity by TEM, Ion/Ioff and 85 C off-current; kill above 1e-13 A.
physics.prior_art: MIT Fink and Abouraddy multimaterial fibers; in-fiber thin-film capillary breakup into filaments; R16 DROP of drawn-coax I-01820; in-batch I-11235. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Geometric draw-down sets 10-50 nm layer thickness with no lithography; thickness control in drawn laminates is genuinely free and kilometre-scale.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 1000-10,000x draw breaks molten Sn-Zn layers (viscosity ~1e-3 Pa s) by Plateau-Rayleigh breakup; crystalline oxide semiconductors cannot co-draw with glass; ribbon tiling needs ~10 nm contact registration.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Draw a glass/oxide/metal laminate preform 1000x on a university draw tower (Clemson, UCF, MIT); TEM layer continuity at 20-50 nm and test any transistor action across the ribbon. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: MIT Fink lab multimaterial fibers (in-fiber diodes, digital fibers with embedded chips); Bilkent iterative-draw nanowires; UCF in-fiber capillary breakup. No drawn memory cell.

title: Wound-film memory: roll-to-roll TFT DRAM coiled like a film capacitor
idea: Ideal: memory sold by the meter. Closest: imprint and print oxide-TFT DRAM arrays on 10 um aluminum/polyimide web at ~10 m/min, wind the web into a cylinder like a metallized-film capacitor, and connect every turn's wordline/bitline buses at the web edges via flame-sprayed 'schoopage' end metallization plus laser-cut edge decoders into parallel banks.

physics.key_insight: Winding is stacking without monolithic yield loss: every web turn can be tested and mapped before winding, unlike a 20-tier stack, where one bad tier scraps the panel.
physics.killer_doubt: Polyimide web moves ~10 ppm/K, ~100 um across 1 m per 10 K, against ~50 nm overlay needed at F=0.25 um. Edge schoopage shorts ~4,700 turns onto one bus.
physics.decisive_experiment: Only after I-10785's rigid-glass arrays work: imprint 2-mask oxide-TFT arrays on 25 um polyimide web at 0.5 um, and measure overlay and TFT yield over 10 m of web. ~$400k.
physics.prior_art: HP self-aligned imprint lithography (SAIL) for roll-to-roll TFTs; metallized-film capacitor schoopage; Thin Film Electronics printed memory. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Winding is the cheapest way to stack area volumetrically; roll-to-roll at ~$2-10/m2 would be striking if TFT memory arrays survived on web.
innovation.killer_doubt: Schoopage end-spray is a blanket contact that shorts every turn's edge together, so separate per-turn buses are impossible; web distortion of ~100-1,000 ppm (0.1-1 mm/m) defeats micron overlay.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Paper and CAD first: per-turn edge interconnect count and a schoopage-compatible bus scheme. Then a single-imprint (SAIL-style) TFT array on polyimide at 1-2 um, measuring yield per m2. ~$200k.
innovation.prior_art: HP Labs self-aligned imprint lithography (SAIL) for roll-to-roll TFT backplanes; metallized-film capacitor winding; flexible oxide TFT-on-foil (Holst Centre, PragmatIC).

title: Thermal arbitrage: keep the bits away from the GPU's heat
idea: HBM sits millimetres from a ~1 kW GPU at 85-95 C (32 ms refresh above 85 C), and server DIMMs run 50-85 C. In a disaggregated design, capacity DRAM (KV pools, cold weights, CXL expanders) moves onto separately liquid-cooled sleds at 30-40 C, linked by optics (B4-14) or CXL. Refresh is set from on-die temperature and canary readings (B4-02), not the 85 C worst case. The cool margin can be spent three ways: (a) 4-30x longer refresh intervals; (b) multi-level rows (B4-05), whose droop budget is a third of single-level; (c) next-generation dies designed to a 'cool spec' with ~30% shorter capacitors.

physics.key_insight: Retention is bought by temperature: capacity DRAM on 35 C sleds could refresh 4-18x less, or a cool-spec die could use a ~30% shorter capacitor.
physics.killer_doubt: Tail cells (GIDL, trap-assisted) have low Ea, so tail retention may gain only 3-5x; LPDDR temperature-compensated refresh already harvests this, worth ~10% of DRAM power. HBM cannot leave the GPU.
physics.decisive_experiment: FPGA DRAM tester on a thermal chuck: measure 1e-6-quantile retention of 1b DDR5 dies at 35, 55 and 85 C to fix tail Ea; about one month and ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: LPDDR4/5 temperature-controlled refresh (MR4); DDR4/5 2x refresh above 85 C; liquid-cooled DIMMs in HPC; C0 N-42. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Capacity memory need not share the GPU's 85-95 C. A 35 C sled buys 4-18x retention, which can be spent on refresh, multi-level margin or shorter capacitors.
innovation.killer_doubt: Tail cells are GIDL or trap-assisted (Ea ~0.2-0.3 eV), which caps the gain at ~3-5x. Refresh is 16-33% of idle DRAM power, so the system gain is ~10-20%.
innovation.decisive_experiment: DRAM Bender sweep of DDR5/LPDDR5 tail-cell retention at 35-95 C on ~20 dies to extract tail Ea. ~$60k; partial data already exist (Liu et al., ISCA 2013).
innovation.prior_art: Liu et al. ISCA 2013 retention vs temperature; JEDEC 2x refresh above 85 C; temperature-compensated self-refresh; liquid-cooled DIMMs; prior batch I-07481 dropped.

title: Bit-plane segmented KV cache with attention-gated plane residency
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: split every FP16 KV vector into a high plane (sign, exponent, top mantissa bits) and a low-mantissa plane stored in separate pages; only high planes stay in HBM, low planes live in CXL/LPDDR or NVMe and are fetched only for tokens whose coarse attention score (computed from high planes alone) lands in the top-k. Resolves 'keep all context' vs 'keep little memory' by holding every token coarsely and few tokens fully, losslessly.

physics.key_insight: Scoring on coarse planes and fetching exact low planes only for the top-k keeps every token losslessly addressable, so long contexts never need eviction.
physics.killer_doubt: The split caps HBM saving at 2x (8 of 16 bits); lossy FP8/INT4 KV already gives 2-4x. Fetching 256 tokens' low planes (~40 MB) at 64 GB/s costs ~0.6 ms/step.
physics.decisive_experiment: vLLM trace study (<$20k): compare FP8-high-plane top-k with lossless refetch against KIVI/KVQuant INT4 and Quest at equal accuracy on RULER. Report HBM bytes and tier traffic per decode step.
physics.prior_art: SpAtten (HPCA 2021) MSB-first progressive fetch; Quest, ShadowKV and InfiniGen top-k KV offload; KIVI and KVQuant low-bit KV. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Scoring from high planes and fetching low planes only for top-k tokens makes KV precision a fetch knob with a lossless fallback, on unchanged HBM.
innovation.killer_doubt: Gain is capped at 2x, which FP8 KV already delivers with negligible loss. NVMe low-plane fetch adds ~80-100 us per layer, ~8 ms per step over 80 layers.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B at 128k context, compare FP8 KV, INT4 KV and high-plane scoring with top-k low-plane fetch. Measure RULER accuracy, HBM bytes and step latency with low planes in CXL versus NVMe.
innovation.prior_art: Same mechanism as R16 I-02063 (HOLD); QuantSpec hierarchical upper/lower-nibble KV (2025); SparQ, InfiniGen and ShadowKV approximate-score fetch; vLLM FP8 KV.

title: Batch blender: Hadamard-mix tensors so bit flips become diffuse noise
idea: Bulk blenders homogenize a batch so that no pocket is off-spec. Tensors are multiplied by a randomized Hadamard transform before quantization and storage, so after the fast inverse transform in the load path, one flipped value is spread at low amplitude across 256-4096 reconstructed values. The same rotation flattens outliers, which allows 3-4-bit quantization.

physics.key_insight: Rotation turns rare catastrophic flips (sign/MSB, super-weights) into diffuse small noise. QuaRot-style rotated INT4 weights already have this property, which could justify relaxed-refresh weight storage.
physics.killer_doubt: Rotation conserves error energy. At 1% BER an INT4 code gains ~0.85 LSB^2 of noise, 10x quantization noise (0.083 LSB^2), leaving ~2.3 effective bits. Long-lived weights accumulate flips.
physics.decisive_experiment: Inject faults at BER 1e-5 to 1e-2 into rotated (QuaRot) and unrotated INT4 Llama weights and plot perplexity against BER. Then measure the retention BER of unrefreshed DDR5 at 85 C on an FPGA rig. ~$80k.
physics.prior_art: QuaRot/SpinQuant Hadamard rotations; EDEN (MICRO 2019) DNNs on approximate DRAM; Phase B card B4-04 (relaxed refresh for mantissa planes).

innovation.key_insight: One randomized Hadamard rotation does two jobs: it flattens outliers for 3-4-bit quantization and caps the peak damage any single stored bit flip can do.
innovation.killer_doubt: Orthonormal transforms preserve error energy. At 1% BER a 4-bit code gains ~0.85 level^2 of noise, ~10x quantization noise (0.083); SNR falls ~24 to ~14 dB whatever the shape.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fault injection into QuaRot-style INT4 weights, KV and activations at BER 1e-5 to 1e-2 with a directional retention model; measure perplexity with and without rotation. ~$15k GPU.
innovation.prior_art: Same mechanism as dropped I-08644. QuaRot, QuIP#, SpinQuant Hadamard rotations; EDEN (MICRO'19) error-tolerant DNNs on approximate DRAM.

title: Return-time-predicted KV hibernation for idle chat sessions
idea: Imposed limit: an idle conversation may hold zero KV bytes in DRAM. When a user goes idle, the KV cache is dropped and only token IDs are kept; a predictor that reads typing indicators, tab focus and the user's past think-times schedules a re-prefill on spare compute a few seconds before the next message is expected.

physics.key_insight: Client signals (typing, tab focus, think-time history) give seconds of warning before the next turn, enough to bring an idle session's KV back from a cold tier just in time.
physics.killer_doubt: Re-prefilling 32k tokens on a 70B model is ~4.6e15 FLOP, ~10 GPU-seconds. Restoring the 10.7 GB of KV from SSD takes ~1.5 s at 7 GB/s, is cheaper, and ships.
physics.decisive_experiment: Replay a chat trace with real think-time distributions. Compare predicted re-prefill against predicted SSD-tier prefetch (LMCache) on GPU-seconds, HBM-GB-hours and TTFT. ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: CachedAttention/AttentionStore (USENIX ATC'24); Pensieve (EuroSys'25); Mooncake KV tiering; LMCache; vLLM recompute preemption.

innovation.key_insight: Token IDs are ~1e5x smaller than KV; a think-time predictor using typing and focus signals can hide KV re-creation inside the user's gap.
innovation.killer_doubt: Re-prefilling a 32k-token 70B context costs ~4.6 PFLOP (~5-9 GPU-s) per resume; NVMe restore in advanced I-08555 takes ~1-2 s with no FLOPs. Merge into I-08555.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Folded into I-08555's experiment: add a re-prefill arm and report GPU-seconds per resume versus NVMe restore across 4k-128k contexts, at measured prediction hit rates. ~$10k extra.
innovation.prior_art: vLLM recompute preemption; InferCept (ICML'24); CachedAttention (ATC'24); HCache; earlier-batch I-08555 (typing-signal NVMe prefetch, advanced) and I-05417 (dropped).

title: Sodium spikes: streaming transformers store only the KV that fires
idea: Like a neuron's Na+ action potential that fires only past threshold, a video/audio streaming model compares each new frame's token KV with the co-located token of the previous frame and stores a new entry only if the change exceeds a learned per-layer threshold; unchanged tokens become 2-byte back-references.

physics.key_insight: Static-camera and screen streams are temporally redundant, so storing only changed-token KV with back-references fits streaming video LLMs, whose KV grows linearly with frame count.
physics.killer_doubt: Prior art already drops ~80% of redundant video tokens; deep-layer KV of an unchanged patch still differs (context mixing, RoPE position), and merged tokens need softmax count bias.
physics.decisive_experiment: On a 7B video LLM, compare per-layer thresholded KV dedup with input-side run-length tokenization at equal KV memory on hour-long static-camera and screen-recording streams, scoring streaming QA accuracy. ~$20k GPU.
physics.prior_art: Run-Length Tokenization (NeurIPS 2024); TimeChat-Online differential token drop (2025); ToMe proportional attention; StreamingVLM, Flash-VStream (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: Static-camera and screen streams repeat most patch tokens from frame to frame, so streaming VLM memory should scale with change, not with frame count.
innovation.killer_doubt: Dropping unchanged patches before the encoder saves KV and compute alike. A per-layer KV back-reference adds ~1.0-1.2x on top (estimate), and duplicated keys skew softmax mass.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On static-camera and screen-recording streams of about 1 hour, compare thresholded KV dedup against RLT-style input dropping and StreamingVLM at equal KV bytes; measure QA accuracy. ~$20k GPU.
innovation.prior_art: Eventful Transformers (ICCV'23) threshold-gated token updates; Run-Length Tokenization (NeurIPS'24); StreamingVLM, InfiniPot-V streaming KV compression [training knowledge].

title: Eliminate cells: vertical charge-coupled shift-register strings
idea: Delete the per-bit capacitor, transistor and staircase: each vertical hole through 128 tiers is a CCD whose tier gates are tied to only 3 clock phases, so charge packets shift up to a single sense node at the top (128 ns worst-case serial access, pipelined bursts).

physics.key_insight: Ganging every third tier onto one of 3 clock phases needs ~3 contacts per block instead of a 128-step staircase; that staircase saving is the genuinely new cost lever.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-01064/N-08. Tier ganging needs selective plane contact (alternating plane metals), and the >10x fewer cleans/CMP per bit water claim is unquantified.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-01064: on 8-16-plane test stacks, make one via that contacts only phase-1 planes after selective lateral recess of phase-2/3 planes (~$100k at a partner line).
physics.prior_art: Duplicate of Phase B N-08 and I-01064; the 3D NAND staircase is the baseline it removes. Vertical CCD memory: none found (via search snippet).

innovation.key_insight: Tie every same-phase tier together: the 128-tier stack needs 3-4 contacts instead of a 128-step staircase, removing a major 3D cost module. Fold this into the I-08879 dossier.
innovation.killer_doubt: The claimed 128 ns worst case for 384 transfers implies a 3 GHz phase clock, ~500x imec's demonstrated 6 MHz. A whole block shifts on every access.
innovation.decisive_experiment: In the I-08879 test chip, add an 8-16-tier vertical stack with phase-tied planes (partner 200 mm line, ~$250k). Measure plane RC, shift energy per bit and CTE versus block size.
innovation.prior_art: imec 3D CCD uses word lines as phase gates (3-WL vertical holes, IMW 2026) (via search snippet); phase-tying of a tall stack was not checked.

title: Eliminate storage-node lithography: transistors electroplate their own capacitor towers
idea: Eliminate the storage-node mask and etch: after building the access transistors, immerse the wafer in a plating bath and turn on every wordline so each working transistor's drain contact sources current and plates its own Ni/Ru nanotower; then add ALD dielectric (N2 purge) and top plate. No argon-sputtered seed is needed because the drains are the seeds.

physics.key_insight: Each access transistor acts as a current source, so plating is self-aligned and dead cells grow nothing: a built-in electrical yield screen.
physics.killer_doubt: Mold-free plating grows isotropically: from 20 nm seeds at ~40 nm pitch, neighbours merge at ~20 nm height, ~60x short of a 1.2 um node. Free AR-100 pillars collapse anyway.
physics.decisive_experiment: Seed-array test wafer (e-beam 20 nm pads, 40 nm pitch, ~$60k): plate Ni or Ru with and without suppressor additives; measure height at first merge by SEM.
physics.prior_art: Template electrodeposition (AAO and track-etch nanowires); SiN-supported DRAM pillar capacitors; transistor-gated self-plating of storage nodes: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Each access transistor as the current source for its own node gives self-alignment and a built-in yield screen. Idsat sets the plating rate, so the spread is ~5-10%.
innovation.killer_doubt: Moldless plating is isotropic: domes merge at ~half pitch (~20 nm), so AR 100 is impossible. Drivers must be powered in electrolyte. Selective electroless already seeds on pads.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A ~$120k test: on a test array of 1k transistors at 1 um pitch with a TEOS hole mold, plate through the transistors, then measure height spread against Idsat. Separately confirm that domes merge on unmolded pads.
innovation.prior_art: Template electrodeposition in AAO (Masuda 1995); bottom-up Co/Ru superfill and selective electroless caps (Intel, IBM); triage N-21 AAO mold and N-82 plated holes [training knowledge].

title: Airbnb for idle cleanroom tools: memory prototyping by the hour
idea: Borrowed from Airbnb monetizing spare rooms: a 10-person team builds a booking, recipe-transfer and wafer-logistics platform over idle tool hours in U.S. university, national-lab and 200 mm commercial cleanrooms, so memory startups route split lots across ALD at one site, etch at another and test at a third.

physics.key_insight: Routing split lots across idle U.S. tools could cut a memory start-up's learning-cycle cost: renting hours instead of building a ~$50M pilot line.
physics.killer_doubt: Cross-site lots break contamination rules (Cu, Au, alkali) and queue-time limits, since high-k and oxide-semiconductor interfaces drift in hours. NNCI sites already rent tools hourly.
physics.decisive_experiment: Run one IGZO 2T0C short loop split across three NNCI sites and the same loop at a single site. Compare Vt spread, Ioff tail and cycle time. ~$150k.
physics.prior_art: NSF NNCI (16 sites) hourly external access; Natcast/NSTC prototyping; MOSIS-style shuttles; Science Exchange-type service marketplaces.

innovation.key_insight: Learning-cycle cost, not physics, gates new memory cells. Split lots across idle U.S. tools could cut a cell team's first-silicon spend by maybe 5-10x.
innovation.killer_doubt: NNCI and Natcast/NSTC already sell tool time. Cross-site contamination rules (Cu, Au, Hf, In) and metrology drift block split lots; integration skill, not tool hours, is scarce.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Broker one 3-site split lot of an IGZO 2T0C test wafer (ALD, etch, test) through NNCI sites. Measure turnaround, cost, contamination refusals and cross-site variation against a single-site run. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: NSF NNCI user facilities; CHIPS NSTC/Natcast prototyping (Albany); NY CREATES; Science Exchange lab marketplace; MOSIS shuttles [training knowledge].

title: Venetian blinds: bit-plane layout fetches only requested precision bits
idea: Tilt Venetian blinds to let in only the light you want. Store tensors transposed into bit-planes across column groups, with a precision-select field in the column command so a 4-bit or 8-bit inference read opens only those planes' micro-rows and moves only those bits, not the full 16-bit words.

physics.key_insight: Precision becomes a fetch knob: bit-plane columns plus micro-row activation move only the planes a kernel needs. Useful for any-precision weights and KV top-k scoring.
physics.killer_doubt: Weights already ship stored at FP8 or INT4. Keeping 16-bit planes so you can read 4 costs 4x capacity. Only multi-precision serving gains, likely ~1.5-3x.
physics.decisive_experiment: GPU emulation of an Any-Precision-style bit-plane layout serving mixed 4/8/16-bit requests on a 70B model. Measure bytes moved and accuracy against separate quantized copies. <$50k.
physics.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024) bit-plane weights; FGDRAM and Half-DRAM fine-grained activation; SIMDRAM vertical layout; Phase B N-70.

innovation.key_insight: A precision-select column command lets one stored tensor serve 4-, 8- or 16-bit reads, moving only needed planes; useful for adaptive-precision KV scoring, not static quantized weights.
innovation.killer_doubt: Static quantization already stores 4-bit weights, so the 2-4x appears only for dynamically varying precision, likely under 20% of decode traffic, and it needs a JEDEC die change.
innovation.decisive_experiment: GPU software emulation: bit-plane KV with MSB-first scoring (Any-Precision style); measure bytes moved and accuracy versus INT4/INT8 on long-context tasks. Pursue a die change only if over 2x. ~$40k.
innovation.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024) bit-plane weights; SIMDRAM/Ambit vertical layouts; Fine-Grained DRAM (NVIDIA, MICRO 2017) partial activation [training knowledge].

title: Memory refinery ASIC: one uniform pool from mixed-vintage used DIMMs
idea: Ideal: all old memory looks like new memory. Closest achievable at trailing nodes: a 28 nm CXL controller with DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 PHYs, chipkill ECC across heterogeneous ranks, per-device health telemetry and hot-page migration to the fastest devices turns decommissioned DIMMs into a qualified capacity tier.

physics.key_insight: One chipkill-protected, telemetry-driven controller over DDR3, DDR4 and LPDDR4 is the right abstraction; the LPDDR4 port reaches phone-scrap supply that DIMM reuse cannot.
physics.killer_doubt: Chipkill needs lockstep devices of one width, so mixed vintages get per-rank ECC only. DDR4 already ships behind commercial CXL cards; a 28 nm tapeout plus PHY IP costs ~$2-5M.
physics.decisive_experiment: FPGA CXL prototype (~$150k) driving retired DDR4 RDIMMs plus reballed phone LPDDR4 on adapter boards: measure per-rank ECC overhead, mixed-rank bandwidth and corrected-error rates over 90 days.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) reuses DDR4 behind CXL; Marvell Structera X and Astera Leo CXL controllers support DDR4 (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: Health telemetry plus hot-page migration toward the best devices could make a heterogeneous used-DIMM pool behave like one qualified capacity tier.
innovation.killer_doubt: Chipkill lockstep across mixed ranks runs at the slowest timing and breaks on mixed x4/x8 widths. Same lever as GreenSKU and Structera X; phone LPDDR harvest is I-06854.
innovation.decisive_experiment: FPGA CXL card with two DDR4 channels of deliberately mixed DIMMs (vendor, speed, x4/x8). Measure lockstep bandwidth loss, chipkill coverage and migration overhead on Redis/memcached traces. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Marvell Structera X; Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Meta TPP page placement; study items I-00224 (HOLD) and I-06854 (ADVANCE).

title: Magnify dictionaries: hardware zstd for in-memory logs and JSON
idea: Magnify compression context with trained multi-MB dictionaries per data type (logs, JSON, traces). A CXL-module decompressor at 50 GB/s serves reads, and the in-memory store keeps everything compressed.

physics.key_insight: Dictionaries matter because small blocks compress poorly. With a 4 KB random-access granule, a trained dictionary lifts zstd from ~2-3x to ~5-8x on logs and JSON.
physics.killer_doubt: 10-20x needs whole-file or columnar (CLP-style) compression, not 4 KB random access. Log/JSON stores are a few percent of DRAM, and software zstd dictionaries already do this.
physics.decisive_experiment: Software trace study (<$30k): zstd with trained dictionaries at 1, 4 and 64 KB blocks on real log, trace and JSON stores. Plot ratio against decode latency. Build hardware only if the 4 KB ratio is >=8x.
physics.prior_art: zstd dictionary training (Meta); IBM z15 on-chip zEDC; Intel IAA; YScope CLP log compression; CXL compressed-memory controllers. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Trained per-type dictionaries let small records (log lines, JSON) compress 5-10x where generic LZ fails, and a near-memory decoder hides the cost.
innovation.killer_doubt: Log and JSON stores already compress in software (columnar stores, CLP, zstd dictionaries) and hold only a few % of fleet DRAM, so the world-level DRAM saving is <<10%.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay one log-analytics and one document-store workload. Compare DRAM per GB ingested for software zstd-dictionary compression against an emulated CXL hardware decompressor at equal query latency.
innovation.prior_art: zstd trained dictionaries (Meta); Intel IAA/QAT; IBM z15 on-chip compression; Marvell Structera inline-LZ4 CXL; YScope CLP log compression.

title: Minify embedding tables to hash encoders plus tiny MLPs
idea: Minify TB-scale recommender embedding tables into multi-hash encoders plus a small MLP that computes each embedding on the fly on tensor cores (deep hash embedding), with no stored rows.

physics.key_insight: The same mechanism as I-06735 without the hot-row cache. Tensor cores make the decoder MLP cheap in FLOPs per dollar, though not in energy.
physics.killer_doubt: With no stored rows, a ~1e7-parameter generator cannot hold the memorised information of hot IDs from a 1e9-row table. Published DHE results come from small datasets, not production NE.
physics.decisive_experiment: Covered by I-06735's experiment: add a DHE arm with no hot rows on Criteo-1TB and report its NE gap against the hybrid (<$10k extra).
physics.prior_art: Deep Hash Embedding (KDD 2021); TT-Rec (MLSys 2021); ROBE (MLSys 2022). From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Embedding rows computed from hash codes by a small MLP on tensor cores, rather than stored, could cut recommender embedding DRAM 10x or more.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-06735 without the hot-ID cache. Pure DHE loses accuracy at billions of IDs, and ~1-10 MFLOP per lookup multiplies inference compute 10-100x; production has not adopted it.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Same as I-06735: DHE against quantized and hashed tables on MLPerf DLRM-DCNv2. Measure AUC, FLOPs per sample, latency and DRAM.
innovation.prior_art: Deep Hash Embedding (KDD 2021), TT-Rec (MLSys 2021), MP-Rec; dup of I-06735 [training knowledge].

title: Minify tier thickness to 6 nm for 1000-tier atomic stacks
idea: Grow alternating MOCVD 2D-semiconductor channel sheets (MoS2 or WSe2, about 1 nm) and hBN/oxide spacers (about 5 nm) so each tier is 6 nm and 1000 tiers fit in a 6 um stack. Gain-cell storage nodes are gated by shared vertical gate holes etched once per 100-tier deck, as in 3D NAND.

physics.key_insight: ~1 nm 2D sheets with ~1.8 eV gaps allow sub-10 nm tiers, 5-8x tighter than 3D NAND's ~45 nm. Workaround: 2D or oxide channels at 20-30 nm pitch, 100-200 tiers.
physics.killer_doubt: 1000 wafer-scale 2D growths at 99.9% per-tier yield leave 37% good stacks; 6 nm steps need +/-3 nm contact landing; no gain-cell storage node fits 6 nm.
physics.decisive_experiment: Grow a 10-tier MoS2/Al2O3 stack at <=450 C and 6-10 nm pitch on 200 mm; map per-tier continuity and mobility through staircase contacts; measure one vertical-gate cell per tier at 85 C.
physics.prior_art: MIT (J. Kim group) low-temperature monolithic 3D TMD stacks, Nature 2024 (training knowledge); Macronix vertical-gate NAND geometry; Phase B N-28.

innovation.key_insight: Deposition-defined tiers at ~6 nm pitch would put many bits in one etchable stack height. Wafer-scale low-temperature TMD growth makes sequential 2D tiers thinkable.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 99.9% per-tier yield, 1000 sequential growths leave 37% of stacks intact. A vertical gate sees a ~1 nm sheet edge. MoS2 (1.8 eV) leaks more than IGZO (3.2 eV).
innovation.decisive_experiment: MOCVD a 10-tier MoS2/hBN superlattice at <=450 C on 200 mm. Build edge-gated FETs through one etched hole. Measure per-tier Ion/Ioff, the spread and tier-to-tier coupling (~$300k). Stop if Ion is under 1 uA.
innovation.prior_art: MIT (J. Kim) growth-based monolithic 3D TMD stacks (Nature 2024); Penn State and Fudan 2D integration; Samsung SAIT 2D channels (training knowledge).

title: Plated-pillar magnetic memory: coincident-current writes, inductive non-destructive reads
idea: Failure mined: plated-wire memory (UNIVAC, Apollo era) read magnetic bits non-destructively with no per-bit transistor but died on hand-assembled wire. Fix: build it monolithically by ALD-coating vertical pillars with a soft magnetic film inside a stack of deposited word planes. Coincident currents in a plane and a pillar write one intersection, and a plane pulse rotates the film so the pillar picks up an inductive or AMR signal without erasing the bit.

physics.key_insight: Unlimited magnetic endurance in a transistorless vertical string; ALD soft-magnetic tubes in DRAM-like holes are a credible process idea.
physics.killer_doubt: The read collapses. A 5x50 nm tube bit holds ~2.5e-16 Wb: a 1 ns rotation gives ~0.2 uV against ~100 uV noise. AMR is even in M: state-blind.
physics.decisive_experiment: Run micromagnetic plus circuit simulation of a 50 nm NiFe tube bit, then fabricate one 200 nm ALD tube with a radial GMR spin-valve and show >=5% state-dependent dR. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: Plated-wire memory (UNIVAC, 1960s-70s spacecraft); Parkin racetrack; cylindrical nanotube domain-wall memories; triage N-82 capacitor-hole racetrack.

innovation.key_insight: Transistorless 3D magnetic bits from one hole etch, with unlimited endurance and no refresh, would clear the triage's write-endurance wall via magnetic order.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 5 nm film round a 40 nm pillar links ~2e-16 Wb per bit, ~0.4 uV inductive signal; coincident writes need ~1 mA per pillar, ~8e7 A/cm2.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fabricate 10-tier test pillars (ALD NiFe/CoFeB liner in 40-100 nm holes) at a university fab; measure write current, half-select disturb and per-bit AMR/inductive read SNR. ~$300k.
innovation.prior_art: Plated-wire memory (UNIVAC, 1960s); IBM racetrack (Parkin); this project's N-82 racetrack-in-capacitor-hole; 3D domain-wall shift registers.

title: Progressive-JPEG bit-plane memory: fetch only needed precision
idea: Satellite and web imagery stream progressive bit planes so receivers stop when good enough. Store tensors bit-plane-sliced across columns (sign/exponent plane first, then mantissa planes); each read requests only the top N planes and only those columns are sensed and sent.

physics.key_insight: Plane-major rows make precision a fetch knob: fetching 4 of 16 planes activates ~1/4 of the rows. Most useful for KV-score screening and batch-1 decode.
physics.killer_doubt: An ACT senses the whole 8 KB row, so column selection saves only I/O. Storing FP16 planes to read 4 uses 4x the DRAM of a static INT4 copy.
physics.decisive_experiment: Software trace study (~$30k): Llama-70B decode at batch 1, 32 and 128 in a plane-major layout. Count rows activated and bytes moved at equal perplexity against a static INT4/FP8 copy.
physics.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024); SpAtten (HPCA 2021) fetches MSBs first; Matryoshka Quantization (2025); BitWeaving bit-sliced scans (SIGMOD 2013).

innovation.key_insight: Mapping each bit-plane to its own mat group would let a low-precision read activate only those mats, cutting activation energy, not just bus bits.
innovation.killer_doubt: Activation senses the whole row; skipping planes needs FGDRAM-style partial wordlines and a JEDEC die change. Static 4-bit weights leave dynamic precision maybe <20% of traffic (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Ramulator2 plus DRAMPower model of plane-to-mat mapping with partial activation, driven by LLM decode traces carrying per-access precision; kill if total DRAM energy falls less than 25%. About $30k.
innovation.prior_art: Fine-Grained DRAM (NVIDIA, MICRO 2017); Half-DRAM (ISCA 2014); Any-Precision LLM bit-plane weights; R22 I-05653 precision-select column command (DROP).

title: Expire-and-regenerate pages: let cells decay, recompute on miss
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: disable refresh entirely; each DRAM page carries a write timestamp, and any page older than its guaranteed retention counts as discarded, so reading it traps to the runtime, which regenerates the data from source (re-decompress weights from flash, recompute activations from checkpoints, refetch KV from a cheaper tier).

physics.key_insight: For clean, regenerable pages, decay can replace refresh: a per-row last-restore timestamp plus a trap on expiry gives zero refresh power with no cell change.
physics.killer_doubt: Decode re-reads weights/KV every ~20-50 ms, past a 10 ms target, and refreshing a 10 ms die costs 64-128% of bandwidth at 32-64 Gb. The 3x Cs cut fails.
physics.decisive_experiment: Trace row reuse intervals for 70B decode and training in Ramulator or an FPGA controller: what fraction of resident bytes is both regenerable and re-touched within 10/32/64 ms. ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: Refrint and eDRAM-cache line decay (expired clean lines invalidated); Smart Refresh (2007); Flikker; our N-64 lease refresh and N-73 weight-streaming die.

innovation.key_insight: A per-page write timestamp plus a regenerate trap turns expiry into a page fault, so data with an authoritative copy elsewhere needs no refresh.
innovation.killer_doubt: Cs is sized by the Cs/Cbl sense ratio, so 10 ms retention saves ~1.2-1.5x Cs, not 3x. KV and cold pages idle >10 ms would regenerate constantly.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Trace study (~$30k): log page reuse intervals for LLM serving and training on GPU hosts, then count bytes idle >10 ms and the regeneration traffic. Pair it with a sense-margin simulation of Cs versus retention.
innovation.prior_art: RANA (ISCA 2018) and ZEM refresh skipping; Flikker; HRM clean-page refetch (DSN 2014); in-study I-10659, I-00496 (DROP), I-03014 (HOLD).

title: Bit-plane memory layout for progressive-precision fetch
idea: MINIFY bits moved by storing tensors bit-plane by bit-plane (all MSBs together, then the next plane, and so on), so an accelerator fetches only the top N planes that the current layer or token needs.

physics.key_insight: One plane-major copy serves several precisions, so precision is chosen per access instead of per stored copy. A software or FPGA demo is cheap.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-08176. Shipping models already store INT4/FP8 (0.5-1 B/param). A 16-plane master copy costs 2 B/param, the wrong direction while DRAM costs 4x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-08176's trace study. No separate experiment is warranted.
physics.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024) serves 3-8-bit models from one bit-plane copy; Stripes and Bit-Fusion bit-serial accelerators.

innovation.key_insight: One plane-major copy serves several precisions. Its value is as the storage layout under I-02172's exact early termination or MSB-plane KV scoring, not as a standalone gain.
innovation.killer_doubt: Published any-precision layouts already do this. Batched decode fetches the most planes any token needs, so realistic saving is ~1.1-1.3x of decode traffic, not 2-4x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Not needed for novelty. If pursued: an FPGA HBM controller replaying batched-decode traces with plane-major layout, measuring bytes moved against a native INT4 baseline. About $50k.
innovation.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024); Matryoshka Quantization (2025); Stripes bit-serial accelerator; in-study I-02632 and I-09970 (DROP).

title: Paper airplane: bit-plane layout so reads fetch only needed precision
idea: A paper airplane flies with only what it needs: weights are stored transposed into bit-planes, so a 4-bit inference pass reads only the top 4 planes of FP16 weights over the link. Implemented as a controller and layout change on an FPGA prototype.

physics.key_insight: An FPGA controller that remaps plane-major weights over a link is a cheap, concrete prototype of fetching precision on demand.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-08176 and I-01714. Reading 4 planes of stored FP16 moves the same link bits as a native 4-bit model but holds 4x its capacity.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-08176's trace study. No separate experiment is warranted.
physics.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024); bit-plane weight layouts in bit-serial accelerators (Stripes, Bit-Fusion).

innovation.key_insight: An FPGA controller with a plane-major layout is the right cheap demo vehicle for the bit-plane family; same core mechanism as I-01714.
innovation.killer_doubt: The top 4 planes of FP16 are the sign plus 4 exponent bits, with zero mantissa, so the pass is unusable without nested integer quantization, which is published.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Software first (~$5k): perplexity of an 8B model reading the top N planes of FP16 versus INT8 plane-major weights, before any FPGA work.
innovation.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024) bit-plane weights; Matryoshka Quantization (2025); in-study I-01714 (duplicate), I-02632 and I-11576 (DROP).

title: Reclaimed server DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Substitute new DRAM purchases with DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs pulled from decommissioned servers: a small team builds an FPGA or off-the-shelf CXL-controller card holding 8-16 used DIMMs, screens them with an on-card pattern tester, and sells them as CXL Type-3 capacity tiers.

physics.key_insight: Retired DDR4 is a real supply buffer: zero wafer starts at ~10-20% of new-bit cost. DRAM has no wear-out, so most retired dies remain good.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-06321. Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL. The CXL tier adds ~70-100 ns, and 5-7-year-old DDR4 shows HCfirst ~10k and VRT drift.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-06321's 1,000-DIMM screening and supply census.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) reuses DDR4 behind CXL; Marvell Structera and Astera Leo support DDR4 reuse.

innovation.key_insight: Retired DDR4 is wafer-free capacity. An FPGA CXL card with pattern screening turns it into a cold tier at ~10-20% of new cost per bit during a 4x spike.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipping: Marvell Structera X and Meta Vistara reuse whole DDR4 DIMMs over CXL. Open-market feedstock may be ~1-2 EB/yr against ~30+ EB/yr of new bits (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Buy 200 retired RDIMMs (~$10k) and test retention, hammer and timing margins on an FPGA rig; publish yield and tail. About $60k, but it settles only the feedstock question.
innovation.prior_art: Marvell Structera X; Meta Vistara; Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); R16 I-00224 (canonical HOLD); ITAD resellers.

title: Piggy bank: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn on CXL expander cards
idea: The 'piggy bank' of savings is the DDR4 sitting in decommissioned servers. Design a PCIe/CXL card around an off-the-shelf CXL memory controller ASIC that hosts 8 used DDR4 RDIMMs, plus a burn-in and test flow, and sell it as a capacity tier. Board design and pilot runs fit within $1M.

physics.key_insight: Retired DDR4 is a real near-term supply buffer: zero wafer starts, ~10-20% of new-bit cost, and shipping CXL controllers already accept DDR4.
physics.killer_doubt: Already deployed at hyperscale. As a capacity tier it adds ~70-100 ns over local DRAM, and 5-7-year-old DDR4 (HCfirst ~10k, VRT drift) needs controller-side mitigation.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed to prove the concept. For the supply model, burn-in 1,000 retired RDIMMs (~$50k): failure, retention-bin and HCfirst rates, plus a census of decommissioned DDR4 GB/yr.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) reuses DDR4 behind CXL. Marvell Structera and Astera Leo support DDR4 reuse (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Retired DDR4 is wafer-free capacity; a CXL tier for cold pages or KV spill monetizes it at roughly 10-20% of new-DDR5 cost per GB.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipping: Marvell Structera X reuses DDR4 and Microsoft GreenSKU did it. The pool is one-time (DDR4 is EOL), and CXL adds ~70-100 ns over local DRAM.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Size the supply: burn-in a few thousand decommissioned RDIMMs to get the fallout rate, plus a survey of retirement volume. If it is under ~1% of annual DRAM bits, it stays a niche.
innovation.prior_art: Marvell Structera X (DDR4-reuse CXL controller), Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024), Azure Pond / Meta CXL pooling studies.

title: Taking out: cold MoE experts moved to router-ahead prefetched DDR4 tier
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out the cold mass: mixture-of-experts models keep only routed-hot experts in HBM, and the rest live in commodity DDR4 behind 28 nm CXL controllers. A tiny predictor runs the next layer's router one layer early so the needed experts stream over CXL before they are used. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)

physics.key_insight: Router-ahead prefetch hides tier latency only when few experts are hot. It suits small-batch or edge MoE serving from trailing-node DDR4.
physics.killer_doubt: At batch >=64 nearly every expert fires each layer. DeepSeek-V3 needs ~350 MB per layer in ~0.5 ms (~700 GB/s); CXL x16 gives ~64 GB/s, so misses stall.
physics.decisive_experiment: Replay DeepSeek-V3 and Mixtral router traces at batch 1-256 through a CXL-DDR4 latency and bandwidth model. Measure the per-layer union of experts and the stall fraction. Software only, ~$20k.
physics.prior_art: Pre-gated MoE (ISCA 2024), MoE-Infinity, ProMoE, Fiddler, HOBBIT, MoE-Lightning; DDR4 reuse behind CXL (Microsoft GreenSKU) (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: At small batch most MoE experts are cold per token; router-ahead prefetch can hide CXL latency and move expert capacity onto depreciated DDR4.
innovation.killer_doubt: At serving batches above ~64 nearly every expert fires each step; a CXL x16 link (~64 GB/s) is ~50-100x below HBM (3-8 TB/s), so offloaded experts stall decode.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay DeepSeek-V3/Mixtral routing traces at batch 1-256: measure the fraction of experts touched per step and the CXL bytes per step against link bandwidth. Software only, under $20k.
innovation.prior_art: Pre-gated MoE (ISCA 2024), MoE-Infinity, Fiddler, KTransformers CPU-DRAM expert offload; Marvell Structera DDR4-reuse CXL controller.

title: Stranded-memory exchange: CXL fabric rents idle DRAM across racks
idea: Inverts 'memory belongs to one server': a row-scale CXL 3 memory fabric plus a spot-market scheduler leases the ~25-35% of installed DRAM that sits stranded to other servers by the minute, with prices that steer tenants.

physics.key_insight: Stranded DRAM is real: servers are provisioned for peak per socket, so pooling recovers capacity without new wafers.
physics.killer_doubt: Microsoft's Pond found ~7% DRAM saving at 16-socket pools, not 20-30%; rack-scale CXL adds ~150-300 ns, and minute-scale leasing needs live page migration.
physics.decisive_experiment: Replay public Azure/Google cluster traces through a pooling simulator for savings versus pool size and latency; largely already done by Pond.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft Pond (ASPLOS 2023); Google far memory (ASPLOS 2019); commercial CXL pooling appliances. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Stranded DRAM is wafer-free capacity. Rack-scale CXL pooling plus price signals recovers part of it, which matters more at 4x prices.
innovation.killer_doubt: Microsoft Pond measured only ~7% DRAM savings from 16-socket CXL pools, not 20-30%. The added ~70-150 ns latency also limits which tenants accept pooled memory.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay public Azure, Alibaba and Borg traces through a pooling-plus-pricing simulator. Measure GB recovered per rack at the p99 SLO, and kill if below 15%. ~$30k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft Pond (ASPLOS 2023); Memtrade marketplace for harvested idle memory (SIGMETRICS 2023); CXL pooling appliances and switches (UnifabriX, XConn, Liqid).

title: Saprotroph recycling: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Saprotrophic fungi turn dead wood into new growth. An FPGA CXL Type-3 card hosts 8-16 salvaged DDR4 RDIMMs from retired servers and takes over the aged chips' 'periphery intelligence': per-DIMM retention profiling, chipkill ECC, adaptive refresh and bad-row remap, so they serve as a slower tier. One board spin plus firmware, ~$800k in 24 months, with revenue from refurbished pools.

physics.key_insight: Retired DDR4 is zero-capex supply during a ~4x price spike. The CXL card's controller absorbs aging through retention profiling, chipkill and row remap.
physics.killer_doubt: Already deployed: Microsoft GreenSKU runs reused DDR4 behind CXL. The card and controller add ~$0.3-0.8/GB and 70-150 ns, so it suits cold-tier pages only.
physics.decisive_experiment: Buy 500 retired RDIMMs. Profile retention and VRT on an FPGA CXL card for 30 days at 85 C, then compare landed $/GB with shipping Structera-class cards. ~$200k.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X DDR4 reuse; ITRenew decommissioned-hardware resale.

innovation.key_insight: Retired DDR4 is wafer-free capacity; an FPGA CXL card with retention profiling and chipkill makes it a trusted slow tier at ~10-20% of new cost/bit during a 4x price spike.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipping: Marvell Structera X and Microsoft GreenSKU reuse DDR4 over CXL; the retired DDR4 pool is finite and shrinks as fleets move to DDR5.
innovation.decisive_experiment: As strategy only: buy 500 retired RDIMMs, profile retention and BER on an FPGA CXL card, and price the tier against new DDR5 contracts. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X DDR4-capable CXL controller; ITAD resale markets [training knowledge, consistent with other R-batch reviews].
