title: Cross-generation CXL reuse of retired DDR4 as tier-2 memory
idea: Time shift of DIMM life: a CXL controller with a DDR4 back end and strong symbol ECC lets hyperscalers move DDR4 pulled from retired servers into CXL boxes attached to new DDR5-only CPUs.

physics.key_insight: Retired DDR4 is zero-capex supply during a ~4x price spike; DRAM barely wears out, so 5-year-old DIMMs keep most of their life.
physics.killer_doubt: Already deployed at hyperscale. Behind CXL it adds ~70-150 ns, so it serves cold pages (~20-30% of footprint); retirement volume (~6-10% of bit demand) cannot cover 20-30% of new capacity.
physics.decisive_experiment: No feasibility test needed; a ~$50k census of retiring DDR4 GB against new-server cold-tier demand settles the realistic supply share.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) reuses DDR4 behind CXL; Marvell Structera X and Astera Leo CXL controllers support DDR4 (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: Retired DDR4 behind a CXL controller with symbol ECC is wafer-free capacity for DDR5-only CPUs: the plainest statement of the reuse lever.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already deployed (GreenSKU, Structera X). DDR4 prices jumped after 2025 end-of-life notices [training knowledge], so value capture, not technology, is open; ~$0.3-0.8/GB card cost per I-00224.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None separate: fold into the I-00224 pilot (1,000 retired RDIMMs retested, a commercial DDR4 CXL expander in a tier-2 cloud, landed $/GB and slowdown).
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X; Meta and Google DDR4-via-CXL reuse (prior study search snippet).

title: Cuban mechanic's almendron: keep old DDR4 alive behind CXL
idea: Havana mechanics keep 1950s cars running with improvised parts. In the same spirit, low-cost CXL Type-3 bridge cards each host 8-16 retired DDR4 RDIMMs and give new DDR5 servers a second-life capacity tier. The controller adds chipkill-class ECC and runs the DDR4 at reduced speed so it lasts longer.

physics.key_insight: Running aged DDR4 below rated speed buys timing margin, a cheap way to tolerate drifted parts behind CXL.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of deployed DDR4-behind-CXL reuse. DRAM wear-out at rated speed is negligible, so slowing it adds margin, not life. Supply ceiling ~6-10% of bit demand.
physics.decisive_experiment: No device test needed; the same ~$50k retirement-volume census as I-08711 bounds how much new DDR5 this displaces.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) reuses DDR4 behind CXL; Marvell Structera X and Astera Leo CXL controllers support DDR4 (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: Same reuse lever framed as cheap bridge cards for 8-16 RDIMMs; running old DIMMs slower cuts power and error rate, not wear.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-08711. DRAM barely wears out, so down-clocking buys little life; 16 RDIMMs draw ~65-95 W per card and need 4+ channels.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None separate: fold into the I-00224 pilot.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X; Azure, Meta and Google DDR4-via-CXL reuse (prior study search snippet).

title: One model per person: users as 1-bit deltas over shared base
idea: From the extreme of a personalized model for every user: each fine-tune is stored as a sign-only 1-bit delta mask with per-matrix scales over one resident base and applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel, so millions of personal models share a single base in HBM.

physics.key_insight: Serving many personal models from one resident base is the right shape; delta size, not base size, decides memory per user.
physics.killer_doubt: BitDelta already does exactly this; a rank-16 LoRA on a 7B model costs ~0.04-0.1 bit per base weight, 10-25x below a 1-bit delta, and S-LoRA/Punica serve thousands.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed; existing BitDelta and S-LoRA results settle it. If pursued, compare BitDelta vs LoRA-16 storage and quality for 1,000 user fine-tunes on one GPU (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: BitDelta (Liu et al., 2024): sign-only deltas with per-matrix scales and a multi-tenant kernel; S-LoRA and Punica multi-adapter serving.

innovation.key_insight: Many fine-tunes over one resident base is the right shape for serving personalized models, and it cuts per-user HBM.
innovation.killer_doubt: BitDelta (2024) published exactly this. A 1-bit delta is still 1/16 of the base (6.25%), while a rank-16 LoRA on 70B is ~0.1-0.3%, so adapters already win by ~20-60x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed. Benchmark BitDelta against S-LoRA quality per byte on 3 personalization tasks in a week of GPU time if a dossier wants the number.
innovation.prior_art: BitDelta (Liu et al., 2024) 1-bit sign deltas with fused multi-tenant kernels; S-LoRA and Punica serve thousands of adapters on one base.

title: Benetton postponement: dye per-tenant fine-tunes at compute time
idea: Benetton knits undyed sweaters and dyes them at the last moment. One base model stays resident and serves thousands of fine-tuned variants. Each variant is stored as a 1-bit sign delta plus per-row scales (or a low-rank adapter), and the 'dye' is fused into the GEMM, so no variant is ever materialized in DRAM.

physics.key_insight: Keeping only deltas resident works: a 70B FP16 base is 140 GB, and a 1-bit sign delta plus scales is ~9 GB, so N tenants cost ~1+N/16 copies.
physics.killer_doubt: BitDelta already fuses 1-bit deltas into the GEMM, and LoRA adapters are ~0.1-1% of the base. Multi-tenant fine-tune hosting is a small slice of DRAM demand.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Reproduce BitDelta or S-LoRA/Punica serving 100 variants on one 8-GPU node and measure resident memory and tokens/s (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: BitDelta (2024) fused 1-bit deltas; S-LoRA, Punica, dLoRA multi-adapter serving; DeltaZip compressed-delta serving. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: One resident base plus 1-bit sign deltas fused into the GEMM serves thousands of full fine-tunes, so memory per extra tenant falls to ~1/16 of a model copy.
innovation.killer_doubt: BitDelta and DeltaZip already do exactly this, and multi-LoRA serving handles adapters. Multi-tenant fine-tune hosting is a few % of inference memory, so the marginal gain is ~1x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. If pursued, benchmark 1-bit deltas against LoRA adapters for 100 tenants of an 8B model: HBM per tenant, tokens/s and quality loss.
innovation.prior_art: BitDelta (Liu et al. 2024); DeltaZip; S-LoRA and Punica multi-adapter serving; multi-LoRA serving in vLLM.

title: Swap fp32 vector-index embeddings for 1-bit codes plus SSD rerank
idea: Substitute full-precision vectors in DRAM with sign-bit codes. Vector databases keep only binary codes in DRAM for Hamming-distance candidate search (popcount on existing CPUs) and read the fp32 vectors of the top ~100 candidates from NVMe to rerank.

physics.key_insight: A 1024-d fp32 vector is 4 KB and its sign code is 128 B. Popcount Hamming search plus an NVMe rerank holds 32x more vectors per GB of DRAM.
physics.killer_doubt: Every major vector DB already ships this. Reranking 100 candidates of 4 KB each caps one ~1M-IOPS SSD near 10k QPS, and vector search is under 1% of DRAM demand.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Benchmark existing binary quantization with rescoring (Qdrant, Weaviate, FAISS) on BEIR or MS MARCO, recall against DRAM per vector (<$10k).
physics.prior_art: DiskANN/SPANN (PQ codes in DRAM, full vectors on SSD); Qdrant, Weaviate, Elasticsearch binary quantization with rescoring; Cohere binary embeddings. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Binary codes in DRAM plus flash rerank cut vector-index DRAM ~25-32x at ~1-point recall loss, using popcount search on commodity CPUs.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipped by every major vector DB. The marginal DRAM saving over current practice is ~1x, and vector indexes are a small share of world DRAM.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed. At most, measure DRAM per billion vectors for binary codes plus rerank against DiskANN PQ at 95% recall@10 on a public 1B-vector benchmark.
innovation.prior_art: DiskANN (Microsoft 2019: PQ codes in DRAM, full vectors on SSD); RaBitQ (SIGMOD 2024); Elasticsearch BBQ; Qdrant and Weaviate binary quantization.

title: Minify vector-DB residency to 1-bit codes plus flash rerank
idea: Minify every resident embedding to a binary sign code (32x smaller than FP32). Candidates are found by popcount Hamming search in DRAM and reranked with full-precision vectors fetched from NVMe.

physics.key_insight: Duplicate of I-00308: the same sign-code Hamming search with a flash rerank. Its value is as stated there, 32x more resident vectors per GB of DRAM.
physics.killer_doubt: Same prior art as I-00308. Embeddings not trained Matryoshka-style lose ~4-8% recall at 1 bit before rerank, which forces deeper rerank lists and more NVMe IOPS per query.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Run the same benchmark as I-00308 (<$10k).
physics.prior_art: Same as I-00308: DiskANN/SPANN, binary quantization with rescoring in Qdrant, Weaviate and Elasticsearch. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Same mechanism as I-00308 (binary sign codes in DRAM, NVMe rerank); merge there. The 32x figure versus FP32 is right, but the practice is already deployed.
innovation.killer_doubt: In-batch duplicate of I-00308, and the market already ships it. The marginal DRAM saving over current vector-DB practice is ~1x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None; fold into I-00308.
innovation.prior_art: Same as I-00308: DiskANN, RaBitQ, Elasticsearch BBQ, Qdrant and Weaviate binary quantization with rescoring.

title: Hashed compositional embeddings plus a learned head cache
idea: Combine the hashing trick (each ID composes its vector from several shared sub-tables via independent hashes) with a small table of fully learned rows for the hottest IDs; IDs are promoted to full rows as their frequency rises and demoted when they cool.

physics.key_insight: Embedding tables are Zipfian. A hot set of full rows plus hashed compositional rows for the tail compresses multi-TB tables 10-100x.
physics.killer_doubt: CAFE (SIGMOD 2024) already does hot-row promotion over a hashed tail. Ads models resist it because ~0.1% AUC loss costs more than the DRAM saved, so tables stay huge.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Reproduce CAFE or QR embeddings on Criteo-1TB or Avazu and report AUC against memory (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: QR trick (Shi, KDD 2020); hash embeddings (2017); DHE (KDD 2021); CAFE (SIGMOD 2024) hot/cold adaptive embeddings; ByteDance Monolith. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Hot IDs get full learned rows while the long tail shares hashed compositional sub-tables. This matches skewed access and cuts embedding-table DRAM 10-50x.
innovation.killer_doubt: CAFE (SIGMOD 2024) already gives hot features unique rows and hashes cold ones, with migration; QR, TT-Rec and ROBE cover the tail. The marginal gain over published work is ~1x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None for novelty. If pursued, reproduce CAFE against QR embeddings on Criteo-1TB at a fixed 0.1% AUC loss and report DRAM per model.
innovation.prior_art: QR compositional embeddings (Shi et al. 2020); CAFE (SIGMOD 2024); TT-Rec (2021); ROBE; Monolith (ByteDance) frequency-filtered hash tables.

title: Eliminate full fine-tune copies with 1-bit deltas over shared bases
idea: Store each fine-tuned variant as the sign of its weight delta plus per-row scales relative to one resident base model, served by a fused dequant-add GPU kernel; it is a software product.

physics.key_insight: The per-variant arithmetic holds: a 1-bit sign delta plus per-row scales is ~1/16 of bf16, a 16x saving per variant against a full copy.
physics.killer_doubt: The headline is ~6x wrong: 100 one-bit deltas add 6.25 base-sizes, so the total is ~7.3x the base, not 1.1x. BitDelta already ships the fused kernel.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Reproduce BitDelta serving 100 Llama-3-8B variants on one GPU node and measure resident bytes and tokens/s (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: BitDelta (2024) fused 1-bit deltas; DeltaZip compressed-delta serving; S-LoRA/Punica for adapters. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: One resident base plus 1-bit sign deltas with per-row scales, fused into the GEMM, cuts the memory of each extra full fine-tune to ~1/16 of a copy.
innovation.killer_doubt: This is BitDelta exactly, already open source. Multi-tenant full fine-tunes are a few % of inference memory, and LoRA covers most variants, so the gain over current practice is ~1x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. At most, benchmark 100 tenants of an 8B model with BitDelta against multi-LoRA: HBM per tenant, tokens/s and quality.
innovation.prior_art: BitDelta (Liu et al. 2024); DeltaZip; Delta-CoMe; S-LoRA, Punica and vLLM multi-LoRA. Same as R28 I-10409 (DROP).

title: Datacenter-wide prompt-prefix KV cache on flash servers
idea: Combine content-addressed storage with LLM prefill: KV blocks for common prefixes (system prompts, documents, tool schemas) are hashed by token sequence and stored once on NAND-heavy cache servers, and inference GPUs fetch matching prefix blocks over RDMA instead of recomputing them or pinning them in HBM.

physics.key_insight: The physics is valid: compute a shared prefix's KV once and fetch it over RDMA, and repeated prefixes stop costing prefill FLOPs and pinned HBM.
physics.killer_doubt: It already ships. Llama-70B KV is ~320 KB/token, so a 4k-token prefix is ~1.3 GB, ~26 ms at 50 GB/s RDMA. It wins only for long, popular prefixes.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Benchmark LMCache or Mooncake against recompute on a shared-prefix chat trace and measure TTFT and HBM per GPU (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: Mooncake (Kimi, FAST 2025); LMCache; CachedAttention (ATC 2024); NVIDIA Dynamo KV offload; SGLang RadixAttention. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Shared prefixes (system prompts, tool schemas, documents) make KV highly redundant across users, so a content-addressed flash tier avoids both recompute and HBM pinning.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already deployed in production by Moonshot (Mooncake), DeepSeek (disk context cache) and the LMCache and vLLM ecosystem, so the marginal gain over the state of the art is ~1x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed. If anything, quantify which share of fleet KV is prefix-shareable across tenants on a public multi-tenant trace.
innovation.prior_art: Mooncake (Kimi); LMCache; CachedAttention (USENIX ATC 2024); DeepSeek on-disk context caching (3FS); vLLM and SGLang prefix caching.

title: Erasure-coded in-memory stores replace triple replication
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: discard replicas and recover lost data from parity; in-memory caches and KV stores stripe objects RS(8,2) across servers' DRAM, with encode and decode done at line rate by a 180 nm XOR/Galois-field engine on the NIC.

physics.key_insight: RS(8,2) costs 1.25x against 3x for replication, saving ~58% of DRAM for replicated in-memory data. The GF math is cheap: ISA-L encodes at ~5-10 GB/s per core.
physics.killer_doubt: Hydra and Carbink already do erasure-coded far memory. Degraded reads fan out to 8 servers (~10-20 us tail), and replicated in-memory stores are a few percent of DRAM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed. Run Hydra's open code against 3x replication on a memcached trace and measure DRAM per object and p99 with one node failed (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: EC-Cache (OSDI 2016); Cocytus (FAST 2016); Hydra (NSDI 2022); Carbink (OSDI 2022, Google). From memory.

innovation.key_insight: For in-memory data that genuinely is replicated, RS(k,m) striping cuts redundancy from 3x to ~1.25x with line-rate NIC coding.
innovation.killer_doubt: Most in-memory caches are not replicated, since misses fall back to the database. Where they are, EC-Cache, Hydra and Carbink already ship this; world DRAM saving <2%.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. At most, survey how much fleet DRAM sits in triple-replicated in-memory stores, using public hyperscaler workload papers.
innovation.prior_art: EC-Cache (OSDI 2016); Cocytus (FAST 2016); Hydra (FAST 2022); Carbink (OSDI 2022, Google); Intel ISA-L and SmartNIC erasure-coding offload.

title: Epigenetic masks: tenant model variants as methylation over shared base
idea: Like methylation silencing genes without changing DNA, each customer fine-tune is stored as a sparse binary mask plus per-row scales over one shared base model, applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel instead of keeping a full copy.

physics.key_insight: The arithmetic holds: a 1-bit mask plus per-row scales is ~1/16 of bf16, so 1,000 full fine-tunes cost ~63 base copies instead of 1,000 (~16x).
physics.killer_doubt: BitDelta already fuses 1-bit deltas into the matmul, and LoRA adapters are 0.1-1% of the base. Multi-tenant full-fine-tune serving is well under 1% of DRAM demand.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing new is needed. Reproduce BitDelta serving 100 Llama-3-8B variants on one 8-GPU node and measure resident GB and tokens/s against S-LoRA (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: BitDelta (2024) fused 1-bit deltas; DeltaZip; ComPEFT sparse ternary residuals; S-LoRA/Punica adapter serving. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: One resident base plus 1-bit sign masks with per-row scales, fused into the matmul, cuts each extra full fine-tune to ~1/16 of a copy.
innovation.killer_doubt: This is BitDelta. A 1/16 mask (~1 GB for 8B) exceeds a rank-16 LoRA (~40 MB), and most tenants already use LoRA, so the gain over practice is ~1x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. At most, compare BitDelta with multi-LoRA serving 100 tenants of an 8B model: HBM per tenant, tokens/s and quality.
innovation.prior_art: BitDelta (Liu et al. 2024), DeltaZip, Delta-CoMe; S-LoRA, Punica, vLLM multi-LoRA. Same as R29 I-02143 (DROP) [training knowledge].

title: Hashing-trick embedding tables at 1% size
idea: Worsen: keep a dedicated row for every user and item ID in TB-scale embedding tables. Flip: hash IDs into a table 100x smaller with multiple hash functions and train with collisions, adding a tiny per-ID sign or scale to separate colliding IDs.

physics.key_insight: A per-ID sign is a cheap collision decorrelator (1 bit/ID, ~125 MB for 1e9 IDs). With multiple hashes, a 100x smaller table keeps most of the tail's information.
physics.killer_doubt: This is feature hashing, hash embeddings and QR embeddings. A per-ID fp16 scale costs 2 B against a 128 B row, capping the gain at 64x, below the claimed 100x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing new is needed. Reproduce QR and hash embeddings on Criteo-1TB at 100x compression, with and without the per-ID sign, and report NE (<$10k).
physics.prior_art: Feature hashing (Weinberger 2009); Hash Embeddings (Svenstrup 2017); QR embeddings (Shi et al. KDD 2020); ROBE (2022). From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Multi-hash collision tables with a tiny per-ID sign or scale can shrink embedding tables by large factors while still separating most colliding IDs.
innovation.killer_doubt: This is the published hashing trick plus weighted hash embeddings. Recommender teams treat ~0.1% AUC as material, and 100x collisions cost more, so production stops near 2-10x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Sweep the compression ratio (2x to 100x) for hash embeddings with per-ID weights against ROBE and QR on Criteo-1TB, and find the ratio where AUC loss reaches 0.1%. About $20k.
innovation.prior_art: Weinberger hashing trick (2009), Svenstrup hash embeddings (2017), QR trick (2020), ROBE, Google Unified Embedding [training knowledge].

title: Precision that ages: KV entries fade from FP16 to 2-bit
idea: Inverts 'a value keeps its precision for life': a background kernel demotes KV entries as they age or lose attention mass (FP16 to FP8 to INT4 to INT2), like a JPEG whose quality fades with distance, while recent and high-attention tokens stay sharp.

physics.key_insight: Making precision a function of token age and attention mass matches how attention decays, and a background requant kernel costs little.
physics.killer_doubt: Production KV is already FP8, so a 3-bit average buys ~2.7x, not 5x. 2-bit keys lose needle and reasoning accuracy at long context, and KIVI/ZipCache already do it.
physics.decisive_experiment: RULER/LongBench at 128k on Llama-3-70B: age-graded 8/4/2-bit against uniform FP8 and KIVI-2, measuring accuracy and HBM bytes. ~$20k of GPU time, mainly to confirm there is no gain over the art.
physics.prior_art: KIVI (2-bit), MiKV (mixed-precision retained KV), ZipCache (saliency-based), KVQuant, vLLM FP8 KV cache.

innovation.key_insight: Bits per KV element can track token importance over time. This is a valid principle, but crowded.
innovation.killer_doubt: The baseline already ships FP8/NVFP4 KV (~4.5 bits including scales). Going to a ~3-bit average adds only ~1.4x, not 5x, and INT2 erodes multi-hop retrieval.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None decisive at <$1M beyond published work. A KIVI/ZipCache ablation over an NVFP4 baseline would only confirm an incremental ~1.3-1.5x.
innovation.prior_art: KIVI (2-bit, FP16 recent window), SKVQ sliding window, MiKV, ZipCache saliency, KVQuant, GEAR; NVFP4 KV cache deployed on Blackwell.

title: Swap fixed-precision KV for age-graded fading precision
idea: Substitute uniform precision with human-like memory decay. KV entries are written at 8 bits; a background kernel requantizes them to 4 bits after ~1k tokens and 2 bits after ~8k, then evicts them, unless their cumulative attention mass marks them salient. This is pure software on unchanged HBM.

physics.key_insight: Duplicate of I-04883: age-graded requantization of KV (8 to 4 to 2 bit) with saliency rescue, as pure software on unchanged HBM.
physics.killer_doubt: Same as I-04883: the FP8 baseline caps the gain near 2.7x. Evicting past ~8k tokens removes the long-range recall that justified long context.
physics.decisive_experiment: Covered by I-04883's experiment.
physics.prior_art: KIVI, MiKV, ZipCache, H2O/SnapKV eviction.

innovation.key_insight: In-batch duplicate of I-04883: age-graded KV precision decay on unchanged HBM.
innovation.killer_doubt: The incremental gain over shipped 4-bit FP KV is ~1.3-1.5x. Requantizing from 8 to 4 to 2 bits accumulates error on tokens later proven salient, and they cannot be re-sharpened.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed. This is covered by existing KIVI/SKVQ/ZipCache results.
innovation.prior_art: Same as I-04883: KIVI, SKVQ, MiKV, ZipCache, PM-KVQ; NVFP4 KV in production.

title: Cascade router sends easy queries to small models first
idea: IFR: every query is answered with the smallest memory possible. Closest with no hardware: a confidence-calibrated cascade routes queries to a 3B model (6 GB) first and escalates to the 400B model only when a verifier flags uncertainty, so fewer replicas of the giant model are needed.

physics.key_insight: Routing easy queries to small models does cut giant-model replicas, and its HBM, roughly by the share of traffic that stays small.
physics.killer_doubt: Already done and shipping. Escalated queries pay both models, and verifier misroutes of ~10-20% erode the claimed 3x HBM cut.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. For the demand forecast: measure the routed share and HBM-hours on a public router benchmark (RouteLLM eval) at iso-quality.
physics.prior_art: FrugalGPT (2023), RouteLLM (2024), Hybrid LLM; production routers such as OpenAI's GPT-5 fast/thinking router.

innovation.key_insight: Routing easy queries to small models cuts giant-model replicas and their HBM roughly by the share of traffic that stays small.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipping. Escalated queries pay for both models, and 10-20% verifier misroutes erode the claimed ~3x HBM cut toward ~2x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. For sizing: measure routed share and HBM-hours on RouteLLM benchmarks at iso-quality.
innovation.prior_art: FrugalGPT (2023), RouteLLM (2024), Hybrid LLM; production routers such as OpenAI's GPT-5 fast/thinking router.

title: Swap greedy tensor allocators for ILP-planned rematerialization and packing
idea: Substitute runtime greedy allocation with a solved plan. One integer program over the training graph decides jointly which activations to keep, recompute or offload and their exact arena offsets, removing fragmentation and peak-coincident lifetimes before the run.

physics.key_insight: Jointly solving keep/recompute/offload and arena offsets removes fragmentation and peak-coincident lifetimes; a correct, useful tool for fixed training graphs.
physics.killer_doubt: Already published: Checkmate solves rematerialization as an ILP and OLLA solves lifetime plus offsets. Gain over today's planners is likely <20%, and MILP on ~1e4-op graphs takes hours.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. To size the residual gain, run Checkmate/OLLA against the PyTorch caching allocator plus selective checkpointing on five transformer configs, measuring peak memory, step time and solve time. ~$20k of GPU time.
physics.prior_art: Checkmate (MLSys 2020) ILP rematerialization; OLLA (Meta, 2022) ILP array lifetime and location; POET (ICML 2022) remat plus paging; XLA rematerialization pass.

innovation.key_insight: Static training graphs allow one offline solve over keep, recompute, offload and arena offsets, removing both fragmentation and coincident peak lifetimes that greedy caching allocators leave.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already published as ILPs. Remaining fragmentation is modest (GMLake measured ~15% average, up to 33% [training knowledge]); over selective recompute plus FSDP, expect ~1.2-1.5x, not 2-4x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Sizing only: run an OLLA/MODeL-style planner on Llama-8B and 70B torch.compile graphs versus selective checkpointing with expandable segments; report peak HBM at equal step time. ~$20k GPU.
innovation.prior_art: Checkmate (MLSys'20) ILP remat; OLLA (Meta 2022) and MODeL (ICML'23) joint lifetime/offset ILP; Moccasin (ICML'23); POET (ICML'22) remat+paging; GMLake (ASPLOS'24).

title: Snapshot-and-restore replaces warm serverless sandbox pools
idea: Reverse 'keep warm' into 'keep cold, restore fast': idle function sandboxes are snapshotted to NVMe and restored in ~5-10 ms by lazily faulting in only the pages the first invocation touches, instead of holding thousands of warm VMs in DRAM.

physics.key_insight: Idle warm sandboxes are stranded DRAM. Lazy restore of the working set from NVMe in ~5-10 ms replaces warm pools at modest tail-latency cost.
physics.killer_doubt: Production already does this: Lambda SnapStart and Firecracker snapshots. The saving depends on the idle fraction, and a 5-10 ms restore lands on p99 cold starts.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Optionally replay the Azure Functions trace with FaaSnap-style restore and report DRAM-GB-hours saved against p99 latency.
physics.prior_art: Firecracker snapshots; REAP (ASPLOS'21); FaaSnap (EuroSys'22); AWS Lambda SnapStart.

innovation.key_insight: Most warm sandboxes sit idle; restoring snapshots from NVMe by lazily faulting the first invocation's working set (~5-10 ms) turns resident DRAM into cheap flash.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipping in Firecracker-based platforms and Lambda SnapStart. Serverless and sandbox pools are likely under 5% of fleet DRAM (estimate), so the fleet-level gain is small.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None for novelty. Size it: replay the Azure Functions and an agent-sandbox trace with REAP-style restore versus keep-warm; report DRAM GB-hours saved and p99 cold start. ~$10k.
innovation.prior_art: REAP (ASPLOS'21), FaaSnap (EuroSys'22), Firecracker snapshots, AWS Lambda SnapStart, Catalyzer (ASPLOS'20) [training knowledge].

title: Carbon backbone documents: schema skeleton shared, only functional groups stored
idea: Organic molecules share a carbon backbone and differ only in functional groups; an in-memory document store (JSON/protobuf caches, Redis hashes) hash-conses each distinct key-set and type layout once as a backbone, and stores each document as a backbone ID plus a packed value vector, with a shape-lookup instruction so a field access stays one dependent load.

physics.key_insight: Hash-consing key-sets so that each document is a shape ID plus packed values removes repeated keys and type tags in JSON-heavy in-memory caches.
physics.killer_doubt: This is the hidden-class (Self maps, V8) technique applied to caches. The 2-3x holds only for small, key-heavy documents; listpack/LZ4 capture much of it. A shape-lookup instruction adds little.
physics.decisive_experiment: Load three public JSON API dumps into Redis and into a shape-shared prototype. Measure bytes per document and p99 GET latency. ~$30k.
physics.prior_art: Self maps and V8 hidden classes; JSON Tiles (SIGMOD 2021); Protobuf/FlatBuffers schema-separated encoding; Redis listpack.

innovation.key_insight: Cached documents share few distinct key-sets; storing each layout once and documents as layout ID plus packed values removes repeated keys, tags and padding.
innovation.killer_doubt: Hidden classes, key-sharing dicts and schema formats already do this; zstd with trained dictionaries compresses JSON blobs ~3-5x [training knowledge], leaving likely under 1.3x extra.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Dump a production Redis or memcached JSON cache; compare shape-sharing against zstd-dictionary and listpack on bytes per document and p99 GET latency. Stop below 1.3x over zstd-dictionary. ~$15k.
innovation.prior_art: Self maps (1989), V8 hidden classes, PyPy maps, Python PEP 412 key-sharing dicts, protobuf and Arrow schemas, Amazon Ion symbol tables [training knowledge].

title: Minify serverless memory: fork thousands from one golden snapshot
idea: Minify per-instance memory: each function runtime is pre-initialized once (imports, JIT, models loaded) and every instance forks copy-on-write from that golden snapshot in microseconds, holding only its private dirty pages (~3-8%).

physics.key_insight: Forking copy-on-write from one pre-initialized golden snapshot leaves each instance holding only its dirty pages, so many more sandboxes fit per GB.
physics.killer_doubt: Prior art ships it: Zygote, Catalyzer sfork and SnapStart. The 3-8% private-dirty figure assumes read-mostly runtimes, but JIT and GC writes re-dirty most of the heap within minutes.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Optionally measure the private-dirty fraction after 1e3 invocations for Python, Node and JVM runtimes forked from a golden snapshot.
physics.prior_art: Android Zygote; Catalyzer (ASPLOS'20) sfork; SEUSS (EuroSys'20); AWS Lambda SnapStart.

innovation.key_insight: Pre-initialised golden images let thousands of instances share read-only pages copy-on-write, each holding only its private dirty pages.
innovation.killer_doubt: Android Zygote has done this since 2008; serverless forks exist. The 10-30x holds only for tiny functions; LLM-tool agent sandboxes likely dirty 20-50% of pages (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: None for novelty. Measure private dirty-page fractions for 1,000 agent sandboxes (Python plus tool runtimes) forked from a golden snapshot over a full task, to size achievable density. ~$10k.
innovation.prior_art: Android Zygote; Catalyzer sfork (ASPLOS'20); SEUSS (EuroSys'20); Mitosis remote fork (OSDI'23); Firecracker snapshot clones; Lambda SnapStart [training knowledge].

title: Ternary weights packed five trits per byte with LUT decode
idea: Box: representation shrink × model training × weights × train time × 3^5 = 243 states in 8 bits + table decode. Models trained natively ternary store five weights per byte and decode via a 256-entry table held in registers or shared memory.

physics.key_insight: 3^5 = 243 <= 256 packs ternary at 1.6 bits per weight, 99% of the 1.585-bit entropy bound; native ternary training makes the packing lossless.
physics.killer_doubt: Already shipped: llama.cpp TQ1_0 packs five trits per byte (~1.69 bpw) and bitnet.cpp uses LUT kernels. Against today's 4-bit deployment the gain is 2.5x, not 10x.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Benchmark public ternary checkpoints (BitNet b1.58 2B4T) against 4-bit-quantized models of equal weight memory on standard evals and tokens/s. ~$10k.
physics.prior_art: BitNet b1.58 (Microsoft 2024) and 2B4T (2025); llama.cpp TQ1_0/TQ2_0 formats; bitnet.cpp TL1/TL2 lookup kernels (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: Ternary-trained models pack five trits per byte (3^5=243 states), 1.6 bpw, decoded by a 256-entry LUT on stock GPUs.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipped: llama.cpp TQ1_0 packs 5 trits per byte at ~1.69 bpw. Against today's 4-bit weights the gain is 2.5x, not 10x, and ternary quality at frontier scale is unproven.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Sizing only: compare a 7B BitNet-b1.58 model with a 4-bit GPTQ model of equal training compute on MMLU/GSM8K, and the HBM GB saved per served token. ~$150k compute.
innovation.prior_art: BitNet b1.58 (2024); llama.cpp TQ1_0/TQ2_0 ternary packing; bitnet.cpp and T-MAC LUT kernels [training knowledge].

title: Map-tile mipmaps: multi-resolution embeddings split across DRAM and flash
idea: Like web maps loading coarse tiles before fine ones, store a 4-bit coarse version of each embedding or retrieval vector in DRAM and its residual refinement levels on flash; the model uses the coarse level by default and fetches residuals only when a confidence check fails.

physics.key_insight: Coarse codes in DRAM with refinement from flash is the right hierarchy for vector indexes: 4-bit or PQ codes need 8-100x less DRAM, and flash serves only reranks.
physics.killer_doubt: This is already standard practice: DiskANN keeps ~32 B PQ codes per vector in DRAM with full vectors on SSD, and FAISS refine plus Matryoshka/residual quantization do coarse-then-fine.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Benchmark against DiskANN on BigANN-100M at equal recall@10 and QPS; continue only if DRAM falls a further >1.5x. ~$10k.
physics.prior_art: DiskANN (NeurIPS 2019), SPANN (NeurIPS 2021), FAISS IndexRefine/IVFPQ, Matryoshka representations (NeurIPS 2022), residual quantization (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: Keep coarse codes in DRAM and put residual refinements on flash, fetched only on low confidence; this keeps ANN and embedding serving mostly out of DRAM.
innovation.killer_doubt: This is DiskANN (PQ codes in DRAM, full vectors on SSD for rerank), shipping since 2019. 32-64 B codes replace ~1.5-3 KB vectors, beating the claimed ~4x (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. Sizing only: DiskANN versus a Matryoshka-style residual tier on a 1B-vector set; report DRAM GB and p99 latency at equal recall@10. ~$20k.
innovation.prior_art: DiskANN (NeurIPS'19), SPANN (NeurIPS'21), FAISS IVF-PQ with refine, Matryoshka embeddings (NeurIPS'22) [training knowledge].

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: DRAM on Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Build 12-16 tiers of oxide-TFT gain cells at F~0.5 um on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in under-used LCD/OLED fabs, which already own panel-scale litho, sputter and PECVD. One panel has ~60x the area of a 300 mm wafer, so even at coarse F it holds ~3-7 TB of capacity-tier memory behind a CXL-style controller.

physics.key_insight: Idle Gen-8.5 display fabs have ~60x a wafer's area per substrate and cheap PECVD and sputter tools. Oxide gain cells need no Czochralski silicon, crucible or EUV.
physics.killer_doubt: Gen-8.5 steppers resolve ~1.5-2 um, not 0.5 um. At F=1.5 um a 16-tier panel holds ~0.3-0.5 TB at ~$10-20/GB, and ppm glass compaction breaks the tier overlay.
physics.decisive_experiment: On a Gen-6 high-resolution line, build a 4-tier IGZO 2T gain-cell test panel at the tightest available rule. Measure tier-to-tier overlay, per-tier D0 and retention maps. ~$800k.
physics.prior_art: ram-venture A1-03 (display-glass IGZO memory, killed on density). Phase B N-38 (Gen 3.5 panel, 64-128 tiers, imprint at 100 nm) is the better version.

innovation.key_insight: A Gen-8.5 panel has the area of ~78 wafers on depreciated tools. Multi-tier oxide gain cells need no Czochralski silicon, quartz crucible, HAR etch or EUV.
innovation.killer_doubt: The economics need F~0.5 um. FPD steppers resolve ~1.2-1.5 um, which gives ~$13/GB (R17), worse than DDR5's $1.48/GB cost, and 16-tier panel CMP is unproven.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Pair with I-07130: on Gen-2 glass, pattern a 4-tier IGZO 2T0C array at ~0.5 um with IL for the array layers. Measure tier yield per cm2, Vt sigma and 85 C retention. ~$500k.
innovation.prior_art: Same core as R17 I-10785 (ADVANCE, merge into it); R01 I-04673; SEL CAAC-IGZO DOSRAM; PragmatIC FlexIC; Phase B N-36, N-38.

title: Eliminate test hardware: bootable signed DIMM health certificate
idea: Eliminate expensive ATE for used-memory trust: a free bootable image runs 8-hour retention, pattern and row-hammer tests on any host and signs the result with the module's SPD serial; ~$600k builds the software, signing service and three pilot broker integrations in 18 months.

physics.key_insight: Zero-hardware delivery runs at native platform speed, so speed-bin and pattern tests are real; it is the software half of I-08260.
physics.killer_doubt: Most stock hosts cannot stretch or disable refresh, so the 8-hour 'retention' test only checks the 64 ms spec; the SPD serial is rewritable, so the signature is forgeable.
physics.decisive_experiment: Not worth separate funding; fold into I-08260. Quick check: on 100 modules, compare MemTest86 Pro results at stock vs BIOS tREFI raised 4x to see whether retention outliers appear.
physics.prior_art: MemTest86 Pro per-module reports with SPD data; ITAD certification practice (R2v3, e-Stewards, Blancco). Adding a signature contributes little.

innovation.key_insight: A free bootable test image removes the ATE cost for used-DIMM grading; a useful on-ramp to the signed-tester scheme in I-08260.
innovation.killer_doubt: The seller controls the host, so a signature from host software attests nothing. SPD serials can be cloned. This is a weaker duplicate of I-08260.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Red-team it: give 5 testers the image and ask them to forge a passing certificate for a failing DIMM by editing SPD or using a VM ($50k). If anyone succeeds, merge into I-08260's hardware-rooted version.
innovation.prior_art: MemTest86 Pro reports; TPM remote attestation; ITAD recertification; in-batch duplicate I-08260.

title: Light-pumped self-restoring cell: photodiode gated by its own charge
idea: Box: cap x Si access nMOS x SA x backside-illuminated die under a uniform LED/laser sheet x thinned Si x BSI image-sensor process. Each cell adds a photodiode in series with a tiny transistor gated by the storage node, so a global light flash tops up only nodes that are already high, refreshing the whole array in parallel without any row activation.

physics.key_insight: A node-gated top-up path refreshes all cells in parallel with zero row activations, which removes refresh bandwidth loss and refresh-induced hammer.
physics.killer_doubt: Bulk photocarriers reach every junction: at 1 W/cm2 a 0-node collects ~0.1-1 pA versus a 13 fA budget; PD plus gating FET doubles the 6F2 cell.
physics.decisive_experiment: Simulate first, then a 180 nm BSI test chip (~$250k): 1T1C plus PD plus gating-FET cells under pulsed LED, measuring 0-node upset rate and 1-node restore at 85 C. Benchmark it against an electrical refresh-rail pulse.
physics.prior_art: Self-restoring 3T/4T dynamic cells with a global refresh rail do this electrically; BSI image-sensor pixels; no optical-refresh DRAM found.

innovation.key_insight: A photodiode gated by the storage node is a light-powered keeper: one global flash tops up only 1-nodes, refreshing every cell with zero activations and no refresh hammer.
innovation.killer_doubt: The cell becomes 2T1C plus a photodiode (>=2x area) to recover 10-20% of bandwidth. At 1-10 mW/cm2 a 0.003 um2 cell gets only ~14-140 fA; stray carriers discharge 1-nodes.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On a 65 nm BSI image-sensor MPW, build 1k self-gated photodiode keeper cells. Under illumination, measure the 0-node upset rate and 1-node hold against flux at 85 C. About $250k.
innovation.prior_art: None found for optical refresh. The inverse, DRAM as image sensor (Micron OpticRAM, 1980s), is old; electrical self-restoring 3T/4T loadless cells need no optics.

title: Cobalt kobold miners: tiny SRAM index picks which KV pages to fetch
idea: Cobalt is named for the kobold that hunted ore; each 16-token KV page gets a 64-byte summary (per-channel key min/max) in SRAM, decode computes upper-bound attention scores from the summaries and fetches only the top 3-5% of pages from DRAM, while the rest of the KV lives in CXL memory or NAND.

physics.key_insight: Per-page key min/max gives a cheap upper bound on attention, so most KV pages need not be read each step; this suits CXL-attached DRAM tiers.
physics.killer_doubt: Quest already does exactly this. On NAND, 5% of a 32k 70B context is ~0.5 GB per token per sequence; batch 64 at 30 tok/s needs ~1 TB/s (~70 SSDs).
physics.decisive_experiment: Run Quest with a CXL/NVMe page store at batch 64 and 32k context; measure step-to-step reuse of selected pages in HBM and the residual tier bandwidth.
physics.prior_art: Quest (ICML'24, per-page min/max key bounds), ArkVale (NeurIPS'24 page digests with recall), ShadowKV, InfiniGen.

innovation.key_insight: Bounding attention scores from page summaries cuts KV traffic about 10-30x, but that mechanism is Quest, published almost verbatim.
innovation.killer_doubt: Exact prior art. Also, with the tail on NAND, ~80 us reads times 80 layer-serial lookups add ~6 ms per token, about 25% of a decode step.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. To keep a sliver of value, measure Quest+ArkVale with a NAND-resident tail on a single GPU to quantify the latency penalty. About $20k.
innovation.prior_art: Quest (ICML 2024) keeps per-page min/max key bounds; ArkVale, ShadowKV, InfiniGen, MagicPIG, RetroInfer offload the tail to CPU/SSD.

title: Geiger-mode avalanche read of a hundred-electron storage node
idea: Shrink the storage node to ~20 aF holding ~100 electrons and wire it as the bias of a SPAD-like junction. At read the junction is armed above breakdown for ~2 ns: a stored '1' tips it into avalanche (gain ~1e5) and a '0' does not, then an active quench resets it.

physics.key_insight: With stored electrons as avalanche seeds (trigger p~0.5), 40 electrons give 1e-12 miss probability: the physical floor is ~100 e- per bit, ~170x below today's 17,700.
physics.killer_doubt: CMOS SPADs need guard rings at ~1-2 um pitch, ~900x a 1b cell; sharing one per bitline re-dilutes 100 e- to 0.46 mV on 35 fF; ~1% afterpulsing.
physics.decisive_experiment: SPAD/CIS MPW (~$200k): 20 aF pinned storage wells transferring into shared SPADs; measure miss and false-fire rates vs electrons stored, dark counts and afterpulsing at 85 C.
physics.prior_art: SPAD and quanta image sensors count single electrons; Phase B N-04 charge-transfer sensing reaches ~0.5 fF without avalanche. SPAD-read memory: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Injecting even ~40 stored electrons into a Geiger-mode junction triggers avalanche almost surely. Gain makes a few-electron bit readable. The value is as an EMCCD-style output stage for CCD strings.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 100-electron node may lose ~60 e per 64 ms, so leakage must be <=0.15 fA, ~90x below the Si tail. SPADs are µm-scale; bitline pitch is 30-40 nm.
innovation.decisive_experiment: TCAD plus a 65 nm SPAD test structure (~$200k) fed metered 10-100 e packets. Measure trigger probability versus dark counts in a 2 ns gate, and the minimum pitch.
innovation.prior_art: Impact-ionisation floating-body Z-RAM (Innovative Silicon); EMCCD gain registers; Fossum quanta-image-sensor jots read single electrons without avalanche [training knowledge]; study's N-04/N-84.

title: Optane's crosspoint kept, PCM swapped for selector-gated capacitor
idea: Optane died largely on cost and PCM endurance, but its stacked crosspoint and OTS selector worked. Place a tiny MIM capacitor in series with the OTS at each crosspoint: the selector's threshold snap acts as a transistor-free access device, turning the array into a refreshed 4F2 multi-deck DRAM.

physics.key_insight: Crosspoint decks remove the lateral access transistor, the main 3D DRAM blocker, and idle chalcogenide PVD tooling exists.
physics.killer_doubt: OTS sub-threshold leakage is ~1e-11 to 1e-9 A at ~0.5 V; on 5 fF at 0.5 V, tau = CV/I ~2.5 us-0.25 ms. Needs ~8 fA: a 1e3-1e5x miracle.
physics.decisive_experiment: Build 1S1C test cells (OTS in series with a 5 fF MIM, ~$100k); measure node decay at 25 and 85 C under V/2 biasing; kill if retention is under 1 ms.
physics.prior_art: Intel/Micron 3D XPoint OTS selectors; Phase B N-85 and N-87 1S1C selector-DRAM; review I-08787 dropped an OTS 1S1C cell.

innovation.key_insight: The 3D XPoint deck architecture plus a capacitor could give a transistor-less stacked 4F2 DRAM on idle chalcogenide tools. The selector, not the deck, is the problem.
innovation.killer_doubt: Hold leakage must be <=3-16 fA (1-5 fF, 0.2 V, 64 ms); an OTS at ~V/2 leaks pA-nA, a 1e3-1e5x gap. OTS endurance (~1e9-1e11) misses 1e13+ hot-row writes.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A ~$60k test: measure the I-V floor of 100 OTS devices (20-40 nm) at 0.2-0.6 V and 85 C with an electrometer, then cycle to 1e11 with a 1 fF series capacitor. Kill if leakage >1 pA.
innovation.prior_art: Intel/Micron 3D XPoint OTS; SK hynix/Micron selector-only memory; triage N-85 crested-barrier 1S1C (the better selector route) [training knowledge].

title: Minify reliability to 1e-3 BER: junk-tolerant stacked memory
idea: Sell memory for noise-tolerant AI tensors at a raw 1e-3 bit error rate: skip sort, burn-in, repair and final test, let each die self-map defects via boot-time BIST, and absorb errors with stochastic rounding and error-resilient training.

physics.key_insight: Error tolerance can be traded for tier yield, but only by bit significance: protect sign and exponent, relax mantissa bits (Phase B N-65).
physics.killer_doubt: At raw 1e-3, a 70B BF16 model takes ~7e7 exponent-MSB flips (a ~0.01 weight becomes ~1e36). Tier yield is set by line shorts killing whole mats, beyond any BER tolerance.
physics.decisive_experiment: Software fault injection (~$50k): inject 1e-5 to 1e-3 random flips into LLM weights and KV, with and without exponent protection; measure accuracy; model block yield versus line-short density per tier.
physics.prior_art: Flikker (ASPLOS 2011); EDEN approximate DRAM for DNNs (MICRO 2019); Phase B N-62 (ECC-paid capacitor) and N-65 (significance-split).

innovation.key_insight: An 'AI-grade' bit: protect sign and exponent, tolerate mantissa errors and map defects at boot, so tall low-yield thin-film stacks ship instead of being scrapped. Re-scope: no 100x claim.
innovation.killer_doubt: 3D-stack defects are clustered (tier shorts, dead lines), not iid, and one shorted tier kills a block. An unprotected exponent-MSB flip turns 1.0 into ~1e38.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Inject clustered fault maps at 1e-3 raw BER into Llama-class inference with exponent-only ECC. Use maps from a 3D oxide test stack or published DRAM error logs. Report perplexity and recovered compound yield. ~$80k.
innovation.prior_art: EDEN approximate DRAM for DNNs (Koppula et al., MICRO 2019); Flikker (2011) [training knowledge]; study N-65 significance split, N-34 defect budget, N-55 spare tiers.

title: Utility meters, not itemized bills: fixed-size recurrent state in SRAM
idea: Borrowed from utility meters that keep a running total instead of every transaction: most attention layers are replaced by fixed-size recurrent/state-space states (a few MB per sequence) held in SRAM, plus a few exact-attention layers over a short local window.

physics.key_insight: Hybrid SSM/attention stacks cap per-sequence state; Jamba-style 1:7 mixing cuts long-context KV ~8x. A real demand-side trend to put in the forecast, not an invention.
physics.killer_doubt: State is not 'a few MB': Mamba-2 2.7B holds ~84 MB/sequence (FP16); a batch of 256 is ~21 GB, so it stays in HBM, not ~50 MB of on-die SRAM.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. For the forecast: tabulate KV+state bytes/token and batch-resident GB for Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next against GQA baselines at 32k-1M context.
physics.prior_art: Jamba (AI21), Samba (Microsoft), Nemotron-H (NVIDIA), Qwen3-Next, MiniMax-01 lightning attention: all shipping hybrids.

innovation.key_insight: Constant-size recurrent state does remove the growing KV term. Frontier labs already ship such hybrids, so a $1M team adds nothing.
innovation.killer_doubt: Not SRAM-sized. Mamba-2 state is ~2 MB per layer (8192x128 at FP16), ~100 MB per sequence. Batch 256 needs ~25 GB, far beyond ~50 MB of L2.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None in scope. Training a competitive hybrid needs well over $1M of compute. Distilling a small model only replicates published Jamba/Samba results.
innovation.prior_art: Jamba, Samba, Zamba, NVIDIA Nemotron-H, Qwen3-Next (Gated DeltaNet), MiniMax lightning attention, Kimi Linear.

title: Lossy NUMA node standard: OS pages tagged by error tolerance
idea: Push a JEDEC/CXL descriptor that publishes each region's raw-BER-vs-refresh curve, plus a Linux 'lossy NUMA node' reached with mmap(MAP_LOSSY). KV caches, media buffers and caches go to 1%-BER regions refreshed rarely; kernel and databases stay on fully protected memory.

physics.key_insight: A standard interface for error-tolerant memory would let ECC-paid or approximate cells (N-62, N-66) ship across vendors and be procured.
physics.killer_doubt: Uniform 1% BER flips BF16 exponent bits catastrophically, so protected bits must be split out; gain is refresh power and bandwidth (~10-20%), not new bits.
physics.decisive_experiment: Linux MAP_LOSSY patch on an FPGA DRAM tester running an LLM KV cache at relaxed refresh; measure accuracy versus raw BER and refresh savings. <$100k.
physics.prior_art: Flikker (MSR, ASPLOS 2011) critical-data refresh partitioning; EDEN (MICRO 2019) approximate-DRAM DNN inference; RAIDR retention-aware refresh.

innovation.key_insight: Its value is as the OS/CXL interface that lets ECC-paid capacitors and approximate multi-level cells (N-62, N-66) deploy across vendors, not as a standalone gain.
innovation.killer_doubt: One BF16 exponent-bit flip scales a value up to 2^128. At 1% BER a 1 GB KV cache has ~8e7 flips; only low mantissa planes (~30-40% of bits) qualify.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Run LLM inference with bit-plane error injection at 1e-6 to 1e-2 BER to find the tolerable byte fraction, then prototype MAP_LOSSY on an FPGA refresh-control platform. Under $150k.
innovation.prior_art: Flikker (ASPLOS 2011) critical/non-critical refresh partitioning; EnerJ approximate types; approximate-DRAM literature; CXL memory tiering.

title: Thousand tiny tapeouts: crowdsourced access-device leakage variants on open PDKs
idea: 10-person constraint: crowdsource the search a small team cannot fund. Publish an open eDRAM access-device test-cell template for open-PDK shuttles (SKY130, GF180, IHP SG13G2). Pay bounties to hobbyists and students whose variants (gate shapes, well-bias tricks, guard rings, stacked devices) beat the baseline in silicon-measured retention, ranked by an automated FPGA tester.

physics.key_insight: Crowdsourced open-PDK shuttles make hundreds of parallel leakage experiments cheap (~$100s per tile); useful for gain-cell circuit IP and recruiting.
physics.killer_doubt: DRAM tails are GIDL/GIJL in 12 nm buried-wordline BCATs, or <1 aA IGZO; 130-180 nm logic FETs leak by subthreshold/junction paths, so results do not transfer.
physics.decisive_experiment: None worth funding for the DRAM tail; at most one ~$10k Tiny Tapeout gain-cell retention tester to validate the bounty pipeline itself.
physics.prior_art: Tiny Tapeout and open-PDK MPW shuttles (SKY130, GF180, IHP); academic gain-cell eDRAM on open PDKs.

innovation.key_insight: Open-PDK shuttles make parallel circuit-level cell experiments almost free. That is better used as a vehicle for testing other ideas' circuits (e.g. I-04691) than for leakage search.
innovation.killer_doubt: The DRAM access-device tail (<=13 fA) comes from buried-wordline GIDL and trap-assisted tunnelling at ~1e19 cm-3 junctions. 130-180 nm open-PDK FETs share none of that structure.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On one SKY130/IHP shuttle, measure 50 access-device variants with an FPGA tester, then check whether the rankings correlate with TCAD of a buried-wordline DRAM transistor. About $30k.
innovation.prior_art: Tiny Tapeout community shuttles; OpenRAM open eDRAM/SRAM generators; university eDRAM retention studies on mature nodes.

title: Magnify contributors: open-source 3D DRAM compiler and PDK
idea: Fund three engineers to release an open-source array generator for SKY130 and GF180, plus a parametric 3D DRAM tier model (tier count, Cs, leakage tail, spares) and a cost and yield calculator, so universities can tape out DRAM arrays on open shuttles.

physics.key_insight: Open array generators and a tier/yield calculator lower the entry cost for university array research. They are useful infrastructure for this study's own models.
physics.killer_doubt: SKY130/GF180 have no DRAM capacitor. A ~2-5 um2 MIM or gain cell is ~1,000x a 1b cell, so tape-outs teach nothing about the 13 fA tail or capacitors.
physics.decisive_experiment: Not needed. If pursued, fund OpenGCRAM extensions plus a public parametric 3D-tier cost model (~$150k) and count external tape-outs after 12 months.
physics.prior_art: OpenRAM (UCSC), OpenGCRAM, DRAM Bender, Ramulator, CACTI-3DD/DESTINY; similar I-05632 dropped and I-04102 held by other critics.

innovation.key_insight: The project needs a parametric 3D-tier cost and yield model internally anyway. Publishing it with a gain-cell eDRAM generator would cheaply seed university array design and U.S. talent.
innovation.killer_doubt: SKY130/GF180 have no DRAM capacitor. A 130 nm gain cell is ~1.5-3 um2, ~2,000x a 1b 6F2 bit (~0.0009 um2), so it trains circuit designers, not cell physics.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Release the tier cost/yield model and a gain-cell macro generator, then count outside tape-outs and citing groups within 12 months (~$150k). Proceed only if at least five outside groups tape out.
innovation.prior_art: OpenRAM SRAM compiler (UCSC/OSU); SKY130 and GF180 open PDKs; academic gain-cell eDRAM macros; R23's open sense-amp IP idea I-05632 was dropped (training knowledge).

title: Open-source DRAM-cell library on US foundry PDKs
idea: Worsen: keep storage-cell know-how locked inside three companies. Flip: spend $1M over 24 months designing, taping out and publishing open-source eDRAM and gain cells (thick-oxide 3T, MIM 1T1C) on SkyWater 130 and 22FDX PDKs with measured retention data, so any US chip team can add dense memory.

physics.key_insight: Measured, open retention data on U.S. PDKs lowers entry cost for gain-cell IP and trains a domestic memory workforce; a useful by-product of any MPW dossier.
physics.killer_doubt: A 130 nm 3T or MIM 1T1C cell is ~1-3 um2/bit, ~500-1,000x a 1b cell (0.0023 um2), with ~ms retention at 85 C. 22FDX is not an open PDK.
physics.decisive_experiment: One Sky130/GF180 shuttle (~$20-50k): 64 kb 3T and MIM 1T1C macros with retention BIST; compare bits/mm2 and 85 C retention against OpenGCRAM and RAAAM published figures.
physics.prior_art: OpenRAM (UCSC), OpenGCRAM open gain-cell compiler, RAAAM GCRAM IP; review I-11121 already dropped the same open-PDK test-chip idea.

innovation.key_insight: An open gain-cell/eDRAM library with measured retention lowers the entry cost for U.S. teams. It is useful test infrastructure for the gain-cell ideas, not a bit-supply lever.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 130 nm cell is ~1-3 um2, >1,000x the 864 nm2 1b cell. The 22FDX PDK is NDA-bound, so it cannot be published. OpenGCRAM already exists.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Not worth funding standalone. If wanted, put a 64 kb SKY130/GF180 gain-cell macro with on-die retention BIST on a free or ~$10k open shuttle and contribute the data to OpenGCRAM.
innovation.prior_art: OpenGCRAM (Stanford/Wong group, arXiv 2507.10849, 2025, built on OpenRAM) (via search snippet); OpenRAM (UCSC/OSU); open SKY130/GF180 shuttles.

title: Short-retention cells matched to ephemeral AI tensors
idea: Combine compiler-known tensor lifetimes with deliberately cheap short-retention cells: activations, KV-cache pages and gradients that are overwritten within 50 ms go to a pool whose cells retain only ~100 ms worst case and are never refreshed. A runtime time-to-live tag per page rewrites or evicts data before expiry, so refresh disappears and the capacitor can be ~3x smaller.

physics.key_insight: Compiler-known lifetimes can drop refresh for genuinely short-lived buffers, and a hardware TTL fault makes the expiry contract checkable.
physics.killer_doubt: KV caches live seconds to minutes, training activations ~0.1-10 s per step; rewriting before expiry is refresh. A 3x smaller Cs needs ~3x lower leakage to keep 100 ms.
physics.decisive_experiment: Instrument vLLM serving and one training run to histogram DRAM page lifetimes; kill if <20% of bytes die within 50 ms. Then disable refresh on an FPGA DDR4 rig. ~$30k.
physics.prior_art: RANA (ISCA 2018) retention-aware eDRAM for DNNs; Flikker; RAIDR; Phase B N-64 lifetime-leased refresh; review I-04810 dropped the same idea.

innovation.key_insight: A compiler TTL tag per page is the right software contract for a retention-class tier. It is folded into I-01854, which pairs it with a cell change.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 100 ms worst case is today's 64 ms cell, so no capacitor saving follows. KV pages live seconds, not 50 ms. RANA, ZEM and N-64 already skip refresh.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Covered by I-01854's trace study. Standalone, disable refresh on one DDR5 FPGA channel and run LLM decode with TTL eviction. Measure bit errors against the refresh-on baseline (~$50k).
innovation.prior_art: RANA (Tsinghua, ISCA 2018); ZEM (IEEE Access 2021); CAMEL eDRAM co-design (2023) (via search snippet); Flikker (ASPLOS 2011); triage N-64.

title: Twin synchronized predictors send only the surprise
idea: Information theory says only unpredicted bits must cross a channel. Run identical stride/context/value predictors on both sides of the memory link; the sender transmits a 1-bit hit flag when the receiver's prediction is right and an XOR residual otherwise, and both update identically so they stay in lockstep.

physics.key_insight: Synchronized twin predictors with 1-bit hit flags are a clean lossless link code for pointer-, stride- and zero-rich traffic at a CXL controller or HBM base die.
physics.killer_doubt: bf16 and fp8 weights and activations are nearly incompressible (entropy ~0.8-0.95 of raw), and measured link compression is 1.2-2x on general code. A CRC replay desynchronizes both predictors.
physics.decisive_experiment: Capture memory-link traces from SPEC, graph and LLM workloads. Simulate stride, context and value twin predictors, and report bits per 64 B line and added latency. Software, ~$20k.
physics.prior_art: T0 bus encoding (Benini 1997); Thuresson-Stenstrom value-locality memory-link compression (IEEE TC 2008); frequent-value encoding; GPU lossless bandwidth compression (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Lockstep predictors at both ends of a link send only residuals, so zero-, pointer- and stride-heavy CPU traffic compresses with no metadata.
innovation.killer_doubt: AI tensors dominate memory bytes and are nearly incompressible (FP8 weights ~1.1-1.3x). Published value-locality link compression gets ~1.3-2x, not 2-5x, and DRAM dies have no predictor logic.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay memory-link traces (SPEC, graph, LLM decode) through stride, context and FCM predictors in software, and measure bits per transferred line. If AI traffic compresses under 1.3x, stop. Under $20k.
innovation.prior_art: Thuresson et al., value-locality memory-link compression (IEEE TC 2008); frequent-value bus encoding; toggle-aware compression (HPCA 2016).

title: Twenty-millivolt bitline-style die-to-die links bounded by kT/C
idea: The true floor on signal swing is thermal noise sqrt(kT/C), ~0.2 mV rms on a 100 fF bonded link, so 20 mV still gives >10 sigma margin. Replace 0.4 V HBM drivers with charge-dump transmitters and cross-coupled latch receivers clocked like a DRAM sense amp (precharge, share, regenerate), with per-lane offset trim stored at boot.

physics.key_insight: The kT/C arithmetic holds (~0.2 mV rms on 100 fF), but it is not the floor. Offset and coupled noise are, and trimmed clocked latches can work at ~20-50 mV.
physics.killer_doubt: PHY plus interposer is only ~0.5-1 of HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit; UCIe-A already reaches ~0.25-0.5 and hybrid bonds ~0.05, so stack gain <=20%. ~10-30 mV switching noise eats margin.
physics.decisive_experiment: Tape out a 28 nm MPW test chip with a 64-lane, 5 mm interposer-class link: charge-dump TX and trimmed StrongARM RX at 20, 50 and 100 mV. Measure BER against aggressor crosstalk, and fJ/bit. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: Ho/Horowitz capacitively driven low-swing wires (JSSC 2008); NVIDIA ground-referenced signaling (~0.54 pJ/bit); UCIe-A and BoW D2D PHYs (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Bonded links are kT/C-limited at ~0.2 mV rms on 100 fF, so sense-amp-style precharge, share and regenerate signalling could run at 20 mV swing.
innovation.killer_doubt: I/O swing is ~15-25% of HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit; activation and datapaths dominate. NVIDIA GRS already reached 0.54 pJ/b; full-swing CV2 on a 50 fF bond is ~0.03 pJ.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A 28 nm MPW: 64 lanes over a 2 mm interposer-like line, with a 20 mV charge-dump TX and a trimmed StrongARM RX. Measure BER at 4-8 Gb/s, crosstalk, supply-noise margin and fJ/bit. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Ho/Horowitz low-swing on-chip wires; NVIDIA ground-referenced signalling (0.54 pJ/b, 2013); capacitively coupled low-swing links; StrongARM latch receivers.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling shares the fab forming-gas recycle loop
idea: Combine the chuck's backside-cooling gas with the fab's existing H2 supply: run 5-15 Torr H2 (thermal conductivity ~0.18 W/m-K vs He ~0.15) under wafers in etch/CVD, recapture it through a palladium-membrane purifier and return it to the forming-gas anneal header.

physics.key_insight: Same core as I-10762: H2 out-conducts He (0.18 versus 0.15 W/m-K) and can be made on site. The recycle loop into the forming-gas header is the only addition.
physics.killer_doubt: The recycle loop is pointless and fragile: ~20 sccm per chuck is ~2.6 g H2/day (cents), cheaper than a Pd purifier, and HBr/halogen traces from chambers poison Pd membranes.
physics.decisive_experiment: Folded into the I-10762 single-chamber trial; a separate test of the recycle loop is not warranted.
physics.prior_art: ESC patents list hydrogen among backside cooling gases (via search snippet); Pd-membrane H2 purifiers are commercial. Duplicate of in-batch I-10762.

innovation.key_insight: Same core mechanism as I-10762 (H2 backside gas instead of helium); adds a Pd-membrane return of used H2 to the forming-gas header.
innovation.killer_doubt: Returning chamber-exposed H2 to gate forming-gas anneals risks F/Cl contamination to save a gas costing ~$2-5/kg; the recycle adds risk without value. Merged into I-10762.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Covered by the I-10762 experiment; add an RGA impurity check of backside-return H2 only if recycling is still wanted. ~$20k increment.
innovation.prior_art: None found for H2 backside gas (one search): chuck patents list He, N2 or Ar (via search snippet). Pd purifiers are commercial.

title: Ephemeral memory: data dies before charge does, so never refresh
idea: Inverts 'stored data must outlive cell retention': a refresh-less DRAM tier holds only AI activations, gradients, KV blocks and packet buffers whose lifetime the compiler/runtime proves is below a guaranteed 10-50 ms retention, with hardware write-timestamps that fault any read past the deadline.

physics.key_insight: A write is a refresh: data provably dead or rewritten within the retention window needs none, and a write-timestamp turns that proof into a checkable fault, not silent corruption.
physics.killer_doubt: The large footprints outlive 30 ms: KV blocks last seconds to minutes and training activations ~0.1-10 s. Refresh is only ~4-8% of active power, and row hammer still needs PRAC.
physics.decisive_experiment: Instrument vLLM serving and a Megatron training run to log byte-weighted data lifetimes. Kill if under 10% of resident bytes die within 30 ms. ~$20k of GPU time.
physics.prior_art: RANA refresh-optimized eDRAM DNN accelerator (ISCA 2018); Smart Refresh (MICRO 2007); ESKIMO semantic refresh (MICRO 2009); GPU eDRAM register files. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: An activation already restores a row; data whose proven lifetime is under worst-case retention never needs refresh, and a hardware deadline fault makes this safe.
innovation.killer_doubt: AI data lives too long: KV caches persist seconds to minutes and training activations ~0.1-10 s per step, against the 10-50 ms window; short-lived data already sits in SRAM.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Trace allocation-to-last-read lifetimes in LLM serving and training HBM, and measure the share of bytes and refresh energy under 32 ms; DRAM-Bender tail retention at 85 C. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: RANA (ISCA 2018) refresh-optimized eDRAM using data lifetime in DNN accelerators; Smart Refresh (2007); RAIDR (2012); Phase B N-64 lifetime-leased refresh.

title: Nested-precision bit-plane memory + self-speculative decoding
idea: INT8/FP8 weights are quantised in a nested (Matryoshka-style) way, so the top 2 or 4 bit planes are themselves a usable low-precision model. The memory controller stores the planes in separate address ranges and streams 'planes 0-1', 'planes 0-3' or all of them, in 512 B-2 KB chunks that match DRAM bursts and pages. Decode is self-speculative: draft k tokens with the top planes only (25-50% of the weight bytes), then verify all k in one batched pass with every plane. No second model is stored.

physics.key_insight: A nested bit-plane layout lets one stored copy also serve as a self-speculative draft, with no second model. A useful serving trick, but not a memory-supply lever.
physics.killer_doubt: A 4-plane draft (50% of bytes) with k=4 and acceptance 0.85 needs ~0.81 weight bytes per token, ~1.2x. Two-plane drafts accept poorly, and batching already amortizes weight reads.
physics.decisive_experiment: Software only: on a Matryoshka-quantized 8B model, measure the acceptance of 2- and 4-plane drafts in vLLM at batch 1-64. Go if >=1.5x tokens/s at batch 16.
physics.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024); Matryoshka Quantization (2025); QSpec quantized self-speculation (2024); R28 dropped the same idea as I-05807. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: With plane-major weight storage, one model serves its own 2-4-bit draft from the same bytes, so speculative decoding needs no second model and no extra capacity.
innovation.killer_doubt: Gain is capped at 1.1-1.8x. Each draft token still reads 25-50% of the weight bytes, and SpecMQuant found that verification compute cancels 4-bit memory savings. A niche software gain.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On one GPU, quantize Llama-3-8B/70B with MatGPTQ and store the weights plane-major. Measure acceptance rate and bytes per accepted token for 2- and 4-plane drafts against EAGLE-style drafters. ~$30k.
innovation.prior_art: Matryoshka Quantization (ICML 2025), MatGPTQ, SpecMQuant (via search snippet); Any-Precision LLM bit-plane serving; QSpec/QuantSpec quantized self-speculation [training knowledge].

title: Battery cell matching: retention-matched rank assembly
idea: Adapted from EV battery packs, which group cells of matched capacity so one weak cell does not limit the pack: dies are binned by measured retention (e.g., 64/128/256 ms classes) on existing testers, modules are assembled only from same-class dies, and the class is written to SPD so the controller sets tREFI per rank instead of for the worst die in a mixed rank.

physics.key_insight: Rank refresh is set by the weakest die. Matching dies by measured retention lets the controller set tREFI per rank.
physics.killer_doubt: VRT cells hop retention states after test, so one-time profiling misses them and 2-4x longer tREFI needs ECC anyway. Temperature-scaled refresh already harvests most margin below 85 C.
physics.decisive_experiment: Profile 200 DDR5 dies at 64/128/256 ms and 45/85 C each month for 6 months on DRAM Bender. Count new failures per bin after binning. <$300k.
physics.prior_art: RAIDR (ISCA 2012); Liu et al. ISCA 2013 retention/VRT study; REAPER (ISCA 2017); AVATAR; DDR5 temperature-based refresh scaling.

innovation.key_insight: Rank refresh is set by its worst die; matching dies by retention class lets most ranks run 2-4x longer tREFI with assembly-flow changes only.
innovation.killer_doubt: Variable retention time: cells jump retention states by >10x over time (Liu, ISCA 2013), so static die binning at 256 ms is unsafe without online profiling or ECC.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Bin 200 DDR5 dies by retention at 85 C, then re-test monthly for 6 months on an FPGA tester; count class downgrades caused by VRT. ~$120k.
innovation.prior_art: RAIDR (2012), AVATAR (2015), REAPER (2017) retention-aware refresh with profiling/ECC; Liu ISCA 2013 VRT study; vendor power/speed binning.

title: Magnify sharing: rack-wide content-addressed memory deduplication
idea: A CXL memory fabric hashes every 4 KB page and keeps one physical copy rack-wide of identical model weights, container images, libraries and zero pages with copy-on-write, so inference fleets running one model on 64-128 accelerators share a single copy.

physics.key_insight: CXL 3.x shared memory lets one physical copy of read-only data (weights, images, libraries) serve many hosts; explicit sharing gets this without hashing every page.
physics.killer_doubt: Weights live in accelerator HBM, and tensor-parallel shards store them once per group, so AI dedup ratio is ~1. Hash indirection adds ~50-100 ns per miss; KSM-class gains are 1.1-1.5x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Snapshot host DRAM of 32 inference and 32 general servers in one rack (~$100k); count rack-wide versus per-host duplicate 4 KB pages, separating file-backed pages that one shared DAX mapping already covers.
physics.prior_art: HICAMP (ASPLOS 2012); Linux KSM; VMware TPS; CXL 3.0 memory sharing; vLLM prefix caching; Phase B B4 notes rejected AI-tensor dedup.

innovation.key_insight: Inference fleets hold many identical bytes (weights, images, libraries); a rack-scale content-addressed CXL pool could keep one copy for 64-128 hosts.
innovation.killer_doubt: The 50-100x needs weights in host DRAM; they live in HBM. Mooncake/vLLM already share prefixes by hash in software, and dedup side channels killed cross-tenant KSM.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Same snapshot study as I-07802: hash 4 KB host-DRAM pages across 64 inference hosts and count duplicates not already shared by software. Kill below 1.3x. ~$50k.
innovation.prior_art: HICAMP (ASPLOS 2012); Linux KSM; Mooncake KV pool (FAST 2025); vLLM prefix caching; Flip Feng Shui dedup attack (USENIX Security 2016).

title: Minify stranded memory with an in-datacenter millisecond spot market
idea: Pool servers' DRAM behind CXL switches and run an internal per-millisecond auction where jobs bid for idle GBs lent by neighbor hosts, with hardware page migration enforcing leases and reclaiming on demand.

physics.key_insight: Prices can reveal which jobs value marginal GBs most, so a pool can lend idle DRAM without central forecasts of each host's demand.
physics.killer_doubt: Pond-style pooling saves only ~7-9% of DRAM. Reclaiming 1 GB over CXL takes ~30 ms plus TLB shootdowns, and allocations live minutes to hours, so millisecond leases add nothing.
physics.decisive_experiment: Trace-driven simulation (~$50k) on public Azure and Google cluster memory traces: compare auction allocation with Pond-style ML placement for DRAM saved and SLA violations.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft Pond CXL pooling (ASPLOS'23); Ginseng market-driven memory allocation (VEE 2014); Resource-as-a-Service cloud proposals. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Price signals could allocate pooled idle DRAM to the jobs that value it most, which matters more at 4x prices.
innovation.killer_doubt: Microsoft Pond measured ~7% savings from CXL pools. Reclaiming a 64 GB lease at ~10 GB/s takes ~6 s of migration, so per-millisecond leases are fiction.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay Azure and Alibaba VM traces in a pooling-plus-auction simulator with realistic migration bandwidth. Kill if GB recovered per rack at p99 SLO beats static pooling by under 5 points. ~$30k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft Pond (ASPLOS 2023); Memtrade harvested-memory marketplace (SIGMETRICS 2023); CXL pooling appliances (UnifabriX, XConn); study item I-04804 (DROP).

title: Eliminate royalty fear: expired-patent freedom-to-operate atlas for legacy DRAM
idea: Eliminate the belief that DRAM is a legal minefield: a ~$400k legal-engineering project maps expired pre-2006 DRAM patents onto a complete 50-90nm stacked-capacitor process and periphery, publishing an open freedom-to-operate atlas and reference flow.

physics.key_insight: Every pre-Nov-2006 patent has expired, so a 50-90 nm stacked-capacitor flow is largely free to operate; the atlas mainly removes legal fear.
physics.killer_doubt: A 50-90 nm node gives ~0.02 Gb/mm2 vs 0.44 at 1b (~25x fewer bits per wafer): ~$20-40/GB cost, uncompetitive even at 4x prices. Subsumed by I-04102.
physics.decisive_experiment: $50k: cost a 65 nm 1 Gb die (bits/wafer, $/GB) against $20/GB contract price before any legal work; if >$15/GB, stop.
physics.prior_art: Commercial patent-landscape/FTO services; CXMT used the Qimonda portfolio. A public atlas: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Pre-2006 DRAM patents are expired, so a 50-90 nm stacked-capacitor flow is legally open; a published map marginally helps specialty and legacy DRAM entrants.
innovation.killer_doubt: Legal risk is not the barrier: a 90 nm 8F2 cell is ~65x the area of a 1b cell, so cost/GB is uncompetitive whatever the royalties.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Interview 10 prospective legacy/specialty DRAM entrants and their counsel (~$50k); if fewer than 3 rank freedom-to-operate cost above capital and yield know-how as a top-3 barrier, stop.
innovation.prior_art: Routine FTO studies by patent firms; legacy and specialty DRAM already made by Winbond, Nanya, ESMT and CXMT without such an atlas.

title: Eliminate lost know-how: retired DRAM engineers' knowledge guild
idea: Eliminate relearning lost US DRAM know-how: a ~$400k program records structured process-knowledge interviews with retired engineers from closed US and European DRAM fabs, builds a searchable knowledge base, and runs a paid advisory guild for new entrants.

physics.key_insight: Tacit yield know-how is real and scarce; structured capture could shorten a new entrant's learning curve.
physics.killer_doubt: Tacit yield learning moves with teams, not transcripts (CXMT/JHICC hired retired engineers); expert networks already sell this at ~$1k/hour, and knowledge from 90-65 nm is ~6 nodes stale.
physics.decisive_experiment: $100k: interview 20 retired integrators and test whether a new fab team solves 5 historical yield excursions faster with the knowledge base than without it.
physics.prior_art: Computer History Museum oral histories; GLG-type expert networks; Chinese DRAM entrants recruiting retired Japanese/Taiwanese/Korean engineers.

innovation.key_insight: Tacit yield and integration knowledge from closed U.S. and European DRAM fabs is perishable and cheap to capture now, before the people retire out.
innovation.killer_doubt: Know-how from 90-40 nm planar fabs transfers poorly to sub-20 nm or oxide 3D processes; it saves an entrant months, not the $15B+ and 3-5 years that gate supply.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Pilot 20 structured interviews (~$60k); have a new-entrant process team score transcripts for actionable yield fixes; continue only if over 25% contain process detail absent from the literature.
innovation.prior_art: Computer History Museum oral histories; expert networks and retired-engineer consultancies; SEMI and CHIPS Act workforce programs.

title: Magnify supplier count 10x with open-source DRAM IP
idea: Fund a DARPA-style open, royalty-free gain-cell memory macro, controller RTL and process module portable to any 22-40 nm logic fab, with qualified PDK decks for GlobalFoundries, TI, SkyWater-class and Intel 16, so ~30 mature logic fabs can make DRAM-class memory chiplets.

physics.key_insight: Idle 22-40 nm logic capacity and open PDKs could make embedded DRAM-class macros without DRAM fabs.
physics.killer_doubt: Si gain cell at 28 nm: ~0.15 um2/bit (~50x 1b's 0.0023), ~10-100 us retention at 85 C; ~43 GB/wafer, ~$58/GB vs $20/GB contract. Not capacity tier.
physics.decisive_experiment: Use existing OpenGCRAM/RAAAM silicon data to cost $/GB per wafer; only an IGZO BEOL module (N-43 class) changes the answer, so test IGZO 2T0C retention on a mature-node BEOL coupon.
physics.prior_art: RAAAM Memory Technologies GCRAM IP for standard CMOS; OpenGCRAM open-source gain-cell compiler (recalled); imec IGZO 2T0C.

innovation.key_insight: A portable, qualified gain-cell macro plus controller RTL lets idle mature logic fabs make on-die and edge memory without DRAM process know-how.
innovation.killer_doubt: Logic gain cells at 22-40 nm are ~0.1-0.2 um2/bit, ~50-100x below 1b DRAM: 30 fabs at ~50k wafers/month add ~0.03-0.1 EB/yr, ~0.1-0.4% of world bits.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Tape out a 2T/3T gain-cell macro on a 22-40 nm MPW, measure 85 C retention, bit area and refresh power; run a BEOL IGZO 2T0C module at a university fab for comparison.
innovation.prior_art: OpenRAM; gain-cell eDRAM macros (Teman, Giterman, Burg groups); Intel and IBM eDRAM; imec and Kioxia IGZO 2T0C; DARPA 3DSoC with SkyWater.

title: Rail yard master: racetrack memory built in U.S. hard-disk head fabs
idea: A rail yard master moves cars along sidings instead of building a track for each car. Magnetic domain-wall racetrack memory uses vertical U-shaped nanowires, each holding ~64 domains shifted by current past one read/write head. It is built in U.S. hard-disk read-head fabs, which already pattern 20 nm magnetic multilayers in volume and are losing HDD demand.

physics.key_insight: Domain-wall shifting has no charge-fluence wear, so it is one of the four endurance-safe write routes; 64 bits per track could beat 1b density ~10x.
physics.killer_doubt: Head fabs build ~1e4-1e5 readers per AlTiC wafer with no CMOS and no HAR verticals; racetrack needs ~1e10 tracks/cm2 with shift errors below 1e-12 per shift, never shown.
