physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into N-82: electroplate 20 nm Co/Ni wires in an AAO or Si mold, write 16 domains, shift 1e9 times, and count shift errors by MFM/TMR readback (~$300k).
physics.prior_art: IBM/Parkin racetrack since 2008, stalled on pinning; Phase B N-82 capacitor-hole racetrack covers the same physics with a better fab route.

innovation.key_insight: Head fabs pattern ~20 nm magnetic stacks at U.S. sites, a real non-DRAM magnetic toolset. Magnetic writes would clear the triage endurance wall.
innovation.killer_doubt: Up to 64 shifts per read require <~1e-12 misplacement per shift; no vertical array has shown it in ~20 years. Head fabs are loaded by nearline demand, not idle.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Electroplate 20 vertical 3 um Ni-Fe/Co wires in a head-fab test lot with a TMR reader at the base. Run 1e9 shift cycles and count displacement errors per shift against the 1e-12 target.
innovation.prior_art: IBM Parkin racetrack (2008 onward); cylindrical domain-wall wires; Everspin U.S. MRAM fab; project N-82 racetrack in the capacitor hole.

title: Seed-bank keeper: pages stored as generator plus seed
idea: A seed bank stores seeds, not forests. A userfaultfd library lets programs register regions produced by deterministic generators (PRNG noise, dropout masks, random projections, synthetic test data, procedurally initialized tensors) as (generator ID, seed, offset). Under pressure the pages are dropped, and on a fault they are regenerated bit-exactly with vectorized Philox at >10 GB/s.

physics.key_insight: Pages that are pure PRNG output compress to (generator, seed, offset), and counter-based Philox can regenerate them bit-exactly on a fault.
physics.killer_doubt: Little memory qualifies: dropout masks are already seed-regenerated, and PRNG pages are likely <5% of a node. At ~2-5 us per 4 KB userfaultfd fault, restore runs ~1 GB/s/thread.
physics.decisive_experiment: Instrument 20 representative training and simulation jobs and count the peak-resident bytes that are pure PRNG output. Below 5%, stop. ~$20k.
physics.prior_art: Philox counter-based RNG (Salmon et al., SC'11); PyTorch/JAX seed-regenerated dropout; Linux discardable/purgeable memory.

innovation.key_insight: Counter-based PRNG output has near-zero Kolmogorov size, so dropping and regenerating it bit-exactly on a fault (Philox >10 GB/s) beats storing or compressing it.
innovation.killer_doubt: Little such data stays resident: dropout masks are already regenerated from seeds, init tensors are overwritten after step one. Likely under 1-2% of node DRAM, not tens of GB (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Instrument 10 training and simulation jobs: sample resident pages and test whether they match a registered generator stream by regenerating and comparing. Stop if matched bytes are under 2% of DRAM. ~$20k.
innovation.prior_art: Random123 counter-based PRNGs (SC'11); FlashAttention and Megatron regenerate dropout masks from seeds; JAX stateless PRNG keys; procedural content generation [training knowledge].

title: Monk with one bowl: eBPF census finds duplicate buffer copies
idea: A monk owns one bowl, not five. An eBPF plus page-hash census tool samples contents across the page cache, socket buffers, user heaps and GPU staging buffers and flags identical data held in two or more places (the NIC-kernel-user-serialize-GPU chain). The team then ships upstream zero-copy patches (io_uring registered buffers, splice, mmap'd page cache) for the top offenders.

physics.key_insight: A content-hash census across page cache, socket buffers, heaps and GPU staging shows where duplicate copies persist, turning zero-copy work into measured DRAM savings.
physics.killer_doubt: In-flight copies live microseconds: at 10 GB/s and ~100 us residency only ~1 MB is duplicated. Persistent duplication (DB buffer pool plus page cache) is already fixed by O_DIRECT.
physics.decisive_experiment: Run the eBPF/page-hash census on 20 storage, proxy and ingest nodes for a week and report persistent duplicate GB per node. Kill if <5% of DRAM. ~$30k of engineering.
physics.prior_art: KSM and VM dedup studies (Difference Engine, OSDI 2008); io_uring registered buffers, splice, MSG_ZEROCOPY; O_DIRECT double-caching fixes; bpftrace/drgn profilers (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: The same bytes often sit in page cache, socket buffers, heap and GPU staging; a content-hash census turns zero-copy work into a ranked, measurable hit list.
innovation.killer_doubt: In-flight copies are transient and small. KSM, O_DIRECT and io_uring already cover the persistent cases, so fleet savings are likely ~2-5%, not 10-25% (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Run the eBPF plus sampled page-hash census on 50 storage, proxy and ingest nodes for 2 weeks; report time-averaged duplicate bytes as % of RSS. Kill if <5%. ~$40k.
innovation.prior_art: Linux KSM page-hash merging; Meta TMO fleet memory work; io_uring registered buffers, MSG_ZEROCOPY, splice [training knowledge].

title: Heat is the wordline: thermally gated access with 1.5 eV activation
idea: Inverts 'access devices are gated by voltage': put an ionic or deep-trap hopping conductor with ~1.5 eV activation energy in series with each capacitor, effectively insulating at 25 C (retention far beyond hours) while a nanosecond pulse in a row heater line takes it to ~400 C, raising conductance ~10^10x long enough to read or write; cells form 2-terminal crossbar stacks.

physics.key_insight: A 1.5 eV-activated series element gives ~1e10 on/off between 85 C and 400 C with no transistor: a two-terminal crossbar cell whose gate is temperature.
physics.killer_doubt: A hot row at 1% duty sees 7e13 x 10 ns: ~8 days cumulative at 400 C. Heating ~1-5 pJ/cell makes a row ~10-40 nJ versus ~2 nJ ACT.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fabricate heater-gated MIM test structures in a university fab (~$200k); measure the conductance Arrhenius slope at 25-450 C and retention at 85 C, then apply 1e10 ns heat pulses and track drift.
physics.prior_art: Thermally assisted switching MRAM (Crocus) and HAMR use heat as the write gate; PCM ns heaters. None found for charge-storage access.

innovation.key_insight: Temperature as the select signal: a 1.5 eV conductor gives ~1e14 on/off between 25 and 400 C, which would be a two-terminal access device with hours of retention.
innovation.killer_doubt: Prefactor bound: with sigma0 <=~1e4 S/cm, a 1.5 eV conductor at 400 C reaches ~6e-8 S/cm; charging 5 fF in 1 ns through 20 nm needs ~2.5 S/cm, ~4e7x more.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Free paper check: fit published sigma(T) for every candidate ionic or hopping conductor. Stop unless one reaches >1 S/cm at 400 C and stays <1e-12 S/cm at 85 C. Only then build a ~$100k microheater test chip.
innovation.prior_art: Thermally assisted MRAM (Crocus); ns PCM microheaters (IBM, Intel/Micron 3D XPoint). Arrhenius-gated DRAM access: none found (training knowledge).

title: Cheap short-living objects: retired server DDR4 reborn as CXL memory
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Collect, retest and bin them, then mount 8-16 on each CXL Type-3 card built around a 28 nm controller, as a cheap cold tier for KV cache and page cache. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)

physics.key_insight: A 28 nm CXL controller plus retired DDR4 needs only trailing-node capacity and no new fab, giving a cold tier for KV and page cache.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-06321 and I-00348. KV cache needs bandwidth: one x8 CXL card at ~32 GB/s delivers ~1/100 of an H100's 3.35 TB/s, so only the coldest KV fits.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-06321's screening and census.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera and Astera Leo CXL controllers with DDR4 support.

innovation.key_insight: Only trailing-node logic and existing DRAM: a 28 nm CXL controller plus retired DDR4 gives a KV and page-cache cold tier with zero wafer starts.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-00348. A custom 28 nm controller needs ~$3-5M in masks and IP (estimate); buying Structera X silicon makes this a reseller, not an invention.
innovation.decisive_experiment: No separate work: covered by the I-00348 retired-RDIMM screening study (~$60k).
innovation.prior_art: Marvell Structera X; Meta Vistara; Microsoft GreenSKU; R11 I-05867 and R22 I-03344 (DROP).

title: Urban-mining line requalifies retired server DRAM
idea: Inverts 'new supply needs new wafers'. Robotic hot-air reflow strips DRAM packages from retired server DIMMs, a 48-hour retention and row-hammer stress screen sorts them, and they are re-mounted on CXL memory-expander cards for pooled tiers.

physics.key_insight: Retired server DRAM has no dominant cell wear-out. Recovered bits use no wafer capacity and arrive in months, a real supply lever during a 4x price spike.
physics.killer_doubt: Desoldering adds a ~260 C reflow, ~1-3% package loss and rework cost for no gain: DDR4 CXL controllers (Marvell Structera X 2404, 12 DIMMs) take whole DIMMs.
physics.decisive_experiment: Desolder and reball 1,000 packages from retired RDIMMs. Compare post-reflow BIST fallout, retention and VRT shift with the same lot tested as intact DIMMs. ~$80k; expect intact reuse to win.
physics.prior_art: Meta Vistara CXL ASIC reusing retired DDR4 (2026) and Marvell Structera X 2404 DDR4-reuse controller (via search snippet); used-RDIMM resale market.

innovation.key_insight: Package-level harvest frees dies from the DIMM form factor for CXL cards. DRAM has no dominant wear-out, so second life is physically sound and needs no wafers.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipping: GreenSKU and Structera X reuse DDR4 over CXL. Reflow and reball add fallout risk, the DDR4 pool is one-time, and CXL adds ~70-100 ns.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Desolder, reball and retest 1,000 retired DDR4 packages. Compare fallout, retention tail and row-hammer threshold against the same lot left on DIMMs. Under $100k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X; R16 I-00224 (HOLD, the canonical reuse review); R26 I-06854 phone LPDDR desolder-to-CXL (ADVANCE).

title: Pinned-photodiode buried node borrowed from image-sensor foundries
idea: MAGNIFY retention by holding the bit in a fully depleted, surface-pinned buried n-well (a CIS pinned photodiode kept dark, dark current ~1-10 e-/s) with a transfer gate and source-follower readout like a global-shutter pixel memory, taped out on a commercial CIS MPW.

physics.key_insight: A fully depleted, surface-pinned node removes interface generation, the main Si leakage path; charge moves through a semiconductor channel, so write endurance is unlimited.
physics.killer_doubt: Dark current doubles every ~6-8 C: 5 e-/s at 25 C becomes ~1,000-3,000 e-/s at 85 C, so 2,000 e- lasts ~0.1-0.5 s. Cells ~0.5 um2, ~200x 1b.
physics.decisive_experiment: Reuse an existing global-shutter CIS test chip, no tapeout: write the storage diode by fill-and-spill, histogram 85 C dark current over 1e6 nodes, and time the transfer. ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: Global-shutter CIS in-pixel pinned storage diodes (Sony, onsemi); 1970s CCD memories; IGZO 2T0C already gives >400 s retention at far smaller area.

innovation.key_insight: A CIS pinned node is the lowest-leakage storage node in silicon (~1-10 e-/s). Its hot-pixel statistics are a ready analogue of the DRAM retention tail.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 0.5-1 um2 the cell is ~600-1,200x the 1b cell. Dark current rises ~100-1,000x from 25 to 85 C. IGZO 2T0C gives >1,000 s retention in far less area.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Only as a test vehicle: on one CIS MPW (~$150k), map dark-current tails of 1e6 pinned storage nodes at 25-85 C, at 1.1 um and the smallest pitch allowed, to calibrate Jot-RAM (N-84) scaling.
innovation.prior_art: Global-shutter in-pixel storage nodes (Sony, Samsung, OmniVision); Jot-RAM N-84 in triage; IGZO/ZTO 2T0C gain cells (imec, N-26) [training knowledge].

title: IBM eDRAM trench sold as merchant pre-capacitored substrate wafers
idea: IBM's deep-trench eDRAM died when its single in-house SOI process ended with GlobalFoundries' 7 nm exit. Disaggregate it: a substrate vendor (Soitec-style) mass-produces blank wafers with a uniform grid of deep-trench capacitors, and any fab, including U.S. legacy logic fabs, builds access transistors and periphery on top aligned to that grid.

physics.key_insight: IBM's native sequence makes the deep trench first, so a pre-capacitored substrate is thermally compatible with a standard FEOL and lets fabs without memory lines host eDRAM-class arrays.
physics.killer_doubt: Deep-trench cells (~0.03 um2) take ~20x commodity DRAM area, about 3 nm SRAM density. BEOL MIM eDRAM (Intel 22 nm) needs no substrate lock-in, and trench placement is product-specific.
physics.decisive_experiment: Buy silicon trench-capacitor (PICS-style) wafers, run a 130-180 nm logic flow on top at SkyWater, and measure strap resistance, node leakage and alignment. ~$700k.
physics.prior_art: IBM/GlobalFoundries deep-trench eDRAM (POWER7-9, z-series); Murata/IPDiA silicon trench capacitors; Intel 22 nm MIM eDRAM (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Moving the deepest etch into a shared, fully used substrate fab is sound capital logic. Trench-first matches IBM's flow order, so FEOL on top is thermally plausible.
innovation.killer_doubt: Density stays at eDRAM level: a ~0.026 um2 22 nm DT cell is ~20x 1b DRAM's area per bit. Logic must also adopt the substrate's fixed grid and buried-strap module.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Etch trench-capacitor coupons, run a 130-180 nm FEOL on top at a U.S. foundry, and measure capacitor leakage, strap resistance and Cs after the full thermal budget. ~$600k.
innovation.prior_art: IBM/GlobalFoundries deep-trench eDRAM (POWER7-9); Murata/IPDiA and TSMC deep-trench silicon capacitors; Soitec engineered substrates; R07 I-04623 [training knowledge].

title: Bicycle gears: bit-plane tiering serves weights at shiftable precision
idea: Store weights transposed into bit-planes: the 4 most-significant planes stay in DRAM/HBM, low planes live in CXL or flash; each request 'shifts gear' by fetching only as many planes as its quality tier needs, and speculative decoding uses MSB-only planes as a free draft model.

physics.key_insight: One bit-plane copy serves several precisions. Its MSB planes double as a speculative draft that shares weights, saving the 2-16 GB a separate draft model occupies.
physics.killer_doubt: Any-Precision LLM already does this. Batches mix quality tiers, so one high-tier request in a 70B batch streams 35 GB of LSB planes per step, 0.55 s over CXL x16.
physics.decisive_experiment: One GPU node (<$30k): serve a Llama-70B bit-plane copy that drafts from its own MSB planes. Measure acceptance rate, tokens/s and resident DRAM against Any-Precision LLM and a separate 8B draft.
physics.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024) single-copy bit-plane multi-precision; Matryoshka Quantization (2025) nested int8/4/2; QSpec (2024) quantized self-draft. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: One bit-plane-major weight copy serves several precision tiers, and its MSB planes double as a free self-speculative draft model with no extra weights.
innovation.killer_doubt: Flash cannot stream low planes per step: a 70B model's 4 low planes are ~35 GB against ~14 GB/s per NVMe drive, ~2.5 s/token; the high tier is unusable.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Software only: store an 8-bit 8B model bit-plane-major, run MSB-4 as draft and all 8 planes as verifier. Measure acceptance rate, HBM bytes per token, and quality at 2-, 3- and 4-plane tiers.
innovation.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (Park et al., ICML 2024) bit-plane weights; Matryoshka Quantization (Google DeepMind 2025); QuantSpec self-speculation from nested quantization.

title: Phylogenetic tree storage for resident model variants
idea: All fine-tuned variants resident on a node form an evolutionary tree. Each node stores 1-bit sign deltas plus per-channel scales relative to its parent, rebuilt on the fly in the GEMM epilogue. Serving 100 variants costs about one base model plus 100 x 1/16 of its size.

physics.key_insight: Variants do form lineages (base, domain, tenant). Deltas against a parent are smaller in magnitude, so per-row scales fit more tightly and fidelity may improve.
physics.killer_doubt: A sign delta costs 1 bit/weight whatever its magnitude, with ~1 bit of entropy. So the tree saves zero memory over flat BitDelta and adds depth-d dequant-adds per GEMM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Simulation only (<$10k): build a 3-level tree of Llama fine-tunes and compare raw bytes, entropy-coded size and perplexity for flat versus tree 1-bit deltas.
physics.prior_art: BitDelta (2024); DeltaZip; delta chains in model hubs (ZipNN). Tree-structured 1-bit serving: none found. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Variants derived from other variants (base to instruct to domain to customer) could share deltas hierarchically, so each level stores only what changed from its parent.
innovation.killer_doubt: Most fine-tunes fork from one base (depth ~1), which is just BitDelta. At depth k, 1-bit errors compound and the epilogue adds k delta passes; depth >2 likely loses quality.
innovation.decisive_experiment: From a public model tree (base, instruct, 10 domain children, 50 grandchildren), compare chained 1-bit deltas with flat-from-base deltas: perplexity drift by depth and decode tokens/s.
innovation.prior_art: BitDelta, DeltaZip, Delta-CoMe, ComPEFT; Hugging Face model-tree lineage metadata. No hierarchical-delta serving found [training knowledge].

title: Colors pick the layer: wavelength-addressed 3D stacks without staircases
idea: Inverts 'each 3D tier needs its own wired wordline contact': give each tier a photoconductive access element made of quantum dots tuned to a distinct absorption band (16 tiers, 16 wavelengths) and run a light pipe per column, so choosing the wavelength selects the tier and all tiers share their electrical lines with no staircase or tier-specific masks.

physics.key_insight: Optical tier select would remove staircase contacts and per-tier masks, the cost that grows fastest as 3D stacks get taller.
physics.killer_doubt: QDs absorb every photon above their gap, so short wavelengths excite all lower-gap tiers. A guiding light pipe needs a core >=~300 nm, against ~40 nm column pitch.
physics.decisive_experiment: Stack three QD photoconductor films with distinct gaps in a university lab (~$100k); measure cross-tier photocurrent selectivity per wavelength and dark leakage at 85 C; kill if selectivity is below 100:1.
physics.prior_art: Wavelength-multiplexed optical and holographic storage addressing; resonant-cavity photodetectors. None found for 3D DRAM tier select.

innovation.key_insight: The target is right: select tiers with a shared broadcast signal instead of contacts, deleting the staircase and per-tier masks. Wavelength is the wrong carrier.
innovation.killer_doubt: Quantum dots absorb every photon above their gap, so the bluest pulse switches all 16 tiers. Light pipes need >=~300 nm pitch against DRAM's ~35 nm, ~70x area loss.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Paper first: show any narrowband selection scheme (e.g., plasmonic absorbers) in which the shortest-wavelength tier does not also fire, at <100 nm pitch. Otherwise a ~$50k two-tier PbS-dot stack confirms crosstalk.
innovation.prior_art: Multi-wavelength optical storage (spectral hole burning, holographic); QD photodetectors; staircase-free phase tying (I-02002). Optically addressed 3D DRAM tiers: none found (training knowledge).

title: Second-life DRAM: retired server DIMMs reborn as CXL pools
idea: Eliminate new wafers for the capacity tier: strip DDR4/DDR5 chips from decommissioned servers, screen with burn-in and row-hammer tests, and mount them behind CXL Type-3 controllers that translate protocol and map out weak rows.

physics.key_insight: Harvesting at chip level, with weak-row maps in the CXL controller, can rescue packages from DIMMs that failed on only a few rows.
physics.killer_doubt: Whole DIMMs plug into CXL cards as they are. Desoldering, baking and reballing add 1-2 reflows, rework loss and a few dollars per package, and buy only weak-row rescue.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-06321, adding a 500-package desolder, reball and retest run to price rework yield and $/GB.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU; DRAM reballing and refurbishment brokers; JEDEC DDR4 post-package repair (PPR) for row remapping.

innovation.key_insight: Chip-level harvest frees dies from the DIMM form factor, and hammer screening plus weak-row map-out is the right trust layer for aged DDR4.
innovation.killer_doubt: Desoldering adds a ~260 C reflow and ~1-3% package fallout for no gain, since DDR4 CXL controllers already accept whole DIMMs. Duplicate of I-00348 and I-00224.
innovation.decisive_experiment: As for I-00348, plus a 100-package reball pilot measuring reflow fallout and retention shift; kill chip-level harvest if fallout exceeds 1%. About $40k.
innovation.prior_art: Marvell Structera X; Meta Vistara (physics R14, via search snippet); Microsoft GreenSKU; R14 I-04852 desolder harvest (DROP).

title: Sourdough starter: persist tokens, regrow KV on demand
idea: Keep only the starter: persist each session's token IDs (2-4 bytes per token) to flash and drop its KV cache (100 KB+ per token on large models) under pressure; a cost model chooses between regrowing KV by prefill on idle compute and fetching a stored copy.

physics.key_insight: Token IDs are ~10^5x smaller than KV, so always persisting them is free insurance. Spilling KV becomes an optional, per-session bet on return probability.
physics.killer_doubt: Regrowing a 32k 70B context costs ~6e15 FLOP (~8 kJ), against ~25 J and ~$0.0005 of NAND wear to re-read 10.7 GB; recompute wins only for short or unlikely-to-return contexts.
physics.decisive_experiment: Trace-driven cost model on a multi-turn chat/agent trace: recompute against NAND fetch against hybrid HCache, sweeping context length and return probability. ~$10k.
physics.prior_art: InferCept (discard/recompute vs swap), HCache (EuroSys'25, restore from hidden states), Cake (compute-or-load) all cover this cost model.

innovation.key_insight: Compute can substitute for memory: token IDs are about 10^5 times smaller than KV. This is already the default eviction policy of every prefix cache.
innovation.killer_doubt: Regrowing a 32k-token context on a 70B model costs ~4.5 PFLOP (5-9 GPU-seconds). Inference GPUs are rarely idle, so flash-stored KV usually beats recompute on cost.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed. Reproduce Cake/InferCept results on a trace to confirm the recompute-vs-load crossover (tokens per GB/s of flash), then fold the result into I-08555's tier policy.
innovation.prior_art: InferCept (ICML 2024) chooses discard, swap or preserve; Cake (2024) computes and loads at once; HCache restores from hidden states; vLLM/SGLang evict and recompute.

title: Retrofit US flexible-packaging converting lines into memory-foil fabs
idea: Partner with U.S. label and flexible-packaging converters, whose vacuum web metallizers, slot-die coaters and gravure units already run at km per hour, add enclosed ISO-5 web paths plus nanoimprint and spatial-ALD modules, and sell memory foil per square metre under a tolling model.

physics.key_insight: Web lines amortise vacuum and transport at ~$1-10/m2. An IGZO 1T1C at 0.08 um2 is ~1.5 TB/m2, so area cost, not density, could set $/bit.
physics.killer_doubt: Converter assets are <10% of a memory line. Spatial ALD and NIL run ~1-10 m/min. A 10 ppm/K web moves ~100 um/m per 10 K vs ~10 nm overlay.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-01819's test: a two-layer self-aligned IGZO TFT array on a 30 cm web at 100 nm rules. Measure overlay, Vt sigma and particle D0 ($500k) before any converter deal.
physics.prior_art: HP Labs SAIL roll-to-roll TFTs; PragmatIC IGZO FlexICs; Thinfilm printed memory; in-study I-01819 (advanced) and I-06468 [training knowledge].

innovation.key_insight: If roll-to-roll memory foil (I-01819) works, U.S. converter sites, web-handling staff and tolling contracts could add capacity fastest, with no EUV, quartz crucibles or helium.
innovation.killer_doubt: Converter halls run at ISO 8-9, 1,000-10,000x ISO 5 particle counts. NIL, spatial ALD, inspection and enclosures are all new capex, so retrofitting saves perhaps 10-20% of line cost (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-01819. After its 100 nm imprint result, build a $50k teardown cost model of one converter line: reusable tools, enclosure cost, and particle counts measured on a running web after an ISO 6 retrofit.
innovation.prior_art: PragmatIC FlexIC fabs; HP Labs SAIL roll-to-roll TFTs; Applied Materials and Buhler vacuum web coaters; in-study advanced I-01819 (training knowledge).

title: Band-offset quantum-well bits stacked along a superlattice pillar
idea: Worse: store each bit on a bulky capacitor needing femtofarads. Flip: etch vertical pillars through a Si/Ge-rich superlattice, wrap each Ge-rich well with a tier gate, and store holes in its valence-band well (up to ~0.5 eV offset) as the bit, sensed as a threshold shift of the shared vertical Si channel, which is capacitorless and has no oxide tunneling, so endurance stays unlimited.

physics.key_insight: A capacitorless heterostructure bit per tier at ~17 nm2/bit would be the ideal 3D cell. The crystalline band offset avoids oxide charge-fluence wear.
physics.killer_doubt: Strained Ge gives dEv ~0.74 eV: tau ~ 1e-13 s * exp(0.74/0.031) ~ 2 ms at 85 C. 1 s needs >=0.92 eV. Ge ni (~2000x Si) refills empty wells.
physics.decisive_experiment: Measure hole retention vs temperature in a Si/Si0.3Ge0.7 QW capacitorless test FET (university epi, $150k). Extract the activation energy; kill unless Ea >=0.9 eV. A wide-gap (GaN/AlN) host is the workaround.
physics.prior_art: Ertosun and Saraswat 1T-QW DRAM with SiGe hole well (Stanford, EDL 2008); floating-body ZRAM; Si/SiGe superlattice 3D DRAM stacks [training knowledge].

innovation.key_insight: Epitaxial band-offset wells store charge with no capacitor and no tunnel oxide in the write path, one of triage's endurance-safe routes: a semiconductor channel.
innovation.killer_doubt: 64 ms at 85 C needs ~0.78 eV (1e12/s attempt rate). Ge-rich wells give ~0.3-0.5 eV after confinement: ns-10 us retention. A 128-cell series string reads in us, not ns.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Grow a 10-period Si/Si0.5Ge0.5 superlattice, etch gated pillars and write holes by GIDL. Measure Vt-decay retention from 25-125 C to extract an Arrhenius barrier. Stop if Ea < 0.7 eV. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Ertosun and Saraswat SiGe quantum-well 1T-DRAM (Stanford, EDL 2008); Z-RAM floating-body DRAM; NEO 3D X-DRAM; Samsung/SK hynix Si/SiGe 3D DRAM stacks (training knowledge).

title: Molybdenite exfoliation: peel only the bit-planes a token needs
idea: MoS2 peels into single layers; weights are stored bit-plane-major in row-aligned tiles (all MSBs of a tile together, then the next bit), and a per-token difficulty predictor fetches 2, 3, 4 or 8 planes, so easy tokens run a lower-precision model from the same single copy without overfetching unused planes.

physics.key_insight: Bit-plane-major tiles let precision change per decode step without overfetch. At batch 1 (phones, laptops), easy tokens could move ~4-6x fewer weight bits.
physics.killer_doubt: Weights are shared across a batch. With 80% easy tokens, P(all 64 easy) = 0.8^64 ~ 6e-7, so datacenter batches always fetch every plane. Truncated 2-bit planes are badly lossy.
physics.decisive_experiment: Batch-1 laptop study (<$20k): Llama-8B in bit-plane layout with a per-token plane predictor. Measure bits fetched, perplexity and tokens/s against a native 4-bit model with the same DRAM footprint.
physics.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM (ICML 2024) bit-plane layout; Matryoshka Quantization (2025); bit-serial accelerators Stripes and Bit-Pragmatic. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Per-token difficulty sets how many weight bit-planes to fetch, so easy tokens move 2-3 planes. It is worthwhile mainly for batch-1 edge decode, where weight streaming dominates.
innovation.killer_doubt: Batched serving loads each weight once per step for 32-256 tokens, so the step fetches the most planes any token needs. Untrained 2-plane truncation also degrades badly.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Train a per-token plane predictor on a nested (MatQuant-style) 8B model. Measure average planes fetched and perplexity at batch 1 and batch 64, on an edge GPU and a server GPU.
innovation.prior_art: Any-Precision LLM bit-plane layout; Matryoshka Quantization nested int8/int4/int2 slices; R16 I-02063 bit-plane family.

title: Swap per-GPU weight copies for an optical weight-broadcast tree
idea: Substitute storage with broadcast. Instead of every accelerator keeping its own copy of the model weights in HBM, a central weight store streams each layer's weights over a WDM optical broadcast tree, timed to the synchronized decode step, so each of N accelerators buffers only the 1-2 layers in flight in SRAM. HBM is left for KV cache and activations.

physics.key_insight: For SRAM-only accelerators or DP-replicated small-TP serving, one central weight copy broadcast per step could free 30-60% of per-GPU HBM for KV. Cerebras already shows a weight-streaming fabric works.
physics.killer_doubt: Tensor/expert parallelism already gives 1/N weight residency, moving ~0.7 GB/step of activations against 70 GB/step broadcast (~100x less). One 70B layer (~0.9 GB) also exceeds on-chip SRAM (~50-130 MB).
physics.decisive_experiment: On an 8xH100 node, use NVLink SHARP multicast to stream layer shards per decode step from one GPU, and compare tok/s/GB-HBM against TP=8 at equal p99 latency. ~$50k cloud.
physics.prior_art: Cerebras MemoryX/SwarmX weight streaming with broadcast to replicas; Megatron tensor parallelism and DeepSeek large-EP serving minimise weight replication.

innovation.key_insight: The per-step weight stream is identical across replicas, so multicast could free weight HBM for KV in SRAM-only accelerators or small-TP replica fleets without a scale-up fabric.
innovation.killer_doubt: Wide TP/EP already keeps one copy per scale-up domain, each GPU reading W/N at ~8 TB/s; broadcast makes every GPU ingest all W (1.4 TB/s, 70B at 20 tok/s).
innovation.decisive_experiment: On an 8xH100 node, stream layer shards each decode step with NVLink SHARP multicast and compare tok/s per HBM GB against TP=8 at equal p99 latency. ~$20k of cloud time.
innovation.prior_art: Cerebras weight streaming (MemoryX/SwarmX broadcast tree), DeepSpeed ZeRO-Inference, NVLink SHARP multicast, DeepSeek wide-EP decode across ~144 GPUs.

title: Turbine-blade eutectic solidification grows built-in vertical nanorod plates
idea: Borrowed from directionally solidified eutectic alloys used in turbine blades: solidify a Si-TaSi2 eutectic ingot so billions of aligned metallic TaSi2 nanorods run through monocrystalline Si, then slice wafers in which each rod is a ready-made vertical capacitor plate or buried bitline, with cells formed around them by one mask.

physics.key_insight: Directional eutectic solidification makes billions of aligned conductors in one thermal step, with no etch or fill: a genuinely unused route to vertical structure.
physics.killer_doubt: Jackson-Hunt (lambda^2 v = const): shrinking micron rod spacing to ~100 nm needs ~100-400x faster growth, metres per hour. Bare rods touch Si, so dielectric still needs an annulus etch.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed to drop. If pursued: laser-zone-melt Si-TaSi2 films at cm/s and measure rod pitch, order and 85 C junction leakage (~$100k).
physics.prior_art: Si-TaSi2 in-situ eutectic composites for field-emission and junction devices (Ditchek, GTE Labs, 1980s, training knowledge); none as memory plates found.

innovation.key_insight: Self-organized eutectic conductors could replace a high-aspect-ratio etch-and-fill with crystal growth. It is a genuinely unseen use of in-situ composites.
innovation.killer_doubt: Si-TaSi2 rods are ~1 um wide at ~1e6-1e7 per cm2. Spacing scales as V^-1/2, so 100 nm pitch needs ~900x faster solidification. Random rod positions cannot align with periodic wordlines.
innovation.decisive_experiment: First, a free paper check: compile published Si-TaSi2 lambda-squared-times-V data and stop if 200 nm pitch needs over 10 cm/min. Only then, one float-zone run at maximum rate with SEM pitch mapping (~$100k).
innovation.prior_art: Directionally solidified Si-TaSi2 in-situ composites (Ditchek, GTE Labs, 1980s) used for field-emitter and Schottky arrays (training knowledge).

title: Federated defect-image library compresses new-fab yield ramps
idea: Worse: every new fab learns its defects alone over 2-3 years. Flip: entrants and toolmakers feed inline SEM/optical defect images and parametric fails into a standardized defect taxonomy. Classifiers train federated (data never leaves each fab) and ship root-cause models and recipe corrections to new lines on day one.

physics.key_insight: The yield ramp burns depreciation (~55% of wafer cost). Shared defect taxonomies could cut root-cause time for entrants with no fab history.
physics.killer_doubt: Ramp speed is set by learning cycles (~60-90-day DRAM cycle time, ~8-12 cycles in 24 months), not by classification. Recipe-specific defects transfer poorly between fabs.
physics.decisive_experiment: Train a federated classifier across 3 university or pilot fabs plus WM-811K. Measure accuracy on a held-out fab's new defect classes against local-only training. ~$300k of software; the ramp claim itself stays untested.
physics.prior_art: KLA and Applied automatic defect classification; PDF Solutions Exensio; academic federated wafer-map classification papers (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Ramp months burn depreciation. Transferring defect-classifier knowledge without moving raw data could shorten a new line's learning curve.
innovation.killer_doubt: Yield learning is recipe- and tool-specific and is the firms' crown-jewel IP. Three makers hold ~90% of DRAM and won't contribute, so the library fills with logic data.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Train a federated wafer-map classifier on public sets (WM-811K, MixedWM38) plus one pilot-line partner. Measure accuracy on a held-out fab against local-only training. Under $200k.
innovation.prior_art: Federated wafer-map defect classification papers (2021-24); PDF Solutions Exensio; KLA Klarity; CHIPS SMART USA digital-twin institute [training knowledge].

title: Hollow-fiber sieving plus pressure swing recaptures fab helium as service
idea: Effect: helium's 2.6 angstrom kinetic diameter lets it permeate polyimide hollow fibers ~100x faster than N2 or Ar. Capture exhaust at chucks, load locks and leak stations, enrich it to 90% through membranes, finish it to 5N by pressure-swing adsorption and refill on site, all sold as helium-as-a-service.

physics.key_insight: The recoverable helium is concentrated: an ESC patent reports ~19.5 of ~20 sccm backside helium is dumped pure through a bleed orifice, before mixing with exhaust (via search snippet).
physics.killer_doubt: Membranes and PSA are the wrong tool: the bleed is already pure and closed-loop control removes it at source; the ~0.5 sccm past the seal dilutes to ~10-25 ppm.
physics.decisive_experiment: Helium mass balance on one etch bay: meter supply, bleed and foreline per chuck for a week. Then retrofit a no-bleed closed-loop backside controller and report helium per wafer and wafer-temperature uniformity. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: Patent family 'Increasing the gas efficiency for an electrostatic chuck' (US 9753463, 11747834, 12493303) (via search snippet); commercial membrane/PSA helium recovery units.

innovation.key_insight: Helium's small kinetic diameter makes membrane enrichment easy where it is concentrated (leak check, tool returns), turning a geopolitical exposure into an on-site loop.
innovation.killer_doubt: Backside helium leaks into chambers and leaves in ~10-50 slm dry-pump N2 ballast at roughly 100-1,000 ppm with fluorocarbon/HF; 70-90% fab-wide recovery from that stream is implausible.
innovation.decisive_experiment: With a fab partner, log helium concentration and flow per exhaust source for one week by mass spectrometer, then cost recovery per Mcf at the measured dilution. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: Industrial-gas helium recovery units (membrane plus PSA) already serve optical-fibre draw, MRI and research labs; the service model is offered by gas majors.

title: Coolant-backed memory wafer: microchannels in the memory layer of a memory-on-logic stack
idea: In a face-to-face memory-on-logic stack (B3-02, or any bonded DRAM-over-logic), etch 100-200 um deep microchannels into the back of the thick memory wafer, away from its devices, and run warm water through them. The memory devices then sit only ~50 um of silicon plus their own BEOL from the coolant, while the logic's heat crosses the memory on its way out. With in-silicon microchannels of the kind Microsoft and Corintis demonstrated in 2025, the memory layer runs ~9-28 K above coolant instead of at the 70-105 C of a cold-plate GPU junction. DRAM retention roughly doubles for every 10 C drop, so a Si 1T1C array at ~45 C holds a 64 ms tail cell for ~1 s.

physics.key_insight: Put the coolant in the memory wafer of a memory-on-logic stack. The memory then sits ~0.5 K above the channel wall, so Si DRAM can survive on ~1 kW logic.
physics.killer_doubt: At 125 W/cm2 with h~1e5 W/m2K, memory runs 13-30 K above coolant, worse over hot spots. Tail Ea of 0.3-0.6 eV gives 3-11x retention; refresh is ~10% of power.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into the N-41 dossier: thin a commercial DRAM die, etch 150 um channels, bond it onto a 125 W/cm2 heater die, and map the retention tail against coolant temperature to extract tail Ea.
physics.prior_art: IBM Zurich interlayer microchannel cooling of 3D stacks; Tuckerman-Pease 1981; Microsoft/Corintis in-chip microfluidics (2025); R18 dropped the cool-spec sled I-11571.

innovation.key_insight: In memory-on-logic stacks the memory tier can sit next to the coolant. 1 W/mm2 across 50 um of Si costs only ~0.3 K, so memory runs ~10-30 K above water.
innovation.killer_doubt: Refresh is ~10-20% of power and bandwidth, so an 8x cut buys ~10-15% at system level. A tail-cell activation energy of ~0.3-0.6 eV may cap the retention gain at 3-10x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Thermal-chuck retention-tail maps of commodity DDR5/LPDDR5 dies at 45, 65 and 85 C on an FPGA tester, extracting the tail activation energy, plus a thermal model of a bonded microchannel stack. ~$80k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft/Corintis in-silicon microfluidics (2025, prior logs); IBM CMOSAIC interlayer 3D-IC cooling; Liu et al. ISCA 2013 retention vs temperature; same family as dropped I-11571.

title: IBM MXT fixed: compression lives in the CXL link, not the core
idea: IBM's Memory eXpansion Technology (2000) doubled effective capacity with hardware compression but died from decompression latency on the CPU critical path, a large L3 requirement and OS changes. Put a 2-4 ns base-delta/zero-run compressor with a metadata cache inside the CXL memory controller, present the OS a fixed larger capacity, and compress only far-tier lines so hot data never pays the latency.

physics.key_insight: Putting compression in the CXL controller, off the CPU critical path, and compressing only far-tier lines fixes the latency failure of MXT. Capacity grows with no new wafers.
physics.killer_doubt: Already commercial. Fleet data show ~20-30% of memory cold at ~3x compression, a ~15-25% gain, not 33-60%. Where host encryption (SEV/TDX) covers the memory, lines are ciphertext and compress ~1.0x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing beyond a replay (~$20k): run public far-memory traces, plus sampled SEV/TDX-encrypted VM pages, through base-delta and LZ4 models to bound the fleet capacity gain.
physics.prior_art: ZeroPoint Technologies CXL compression IP; Marvell Structera A inline LZ4; OCP hyperscale CXL tiered-memory compression; IBM MXT (2000).

innovation.key_insight: It diagnoses MXT's failure correctly: compress only far-tier lines behind CXL, where ~150-250 ns already hides decompression, so ~1.5-2x ratios become capacity.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already productized: Marvell Structera A ships inline LZ4 and ZeroPoint licenses compression IP. Incompressible or encrypted pages (~1.0x) overflow a fixed advertised capacity, forcing OS ballooning.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Not needed for novelty. To size it: replay fleet memory dumps through LZ4 and BDI at 64 B to 4 KB granularity and measure capacity at p99 compressibility. About $20k.
innovation.prior_art: IBM MXT (2000-01); Marvell Structera A inline LZ4 (2024); ZeroPoint Technologies IP; R17 I-05749 and R28 I-09017 (DROP).

title: Hash-deduplicating base die stores shared KV prefixes once
idea: Worsen: store the same system-prompt KV cache separately for every user. Flip: the memory base die hashes each 4 KB block on write and keeps a content-addressed table, so identical prefix blocks across users map to one physical copy with copy-on-write, transparent to the host.

physics.key_insight: Shared system-prompt and agent prefixes make KV highly redundant, and deduplication raises effective capacity 2-5x on those workloads.
physics.killer_doubt: A KV block depends on every earlier token, so the only duplicates are exact prefixes. Software already shares these with no silicon; hardware hashing likely adds <5% capacity.
physics.decisive_experiment: Replay production chat and agent traces (<$20k) and measure the dedup ratio that 4 KB content hashing finds beyond vLLM APC / RadixAttention. Close the idea if the gain is under 5%.
physics.prior_art: vLLM automatic prefix caching, SGLang RadixAttention, HICAMP content-addressed memory (ASPLOS 2012), Linux KSM.

innovation.key_insight: Shared system prompts make KV highly redundant across users; content-addressed blocks store each shared prefix once.
innovation.killer_doubt: Host software already deduplicates exactly (vLLM automatic prefix caching, SGLang RadixAttention) with no hashing hardware. Base-die hashing adds latency and recovers nothing the scheduler misses.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Measure the duplicate 4 KB blocks left in HBM after RadixAttention on an agent-heavy trace. If under 10%, hardware dedup is moot. Software only, under $10k.
innovation.prior_art: vLLM automatic prefix caching; SGLang RadixAttention; hardware-deduplicated memory (HICAMP, ASPLOS 2012).

title: Index-list gather engine returns only packed useful words
idea: Ideal: the memory already knows which words you need. Closest achievable: the host sends a list of 4-8 byte indices (embedding rows, sparse nonzeros, KV pages) over the command path, and the base die does bank-parallel fetches and returns densely packed 64 B lines holding only the requested words.

physics.key_insight: Packing sub-line words saves link bytes for truly sparse 4-8 B gathers, and the base-die command path is the right place to do it.
physics.killer_doubt: Each word still opens a 1-2 KB page, so activation and on-die movement (~2/3 of ~3.5 pJ/bit) stay. Embedding rows are 128-512 B, so most traffic gains <=1.3x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Run a trace-driven Ramulator2 study of DLRM, SpMV and paged-KV gathers with packed returns. Report link bytes and total pJ per useful bit. Software, ~$30k.
physics.prior_art: Impulse memory controller (Utah 1999), GS-DRAM (MICRO 2015), TensorDIMM (MICRO 2019), RecNMP (ISCA 2020), Samsung AxDIMM (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: For sub-64 B random words (graphs, sparse matrices, small embeddings), memory-side gather-and-pack removes the 80-95% of link bytes that are wasted.
innovation.killer_doubt: AI's dominant bytes (weights, 2 KB+ per-token KV, 128-512 B embedding rows) are already 64 B-granular, so the gain is limited to perhaps <10% of HBM traffic.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Profile LLM decode, DLRM and GNN traces for the share of 64 B lines with <25% useful bytes. If it is under 10% of bytes, stop; otherwise model a base-die gather unit in Ramulator. Under $50k.
innovation.prior_art: Impulse memory controller (Utah, 1999), GS-DRAM (MICRO 2015), RecNMP (ISCA 2020), Samsung AxDIMM embedding lookup in the buffer chip.

title: Poor man's HBM on commercial HDI substrates
idea: Substitute the silicon interposer with a commercial mSAP HDI board (15 um lines) carrying bare LPDDR5X dies flip-chipped within 3 mm of an FPGA/ASIC, running a 1024-bit bus at a modest 2-3 Gb/s per pin.

physics.key_insight: LPDDR beside the ASIC on an organic substrate gives a few hundred GB/s with no TSVs or CoWoS: real cost relief for mid-tier accelerators.
physics.killer_doubt: A 1024-bit bus needs ~32 x32 LPDDR dies (~50-70 mm2 each), which cannot sit within 3 mm. Apple M-Ultra already ships 1024-bit LPDDR5 at ~800 GB/s.
physics.decisive_experiment: Lay out a 1024-bit LPDDR5X ring on 15 um mSAP; run SI/PI and a cost model against packaged on-substrate LPDDR5X (Grace/SOCAMM style). ~$150k; expect parity, not a step change.
physics.prior_art: Apple M1/M2 Ultra 1024-bit in-package LPDDR5; NVIDIA Grace on-package LPDDR5X; SOCAMM; Phase B N-74 (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Wide, slow, short-reach LPDDR on cheap organic substrate trades bandwidth density for cost, sidestepping TSVs and CoWoS; a valid capacity tier beside or instead of HBM.
innovation.killer_doubt: LPDDR5X dies are x32, so 1024 bits need ~32 dies (~2,000 mm2) within 3 mm of the ASIC; ~10 native-speed dies give ~400 GB/s, a third of one HBM3E stack.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Floorplan and signal-integrity study: place LPDDR5X dies around a 600 mm2 ASIC on mSAP HDI, simulate 2.5-9.6 Gb/s channels, and compare GB/s per mm of shoreline and $/GB/s against HBM3E. Under $50k.
innovation.prior_art: Apple M-series Ultra ~1024-bit in-package LPDDR5 (~800 GB/s); NVIDIA Grace LPDDR5X; SK hynix LLW for Apple R1; Eliyan HBM-on-organic; JEDEC Wide I/O 2.

title: Reverse fab: harvest, retest and rebin retired server DRAM
idea: First principle: DRAM has effectively unlimited endurance and no dominant wear-out, so a 5-year-old die is physically almost as good as new. Build automated lines that desolder DRAM packages from retired DIMMs and boards, reball them, run full BIST, retention and row-hammer binning, and assemble certified second-life modules.

physics.key_insight: Correct first principle: DRAM has no dominant cell wear-out, so second-life bits are nearly as good as new and need no wafer capacity.
physics.killer_doubt: Field data show correctable-error incidence rising with DIMM age (Schroeder 2009). Die-level harvest adds reflow loss and cost, and cannot make DDR4 dies serve DDR5 sockets.
physics.decisive_experiment: Reball 1,000 harvested packages and compare BIST fallout and retention with intact DIMMs. Then age-stratify CE rates on 200 DIMMs over 3 months. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: Meta Vistara and Marvell Structera X reuse whole DDR4 DIMMs via CXL (via search snippet); Schroeder et al. 2009 DRAM field study (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: The first-principles premise holds: a five-year-old DRAM die is nearly as good as new, so recovered bits arrive in months rather than fab-years.
innovation.killer_doubt: Same mechanism as I-04852 and R16 I-00224. R16 put retiring DDR4 at ~5-7 EB/yr (~15% of bit output), but resale channels and CXL controllers already capture it.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Covered by I-04852: measure desolder/reball fallout and the retention tail on 1,000 harvested packages against controls left on DIMMs. Under $100k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X; ITRenew/Iron Mountain resale; R16 I-00224 and I-10802.

title: OMI done right: generation-agnostic CXL buffer reuses retired DDR4
idea: IBM's OpenCAPI Memory Interface (and FB-DIMM before it) died tied to one CPU vendor and one buffer supplier. Fix: an open CXL Type-3 card whose buffer drives DDR3, DDR4 or DDR5 on its back side, so DIMMs pulled from retired servers go back into new servers behind CXL, with the buffer adding ECC and patrol scrub to manage aged parts.

physics.key_insight: OMI and FB-DIMM died of single-vendor lock-in, not physics; an open generation-agnostic CXL buffer with ECC and patrol scrub is the right way to manage aged parts.
physics.killer_doubt: Already shipping as commercial CXL-DDR4 controllers. DDR3 adds 4 Gb dies at a third of DDR4 bandwidth, not worth a PHY. Retiring server DRAM is ~6-10% of bit demand.
physics.decisive_experiment: Buy a commercial CXL-DDR4 card (~$20k), fill it with 5-7-year-old RDIMMs, and log 30 days of corrected errors, retention and row-hammer events under production traces; nothing new needs building.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) reuses DDR4 behind CXL; Marvell Structera X and Astera Leo CXL controllers support DDR4 (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: OMI and FB-DIMM died of single-vendor lock-in; an open, generation-agnostic CXL Type-3 buffer with ECC and patrol scrub lets retired DIMMs serve new CPUs.
innovation.killer_doubt: Marvell Structera X already drives DDR4 behind CXL. DDR3's 4 Gb dies give ~16 GB per DIMM at ~2-3x DDR5 watts per GB, so the generation-agnostic part adds little.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Price a three-PHY versus DDR4-only controller (die area and NRE from a PHY IP quote) and count DDR3 versus DDR4 GB in 2026 ITAD lots. Drop DDR3 support if under 10% of reusable GB. ~$20k.
innovation.prior_art: IBM OMI / Microchip SMC 1000; FB-DIMM AMB; Marvell Structera X (DDR4/DDR5 CXL); Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024) [training knowledge].

title: Page-age compression ladder across ns-to-hour timescales
idea: Time-scale tiering: hardware in the CXL expander compresses pages by idle age. Pages idle for 1 s get LZ4, 1 min gets zstd with dictionary, and 1 h gets deduplicated, compressed and parked in flash, while hot pages stay raw.

physics.key_insight: Idle-age tiered compression is pure logic and adds capacity without wafers.
physics.killer_doubt: Fleet data show ~20-30% cold memory at ~3x compression, a ~15-25% saving, not 1.6-2.5x. Hyperscalers and CXL-compression vendors already ship it.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed beyond replaying a public memory trace (e.g., Google/Meta far-memory data) through an LZ4/zstd age ladder simulator, about $20k.
physics.prior_art: Google software-defined far memory (zswap, ASPLOS 2019); Meta TMO (ASPLOS 2022); OCP hyperscale CXL tiered-memory expander with compression; ZeroPoint.

innovation.key_insight: Much fleet DRAM holds pages idle for seconds or longer; age-graded compression plus flash offload recovers capacity with logic only, no wafers.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already deployed at scale: Meta TMO reports ~20-32% memory savings, not 1.6-2.5x, and Marvell Structera CXL expanders already offer inline LZ4 compression.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay a production page-access trace through a simulator of the three-tier ladder; compare effective capacity and p99 latency against zswap plus TMO-style offload; proceed only if gain exceeds 1.3x.
innovation.prior_art: Google software-defined far memory (ASPLOS 2019), Meta TMO (ASPLOS 2022), Linux zswap, Marvell Structera, ZeroPoint Technologies compression IP.

title: Semantic snapshots: background apps keep only re-creatable state
idea: Imposed limit: a background phone app gets 2 MB. The OS makes each app serialize a semantic snapshot (navigation stack, form inputs, scroll positions, auth tokens) and then discards its heap; on relaunch the app rehydrates from the snapshot and a cached UI layout instead of restoring the whole heap.

physics.key_insight: Phone DRAM is sized partly for warm apps; forcing small, re-creatable state would decouple perceived warmth from resident heap.
physics.killer_doubt: Android saved-instance state, the low-memory killer, the cached-app freezer and zRAM already do this; on-device LLMs (Apple Intelligence needs 8 GB) now set phone RAM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Profile 50 popular apps on 6 GB vs 12 GB Android phones (~$50k): measure relaunch time and state loss after forced process death, and whether OEM RAM tiers could shift.
physics.prior_art: Android saved-instance state and process-death restore; iOS state restoration; Android cached-app freezer; zRAM swap.

innovation.key_insight: Re-creatable app state is kilobytes while warm heaps are hundreds of MB. OS-enforced semantic snapshots would trade heap residency for relaunch work.
innovation.killer_doubt: Android saved-instance state and low-memory-killer already do this. Phone DRAM growth is now driven by on-device models (a 3B INT4 model is ~2 GB resident), not warm apps.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Trace 20 top Android apps under 2 MB background caps and measure relaunch latency against warm resume ($100k). Compare the freed GB with the resident size of on-device AI models.
innovation.prior_art: Android onSaveInstanceState/SavedStateHandle and LMK, iOS state restoration, Marvin (USENIX ATC 2020) mobile memory management.

title: Client-parked compressed KV state between conversation turns
idea: After each turn, the server sends the user's device or the nearest edge PoP a compressed, encrypted latent state of ~0.5-2 MB (MLA-style low-rank KV or a distilled gist-token set). The next request uploads it back. The datacenter then holds no per-session state across gaps of minutes to days.

physics.key_insight: If session state really could be distilled to ~1 MB without losing quality, that compression would cut server KV residency directly. Parking it on clients is secondary.
physics.killer_doubt: Even MLA KV is ~70 KB/token: 8k tokens is 560 MB, ~4 minutes of uplink at 20 Mb/s. Idle KV already moves to NVMe (DeepSeek, Mooncake), not DRAM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Software study (<$50k): score gist or KV distillation at 0.5-2 MB per 8k-32k-token session on multi-turn benchmarks against full KV. If quality holds, use it server-side first.
physics.prior_art: CacheGen (SIGCOMM 2024) compresses KV into bitstreams for network transfer; gist tokens (Mu 2023); Mooncake and LMCache SSD KV tiers. Client parking: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Session state between turns need not sit in datacenter memory. An idle session can live anywhere cheap, and a compact latent would make it portable.
innovation.killer_doubt: Exact 32k-token 70B KV is ~10 GB (MLA ~2.3 GB), so 0.5-2 MB needs ~1000x lossy gisting. Resending ~100 KB of tokens and re-prefilling already makes servers stateless.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Compress 32k-token sessions of an 8B model to 1 MB gist latents. Measure next-turn answer quality and prefill FLOPs against exact KV restore from server NVMe and against plain re-prefill.
innovation.prior_art: Stateless chat APIs that resend history; gist tokens (Mu et al. 2023); AttentionStore/CachedAttention (ATC 2024), LMCache and Mooncake KV tiers.

title: IBM MXT, fixed: compression moved behind CXL where latency is free
idea: MXT (2000) compressed all memory in 1 KB sectors behind a 32 MB L3, so every miss paid decompression and the extra cache chip cost more than the DRAM saved. Put an LZ4/zstd engine inside a CXL Type-3 expander that already costs ~150-250 ns, compress at 4 KB with a 64 MB uncompressed hot-line buffer, and expose 2-3x physical capacity as plain memory.

physics.key_insight: Correct diagnosis of MXT: compression latency is free only where a hop already costs ~200 ns, so CXL Type-3 expanders are the right host.
physics.killer_doubt: Already commercial. AI-era data (BF16/FP8 weights, KV, activations) compresses losslessly only ~1.1-1.3x, so the capacity gain collapses exactly where DRAM demand grows.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing is needed for the concept. To bound effective capacity per workload, dump pages from LLM serving and general servers and measure LZ4/zstd ratio distributions (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: IBM MXT (2000); OCP hyperscale CXL tiered-memory expander with inline compression; ZeroPoint Technologies; Google zswap far memory. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: MXT's error was putting decompression on the cache-miss path. A CXL expander already pays ~150-250 ns, so inline LZ4 can hide there and turn a 2-3x ratio into capacity.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already being commercialized. Capacity depends on the data: incompressible or encrypted pages (~1.0x) overflow the advertised 2-3x and force OS ballooning, the integration problem that kept MXT niche.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None for novelty. A user would benchmark a shipping compressed CXL expander on fleet page traces for effective ratio, tail latency and overflow events under 10% incompressible churn.
innovation.prior_art: IBM MXT (2000-01); IBM POWER Active Memory Expansion with on-chip compression; ZeroPoint Technologies compressed-memory IP; commercial CXL compression controllers (screener note).

title: Minify graphs with gap-coded adjacency and hardware decoder
idea: Minify web and social graph adjacency using WebGraph-style reference copying, gap and zeta coding. A near-memory decoder streams neighbor lists at line rate to the graph engine.

physics.key_insight: WebGraph reaches ~2-3 bits/link on web graphs, against 32-64 bits for raw adjacency, so a 10-20x footprint cut is real for web-crawl graphs.
physics.killer_doubt: Social graphs compress only to ~8-12 bits/edge (~3-4x). Software decoders (Ligra+) already run near uncompressed speed, and SpZip built the hardware. Graph analytics is a tiny share of DRAM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Nothing new is needed at first. Benchmark Ligra+ and WebGraph-decoded BFS and PageRank on Twitter and ClueWeb against SpZip's published results. Add hardware only if software decode is >2x slower (<$20k).
physics.prior_art: WebGraph (Boldi-Vigna 2004); Ligra+ (DCC 2015); Log(Graph) (PACT 2018); SpZip hardware decompression (ISCA 2021). From memory.

innovation.key_insight: WebGraph gap and zeta coding cuts adjacency to a few bits per edge. A line-rate decoder would remove the decompression cost.
innovation.killer_doubt: Software already does this: GBBS/Ligra+ run the 128B-edge Hyperlink2012 graph on one 1 TB server, and SpZip (MICRO'21) decompresses in hardware. Graph analytics is a small DRAM share.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Model a near-memory decoder against GBBS compressed-graph software on a 1 TB server for BFS, PageRank and CC, using a SpZip-style simulator. If the speedup is under 1.5x, drop. About $40k.
innovation.prior_art: WebGraph (Boldi-Vigna 2004), Ligra+ (DCC 2015), GBBS (SPAA 2018), SpZip (Yang, Emer, Sanchez, MICRO 2021) [training knowledge].

title: Minify replica count: consolidate long-tail models by global routing
idea: Minify how many places each model's weights must be resident: a global router concentrates all traffic for each long-tail model onto the fewest replicas that meet the SLO, and cold models page in from NVMe in under a second.

physics.key_insight: Long-tail fine-tune fleets keep >=1 warm replica per model; pooling them onto shared GPUs with fast loading frees much pinned HBM, mainly for multi-tenant model hosts.
physics.killer_doubt: Prior art already ships it. 'Under 1 s' load holds only to ~13B: 70 GB FP8 at ~55 GB/s PCIe5 x16 takes ~1.3 s even before NVMe striping limits.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. For the forecast: replay a public multi-model trace (Azure LLM, BurstGPT) through ServerlessLLM-style pooling and report GB-HBM-hours per model at a fixed p99 TTFT SLO.
physics.prior_art: ServerlessLLM (OSDI'24), AlpaServe, S-LoRA/Punica multi-adapter serving, Alibaba Aegaeon (SOSP'25) token-level multi-model GPU pooling.

innovation.key_insight: Long-tail fine-tune fleets pin at least one warm replica per model; pooling them onto shared GPUs with fast weight loading frees real pinned HBM for multi-model hosts.
innovation.killer_doubt: Already shipping in research and production. 'Under 1 s' cold start holds only to ~13B: 70 GB FP8 over PCIe5 x16 (~55 GB/s) takes ~1.3 s before NVMe limits.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed for novelty. For sizing only: replay a public multi-model trace (Azure LLM, BurstGPT) through ServerlessLLM-style pooling and report HBM GB-hours per model at a fixed p99 TTFT.
innovation.prior_art: ServerlessLLM (OSDI'24), AlpaServe, S-LoRA/Punica multi-adapter serving, Alibaba Aegaeon GPU pooling (SOSP'25), serverless LLM hosts (Together, Fireworks).

title: Demoscene 64k coder: neural texture compression plugin for game engines
idea: Demosceners fit whole worlds in 64 KB. An Unreal/Godot plugin encodes each material's texture stack (albedo, normal, roughness and more) into a small latent grid plus a tiny MLP decoded in the shader at sample time, replacing block-compressed mip chains. A 4-person team can build it in 24 months.

physics.key_insight: Textures dominate game and VR memory, and neural texture compression gives a 4-8x VRAM cut over BCn when decoded at sample time.
physics.killer_doubt: VRAM is saved only with decode-at-sample. GPUs lacking matrix cores (consoles, mobile, VR) transcode to BCn on load instead, saving disk, not DRAM. NVIDIA ships the SDK.
physics.decisive_experiment: None for novelty. For the forecast: measure frame-time cost and VRAM cut of NTC decode-at-sample on 3 GPU tiers in one Unreal scene.
physics.prior_art: NVIDIA RTX Neural Texture Compression SDK and SIGGRAPH'23 random-access neural texture paper; AMD neural block compression research.

innovation.key_insight: Textures dominate game and VR memory, and neural texture compression decoded at sample time cuts VRAM 4-8x versus BCn.
innovation.killer_doubt: VRAM is saved only when decoding at sample time; consoles, mobile and VR without matrix cores transcode to BCn on load, saving disk, not DRAM. NVIDIA already ships the SDK.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None for novelty. For sizing: measure frame-time cost and VRAM cut of decode-at-sample NTC on three GPU tiers in one Unreal scene.
innovation.prior_art: NVIDIA RTX Neural Texture Compression SDK and SIGGRAPH'23 random-access neural textures; AMD neural texture block compression; DirectX cooperative vectors.

title: Bootstrapped T-switch gain cell zeroes leakage across its write path
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality + #25 Self-service: write the gain-cell storage node through two series transistors and drive their middle node from the cell's own source-follower output, the guard trick from electrometers and sample-and-hold circuits. The inner transistor then sees ~0 V drain-source, so subthreshold leakage collapses.

physics.key_insight: Equipotential guarding is sound: subthreshold leakage scales with 1-exp(-Vds/kT), so holding the mid node within 0.5 mV of the storage node would cut it ~50x.
physics.killer_doubt: In-cell source followers carry Vgs ~0.4 V and ~20 mV mismatch: 20 mV residual gives only ~1.9x, and 1 nA follower bias per cell is ~1 A per Gb.
physics.decisive_experiment: 28 nm MPW eDRAM macro (~$150k): 3T vs bootstrapped 5T cells, 1 Mb retention distributions at 85 C. Kill if tail gain <10x at <1.5x area with zero static bias.
physics.prior_art: Electrometer guards; bootstrapped sample-and-hold switches; Giterman/Teman 4T feedback gain cells (~2016-18); IGZO access transistors already reach ~1 aA.

innovation.key_insight: A guard-driven T-switch zeroes drain-source voltage across the inner write FET, suppressing subthreshold leakage in Si gain-cell eDRAM. It is cheap to verify on an MPW.
innovation.killer_doubt: Junction, GIDL and gate leakage remain. A live source follower per cell draws static current. Realistic gain is ~10x, against IGZO's native ~1e3x lower off-current.
innovation.decisive_experiment: 28/40 nm MPW (~$150k) with 2T, 3T-guarded and 4T internal-feedback gain-cell arrays. Measure retention tails at 85 C, area and standby power per bit.
innovation.prior_art: Internal-feedback/leakage-compensated 4T gain cells (Teman, Meinerzhagen, Burg et al., ~2014); T-switch in sample-and-hold circuits [training knowledge].

title: Open capacitorless memory macro qualified at every U.S. logic fab
idea: Ideal: every fab already in the country is a memory fab. Closest: a CHIPS-funded open PDK macro (gain-cell array, sense amps, refresh controller) qualified on Intel 18A, TSMC Arizona, GlobalFoundries and SkyWater flows, so any U.S. chip can carry hundreds of MB on-die and GB-class stacked working memory without a DRAM fab.

physics.key_insight: If a qualified open gain-cell macro exists, every U.S. logic wafer start can carry memory without per-customer memory IP or NDA friction.
physics.killer_doubt: Si gain cells in FinFET or GAA retain ~10-100 us at 85 C and give only ~1.5-2x HD-SRAM density. Leading foundries will not publish 18A or N4 macros openly.
physics.decisive_experiment: Tape out a 2T/3T gain-cell macro on SkyWater 130 and GF 22FDX MPWs. Measure 85 C retention distributions, refresh power and bits/mm2 against foundry SRAM. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: Academic Si gain-cell eDRAM macros (Teman, Burg, Giterman); OpenRAM compiler; Phase B N-35 BEOL oxide gain cells (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Qualifying one gain-cell macro across U.S. logic flows makes on-die MB-scale memory a standard block, trimming off-chip DRAM demand for caches and KV buffers.
innovation.killer_doubt: At ~0.03 um2/bit a GB needs ~300 mm2 of a ~$25k logic wafer, ~$100-150/GB against ~$20/GB contract DRAM. Foundries will not open their 18A or N4 PDKs.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Port an OpenRAM-style 2T gain-cell macro to SKY130 and GF 22FDX MPWs. Measure retention, refresh power and bits/mm2 at 85 C, then publish the cost per MB against SRAM and HBM. ~$250k.
innovation.prior_art: OpenRAM on SKY130 (UCSC); Bar-Ilan/EPFL Si gain cells; imec IGZO 2T0C BEOL; SEL NOSRAM; R07 I-01411 (DROP) [training knowledge].

title: Thermophoretic wafer shielding allows ISO-7 cleanrooms for DRAM fabs
idea: Effect: thermophoresis. Every exposed wafer is held 10-20 K warmer than the gas around it inside sealed carriers and tool mini-environments; the thermophoretic force pushes sub-100 nm particles away from the warm surface, cutting deposition velocity by more than 100x, so the ballroom can be ISO 7 instead of ISO 3-4.

physics.key_insight: Thermophoresis is real and nearly size-independent: a 10 K/mm gradient gives ~0.03 cm/s outward drift, beating diffusion deposition for particles down to ~10-20 nm.
physics.killer_doubt: FOUP/EFEM mini-environments already let ballrooms run ~ISO 5-6 (est.). Scanners hold wafers to ~mK, and a 10 K offset expands 300 mm Si ~8 um. AMC is untouched.
physics.decisive_experiment: Count 20-100 nm particle adders on bare wafers held 0, 5, 10 and 20 K above ambient in an ISO-7 room and an ISO-4 room, using a surface scanner. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: Ye, Pui, Liu, Fissan et al. on thermophoretic wafer deposition (J. Aerosol Sci. ~1991, from memory); Sandia thermophoretic EUV-mask protection; SMIF/FOUP mini-environments.

innovation.key_insight: A 10-20 K wafer-to-gas gap drives sub-micron particles away at ~0.2 mm/s, faster than diffusion deposition, so particle protection can travel with the wafer instead of the building.
innovation.killer_doubt: FOUP/EFEM mini-environments already isolate wafers, so the ballroom sets little yield. Cleanroom systems are ~5-10% of fab capex (estimate), so ISO 5 to ISO 7 saves ~2-4%.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Expose heated (+15 K) and ambient bare wafers in ISO 5 and ISO 7 air inside a FOUP-like enclosure for 24 h, then count added particles >20 nm on a wafer inspector. Under $100k.
innovation.prior_art: Stratmann/Fissan heated-wafer thermophoretic suppression (late 1980s); Sandia/Intel thermophoretic EUV-mask protection; FOUP/SMIF mini-environment fabs [training knowledge].

title: Lunar-base abundant-element PDK: a gain cell from only eight elements
idea: A Moon-base fab could use only regolith-abundant elements, so impose that rule in a university nanofab: build a 2T gain-cell array from Si, O, N, Al, Ti and H (plus B/P dopants) only, with poly-Si channels, LPCVD SiO2/Si3N4, ALD Al2O3, sputtered Al and TiN, and contact lithography on 100 mm wafers. Benchmark retention against a W/ZrO2 reference.

physics.key_insight: Shows W, Hf, Zr, In and Ga are not physically required; a chokepoint-free element list is a useful resilience constraint for any U.S. memory flow.
physics.killer_doubt: Poly-Si TFT off-current ~0.1-1 pA versus the 13 fA tail: a 1 fF node keeps 0.2 V only ~0.2-2 ms. Contact-litho density is ~1e4-1e5x below 1b.
physics.decisive_experiment: No device run needed; it would reproduce 1970s data. Cheaper: a paper audit of which chokepoint elements DRAM truly needs (W to Mo/Ru, Hf to Zr), costed per wafer.
physics.prior_art: 1970s 3T/2T gain-cell DRAM (Intel 1103 3T cell); modern Si gain-cell eDRAM; poly-Si TFT memory studies.

innovation.key_insight: A useful supply-chain stress test: it shows which DRAM elements (W, Hf, Zr, In, Ga) can really be substituted at trailing nodes.
innovation.killer_doubt: Without In/Ga/Zn the channel must be poly-Si. Off-current ~1e-13 A/um gives ~2 ms retention on a 1 fF node, against 64 ms or more needed.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Paper exercise first: mass per GB and available substitutes for W, Hf and Zr in a DDR5 bill of materials. Fab a ~$50k poly-Si 2T array only if a non-substitutable element appears.
innovation.prior_art: 1970s 3T silicon-gate DRAM (Intel 1103); poly-Si TFT gain cells; Mo already replacing W in 3D NAND wordlines.

title: Self-service: read-write-read self-reference removes matched sense amp pairs
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: each read samples the bitline after charge sharing, writes a known '1', shares again and samples a second time, comparing the cell with itself on one capacitor pair; device mismatch, reference bitlines and dummy cells cancel, so sloppy TFT or 180 nm transistors can serve as the sense amp.

physics.key_insight: Sampling one cell twice (its data, then a written '1') through one comparator cancels amplifier offset and Cs/Cbl spread: a reference-free, single-ended read suited to TFT periphery over 3D arrays.
physics.killer_doubt: Destructive 1T1C read needs one amp per bitline (~0.2-0.3 um2 at 1b pitch); a 180 nm amp is ~50x larger. Read grows to ~3x tRC (~135 ns), ~3x array energy.
physics.decisive_experiment: IGZO TFT test chip (university fab, ~$250k): 64 1T1C cells per bitline with a self-referenced auto-zeroed comparator; measure residual offset, read BER versus Cs (1-5 fF), and total read latency at 85 C.
physics.prior_art: Offset-cancelling bitline sense amps in recent production DRAM nodes; destructive self-reference reads in MRAM and FeRAM since the early 2000s.

innovation.key_insight: Sampling one bitline twice through the same comparator cancels device offset and removes reference bitlines, so sloppy TFT or 180 nm devices could sense.
innovation.killer_doubt: Each read costs an extra write plus a restore (~3x tRC, ~2x array energy). Auto-zero and offset-cancelling sense amps already cancel 20-50 mV mismatch without the extra write (N-27).
innovation.decisive_experiment: SPICE plus a 180 nm MPW test array: compare self-reference with auto-zero (N-27) on sense margin, tRC and energy per read, at 50 mV injected offset, on 1T1C and IGZO cells. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: MRAM destructive self-reference sensing (Jeong et al., JSSC 2003); offset-cancellation DRAM sense amps; study N-27 auto-zero TFT sense amps [training knowledge].

title: Alien measures memory in entropy: sell 'effective GB' modules
idea: Aliens count entropy, not bytes. Memory makers sell CXL modules whose controller does inline ANS/LZ compression, cache-line dedup and zero-page elision, plus fabric-wide dedup of identical pages (model weights, OS images, KV-cache prefixes) across 1,000 hosts. They price per effective GB.

physics.key_insight: Pricing per effective GB pushes compression into the memory controller, where it is cheapest; random-access line compression gives ~1.5-2x on general server data.
physics.killer_doubt: Dedup across 1,000 hosts cannot be load/store: multi-hop CXL lookups add ~0.5-1 us. BF16 weights compress only ~1.3x and accelerator weights sit in HBM, so 10x falls to ~2x.
physics.decisive_experiment: FPGA CXL Type-3 prototype (~$200k) with LZ4-class line compression and a hash-dedup table; replay host-memory snapshots from 20 inference and 20 general servers; measure effective capacity ratio and added load latency.
physics.prior_art: IBM MXT compressed main memory (2001); ZeroPoint CXL compression IP; HICAMP (ASPLOS 2012); Linux KSM. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Pricing per effective GB shifts data-reduction risk to the vendor, as storage arrays did; fleets with identical weights and prompt prefixes are the one place 10x is plausible.
innovation.killer_doubt: Weights live in HBM; prefix sharing is already software (vLLM, Mooncake). Confidential VMs (SEV-SNP/TDX) hold ciphertext that neither compresses nor dedups, capping general workloads near 1.5-2x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Snapshot host DRAM of 100 AI-inference nodes and 100 general cloud hosts; compute 64 B-line LZ4 ratio and cross-host 4 KB duplicate fraction, excluding encrypted VMs. Kill below 2x effective. ~$60k.
innovation.prior_art: Marvell Structera A inline-LZ4 CXL expander; ZeroPoint compression IP; IBM MXT; HICAMP dedup (ASPLOS 2012); storage effective-capacity pricing [training knowledge].

title: Compact-then-sleep: compress, pack, partial-array self-refresh
idea: The memory controller (phone SoC or server CXL controller) carries a hardware compaction engine. When it detects idle, it walks live pages, LZ4-compresses them (2-3x is typical for Marvell-class engines), packs them into the lowest segments and updates a remap table. It then issues partial-array self-refresh (PASR) masks that leave the vacated segments unrefreshed. Combined with B4-02's ECC-stretched self-refresh interval (1 s at 85 C, longer when cool). On wake, pages decompress on first touch (us-scale, like a minor fault) or eagerly in the background.

physics.key_insight: Compaction before self-refresh lets partial-array masks stop refresh on vacated segments; useful for phones and idle CXL pools.
physics.killer_doubt: Saves idle refresh only (~0.5 W per 64 GB RDIMM); the /32-48 comes from N-63's ECC-stretched interval, compaction gives 2-3x. Adds no bits; ~16 s break-even.
physics.decisive_experiment: None needed: a zram-plus-PASR measurement on an LPDDR5 phone board would confirm the known 2-3x idle refresh saving within a week.
physics.prior_art: LPDDR PASR; RAMZzz (SC 2012) migrates pages to power down ranks; GreenDIMM (MICRO 2021); Android zram and compaction. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Compressing before self-refresh lets PASR switch off the vacated segments. On phones, idle DRAM power directly sets standby life.
innovation.killer_doubt: Only idle refresh power improves (~0.49 W per 64 GB RDIMM), with no cost/bit or capacity gain. Linux zram plus LPDDR PASR already captures much of it; ~16 s break-even.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On an LPDDR5 phone dev board, script zram compaction and PASR masks at idle. Measure standby DRAM power and wake latency over 1-week user traces. ~$50k.
innovation.prior_art: LPDDR partial-array self-refresh; Linux zram/zswap and compaction; RAMZzz rank power-down via page migration (SC 2012) [training knowledge]; GreenDIMM sub-array power-down.

title: Functional pages: page-table entries that point to generators
idea: Much DRAM holds data derivable from a short program: hashed embeddings, lookup tables, procedural textures, constant or zero-filled arrays. Add a page-table entry type whose payload is a generator-kernel ID plus parameters; a near-memory engine synthesizes the requested 64 B line on read and caches it in a small buffer, so the bits are never stored.

physics.key_insight: The right framing: the floor is Kolmogorov complexity. Seeded-PRNG content (random projections, hashed weights, SeedLM codes) defeats line compressors yet is trivial to generate.
physics.killer_doubt: Zero pages and BDI compression already catch cheap generators. An MLP generator needs ~1 MFLOP, ~1 us per line versus 50-100 ns DRAM. In-kernel recomputation needs no new PTE type.
physics.decisive_experiment: Dump memory from 50 production servers and classify 64 B lines as zero/constant, BDI-compressible or neither. Test the residue for PRNG or affine generators. Advance only if >5% is generator-only (<$40k).
physics.prior_art: Linux zero page and KSM; Base-Delta-Immediate (PACT 2012); userfaultfd lazy fill; SeedLM (Apple 2024) PRNG-seed weights. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: A page-table entry naming a generator kernel and parameters would let a near-memory engine synthesize lines on read, so memory is bounded by description length, not raw size.
innovation.killer_doubt: Little live DRAM is generable per 64 B line. Zero pages (~10-20% of Meta's swapped pages) are already deduped, DHE rows need a full MLP, and software can compute instead.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Snapshot 5 production-like workloads. Classify pages that a generator under 1 KB can reproduce (constant, strided, PRNG, affine). If they are under 5% beyond zero pages, drop. About $40k.
innovation.prior_art: Zero-content augmented caches (Dusser 2009), KSM zero-page merging, Random123 seed regeneration; R33 I-07662 (DROP) [training knowledge].

title: Overbuild 120 tiers, fuse to 100: tier-level sparing
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: deliberately deposit ~20% more tiers than the product needs, add a per-block tier-remap register, and e-fuse out any tier that fails test (shorts, Vt outliers, weak capacitors). The process window can then be loosened (faster deposition, cheaper precursors) because whole-tier defects become yield-neutral.

physics.key_insight: Tier-granular remap makes random tier defects yield-neutral: a correct design rule every 3D-DRAM dossier should carry, not a standalone invention.
physics.killer_doubt: At 0.01 defects/tier/die over 1,000 blocks, one spare tier per block gives 99.95% die yield; 20% overbuild adds ~20% etch depth. Loosened windows cause systematic, unsparable defects.
physics.decisive_experiment: Desk yield model (<$50k) on published tier-defect data: 1-2 spare tiers per block plus vertical-bitline column sparing vs 20% overbuild; list defect classes (vertical BL shorts) tier sparing cannot fix.
physics.prior_art: 3D NAND spare blocks and word lines with bad-block tables; DRAM row/column redundancy; SK hynix 5-tier 3D DRAM at 56.1% yield.

innovation.key_insight: Spare whole tiers so tier-wide defects stop compounding with stack height. This is a useful yield feature for any 3D DRAM dossier, not a standalone invention.
innovation.killer_doubt: Through-hole and HAR-etch defects kill every tier in a string, so sparing cannot fix them; 20% more tiers means ~20% more deposition and a 20% deeper etch.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Monte Carlo yield model (~$50k) fed with published 3D-NAND defect classes: what share of killers is tier-wide versus through-hole, and the net cost/bit at 100+20 versus 100 tiers.
innovation.prior_art: Row/column/block redundancy is universal; 3D NAND uses dummy word lines and bad-block remapping; HBM has spare TSVs and channel repair [training knowledge].

title: Thousand-composition sputter library hunts for k-over-100 dielectrics
