idea: MAGNIFY experiment throughput ~1000x: co-sputter three targets with deliberate thickness gradients onto one 150-mm wafer pre-patterned with 1,000 MIM test capacitors, then auto-probe k, leakage at 1 V and breakdown overnight, screening ternary oxide spaces such as Ti-Zr-La-O weekly.

physics.key_insight: Measuring k, leakage and breakdown on one wafer at final thickness is the right screen; libraries cheaply map the k-versus-band-gap frontier.
physics.killer_doubt: k and band gap trade off (Eg near ~3 eV at k 70-100); 50-100 nm sputtered films overstate k versus 5-8 nm ALD in 60:1 holes with interfacial dead layers.
physics.decisive_experiment: Run the library at 6 nm on TiN/Ru with a 450 C anneal; go only if any spot shows EOT <=0.4 nm at <=1e-7 A/cm2 and 0.8 V. ~$150k.
physics.prior_art: Van Dover et al. Bell Labs Zr-Sn-Ti-O composition spread (Nature 1998); Intermolecular combinatorial high-k programme with Elpida for DRAM (~2010).

innovation.key_insight: Composition-spread MIM libraries make dielectric screening fast and cheap. They are useful lab infrastructure, not an invention.
innovation.killer_doubt: Planar sputtered spreads do not predict ALD films in 60:1 holes. Known k 80-150 oxides (rutile TiO2, STO) leak ~1e-6 to 1e-5 A/cm2, and k 40->70 buys only 1.75x charge.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None worth funding standalone. If pursued, run ALD gradient libraries on Ru/RuO2 bottom electrodes for the 5 best DFT candidates (~$150k), judged at EOT <=0.4 nm and 1e-7 A/cm2.
innovation.prior_art: van Dover et al., Bell Labs, Nature 1998 (Zr-Sn-Ti-O spread); Intermolecular HPC programs with DRAM makers (Elpida); SNU Hwang group TiO2/STO [training knowledge].

title: Token-synchronous memory: decode sweeps restore every row each token
idea: Align the workload clock with the leakage clock: LLM decode reads all dense weights and active KV each token (~20-50 ms) and every DRAM read restores its row, so the refresh engine is removed from the die; a 1-bit-per-row coverage bitmap faults if any row goes unread for one retention window, and sparse MoE experts live in an NV tier.

physics.key_insight: Each decode step's weight and KV sweep does restore its rows. A 1-bit-per-row coverage map lets the controller skip refresh for rows already read.
physics.killer_doubt: Decode steps of ~20-50 ms straddle the 32 ms tREFW (16 ms hot), and idle KV stays unread. Refresh is only ~5-20% of bandwidth, and REF-borne TRR is lost.
physics.decisive_experiment: Replay vLLM decode traces (dense 70B and MoE) through a Ramulator2 HBM3 model with a row-coverage bitmap. If >20% of rows miss a 32 ms window, stop. <$50k.
physics.prior_art: Smart Refresh (Ghosh and Lee, MICRO 2007) skips refresh for recently accessed rows; RANA (ISCA 2018) for NN eDRAM; Phase B N-73, N-64.

innovation.key_insight: Weight-streaming decode activates every weight row each 20-50 ms token, inside the 32-64 ms window, so refreshing those rows is redundant; a coverage bitmap makes skipping safe.
innovation.killer_doubt: Gain caps at the refresh tax on weight rows only (~5-10% bandwidth); KV, activations, OS pages and idle servers still need refresh, so the engine cannot leave the die.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay vLLM decode traces in Ramulator 2 with per-row last-activation times; measure the share of rows touched within 32 ms and the bandwidth recovered by skipping their REFs. ~$30k.
innovation.prior_art: Smart Refresh (Ghosh and Lee, MICRO 2007) skips recently accessed rows; RANA (ISCA 2018) skips eDRAM refresh using DNN data lifetime [training knowledge].

title: Moth-ear minimal-periphery eDRAM compiler for open U.S. PDKs
idea: Noctuid moths detect bats with ears of just two neurons. An open-source compiler for SkyWater 130/GF180 generates 3T gain-cell eDRAM macros with radically minimal periphery: single-ended inverter sensing, shared counter refresh and standard-cell decoders. Two shuttles validate it for ~$700k in 24 months.

physics.key_insight: Minimal-periphery 3T gain-cell macros on open US PDKs are cheap to prove and could seed a domestic memory-design base.
physics.killer_doubt: Already exists as OpenGCRAM. At 130-180 nm a 3T cell is ~1-2 um2, under ~1 Mb/mm2, so one GB needs ~8,600 mm2: no effect on the RAM supply.
physics.decisive_experiment: Port OpenGCRAM to SKY130/GF180, then measure 85 C retention and refresh power on one shuttle. If density is not 2x SRAM with refresh included, stop. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: OpenGCRAM (Stanford, arXiv 2507.10849, via search snippet), built on OpenRAM; RAAAM commercial 3T gain-cell compiler.

innovation.key_insight: An open gain-cell macro compiler on SKY130/GF180 gives domestic mature fabs a block 2-3x denser than SRAM and trains memory designers.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 130 nm 3T cell is ~1-2 um2 against ~0.001 um2 for 1b DRAM, >1,000x less dense, with ms-scale retention; it does not touch DRAM supply.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Not needed for this study. If funded: one SKY130 MPW (~$10-50k) of compiler output, measuring retention distribution at 85 C and density against OpenRAM SRAM macros.
innovation.prior_art: OpenRAM on SKY130 (Guthaus, UCSC); open gain-cell compilers (OpenGCRAM, 2025) [training knowledge]; Teman/Giterman and Burg gain-cell eDRAM; similar I-01800 dropped.

title: Wired-NOR zero-detect lines suppress all-zero bursts at sense stripes
idea: Satellites downlink only non-trivial data: each SA group pulls down a wired-NOR line if any latched bit is 1, so all-zero 64-byte sectors return a 1-bit flag instead of a full burst over global I/O and pins. Sparse AI activations and zero-padded KV pages benefit most.

physics.key_insight: Zero detection at the sense-amp stripe is nearly free and saves pin energy and bandwidth on all-zero sectors, compression with no decompression latency.
physics.killer_doubt: All-zero 64 B sectors are rare in dense BF16/INT4 weights and KV (est. <5%), and 2:4 sparsity leaves none. It needs a JEDEC protocol change for ~1-5% I/O energy.
physics.decisive_experiment: Software trace study (~$30k): share of all-zero 32/64 B sectors in LLM weights, KV cache, activations and OS pages across real serving workloads. Stop if below 10% of traffic.
physics.prior_art: Zero-content caches and zero-value compression (ISCA/ICS literature); DDR4/DDR5 data-bus inversion; ZeroPoint compression IP; OS zero-page deduplication.

innovation.key_insight: Detecting zeros at the sense stripe, before global I/O, saves both internal datapath and pin energy on all-zero sectors; controller-side compression saves only pin energy.
innovation.killer_doubt: Whole all-zero 64 B sectors are rare. At 90% element sparsity only 0.9^32 = 3.4% of BF16 sectors are all-zero, and paged KV caches avoid padding.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Trace study: measure the fraction of all-zero 64-byte sectors in LLM inference activation, KV and gradient traffic (vLLM, PyTorch), and model the energy saved with DRAMPower. ~$30k, weeks.
innovation.prior_art: LPDDR5 Write-X pattern writes; NVIDIA A100 compute data compression for sparse data; zero-content augmented caches (Dusser et al., 2009) [training knowledge].

title: Eliminate shred-everything policy: volatile-memory sanitization clause
idea: Eliminate the security rule that sends decommissioned DRAM to shredders: a ~$300k study measures room-temperature data remanence after power-off and drives a 'power-cycled DRAM is sanitized' clause with a verification test into NIST SP 800-88 guidance and corporate disposal policies.

physics.key_insight: Room-temperature DRAM remanence lasts seconds to minutes, so a DIMM unpowered for an hour holds no recoverable data; shredding DIMMs has no physical basis.
physics.killer_doubt: Guidance exists: manuals citing NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 treat DRAM as volatile, sanitized by power removal and a 5-10 min wait (via search snippet). Shredding volume is unmeasured.
physics.decisive_experiment: Survey 30 ITAD firms and 20 enterprises (~$50k) for the share of DIMMs destroyed; only if material, measure 24-hour remanence of 50 DDR4 and DDR5 DIMMs at 25 C.
physics.prior_art: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 volatile-memory guidance as quoted in Rohde & Schwarz security manuals (via search snippet); Halderman et al. cold-boot attacks, 2008.

innovation.key_insight: Shredding policies, not physics, can pull reusable DIMMs out of supply; an auditable verification test lets disposal policies accept power removal.
innovation.killer_doubt: Vendor manuals citing NIST 800-88 already treat 5-10 min power removal as DRAM 'Clear' (via search snippet); cold-boot work measured seconds-to-minutes room-temperature remanence. Little left to change.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Survey 30 ITAD firms and 20 enterprise disposal policies for the fraction of retired DIMMs shredded; drop if under 10%. ~$30k. Remanence physics needs no new study.
innovation.prior_art: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 (via vendor-manual search snippets); Halderman et al., cold-boot attacks (USENIX Security 2008); IEEE 2883-2022 sanitization standard.

title: Roll-to-roll web: stream tiles depth-first through every layer
idea: Activations are treated like the web in a roll-to-roll line. Each input tile runs through all layers (or a deep stage) before the next tile enters, and the overlap 'splice' halos at tile edges are recomputed. Full feature maps are never written to DRAM; only a moving web of tiles stays in on-chip SRAM. The compiler picks tile size the way a line picks web width, trading halo recompute against buffer size.

physics.key_insight: Depth-first tiling with halo recompute trades ~5-15% more FLOPs for never writing intermediate feature maps; valuable for CNN and edge-vision DRAM traffic.
physics.killer_doubt: A transformer attention layer sees the whole sequence, so the halo becomes 100% after one layer. AI DRAM is dominated by weights and KV, not activations.
physics.decisive_experiment: Compile a diffusion U-Net and a ViT with DeFiNES-style depth-first scheduling; measure DRAM bytes saved against recompute. Expect gains only in the conv stages.
physics.prior_art: Fused-layer CNN accelerators (Alwani, MICRO 2016), MCUNetV2 patch-based inference, DeFiNES depth-first scheduling, TVM/XLA fusion.

innovation.key_insight: Depth-first tile fusion with halo recompute removes intermediate DRAM traffic in conv stacks. This is valid and well known.
innovation.killer_doubt: DiT and video models use global self-attention, so after one attention layer the halo becomes the whole image. The 10-50x claim holds only for conv or local-window stacks.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None decisive. Compiler-fusion results already exist. Profiling a DiT step would confirm that attention blocks force full feature-map materialization.
innovation.prior_art: Fused-layer CNN accelerators (Alwani, MICRO 2016), MCUNetV2 patch inference (2021), DeFiNES (2023), TVM/XLA fusion, FlashAttention-style tiling.

title: Apollo core-rope weaver: frozen weights in via-programmed ROM chiplets
idea: Apollo's flight software was literally woven into core-rope ROM. Production model weights that won't change for a year are mask-programmed into dense, multi-bit, stackable via-ROM chiplets on a mature node and co-packaged beside the accelerator. HBM then holds only KV cache and activations.

physics.key_insight: Same mechanism as I-01226. Multi-bit, stacked via-ROM chiplets are the right fix for density, and offloading weights to non-DRAM would leave HBM for KV cache.
physics.killer_doubt: Even at 2 b/cell and 8-high stacks, 70 GB needs ~2,900 mm2 of footprint against ~240 mm2 for two HBM4 stacks. NAND-based HBF does the same job ~50x denser.
physics.decisive_experiment: Folded into I-01226's desk study. Add a stacked-ROM arm (2 b/cell, 8 dies, hybrid bond) and compare GB per package footprint and $/GB against HBF and HBM3E.
physics.prior_art: Taalas hard-wired model silicon (per press), High Bandwidth Flash (SanDisk/SK hynix MoU 2025), multi-level implant/via ROM in MCUs.

innovation.key_insight: Same mechanism as I-01226; multi-bit, stacked via-ROM chiplets fix some density, and moving weights off DRAM leaves HBM for KV cache.
innovation.killer_doubt: ROM at ~$3-8/GB is disposable after a 6-12-month model life; HBM at ~$20/GB is reused 5 years (~$4/GB-year), so ROM loses below ~2-year lifetimes. HBF is ~10x cheaper still.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Folded into I-01226's desk study. Add a stacked arm (2 bit/cell, 8 dies, hybrid bond) comparing GB per package footprint and $/GB-year against HBF and HBM3E.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas/AMD hardwired-weight silicon; YOLoC ROM-CiM (2022); High Bandwidth Flash (SanDisk/SK hynix, OCP spec Aug 2026).

title: Memory that rots on purpose: nanoimprinted foil for short-lived data
idea: Inverts 'memory must keep data until overwritten': roll-to-roll nanoimprint (~100 nm) 1T1C oxide-TFT arrays on metal foil with small leaky cells (1-10 ms retention, no refresh circuitry), laminate ~50 foils into a block, and let accelerators store only activations, gradients and KV pages consumed within the retention window, recomputing on rare loss.

physics.key_insight: Matching memory lifetime to data lifetime is sound, and oxide TFTs need no EUV; a cheap, slow, deliberately leaky tier for transient AI data is a legitimate product shape.
physics.killer_doubt: Steel foil (10-17 ppm/K) moves 3-5 um per kelvin over 30 cm, ~100x a 30 nm overlay budget for 100 nm TFTs. Activations live 0.1-10 s, not 1-10 ms.
physics.decisive_experiment: Measure layer-to-layer overlay of two nanoimprint levels across a 30 cm roll-to-roll web on a pilot line (~$100k); kill if 3-sigma overlay exceeds ~30 nm, then test IGZO 1T1C retention at 100 nm.
physics.prior_art: HP SAIL self-aligned roll-to-roll imprint TFTs; PragmatIC/Arm PlasticARM flexible IGZO processor with on-chip RAM (2021); display-fab oxide TFT panels.

innovation.key_insight: Lifetime-typed data could live in ms-retention cells with no refresh circuitry. The real lever, roll-to-roll layers at ~$1-5/m2, belongs to the long-retention R2R IGZO dossier I-01819.
innovation.killer_doubt: Ms windows hold little: KV pages live seconds to hours, training activations ~0.1-1 s, so likely <10% of capacity qualifies. Leaky-by-design oxide TFTs save nothing.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Histogram HBM capacity by data lifetime in PyTorch training and vLLM serving traces (<$50k). Proceed only if >30% of capacity lives under 10 ms; otherwise fold into I-01819.
innovation.prior_art: HP Labs SAIL roll-to-roll TFTs; PragmatIC IGZO FlexICs; RANA (ISCA 2018) refresh skipping for short-lived DNN data; this study's I-01819 (training knowledge).

title: HP's The Machine fixed: pooled memory racks with a refurbishment loop
idea: HPE's The Machine died betting on an unready memristor. Build the same memory-centric fabric with today's DRAM in CXL-attached pooled racks, sold as a service. Modules are hot-swapped, tested, refurbished and redeployed to lower tiers instead of retiring with the server.

physics.key_insight: Stranded DRAM and retired modules are wafer-free supply. Pooling plus redeployment matters more at ~4x contract prices.
physics.killer_doubt: Microsoft Pond measured ~7% DRAM savings from 16-socket CXL pools, not 20-40%. DDR4 reuse behind CXL is already deployed. CXL adds ~70-150 ns latency.
physics.decisive_experiment: None physics-relevant. A market pilot: refurbish 1,000 retired DDR4 RDIMMs into CXL expanders and measure test fallout and $/GB vs new DDR5 (~$200k).
physics.prior_art: Microsoft Pond (ASPLOS 2023) and GreenSKU DDR4-over-CXL reuse; Memtrade; CXL pooling appliances (UnifabriX, XConn, Samsung CMM-B) [training knowledge].

innovation.key_insight: Under a 4x price spike, giving retired modules a second life over CXL adds real supply. Pooling also recovers stranded capacity without new fabs.
innovation.killer_doubt: Pond (ASPLOS 2023) estimated only ~7-9% DRAM savings from pooling, not 20-40%. Hyperscalers and CXL vendors already run pooling and DDR4 reuse (training knowledge).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Desk study (~$30k): from public Azure and Alibaba cluster traces, compute the stranded DRAM recoverable by 8-16-socket pools and the second-life module supply. Continue only if net bits exceed 15% after CXL latency limits.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft Pond and GreenSKU DDR4 reuse via CXL; Meta TPP; Astera Labs, Samsung CMM-B, Liqid, UnifabriX pooling; in-study I-06854 and I-01312 (training knowledge).

title: Po: the worst transistor is the best — cryo poly-Si 3D stack
idea: Po: the worst transistor is the best. Extracted: build 128-tier 1T1C stacks with cheap, leaky low-temperature poly-Si TFT access devices using a NAND-like single-hole etch and no EUV, then run the module at ~150 K where trap-assisted leakage drops by orders of magnitude, turning unusable cells into seconds-retention DRAM.

physics.key_insight: Temperature is a real leakage knob: SRH generation (Ea ~0.56 eV) falls ~1e9 from 300 to 150 K; commercial DDR3 at 77 K retains 4,096 s.
physics.killer_doubt: Grain-boundary trap-assisted tunnelling and GIDL (Ea <=0.15 eV) fall only ~30-300x at 150 K; warm IGZO already reaches aA/um; cooling costs ~2.5-4 W per W.
physics.decisive_experiment: Measure Ioff from 300 K to 120 K at hold bias on 1,000 small-gate SPC/LTPS poly-Si TFTs; compare the 1e-4 leakage tail with IGZO at 300 K. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: Cryogenic DRAM work (Rambus/Microsoft 2017, CryoRAM, CryoGuard); our B5-14 77 K oxide stage; Kioxia OCTRAM and IGZO 2T0C win without cooling.

innovation.key_insight: At 150 K, cooling costs ~3-7 W at the wall per W removed (versus ~10-19 at 77 K). SRH generation falls ~1e10, which could rescue leaky NAND-style poly-Si devices.
innovation.killer_doubt: Room-temperature IGZO already reaches aA leakage (>200 s at 95 C) with no cryostat. Field-driven GIDL and grain-boundary tunneling do not freeze out, and the 3D capacitor is still unsolved.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Cryo-probe poly-Si TFTs (university or NAND-like test structures, ~$100k) at 150 K and 2-3 V bias. Kill if off-current is >=1e-17 A or no better than IGZO at 300 K.
innovation.prior_art: Cryogenic DRAM (Rambus/Microsoft 2017, CryoRAM, CryoGuard); Kioxia cryogenic 3D NAND (Sanuki et al.); no cryogenic poly-Si 3D 1T1C found (via search snippet).

title: Single carbon nanotubes coated as 1-micron coaxial storage capacitors
idea: Coaxial capacitance per length is 2*pi*eps/ln(r2/r1): a 1 nm-radius nanotube with 2 nm ZrO2 and a TiN shell gives ~2 fF/um, so a 1 um tube suffices at 10 nm pitch. Grow vertical tubes by methane CVD from Fe catalyst dots on each vertical-transistor drain.

physics.key_insight: Coax arithmetic is right: 1 nm core, 2 nm k~35 shell gives ~1.8 fF/um geometric, and a grown AR-100 pillar avoids the fluorocarbon HAR etch.
physics.killer_doubt: SWCNT quantum capacitance ~0.4 fF/um in series cuts it to ~0.33 fF/um; inner-surface field ~9 MV/cm at 1 V; one tube per site at 10 nm pitch, 1.7e10/die, unshown.
physics.decisive_experiment: Grow vertical SWCNTs from e-beam-defined Fe dots at 20-40 nm pitch on TiN; count single-tube-per-site yield over 1e6 sites. Below ~99.99%, drop permanently.
physics.prior_art: CNT-forest MIM capacitors in academia; CNT vias (Infineon, imec). No single-tube DRAM storage capacitor found. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Coaxial geometry is right: C/L = 2*pi*eps/ln(r2/r1) favors a thin core, and growing electrodes rather than etching them avoids the fluorocarbon HAR etch.
innovation.killer_doubt: 2 nm ZrO2 on a 1 nm core sees 4.5 MV/cm at 0.5 V and leaks. A safe 5 nm film forces ~24 nm pitch, only ~1.5x over 864 nm2.
innovation.decisive_experiment: No devices: analytic/TCAD leakage for curved 2-5 nm ZrO2 at 1 nm radius, plus a literature yield check on single-CNT-per-site vertical growth. Kill unless both pass. ~$20k.
innovation.prior_art: Early-2000s vertical-CNT transistor and electrode research (e.g., Samsung SAIT; unverified); CNT-forest supercapacitors; Phase B N-21 grown AAO molds.

title: Papermaker's book: roll-to-roll foil memory laminated 800 sheets deep
idea: A papermaker makes thick books from cheap sheets. Print single-tier oxide-TFT gain-cell memory on 10 um polyimide foil by roll-to-roll nanoimprint at ~100 nm rules, then laminate ~800 sheets per cm with anisotropic conductive film and edge-plated through-stack bus lines into a memory 'book'.

physics.key_insight: Lamination solves packaging of foil arrays: modest 8-32-sheet edge-plated stacks (3D-Plus style) could package I-01819 foil dies into module-sized parts.
physics.killer_doubt: Stacking leaves $/bit unchanged and HBM already reaches ~300-400 GB/cm3; 800 laminations at 99.9% yield each give 45%; PI at 0.12 W/mK gives ~800 K/W through 1 cm.
physics.decisive_experiment: Laminate 32 test foils (daisy chains plus TFT monitors) with ACF and edge plating (~$150k); measure per-interface yield, contact resistance and in-stack thermal resistance before building any memory.
physics.prior_art: Irvine Sensors and 3D-Plus edge-plated laminated die stacks; HBM and 3D NAND already exceed the claimed volumetric density.

innovation.key_insight: Laminating tested sheets builds tiers from known-good layers, so yield does not compound as it does over 64 monolithic tiers. Worth keeping as a packaging option for I-01819.
innovation.killer_doubt: Volume is not a cost axis: $/GB equals per-sheet $/GB. ACF film is ~15-25 um thick, more than the 12.5 um sheet pitch, so 800 sheets/cm cannot be built.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Laminate 16 printed test foils with thin ACF and edge-plated buses. Measure contact yield per sheet edge and bus resistance and capacitance, then project to 100 sheets. Folds into I-01819's demo.
innovation.prior_art: Irvine Sensors and Vertical Circuits edge-wired die stacks; SAIL roll-to-roll TFTs (HP Labs); project Phase B N-38 panel-level tiers.

title: Legacy-node always-on island lets modern DRAM fully power down
idea: Put a 32-64 MB refresh-free die on the package (180 nm thick-oxide or loadless cells) holding page tables, kernel and wake state. Modern DRAM banks then enter deep power-down with no refresh when idle, flushing or discarding their contents.

physics.key_insight: Correct that idle refresh (16-33% of idle power) only needs to protect a few tens of MB of kernel and wake state.
physics.killer_doubt: 180 nm SRAM at ~4.6 um2/bit makes 256 Mb ~1,180 mm2, beyond reticle; LPDDR partial-array self-refresh already refreshes only a chosen segment, no extra die.
physics.decisive_experiment: Phone trace study: standby power with LPDDR5 partial-array self-refresh restricted to a 64 MB segment versus full self-refresh; if PASR captures >90% of savings, the island adds nothing.
physics.prior_art: LPDDR partial-array self-refresh and deep power-down modes; OS suspend-to-disk; Flikker-style critical-data refresh partitioning.

innovation.key_insight: Separates must-persist state from bulk DRAM so idle banks can power off. The useful part is the OS policy, not a legacy-node die.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 180 nm SRAM cell is ~4.6 um2, so 32 MB (256 Mb) needs ~1,200 mm2 of array. Phones keep 8-16 GB resident, and discarding it costs relaunch energy.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Do an Android/server trace study: idle self-refresh share against app-relaunch energy when DRAM contents are discarded, with a PASR plus on-SoC SLC prototype. Under $100k.
innovation.prior_art: LPDDR PASR and deep power-down modes; OS-assisted sub-array DRAM power-down research (e.g. GreenDIMM); 32+ MB always-on SoC system-level caches.

title: Row-granular decompressor in the sense-amp stripe, after IBM MXT
idea: Failure mined: IBM's MXT compressed main memory died on decompression latency and a costly controller far from the DRAM. Fix: put a wide, row-granular decompressor (zero-run coding plus 4-bit quantization tables for AI weights, KV caches and activations) right after the secondary sense amps. Its work overlaps the activation's tRCD and rows are stored compressed, so effective capacity multiplies with no added latency.

physics.key_insight: Compressed rows raise useful bits per activation, cutting activation energy per value. The HBM4 logic base die, not DRAM-process periphery, is the natural home.
physics.killer_doubt: 4:1 quantization is the application's choice, not a memory gain. Lossless gain on dense int4 weights is ~1.1-1.3x, on activations ~1.5-2x. Decompressing before the I/O saves no link pJ/bit.
physics.decisive_experiment: In software, trace LLM weights, KV cache and activations in production formats and measure the lossless row-granular ratio net of metadata. If below 1.5x for weights plus KV, stop. ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: IBM MXT; LCP (MICRO 2013); Compresso (MICRO 2018); Buddy Compression (ISCA 2020); ZeroPoint Technologies compression IP; Samsung HBM-PIM, SK hynix AiM.

innovation.key_insight: Decompression overlapped with tRCD hides MXT's latency; zero-run coding of sparse activations and KV caches could add ~1.3-2x effective capacity without new cells.
innovation.killer_doubt: The 10x double-counts 4:1 quantization software already applies; DRAM-process logic (3-4 metals, slow FETs) makes row-wide decoders costly, and variable-length rows need remap metadata.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Trace study: compress real INT4/FP8 weights, KV caches and activations at row granularity (2-8 KB) with zero-run and table codes; report gain beyond quantization net of metadata. Proceed only if >1.5x. ~$40k.
innovation.prior_art: IBM MXT (2001); LCP (MICRO 2013); Buddy Compression (ISCA 2020); Marvell Structera A inline LZ4; ZeroPoint compression IP; study N-69.

title: Compiler swaps pointer structures for succinct ones with rank/select instructions
idea: IFR: indexes sized at the information-theoretic minimum. Closest: a profile-guided compiler pass replaces read-mostly maps, sets and trees with succinct equivalents (Elias-Fano, wavelet trees, compressed tries) backed by new rank/select instructions.

physics.key_insight: Profile-guided choice of data-structure representation could shrink read-mostly maps and graphs without programmer effort; succinct encodings are the right target for cold indexes.
physics.killer_doubt: Rank/select instructions largely exist (x86 POPCNT+PDEP+TZCNT, ARM SVE2 BDEP/BEXT); swapping mutable containers needs proven read-only phases, so coverage is likely <10% of heap.
physics.decisive_experiment: Census five production-like services (search index, KV store, BWA genomics, graph DB, ads) for the heap share held in read-mostly maps and trees; kill if under 15%. ~$20k of engineering.
physics.prior_art: Data-structure selection tools: Chameleon (PLDI 2009), Brainy (PLDI 2011), CollectionSwitch (CGO 2018); SDSL; BMI2 and SVE2 bit-permute instructions (from memory).

innovation.key_insight: Profile-guided selection can find read-mostly maps, sets and trees whose information-theoretic size is far below their pointer size, then freeze them into succinct form.
innovation.killer_doubt: The compiler must prove immutability and keep iteration semantics. Most of the win sits in a few hand-tuned indexes, so automatic gain is likely <10% of heap (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Heap census of 20 production JVM/C++ services: measure the bytes in maps, sets and trees that are read-mostly after init, and their succinct size. Kill if that is <10% of heap. ~$50k.
innovation.prior_art: Automatic data-structure selection: Chameleon (PLDI'09), Brainy (PLDI'11), CollectionSwitch (CGO'18); succinct libraries SDSL, sux4j [training knowledge].

title: Potassium hydroxide on (110) silicon etches crystal-perfect vertical cell walls
idea: Align lines along <112> on (110) Si and etch in KOH so the slow {111} planes form atomically smooth vertical walls 20-40 nm thick at >100:1 aspect ratio; a deposited oxide/TiN wordline stack crossing the walls turns each wall into a vertical string of DRAM cells.

physics.key_insight: KOH {111} planes on (110) Si give litho-free, atomically smooth single-crystal walls from a wet bench. A cheap c-Si template, if a cell topology existed.
physics.killer_doubt: At 1:160 selectivity a 3 um etch undercuts ~19 nm per side, more than a 30 nm wall. Wet drying collapses 100:1 walls. {111} Dit is ~3x (100).
physics.decisive_experiment: E-beam lines on a (110) wafer (~$30k), TMAH/KOH etched 3 um deep with supercritical dry. Map wall thickness and taper vs depth, and Dit on {111} MOS caps. Before that, a cell topology on paper.
physics.prior_art: Kendall (1975-79) KOH (110) vertical walls; KOH X-ray gratings; horizontal c-Si tiers via Si/SiGe epi (Samsung VS-DRAM, imec 120 bilayers) [training knowledge].

innovation.key_insight: Crystallographic {111} walls give single-crystal, atomically smooth vertical Si sheets without DRIE or EUV. They could serve as a low-Dit channel option for vertical-channel 4F2 transistors.
innovation.killer_doubt: KOH (110):(111) selectivity of ~100-400 erodes walls by 2h/R: a 3 um etch removes 15-60 nm, the entire 20-40 nm wall. No capacitor or tier isolation; potassium is CMOS-hostile.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Pattern oxide-masked <112> lines on (110) wafers and etch 2-3 um deep in K-free TMAH. Use TEM to map wall taper and roughness, then measure Dit and 85 C off-current on gated wall FETs. ~$80k.
innovation.prior_art: (110) KOH vertical-wall MEMS (1970s on); TMAH-etched {111} FinFET fins; Samsung/SK hynix VCT and Si/SiGe 3D DRAM already give crystalline channels (training knowledge).

title: HBF weight tier with read-disturb-aware 'weight mode'
idea: HBF stacks NAND dies on TSVs behind an HBM-like interface (OCP spec August 2026: 256 GB/die, 512 GB per 16-high stack, ~1.6 TB/s read). Weights are written once per deployment, while KV and activations stay in DRAM. Each decode step reads every weight page, so a page sees 1e5-3e6 reads per day. Read disturb (pass-voltage stress on the unselected wordlines of a block) then forces periodic reclaim, that is, a rewrite. The 'weight mode' has four parts: program weights in pSLC, or TLC with relaxed retention; interleave each tensor across many blocks so read counts stay even; track per-block read counters and relocate before the disturb limit; and keep a second replica on another die to alternate reads when the disturb budget is tight.

physics.key_insight: Read disturb, not write endurance, is HBF's real wear-out for inference; per-block read-rate arithmetic must enter any HBF dossier.
physics.killer_doubt: Disturb counts per block: 1.6 TB/s over 512 GB gives each ~500-page pSLC block ~1.3e8 reads/day; a ~1e6 limit forces ~130 rewrites/day, ~2.4e5 P/E in 5 years.
physics.decisive_experiment: Raw 2xx-layer 3D NAND on an ONFI tester (~$50k): apply 1e7-1e9 block reads in pSLC mode at 55-85 C and track RBER growth to set the true reclaim interval.
physics.prior_art: SanDisk and SK hynix High Bandwidth Flash (2025-26); SSD read-disturb counters and relocation are standard FTL practice. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: Weights are written once and read 1e5-3e6 times a day, so HBF wears by read disturb, not P/E cycles. Interleaving tensors and alternating replicas spread the disturb budget.
innovation.killer_doubt: SSD firmware has run per-block read counters and read reclaim for 15+ years; the SanDisk/SK hynix HBF controller will include them, leaving no defensible invention.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay LLM decode read traces on raw pSLC/TLC NAND with a tester. Measure RBER growth vs reads per block, and relocation write amplification with and without replicas. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: SanDisk/SK hynix High Bandwidth Flash (2025-26); SSD FTL read-disturb management (read counters, read reclaim); stage-2 R32 cites HBF for weight streaming.

title: Weimer's 1962 TFT reborn: panel-fab memory on Gen-8 glass
idea: Revive RCA's thin-film transistor for memory: build 4-tier oxide-TFT DRAM-like arrays on Gen-8.5 glass in idle LCD and plasma panel fabs at ~1 um features, accept 1% defective cells across huge panels with block codes, and sell them as cheap capacity modules.

physics.key_insight: Block codes that tolerate 1% defective cells relax panel-scale defect density, the right lever for huge glass substrates.
physics.killer_doubt: At F=1 um a ~12F2 gain cell gives ~10 GB/m2 per tier; at ~$150/m2 per tier that is ~$15/GB, ~10x DDR5's $1.48 cost. Stacking does not lower $/GB.
physics.decisive_experiment: Settled by I-00145's single-tier panel run; the 1%-defect block-code part is an FPGA study on measured panel defect maps.
physics.prior_art: Weimer TFT (RCA, 1962); SEL CAAC-IGZO memories; memory-in-pixel LCDs; Phase B N-34 defect-budget co-design; sibling I-03879 dropped at 2 um.

innovation.key_insight: Accept ~1% defective cells across a panel and cover them with block codes, so panel yield is not the gate. That twist should be folded into I-00145.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 1-1.5 um rules, 4 tiers give ~7-16 GB/m2 per tier, about $10-22/GB. That is 7-15x DDR5's $1.48/GB cost and viable only while contract prices stay near $20/GB.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Merge into I-00145. Add a defect-map study: on one partner panel run, measure the cell-fail clustering and size the block-code overhead needed for 1e-15 UBER (~$50k analysis on top).
innovation.prior_art: Near-duplicate of I-00145. RCA Weimer TFT (1962); SEL CAAC-IGZO memory; memory-in-pixel LCDs; Phase B N-38 (training knowledge).

title: Apollo core-rope ROM reborn as via-coupled multi-layer weight store
idea: Apollo's rope memory encoded bits as whether a sense wire threaded a core. Encode frozen AI weights as presence or absence of via stubs coupling word lines to sense lines across 8 metal-layer pairs of an existing 40-nm logic process (one custom via mask per layer); pulsing a word line induces charge only on sense lines with a stub, so there is no DC sneak path.

physics.key_insight: Capacitive crosspoint coding avoids DC sneak paths, so a transistor-free multi-layer ROM in standard BEOL is sound in principle for frozen weights.
physics.killer_doubt: A via stub adds ~4 aF to an ~8 fF, 512-cell sense line: ~0.5 mV. At 40 nm, ~120 nm metal pitch makes 8 planes ~2,000 nm2/bit, worse than DRAM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Field-solve stub coupling on a 40 nm stack, then tape out a 4 kb array on an MPW (~$80k); kill if signal <10 mV at 64 cells per sense line.
physics.prior_art: IBM card capacitor read-only storage on System/360 (1960s); Apollo core rope; via and contact mask ROM; hardwired-model chips (Taalas).

innovation.key_insight: Capacitive via-stub coupling makes a transistor-less ROM in stacked BEOL planes with no DC sneak path. It is a neat cell for immutable weights.
innovation.killer_doubt: '4F2 at 40 nm' assumes an 80 nm metal pitch. Real 40 nm-node M1 pitch is ~120-140 nm, upper metals 2-4x wider: density ~5x worse than DRAM's 864 nm2.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Layout-accurate density plus SPICE coupling-margin study on a real 40 nm PDK (~$30k). If the margin is >=20 mV at 128 crossings, tape one MPW block.
innovation.prior_art: Apollo core rope; ROM compute-in-memory (YOLoC 2022, Hidden-ROM 2023); Taalas hardwired-weight silicon (per R16 source log) [training knowledge].

title: Airport baggage conveyor: vertical charge-coupled bit strings in 3D stacks
idea: Like bags riding a conveyor to one scanner, deposit a 3D-NAND-style stack of 64-128 gate layers around a vertical wide-gap channel (e.g., Ga2O3 or ZnSnO) and clock charge packets up and down it CCD-style; a single sense/restore node at the top of each string reads and rewrites packets as they pass. A bit is a potential well under a gate, so each tier costs one deposition, not a transistor plus capacitor.

physics.key_insight: Indium-free ZnSnO is a useful materials hedge for the vertical CCD family; one sense/restore node per string regenerates every packet each pass.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-08763, N-08 and imec's 3D IGZO CCD. a-Ga2O3 mobility is likely <1-5 cm2/Vs with deep traps; ~100 transfers per pass need CTE >=0.999.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into the I-08763 test chip: add ZnSnO and a-Ga2O3 channel splits on the same planar CCD mask; compare CTE versus clock and 85 C hold. ~$50k extra.
physics.prior_art: imec IEDM 2024 planar and IMW 2026 vertical 3D IGZO CCD; in-study I-10793 and I-01064 (ADVANCE); Phase B N-08.

innovation.key_insight: An indium-free ZnSnO channel is a useful resource hedge for the CCD family. Otherwise it duplicates I-00033's regenerating sense node at the top of each string.
innovation.killer_doubt: ~100 tiers at 3 gates/bit means ~300 transfers per pass: 99% charge needs CTE >=0.99997, against imec's demonstrated >98%. a-Ga2O3 mobility of <~1 cm2/Vs also slows transfers.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Add ZnSnO and a-Ga2O3 channel splits to the I-08763 planar CCD mask (~$50k extra); compare CTE versus clock and 85 C dark fill against IGZO.
innovation.prior_art: imec IGZO CCD (IEDM 2024 planar; IMW 2026 vertical, via prior search logs); in-study I-10793, I-04245; Phase B N-08.

title: Swap per-bit access transistors for vertical CCD charge-packet strings
idea: Reuse the 3D NAND stack: each vertical poly or IGZO channel works as a CCD in which the 128 tier gates, clocked in three phases, shift ~40 charge packets up and down to a regenerating sense amplifier at the top. There is no contact, capacitor or access transistor per bit, and each pass through the amplifier refreshes the packet.

physics.key_insight: 3D NAND tools plus amplifier-per-string regeneration avoid EUV and per-bit contacts; streaming a whole string costs only ~0.2 pJ/bit of gate CV2 at 3 V.
physics.killer_doubt: Overclaimed: a 150 nm hex hole is ~19,500 nm2, so 40 packets give ~490 nm2/bit before slits, not 250. 20 ns average needs ~3 GHz clocks; poly-Si traps cut CTE.
physics.decisive_experiment: Covered by the I-08763 planar CCD chip: add a poly-Si channel split and a 120-transfer recirculating loop to measure cumulative loss and 85 C dark fill. ~$50k extra.
physics.prior_art: Phase B N-08; imec IGZO CCD (IEDM 2024, IMW 2026); 1970s Fairchild and Intel CCD memories; in-study I-10793, I-05275.

innovation.key_insight: The clearest 3D-NAND tool-reuse case: DUV only, no per-bit contact, and refresh comes free with each pass through the top amplifier.
innovation.killer_doubt: Overclaimed: a ~150 nm hole (~19,500 nm2) holding 40 packets is ~490 nm2/bit before slits, not 250. A 20 ns average needs ~3 GHz phase clocks; poly-Si traps cut CTE.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Covered by the I-08763 chip: add a poly-Si split and a 120-transfer recirculating loop to measure cumulative loss and 85 C dark fill (~$50k extra).
innovation.prior_art: Phase B N-08; imec IGZO CCD (IEDM 2024, IMW 2026); Intel 2416 and Fairchild CCD memories; in-study I-10793, I-04245.

title: Hitachi's single-electron grain memory stacked in 64 cheap tiers
idea: Hitachi's room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano, 1990s) stored a few electrons in grains of 3-4 nm polysilicon and died because random grains caused wild threshold scatter. Tame the scatter with per-cell write-verify calibration and a 3-cell majority code, and exploit its simplicity of thin films with no capacitor or deep etch by depositing 64 tiers gated by one shared vertical-gate hole pattern.

physics.key_insight: Few-electron storage needs no capacitor or deep etch. Per-cell write-verify and majority coding are the right tools for the random threshold scatter of grains.
physics.killer_doubt: Current through 3-4 nm poly-Si grain channels is ~nA, so sensing takes microseconds. ~7e13 hot-row writes of 5 e- push ~1e8 C/cm2 through a few-nm2 barrier, beyond any Qbd.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fabricate 1,000 Yano-type 3 nm poly-Si cells on a university line. Measure read current, Vt scatter after write-verify, retention at 85 C and endurance to 1e10 cycles. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: Hitachi/Yano poly-Si single-electron memory (1993-98); SunRise Memory quasi-volatile 3D NOR; nanocrystal flash (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Few-electron storage needs only thin films and one shared vertical-gate hole, so tiers are cheap depositions. Write-verify can absorb part of the grain scatter.
innovation.killer_doubt: Few-electron windows sit near RTN and grain scatter, and 3x majority triples area. Tunnel writes need >=3e8 cycles (C0-1), not shown. Grain-limited strings read at nA, i.e. us sensing.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fabricate poly-Si nanowire grain cells in a university fab. On 1,000 devices, measure the post-write-verify Vt window and sigma, 85 C retention and endurance to 1e10 cycles. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Yano et al., Hitachi single-electron memory (128 Mb prototype, 1998); Tiwari IBM nanocrystal memory (1996); SunRise quasi-volatile 3D NOR; Phase B N-10 [training knowledge].

title: Datacenter fleets as ore: reverse-fab reclaim of retired DRAM dies
idea: Scale shift from fab to fleet: DIMMs retired after 4-6 years are laser/chemically decapped, dies are retested and rebinned, then re-assembled onto new substrates or CXL expander cards as capacity-tier memory with stronger ECC.

physics.key_insight: Retired fleet DRAM has no cell wear-out, so recovered bits use no wafer capacity and arrive within months during a ~4x price spike.
physics.killer_doubt: Decapping and re-bumping molded FBGA dies damages pads and yield (est. 50-80% recovery), while whole retired DIMMs already plug into DDR4 CXL expanders with zero rework.
physics.decisive_experiment: Chemically decap and re-bump 500 dies from retired RDIMMs. Compare BIST fallout, retention and VRT with the same lot reused as intact DIMMs behind a CXL controller. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: Marvell Structera X and Meta CXL reuse of whole retired DDR4 DIMMs; Microsoft GreenSKU; refurbished-DIMM resellers; failure-analysis decap labs.

innovation.key_insight: Retired DRAM dies show little wear-out, so retest and rebinning recover wafer-free bits. Die-level reclaim could restack them into denser CXL packages.
innovation.killer_doubt: Decap plus re-bump costs more than reballing whole packages, which GreenSKU and Structera X already reuse. Decap fallout is likely 10-30% (estimate), and the DDR4 pool is one-time.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Decap 200 retired DDR4 FBGA packages chemically and by laser, re-bond the dies on a test substrate, and compare yield, retention tail and cost per GB with reballed whole packages. Under $150k.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); Marvell Structera X; ITAD resale; failure-analysis decap; in-study I-04852, I-05321, I-06172 (all DROP).

title: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D antifuse stack made rewritable with selector-charged capacitors
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D poly-diode antifuse memory (bought by SanDisk in 2005) stacked cheaply at ~4 masks per layer but died for being write-once. Keep the stacked poly pillar process and swap the antifuse for a small planar MIM capacitor charged through a bidirectional punch-through n-p-n selector, giving 1S1C dynamic cells with unlimited endurance, refreshed like DRAM.

physics.key_insight: Matrix's ~4-mask-per-deck poly pillar stack is the right cost template, and swapping the antifuse for a capacitor removes the write-once failure.
physics.killer_doubt: Hold bias ~V/2 sits across a poly-Si selector. Its own ms-scale refresh at ~50-100 fJ/bit per refresh is 70-140x DDR5's ~0.7 pW/bit refresh power.
physics.decisive_experiment: Build 40 nm poly-Si n-p-n punch-through selectors with 1 fF MIM stubs on a 4-deck test chip. Map I(V/2) at 85 C to the 1e-6 tail and the write/hold current ratio. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: Matrix Semiconductor 3D poly-diode OTP (SanDisk); epitaxial-Si punch-through RRAM selector (IEEE EDL ~2012, from memory); our N-85 crested-barrier 1S1C.

innovation.key_insight: Matrix's ~4-masks-per-deck poly-diode stacking, with a capacitor replacing the antifuse, gives transistor-free DUV decks with unlimited write endurance.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 4F2 planar MIM at F=40 nm holds ~0.2 fF. Poly-Si junction leakage (~10-100 fA at 85 C, estimate) gives ~0.2-2 ms retention: 30-300x more refresh than 64 ms.
innovation.decisive_experiment: University fab, ~$150k: build 2-deck poly-Si punch-through selectors on 0.2 fF MIM caps. Measure hold leakage at 25-85 C, V/2 disturb across 1k half-selected cells, and retention distributions.
innovation.prior_art: Matrix Semiconductor/SanDisk 3D OTP; Phase B N-85 crested-barrier 1S1C (the better selector route); in-study I-08759, I-04677 (both DROP).

title: Federal commons for dead refresh-free memory IP plus shared qualification line
idea: Most refresh-free memory ventures (T-RAM, Z-RAM, Kilopass, Spin Memory and others) died less from physics than from missing reliability data and qualified second sources. Fix: a federal program buys or licenses their patent estates into an open pool and funds a shared U.S. qualification line that runs JEDEC-style retention, endurance, disturb and soft-error testing on every revived cell and publishes the failure-rate data.

physics.key_insight: Every new cell lacks published retention, disturb and soft-error failure-rate data. A shared JEDEC-style qualification lab is genuinely useful infrastructure.
physics.killer_doubt: The premise is half wrong: Z-RAM and T-RAM stalled on margin and variability at scale. Patents filed 2003-2010 expire by ~2030. A real qualification line costs >$50M.
physics.decisive_experiment: Audit the named estates for expiry, live claims and documented failure modes. If <30% of claims survive past 2030, drop the pool and fund only an open reliability-test lab.
physics.prior_art: CHIPS Act NSTC/NAPMP prototyping programs; SEMATECH-style consortia; JEDEC qualification flows.

innovation.key_insight: Reliability data and qualified second sources, not only physics, gate alternative memories; an open qualification line attacks that shared bottleneck.
innovation.killer_doubt: Premise weak: Z-RAM and T-RAM faded after AMD, Hynix and GlobalFoundries trials, largely on scaled-node retention/variability; their 1998-2010 filings expire by ~2030 anyway.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A $50k audit: for each dead refresh-free venture, document failure cause and patent expiry; proceed only if >=3 died of data/qualification gaps on still-live patents.
innovation.prior_art: SRC/NSTC programs and JEDEC qualification norms; Z-RAM licensed by AMD and Hynix, then dropped; T-RAM with GlobalFoundries; standard patent pools.

title: Biologist's self-assembly: block copolymers draw 5 nm cells
idea: Cells build structures by self-assembly. High-chi silicon-containing block copolymers on sparse ArF guide patterns define a 10 nm-pitch hexagonal array of vertical nanowire access transistors, each with an oxide-semiconductor storage node instead of a capacitor. Spin-coat and anneal from U.S. chemical suppliers replace 5-7 EUV layers.

physics.key_insight: Periodic DRAM arrays suit self-assembly: a guided block-copolymer hex lattice at proven ~20-30 nm pitch can replace EUV hole layers in a 4F2 vertical-channel cell (Phase B N-30).
physics.killer_doubt: At 10 nm pitch a 5 nm wire leaves ~2.5 nm per side for oxide, wordline and isolation. The node holds ~0.01 fF (~70 e-/V); ~1.5 nm LER swamps Vt.
physics.decisive_experiment: University-fab run (~$300k): guided high-chi block-copolymer hex lattice at 10-12 nm pitch on ArF guides; measure defects over 1 cm2, CD and LER after transfer into oxide, then attempt a gate wrap.
physics.prior_art: imec and IBM DSA contact-hole multiplication; high-chi sub-10 nm block copolymers (MIT, UT Austin); 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM (Samsung, CXMT); Phase B N-30.

innovation.key_insight: DSA on sparse ArF guides can print sub-10 nm hex arrays with spin-and-bake tools, attacking EUV cost and U.S. chemistry supply at once.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 10 nm pitch the node is ~2-5 aF (~10-30 electrons at 1 V), readable only by a second gain transistor that breaks 4F2; DSA defectivity remains far above targets.
innovation.decisive_experiment: University nanofab: PS-PDMS DSA on ArF guide posts to 10-12 nm-pitch hex holes over 1 cm2; SEM placement error and missing/merged-hole density. Kill above 1 per cm2. ~$200k.
innovation.prior_art: DSA hole patterning (IBM, imec, MIT Ross/Berggren PS-PDMS); Samsung vertical-channel 4F2 DRAM; study item I-04680 (DROP, same mechanism) [training knowledge].

title: Americium credit: U.S. tax credit per gigabyte of DRAM avoided
idea: Named for the Americas, a CHIPS-style federal credit pays data-center operators per GB-year of DRAM avoided against a certified baseline (via compression, pooling, reuse) measured by a standard telemetry audit, and federal procurement favors software that publishes bytes-per-transaction figures.

physics.key_insight: Treating avoided DRAM as a 'negabyte' supply lever is the right accounting frame, and federal procurement disclosure of bytes per transaction is cheap and executable without Congress.
physics.killer_doubt: At $20/GB DRAM (~$4/GB-year amortized), the market already pays far more than a plausible credit. Counterfactual baselines invite gaming like the FERC demand-response cases, plus Jevons rebound.
physics.decisive_experiment: Model a $0.5-1/GB-year credit against the 4x price signal using public capex data. Pilot only the procurement-disclosure half with one agency (GSA) for software buys.
physics.prior_art: Energy-efficiency analogues: EU white certificates, 179D deduction, utility demand-response baselines; no memory-specific credit found.

innovation.key_insight: Counting avoided DRAM as domestic 'negabyte' supply is the right accounting frame, and procurement disclosure of bytes per transaction is executable without Congress.
innovation.killer_doubt: The 4x price spike already pays ~$4/GB-year for efficiency; a plausible $0.5-1/GB-year credit adds <25%. Counterfactual baselines invite gaming, and Jevons rebound eats savings.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Model a $0.5-1/GB-year credit against the price signal on public capex data, then pilot only the disclosure half with one agency (GSA) software buy, using the I-07673 telemetry as audit.
innovation.prior_art: Energy Star and utility demand-response baselines (gaming record), CHIPS Act credits; no memory-avoidance credit found.

title: Cloud DFT screen for a k-70 dielectric that ALD can grow
idea: Worsen: keep the k ~40 ZrO2 stack forever. Flip: spend ~$300k of cloud compute on a high-throughput DFT and phonon screen of rutile and alloyed oxides (Ti-Ge-Sn-O, Hf-Ti-O) for k >= 70 with band gap >= 4 eV and ALD growth below 450 C, then test the top five in a university ALD within 24 months.

physics.key_insight: Computation can prune ternary oxide space before costly ALD; a >=4 eV band-gap filter is the right gate for DRAM leakage.
physics.killer_doubt: A ~1,800-oxide HSE screen already exists; its standout (rocksalt BeO) is a metastable high-pressure phase. Even k 70 cuts AR only 75 to ~45, 1.6x.
physics.decisive_experiment: Refilter the published 1,800-oxide dataset for cations with mature ALD precursors; grow the top three at 6 nm and 400 C; go if EOT <=0.35 nm at <=1e-7 A/cm2. ~$200k.
physics.prior_art: Yim, Han, Hwang et al., NPG Asia Materials 2015: ~1,800 oxides screened for k and band gap (via search snippet); Materials Project DFPT dielectric data.

innovation.key_insight: DFT can prune the oxide space before any deposition. But the k-bandgap trade-off is the real constraint, and the screen has already been run.
innovation.killer_doubt: No known oxide reaches k>=70 with Eg>=4 eV. DFT k for soft-mode oxides errs by ~30-50%, and thin-film dead layers cut k further. N-04 circuits give 10x versus 1.75x.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Re-mine the existing Materials Project dielectric set (~$20k): count ALD-growable phases above the k*Eg^2 frontier. Kill if fewer than 3 exist.
innovation.prior_art: Yim et al., NPG Asia Materials 2015 (automated ab-initio high-k screen, SNU); Petousis et al., Scientific Data 2017 (Materials Project dielectrics) [training knowledge].

title: Thermally drawn fiber preforms yield coaxial capacitor bundles
idea: Adapt optical-fiber drawing: build a macroscopic preform of metal/glass/metal coaxial rods, draw it ~1000x down to 30 nm features over km lengths, slice it into thin wafers of parallel coaxial capacitors, and hybrid-bond them onto access-transistor wafers.

physics.key_insight: Capacitor height becomes slice thickness, decoupling aspect ratio from plasma etch; hollow drawn nanochannel glass already reached ~33 nm channels, a workable template variant.
physics.killer_doubt: Liquid-metal cores below ~100 nm break up by Rayleigh-Plateau in ~ms during the draw; a multi-fibre lattice cannot register to a 40 nm-pitch transistor array after bonding.
physics.decisive_experiment: Draw a hollow nanochannel-glass slice (50 nm pores, 5 um thick), ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN, bond to an oversized-pad array; measure Cs spread and opens/shorts over 1e6 pads. ~$400k.
physics.prior_art: NRL nanochannel glass, 33 nm channels (Tonucci et al., Science 1992); multimaterial fibre drawing (MIT, Bilkent); our N-21 AAO-Cap grows a registered mold in place.

innovation.key_insight: In a drawn and sliced bundle, capacitor height is set by slice thickness, not by etch aspect ratio.
innovation.killer_doubt: Drawable glasses have k~3-10 (ZrO2 ~40): a 30 nm coax gives ~1 fF/um, needing ~5 um slices. Metal cores break up far above 30 nm; bond pitch ~0.4-1 um.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Iterative stack-and-draw of a Sn/In-core borosilicate coax preform (~$150k, a fiber-draw lab). Report the smallest continuous metal core and the slice-face flatness. Kill above 200 nm.
innovation.prior_art: MIT Fink group multimaterial thermally drawn fibers; Yaman et al., Nature Materials 2011 (iterative size reduction, nanowire arrays) [training knowledge].

title: Gleaner's cool tier: sense-marginal dies for liquid-cooled racks
idea: Farmers glean the field after harvest. Dies that fail sense margin only above ~75 C are binned as cool-tier DDR5/HBM, sold at standard JEDEC timings into liquid- and immersion-cooled racks that hold devices under 60 C.

physics.key_insight: Retention-limited fails improve ~2x per 10 C. Dies that fail only above 75 C stay usable in cold-plate or immersion-cooled servers.
physics.killer_doubt: Temperature grades and downgrade channels already exist. Hot-only margin fallout after repair is likely ~1-3%. HBM next to a GPU runs 85-95 C even when liquid-cooled.
physics.decisive_experiment: With one vendor or OSAT, re-test 10k hot-test rejects at 60 C with 2x margin and a VRT soak. If <2% of output is recovered, stop. ~$150k.
physics.prior_art: Commercial vs industrial temperature grades; Micron SpecTek downgraded components; DDR5 2x refresh above 85 C.

innovation.key_insight: Dies that fail sense margin only when hot are usable in liquid-cooled racks held under 60 C; a temperature-graded SKU turns some yield loss into salable bits.
innovation.killer_doubt: Hot-only sense fails are likely ~1-3% of dies after redundancy, not 3-8%; temperature grades and downgraded parts already exist, and cooling excursions add field risk.
innovation.decisive_experiment: With a test house, bin 10k reject DDR5 dies by failing temperature; measure the share passing JEDEC timing at or below 60 C through 1,000 h burn-in. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: Commercial versus industrial temperature grades; Micron SpecTek downgraded components; routine speed and temperature binning [training knowledge].

title: Clonal-selection retention profiler RTL for commodity DDR5 on FPGA
idea: Like adaptive immunity, an FPGA controller (DRAM Bender-class) 'challenges' rows with stretched refresh and worst-case patterns. Failing rows are clonally expanded into a Bloom-filter list kept at 64 ms, and negative selection re-tests them to purge false positives and catch VRT drift. Everything else refreshes at 256 ms. Three engineers for 24 months plus $80k of boards, ~$900k total, produce licensable controller RTL.

physics.key_insight: Bloom-filter weak-row lists with re-testing for variable retention can cut refresh ~4x with no die change. The value is licensable RTL.
physics.killer_doubt: VRT and data-pattern dependence create new weak cells after profiling, and retention halves per ~10 C. DDR5 on-die ECC and remapping hide fail bits. Standard REF cannot skip rows.
physics.decisive_experiment: On DRAM Bender with 20 DDR5 DIMMs, profile at 85 C, then run 256 ms refresh for 30 days with ECC logging and count escapes per GB-day. ~$150k.
physics.prior_art: RAIDR (ISCA 2012, Bloom filters), AVATAR (DSN 2015), REAPER (ISCA 2017), BEER/HARP on-die-ECC profiling (MICRO 2020/2021).

innovation.key_insight: Retention profiling with a Bloom-filter weak-row list can cut refresh ~4x on commodity parts and could ship as licensable controller RTL.
innovation.killer_doubt: DDR5 on-die ECC hides raw retention failures and VRT cells drift, forcing guardbands; RAIDR, REAPER and HARP already map this, and DDR5 refresh is internally sequenced.
innovation.decisive_experiment: DRAM Bender on 20 DDR5 parts: profile at 256 ms and 85 C, then run 30 days of ACT-only weak-row refresh with REF thinned; count escapes from VRT and on-die ECC. ~$80k.
innovation.prior_art: RAIDR (ISCA 2012), AVATAR (DSN 2015), REAPER (ISCA 2017), HARP (MICRO 2021); DRAM Bender (2022); study N-42/N-63.

title: Self-assembled diode dots: block copolymers replace EUV for every cell
idea: Inverts 'lithography must define each access device': coat a PS-b-PDMS block copolymer guided by coarse 193 nm trenches into 10 nm-pitch dot arrays, then convert each dot by sequential infiltration synthesis into a vertical oxide Schottky diode atop a MIM nanocapacitor, mapping out defective dots at test.

physics.key_insight: Coarse 193 nm guides plus BCP self-assembly can define 10-30 nm dot lattices with no EUV; defect remapping at test makes per-site defectivity tolerable.
physics.killer_doubt: A single rectifying Schottky diode passes charge one way, so cannot write both 0 and 1; a 5 nm MIM dot holds ~0.05-0.1 fF (~400 e-) even at AR ~20.
physics.decisive_experiment: SIS-convert a PS-b-PDMS dot array on TiN and measure single-dot I-V by conductive AFM (~$100k): need rectification >1e4 at 1 V and reverse leakage <1 fA; then prove a bidirectional write path.
physics.prior_art: Our B2-11/N-30 DSA honeycomb and B2-20 SIS lamellae (ALIVE); imec 37 nm BCP contact multiplication; 1D1C crosspoint proposals.

innovation.key_insight: Graphoepitaxial DSA on coarse 193 nm guides, plus SIS conversion of the dots, could give EUV-free 10 nm-pitch device sites. Worth keeping as a patterning module, not as this cell.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 10 nm-pitch planar MIM (5x5 nm, k=40, 5 nm) is ~2 aF, about 11 electrons at 1 V; charge-transfer sensing needs ~0.5 fF, 250x more. Diodes cannot write 0s.
innovation.decisive_experiment: For <$150k: make DSA+SIS dot arrays in guided trenches and measure dot-placement defects per cm2 and single-dot rectification by conductive AFM. A capacitor of >=0.3 fF at 10 nm pitch must close on paper first.
innovation.prior_art: DSA dot and contact-hole patterning (IBM, imec, Intel, MIT Ross/Berggren PS-PDMS); Argonne sequential infiltration synthesis; diode-access crosspoint memories (3D XPoint, Samsung diode PRAM).

title: Threshold-switch crossbar capacitors: 64 decks, refreshed constantly
idea: Inverts 'an access device must hold the bit for 64 ms': put a chalcogenide ovonic threshold switch in series with a tiny MIM capacitor at every crossbar node, stack 64 self-aligned decks with two KrF masks each, accept us-to-ms retention set by OTS leakage, and refresh whole decks in parallel from base CMOS.

physics.key_insight: A 4F2 transistor-free crosspoint, with two KrF masks per deck and 64 decks, is the cheapest conceivable patterning if a two-terminal access device could hold charge.
physics.killer_doubt: Half-select OTS leakage ~0.1-1 nA on 1 fF gives ~us retention: ~100 fJ x 1e5/s is ~80 W/GB; 10 years is ~3e13 firings versus ~1e8-1e11 reported.
physics.decisive_experiment: 1S1C coupons (~$100k): measure node droop through an OTS at V/2 bias, the stored window loss to Vhold, and endurance to 1e11 firings. Kill if retention <1 ms or endurance <1e12.
physics.prior_art: Intel/Micron 3D XPoint OTS selectors; academic 1S1C selector-capacitor crossbar concepts (not verified here).

innovation.key_insight: A two-terminal selector plus a planar MIM at each crosspoint gives transistor-free 4F2 decks at KrF. An 80 nm-pitch MIM holds ~0.45 fF, enough with charge-transfer sensing.
innovation.killer_doubt: At us-ms retention every OTS switches 1e3-1e6 times/s: 3e11-3e14 cycles in 10 years, beyond OTS endurance. ~1000 half-selected cells at ~nA sneak swamp a sub-fC read.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fabricate 1S1C crosspoint test arrays (GeSe OTS plus TiN/ZrO2 MIM) at a university fab. Measure hold leakage at Vth/2, read signal against line length, and OTS cycling to 1e12 at 85 C. About $300k.
innovation.prior_art: 3D XPoint OTS selectors (Intel/Micron); selector-only and self-selecting chalcogenide memories (SK hynix, Micron); 1S1R crosspoint stacks.

title: Vacuum as the insulator: field-emission two-terminal crossbar storage cell
idea: Reverse insulator and conductor: each storage node is a metal island over a sealed 3-5 nm vacuum gap to a sharp emitter at a wordline/bitline crossing; below the Fowler-Nordheim threshold the gap passes essentially nothing, while ~2x the field drives uA emission to charge or discharge it in ns.

physics.key_insight: Vacuum is a wear-free, trap-free barrier: a 3 nm gap tunnels ~exp(-65) at rest, and Fowler-Nordheim gives ~1e12 on/off under V/3 biasing, a genuine crossbar selector.
physics.killer_doubt: No gain stage: a 20x20 nm island over 4 nm vacuum is ~0.9 aF, ~5 e- at 1 V, ~90 uV on 10 fF. A sense transistor makes it N-09.
physics.decisive_experiment: Sacrificial-release 5-10 nm W/Pt emitter gaps onto the floating gate of a reference MOSFET (~$250k): measure write-current spread, 85 C retention and drift after 1e10 pulses.
physics.prior_art: Phase B N-09 nanogap floating node (ALIVE-SPEC); NASA Ames nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors (training knowledge); Spindt field-emitter arrays.

innovation.key_insight: Vacuum is a wear-free, trap-free barrier, and Fowler-Nordheim gives ~1e11-1e12 selectivity at V/3 for nA-class writes: a genuine transistor-free selector.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 20x20 nm island over 4 nm vacuum is ~0.9 aF: ~5 electrons at 1 V, ~90 uV on a 10 fF bitline. In-cell gain reinstates the transistor.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Do not fund standalone; fold into N-09: release 4-8 nm emitter gaps over a MOSFET floating gate (~$250k), then measure write spread, 85 C retention and emitter drift after 1e10 pulses.
innovation.prior_art: Phase B N-09 vacuum-nanogap floating node; NASA Ames nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors (Han, Meyyappan); Spindt field-emitter arrays [training knowledge].

title: Josephson-era missing memory: 77 K thin-oxide 3D NAND as DRAM
idea: IBM's Josephson program (cancelled 1983) and later cryogenic computing stalled for lack of dense, cheap cold memory. At 77 K leakage collapses, so a 3D NAND-style vertical string with a 1.5-2 nm direct-tunneling oxide instead of ~7 nm Fowler-Nordheim oxide programs at ~3-5 V in tens of ns, suffers little hot-carrier wear and holds charge for hours.

physics.key_insight: At 77 K thermal leakage paths freeze, so barrier tunnelling alone sets retention. Cold computing does lack dense memory.
physics.killer_doubt: Direct tunnelling is temperature-insensitive. Writing in ~10 ns and holding for 1e4 s needs a ~1e12 current ratio; 2 nm SiO2 gives ~1e6-1e8 between ~4 V and ~0.3 V.
physics.decisive_experiment: Make 2 nm-oxide floating-gate capacitors. Measure charge loss at 300 K and 77 K from 1 ms to 1e4 s, and write speed at 3-5 V. Any hours-scale retention would revive the idea. ~$150k.
physics.prior_art: IBM Si-nanocrystal memory with 1-2 nm tunnel oxide (Tiwari 1996); Phase B N-94 (77 K oxide gain cell) is the stronger cold path (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Swapping Fowler-Nordheim for low-voltage direct tunneling could cut write voltage and wear in NAND-tool charge-trap strings; the room-temperature quasi-volatile version is Phase B N-10.
innovation.killer_doubt: Direct back-tunneling through 1.5-2 nm oxide is temperature-insensitive (estimated retention of us to seconds), so 77 K cannot deliver hours, while LN2 cooling adds ~10-15% overhead.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Measure charge loss versus time at 300 K and 77 K on SONOS capacitors with 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5 nm tunnel oxides in a cryoprober; stop if the 77 K retention gain is below 10x. University fab, ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: Tiwari et al. nanocrystal memory with ~2 nm oxide (IBM, APL 1996); Phase B N-10 direct-tunnel 3D AND; SNU CryoRAM model (ISCA 2019) (training knowledge).

title: Tire retreading: CXL rehab buffer gives retired DRAM second life
idea: Truck fleets retread tires instead of buying new. Sell a CXL memory-expander buffer chip whose periphery profiles retired DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs in situ (per-row retention margin, weak-column sensing), applies per-region refresh rates and column remaps, and pools them as tier-2 memory under strong ECC, fed by hyperscaler decommissioning streams.

physics.key_insight: The same reuse play as I-03344, through a custom buffer chip. The water argument holds: a reused GB avoids nearly all of its fab water.
physics.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-03344. A buffer chip cannot reach the DRAM's internal sense amps, so weak-column sensing reduces to timing-margin tests. An ASIC tapeout costs ~$10-30M.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold into I-03344. Run its FPGA profiling first, and tape out an ASIC only if profiling qualifies >90% of retired DIMMs at <$0.5/GB landed.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft GreenSKU; Marvell Structera X and Astera Leo CXL controllers; batch-mate I-03344.

innovation.key_insight: Same mechanism as I-03344, but as a buffer ASIC with in-situ per-row retention profiling and per-region refresh; the water and fab-avoidance argument is real.
innovation.killer_doubt: Duplicate of I-03344 and of shipping CXL controllers; a new buffer ASIC needs over $10M in masks and IP, ten times the budget.
innovation.decisive_experiment: FPGA CXL card profiling 500 retired DIMMs; justify an ASIC only if per-row refresh tuning adds over 20% usable capacity versus simple binning. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: Marvell Structera X; Microsoft GreenSKU (ISCA 2024); REAPER/AVATAR retention profiling [training knowledge].

title: Run cache-sized services on gigabyte-LLC CPUs with minimal DIMMs
idea: Box: substitute × existing large-L3 CPUs (~1 GB stacked SRAM) × whole working set × deployment time × minimal DIMM population. Routers, rate limiters, feature-flag and session services whose working sets fit in ~1 GB are pinned to large-cache parts already in the fleet, with one small DIMM per channel.

physics.key_insight: Some fleet services have sub-100 MB working sets yet get default 256-512 GB boxes; right-sizing DIMM population is a free DRAM lever.
physics.killer_doubt: Genoa-X's 1,152 MB L3 is twelve private 96 MB CCD slices, so a 1 GB working set fits no core's cache. The savings duplicate ordinary VM right-sizing and pooling.
physics.decisive_experiment: Pin per-CCD instances of 20 candidate services on a Genoa-X host with 32 GB total DRAM; measure LLC miss rate and p99 latency against the default box. ~$50k.
physics.prior_art: AMD 3D V-Cache EPYC (Milan-X, Genoa-X); hyperscaler VM right-sizing; Pond CXL memory pooling (ASPLOS'23).

innovation.key_insight: Installed SRAM capacity could stand in for DRAM in tiny-working-set services. The underlying problem is real: stranded DRAM.
innovation.killer_doubt: Genoa-X's 1.1 GB L3 is twelve private 96 MB CCD slices, so 1 GB working sets are not resident. Small services are already bin-packed: stranded DRAM is ~25%, not 80-95%.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Pin a 1 GB-working-set Redis or rate-limiter on a 9684X with one DIMM per channel. Measure DRAM bandwidth and p99 against a standard host. About $15k. A null result is expected.
innovation.prior_art: AMD 3D V-Cache (Milan-X/Genoa-X); Microsoft Pond and CXL pooling for stranded memory; standard Kubernetes bin-packing.

title: Core-rope via-programmed 3D weight store, one sense per rope
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope, where a bit was set by whether a wire threaded a core: inference weights are encoded by whether a BEOL via links a rope wire to a shared sense node, written by maskless laser/e-beam via patterning in a mature U.S. fab and stacked 16 metal decks high, with one sense amp per 64 rope wires. Static weights leave DRAM, which keeps only activations and KV cache.

physics.key_insight: Fixed-model weights in via ROM need no refresh, capacitor or EUV and can sit in logic BEOL beside compute, removing weight traffic entirely for frozen models.
physics.killer_doubt: Via ROM at 64 nm pitch is 0.0041 um2/bit per deck, ~4x worse than 1b DRAM; BEOL offers ~4-5 tight decks; maskless e-beam writing ~1e10 vias/cm2 lacks production throughput.
physics.decisive_experiment: Desk cost model (~$20k): $/bit for via ROM in 12-28 nm BEOL with 2 custom via masks vs DDR5 at $1.48/GB, including model-churn write-off every 6-12 months.
physics.prior_art: Mask/via-programmable ROM (decades old); hardwired-weight inference ASICs from startups, e.g. Taalas (recollection, not verified this session).

innovation.key_insight: Static inference weights do not need DRAM. A via-programmed BEOL ROM in a mature U.S. fab removes refresh and EUV for that share.
innovation.killer_doubt: Models churn every ~6-12 months. 16 decks means ~32 extra metal layers. An 8B, 4-bit model needs ~1.6e10 e-beam vias per die. Passive via crosspoints lack selectors.
innovation.decisive_experiment: MPW test chip (~$200k) of a 2-4-deck via-programmed capacitive crosspoint ROM measuring read margin, sneak paths and bits/mm², plus a cost model against LPDDR at model lifetimes of 6-24 months.
innovation.prior_art: Mask/via ROM (decades old); ROM-based CIM (e.g., YOLoC, DAC 2022); hardwired-model LLM ASICs (e.g., Taalas) [training knowledge].

title: Via-ROM for frozen AI weights: nothing to refresh
idea: Inverts 'working memory must be rewritable': store fixed model weights as present/absent or size-coded (2-bit) vias in a dense crosspoint read-only array using two custom mask layers on a mature node; changing the model re-spins only the via mask, and only activations use DRAM.

physics.key_insight: Size-coded vias give 2 bits per site, and re-spinning only one via mask per model keeps NRE near $0.1-0.3M on a mature node.
physics.killer_doubt: '2-4 bits per F2' is 4-8x high: a crosspoint site is >=4F2, so 2-bit vias give 0.5 bit/F2; at F=45 nm ~4,000 nm2/bit, ~4x below 1b DRAM, before selectors.
physics.decisive_experiment: Duplicate of I-02068; fund only inside I-03028's MPW: measure 2-bit via-size resistance distributions (4 levels) and read margin with a diode selector across 0-85 C.
physics.prior_art: Multi-level via/implant-coded mask ROM (1990s); Taalas hardwired-model chips (2026); covered by the I-03028 dossier. From memory, unverified.

innovation.key_insight: Same mechanism as I-02068, using masks. Size-coded 2-bit vias on a mature node reach near-1b-DRAM density with zero refresh, and only the via mask is re-spun per model.
innovation.killer_doubt: Taalas already hardwires weights with ~2 masks per model. Each update costs masks and an ~8-12 week fab turn while models change every ~3-6 months; 4-level vias face CD spread.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Tape out a size-coded 2-bit via array on a mature-node MPW (130/65 nm). Measure 4-level resistance distributions and read margin over ~1e6 vias, plus margin across temperature. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1 mask-ROM weights (AMD acquiring, via search snippet, prior logs); NOR/NAND mask ROM; multi-level implant-coded mask ROM (1990s) [training knowledge]. Dup of I-02068.

title: Yield firewall: spare tiers per block plus pre-tested tier groups
idea: Build 64 + s tiers per block and fuse out up to s defective tiers per block through the tier decoder (B3-08 makes tier selection programmable), so one killer defect in one tier no longer kills a block. For very tall stacks, build tiers in groups of 8 on separate carriers, run parametric tests on each group (vertical-bitline continuity, leakage, Vt maps from built-in test structures), and stack only good groups by die-to-wafer hybrid bonding. That turns a multiplicative 64-tier yield into a sum of 8-tier yields plus bond yields.

physics.key_insight: Tier-granular sparing makes random tier defects yield-neutral at ~6% area. It is a design rule every 3D-memory dossier should carry, not a standalone invention.
physics.killer_doubt: Separately built 8-tier groups need joins at bitline pitch (~40-80 nm) against a ~0.4-1 um hybrid-bond pitch. Eight carriers give up single-etch amortization, and test structures miss in-array defects.
physics.decisive_experiment: Not as a standalone project. Inside the 3D dossiers, run Monte Carlo yield on per-tier killer densities measured from an 8-16-tier test stack, comparing sparing with grouping on cost per good bit.
physics.prior_art: 3D NAND spare blocks, word lines and bad-block tables; DRAM row/column redundancy; HBM known-good-die stacking; R06 dropped the same sparing rule as I-02910.

innovation.key_insight: Programmable tier decode makes tier-level sparing cheap (~6% area), and the arithmetic is right: 0.99^64 is about 53%, so 3D DRAM needs some tier redundancy.
innovation.killer_doubt: Dominant 3D defects (blocked or bowed HAR holes) are vertical and kill every tier of a string, which tier spares miss. Pre-tested 8-tier groups need 8 substrates per stack.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Desk study: a yield model fed with the published 3D NAND defect Pareto (vertical vs per-tier), plus a cost model of 1 vs 8 substrates. ~$20k, folded into the I-11545 dossier.
innovation.prior_art: DRAM row/column redundancy; 3D NAND bad-block and wordline management; HBM known-good-die and spare TSVs [training knowledge].

title: Selective-assembly die pairing matches complementary defect maps
idea: Bearing makers measure parts and mate oversized balls with undersized races; record each die's failing and weak-row map at wafer test and pair dies into stacks or ranks whose bad addresses do not overlap, so cheap module-level mirroring or spare sharing covers one die's holes with its partner's good rows.

physics.key_insight: Cross-die sparing in stacks or ranks can rescue dies that exceed their own redundancy, if the controller remaps a bad row to a partner's good row.
physics.killer_doubt: Random pairing already gives near-zero overlap: 100 bad rows each among ~2M rows gives ~0.005 expected collisions. Matching adds nothing; lockstep remap logic is the real cost, rescuing ~1-3%.
physics.decisive_experiment: None separate: a Monte Carlo on vendor fail-bit maps (~$20k) shows random pairing suffices. The remap test belongs with host-level row retirement (I-06365).
physics.prior_art: Selective assembly in bearing manufacture; DDR5 PPR/sPPR; ArchShield fault-map remapping (ISCA 2013).

innovation.key_insight: Wafer-test fail maps are free data; pairing dies with non-overlapping weak rows lets a buffer or base die borrow spare rows across dies.
innovation.killer_doubt: Mature DRAM loses only a few % of dies after on-die redundancy; mirroring halves capacity, and spare sharing needs a remap layer (base die, CXL controller). Gain ~1-3 yield points.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Mine wafer-sort fail-bit maps from a partner fab, or 500 reject dies on DRAM-Bender; simulate pairing with a 1k-entry cross-die remap table and count rescued dies versus PPR alone. ~$60k.
innovation.prior_art: Redundancy sharing across stacked dies (Jiang et al., ICCAD 2010); wafer matching for W2W yield (Reda et al., 2009); DDR5 PPR [training knowledge].

title: Predictive-coding memory link transmitting only prediction errors
idea: The visual cortex sends mostly prediction errors, not raw images. Identical lightweight predictors (last-value, stride, zero-run) sit at both ends of a CXL/DIMM link on FPGA, and only the entropy-coded XOR residual crosses the wire. FPGA prototype, ~$600k in 18 months.

physics.key_insight: Synchronized predictors at both ends of a link send only residuals, a cheap FPGA-demonstrable way to buy link bandwidth.
physics.killer_doubt: Interleaved multi-stream traffic defeats per-line last-value and stride prediction. Realistic saving is ~1.2-1.5x of link bits, and the link is only part of access energy. Coding adds ~2-5 ns.
physics.decisive_experiment: Replay published server and AI memory traces through the predictor pair in software and measure residual entropy. If the bit saving is below 1.5x, stop. ~$30k.
physics.prior_art: Base-Delta-Immediate (PACT 2012), FPC, DBI bus encoding in DDR4/GDDR, NVIDIA compute data compression, link-compression literature.

innovation.key_insight: Mirrored predictors at both ends of a link send only residuals; a cheap FPGA proof, and residual coding stacks with any link PHY.
innovation.killer_doubt: General memory traffic compresses ~1.3-1.5x, I/O is only part of the 10-20 pJ/bit, every miss pays 2-5 ns of codec latency, and link compression is decades old.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Replay SPEC, graph and LLM memory traces through last-value, stride and zero-run predictors in software; measure bits saved and codec latency. Stop below 1.5x. ~$20k, not $600k.
innovation.prior_art: Memory-link compression (Thuresson et al., IEEE TC 2008); base-delta-immediate compression (PACT 2012); GPU delta colour compression; value prediction (Lipasti 1996) [training knowledge].

title: Token-ring wordline sequencer for append-only KV-cache mats
idea: KV-caches append and stream tokens in order, so dedicated mats replace the row decoder with a token passed along a chain of shift-register stages (one per 8 wordlines plus a 3-bit local predecoder), allowing random access only at block granularity. Everything is drawn at DUV pitch.

physics.key_insight: Append-only KV-cache mats touch rows in order, so a shift-register token can replace row predecode and be drawn at relaxed DUV pitch.
physics.killer_doubt: Pitch-matched sub-wordline drivers at VPP ~3 V, not predecoders, dominate row periphery; decoder logic is ~3-5% of die (est.), so cutting 60% saves ~2-3%.
physics.decisive_experiment: Desk layout study (~$30k) of a 1b-class mat: row-decoder versus sub-wordline-driver area, then with a token chain; plus a paged-attention trace replay measuring the share of non-sequential row hits.
physics.prior_art: Serial-access memories (video-RAM SAM ports, FIFO DRAMs); display gate-driver-on-array shift registers; imec block-addressable CCD buffer memory.

innovation.key_insight: Append-only KV streams let dedicated mats trade random row access for sequential access, so the row path could be drawn at relaxed DUV pitch.
innovation.killer_doubt: Sub-wordline drivers, not predecoders, dominate row periphery. A flip-flop per 8 wordlines is larger than a predecoded NAND gate, so the saving is a few % of die (estimate).
innovation.decisive_experiment: Layout study in a 28 nm PDK: predecoded row decoder versus a shift-register token chain at 8-wordline pitch. Replay vLLM paged-attention traces to measure how often block-granular access suffices. ~$50k.
innovation.prior_art: LCD gate-on-array shift-register gate drivers; VRAM serial-access ports and FIFO memories [training knowledge].
