physics.decisive_experiment: 40 nm CMOS test chip: transfer 100-500 e packets into gated SPADs at 1 um pitch. Measure trigger and false-trigger rates and the junction-leakage tail at 85 C. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: Z-RAM impact-ionisation floating body (Innovative Silicon); EMCCD gain registers; Fossum quanta-image-sensor jots read single electrons without avalanche.

innovation.key_insight: Avalanche gain turns a ~100-electron packet into a full-swing digital event, so the storage node could be a planar diffusion if dark counts and leakage were negligible.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 0.02 fF node (~125 e-) drains in ~20 ms at a 1 fA junction-leakage tail; CMOS SPAD breakdown is ~10-25 V, far above the 3 V wordline floor.
innovation.decisive_experiment: On a 180 nm SPAD-capable shuttle, couple a gated diffusion to a SPAD; measure trigger probability for 0 versus 100 injected electrons, plus dark-count and afterpulse errors at 85 C. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Z-RAM impact-ionisation floating body; EMCCD gain registers; Fossum QIS reads single electrons without avalanche [training knowledge]; similar idea I-05065 dropped elsewhere.

title: Charge-gated Mott channel amplifies a few hundred stored electrons
idea: Effect walk: filling-controlled Mott transition. The storage node gates a 3-nm channel of a correlated oxide (strained NdNiO3 or electron-doped Sr2IrO4) poised at its metal-insulator boundary, so a few hundred stored electrons (~0.1-0.3 e per unit cell under a 100 nm2 gate) swing channel resistance ~100x for a gain read.

physics.key_insight: A steep nonlinear element on the storage node to cut needed charge is the right goal; triage confirms reading few-hundred-electron nodes is solvable.
physics.killer_doubt: 300 e under 100 nm2 is 3e14 cm-2: at EOT 1 nm the node must sit at ~14 V. Electrostatic gates reach ~3e13 cm-2; NdNiO3 is metallic at 300 K.
physics.decisive_experiment: Gate a 3 nm SmNiO3 film (TMI ~400 K) through 3 nm HfO2 at room temperature; kill if resistance changes <3x at 1.5 V, versus a Si MOSFET's 100x per 120 mV. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: Field-effect gating of NdNiO3 (Scherwitzl et al. 2010) and ionic-liquid nickelate gating; Mott-FET proposals (IBM, 1998); oxide 2T0C gain cells already give in-cell gain.

innovation.key_insight: A filling-controlled Mott channel could give large current gain from a tiny stored charge, removing the high-aspect-ratio capacitor.
innovation.killer_doubt: 0.1 e/u.c. is ~7e13 cm-2 (~6 MV/cm in HfO2); a ~0.006 fF gate holding 300 e needs ~8 V. NdNiO3 is metallic at 300 K; IGZO gain cells suffice.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Solid-gated SmNiO3 or VO2 Hall bar, <=5 nm thick under a 3 nm HfO2 gate (~$150k, university oxide MBE/PLD). Kill if resistance swing is <10x at <=2 V.
innovation.prior_art: Mott-FET proposals (Newns et al., IBM 1998); SmNiO3/VO2 gating (Ramanathan); ferroelectric nickelate gating (Ahn, Yale; Triscone, Geneva) [training knowledge].

title: Swap layer-by-layer 3D stacking for rolling one patterned membrane
idea: Pattern one planar layer of thin-film gain cells with DUV on a strained SiNx bilayer, release it, and let the built-in strain roll it into a 20-winding tube. Each winding becomes a memory tier, and the tiers connect through edge contacts along the roll axis.

physics.key_insight: Strain-driven self-rolling compacts a planar array ~40-60x in footprint with one release etch, which could pack bits under an accelerator.
physics.killer_doubt: Rolling creates no bits: 20 windings need 20x footprint of patterned area, so $/bit equals planar DUV TFT cost (~20-50x 1b). R=5 um bends a 100 nm stack 1%.
physics.decisive_experiment: Roll a released SiNx bilayer carrying a 32x32 IGZO TFT array (~$150k university fab); measure Vt shift, yield per winding and edge-contact yield at the tube end.
physics.prior_art: Rolled-up nanomembranes (Prinz; Schmidt group, IFW Dresden): rolled capacitors, microbatteries, sensors (training knowledge); rolled memory arrays: none found.

innovation.key_insight: Strain-driven rolling multiplies the area per footprint by ~pi x N. That is a volume-density trick, worth something only where footprint is the constraint.
innovation.killer_doubt: Rolling folds already-patterned area. Cost scales with patterned area (~63x footprint for 20 windings), so cost per bit stays planar. Contacting 20 windings needs a staircase.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A ~$150k test: roll a 5-winding IGZO TFT membrane, then measure winding-to-winding contact yield and TFT shift after rolling. Model the cost per patterned area first. It decides the idea before any fabrication.
innovation.prior_art: Rolled-up nanotechnology (O. G. Schmidt, IFW Dresden/TU Chemnitz): rolled-up capacitors, batteries and TFTs [training knowledge].

title: Apical-meristem nanowires grow stacked transistors along their own axis
idea: Shoots add segments at the tip; grow vertical Si nanowires by catalyst-tip (VLS) growth from the pad lattice while switching dopant and Ge gases every ~25 nm, so each wire holds 16 axial n+/p/n+ transistor segments, then fill around the forest with alternating spin-on dielectric and conductor layers that become wordline tiers timed to the segments.

physics.key_insight: Growing every tier's channel in one axial run would bypass stack deposition. Axial-doped nanowires show that tier-free channel formation is conceivable.
physics.killer_doubt: Sixteen n+/p/n+ segments on one wire share n+ nodes: a series string with no storage element. The VLS dopant reservoir grades junctions over ~20 nm, against 25 nm segments.
physics.decisive_experiment: Grow 4-segment n+/p/n+ Si nanowires (Au and Al catalysts) at 20-40 nm diameter. Map junction abruptness by atom probe and the kink rate over 1e6 wires. University CVD, ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: Axial-doped VLS nanowire FETs (Lieber group); Unisantis vertical SGT; atom-probe Au incorporation in VLS Si (Lauhon group) (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Growth-defined vertical doping profiles could set every tier's channel in one deposition step, trading lithography for chemistry; the instinct matches deposition-defined tier economics.
innovation.killer_doubt: VLS reservoir effects smear axial junctions over ~the wire diameter (20-40 nm), versus 25 nm segments; Au is a mid-gap leakage killer; 16 series transistors form a string, not cells.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Grow 40 nm Al- or Cu-catalysed Si wires with 4 dopant switches; measure junction abruptness by APT/SIMS and gate-all-around leakage per segment. University CVD, ~$150k; stop if transitions exceed 10 nm.
innovation.prior_art: Lieber (Harvard) axial-heterostructure nanowires; Lund University vertical nanowire GAA MOSFETs; IBM VLS Si nanowire work (training knowledge).

title: Eliminate writability for frozen weights: via-programmed 3D ROM replaces DRAM
idea: Encode a deployed model's weights as present/absent vias in 4-8 stacked metal layers written by maskless e-beam on mature-node wafers, read by low-swing sensing with no refresh or capacitor, with only activations kept in DRAM.

physics.key_insight: Frozen weights need neither writes nor refresh, so read-only bits from a mature U.S. logic fab could offload HBM capacity without capacitors or EUV.
physics.killer_doubt: Stacked present/absent-via decks lack per-bit selectors, so sneak paths through shorted vias defeat crosspoint reads; one deck at 64 nm pitch is ~4,100 nm2/bit, ~4x below 1b DRAM.
physics.decisive_experiment: Do not fund separately; fold into I-03028's 28 nm MPW NOR-ROM macro and $/GB model versus HBF. A selector-less 1k x 1k via crosspoint test chip would show the sneak-path margin collapse.
physics.prior_art: Mask ROM since the 1970s; e-beam direct-write ROM coding; Taalas hardwired-model chips (2026); I-03028 (R16). From memory, unverified.

innovation.key_insight: Frozen weights need no writes, so endurance and refresh vanish. Maskless via writing removes the per-model mask set that limits hardwired-model chips.
innovation.killer_doubt: Multi-beam writers need ~10 h per mask plate; a 300 mm wafer is ~5x that area, so 4-8 via layers is ~200+ tool-hours per wafer. Diode-less via crosspoints short rows.
innovation.decisive_experiment: E-beam write a 1 Mb via crosspoint with resistive via fill on a university tool. Measure read margin vs array size, plus write time per cm2, then feed a per-model cost model against HBM. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1 mask-ROM weights, AMD acquiring (via search snippet, prior logs); Matrix Semiconductor 3D OTP; eASIC via-configurable ASICs; Multibeam direct-write e-beam [training knowledge].

title: Scrap remelt: near-capacity code, refetch master copy on decode failure
idea: Foundries simply remelt bad castings. Clean data that can be fetched again (page cache, model weights, container images) sits in 1%-BER cells under a near-capacity 4 KB LDPC code with only about 10-12% overhead and a deliberately high failure rate of about 1e-6 per page read. When decoding fails, the page is refetched from SSD or a remote master, which is cheap because it is rare.

physics.key_insight: Clean data has a master copy, so detection plus refetch can stand in for correction. That also makes non-iid failures (dead rows, VRT bursts) survivable.
physics.killer_doubt: At p=1e-2 and 4 KB, the finite-length bound gives 12.3% overhead at FER 1e-15 and 10.9% at 1e-6. That saves ~1.4 points, and a 64 B read pulls 4 KB.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold this into I-10425. On DRAM Bender data, compare a CRC+refetch tier with an LDPC tier for page cache, measuring refetch rate, decoder pJ/bit and p99 page latency (<$50k extra).
physics.prior_art: HRM Par+R (Luo et al., DSN 2014): parity detection plus a clean-copy reload from disk (via search snippet); cache designs that refetch clean lines.

innovation.key_insight: Clean, refetchable data needs only error detection plus a cheap refetch, so a code can be tuned for throughput rather than a 1e-15 frame-error guarantee.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 4 KB, 1% BER, the ML bound needs ~10.9% parity at FER 1e-6 versus ~12.3% at 1e-15: ~1.5 points saved, not half. 64 B reads decode 4 KB.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None needed beyond the finite-length bound computed above. Fold the refetch fallback into the I-10425 / R21 I-01312 controller as a policy for clean pages.
innovation.prior_art: Heterogeneous-Reliability Memory (Luo et al., DSN 2014) recovers clean pages from storage; Linux hwpoison clean-page drop; in-study R17 I-02525 (DROP) and R28 I-10420 (HOLD).

title: Defect-budget co-design: 100x pattern-defect tolerance to unlock cheap patterning
idea: Every 128-bit word carries 16 BCH (t=2) check bits instead of 8 SECDED bits, decoded in fast logic-process periphery (bonded or under-array). A small CAM remaps the few residual failing words found at test; mat-level sparing (NAND bad-block style) handles clustered pattern defects (line opens, shorts). Retention-weak cells are remapped too. This turns patterning defectivity from a yield killer into a few percent of area overhead.

physics.key_insight: For iid defects the arithmetic holds: t=2 BCH on 144-bit words at p=1e-4 leaves ~62 three-defect words per 16 Gb die, remappable in a small CAM.
physics.killer_doubt: Patterning defects cluster (one particle kills 1e2-1e4 cells), not iid at 1e-4 (1e7/cm2); ~12,500 two-defect words per die keep zero soft-error margin. DDR5 on-die ECC exists.
physics.decisive_experiment: Analysis only (<$100k): take fail-bit maps from a DSA or NIL line-array test vehicle, fit spatial clustering, and compare yield under word-level BCH versus mat sparing.
physics.prior_art: DDR5 on-die SEC (128+8), HBM ECC, NAND bad-block management, row/column redundancy; C0 rated N-34 KNOWN+TWIST. From memory.

innovation.key_insight: The arithmetic holds: t=2 BCH over 144 b at p=1e-4 leaves ~60 failing words per 16 Gb die, so random single-cell defects cost only ~6% in check bits.
innovation.killer_doubt: Patterning defects cluster (a bitline bridge kills 512-1,024 cells) and redundancy already handles them. Hard faults at 1e-4 consume VRT/soft-error margin; overlay, not defects, blocks cheap patterning.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Map failing-bit spatial classes (single, line, cluster) on ~100 reject DDR5/LPDDR5 dies with DRAM Bender. Then model ECC-plus-sparing yield under NIL and DSA defect signatures. ~$80k.
innovation.prior_art: Row and column redundancy (decades); DDR5 on-die SEC ECC adopted for scaling yield; ArchShield (ISCA 2013); NAND bad-block management.

title: Accordion-folded single membrane becomes 26 tiers of crystalline cells
idea: Process one planar single-crystal membrane (SOI device layer) with lateral access transistors in a strip pattern, release it, then fold it accordion-style like a road map using prestressed hinge lines. N folds yield N tiers that all came from one high-quality planar process.

physics.key_insight: Folding a single membrane processed once in a planar flow gives single-crystal access FETs in every layer; fold-edge wiring replaces TSVs.
physics.killer_doubt: Fold radius >=33 um gives >=67 um layer pitch: an HBM-style stack, not 3D tiers; 26 layers at 90% each yield 0.9^26 = 6.5% without known-good-die.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fold a 5-layer 2 um SOI test membrane with neutral-plane Cu hinge lines (~$150k); measure wire yield and resistance through 1,000 -40/125 C cycles, plus continuity of a 1 um-pitch fold bus.
physics.prior_art: Our own B3-15/N-54 origami stack (ALIVE, same mechanism); imec W2W hybrid bonding at ~300 nm pitch interconnects better.

innovation.key_insight: Folding puts single-crystal lateral transistors in every tier from one planar process, avoiding the channel-quality limits of deposited 3D tiers.
innovation.killer_doubt: Each tier's area is still lithographed separately, so cost per bit is planar (1x) plus fold yield loss; 3D pays only when one etch patterns all tiers. Registration is ~um.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Start with a $0 cost model: folding leaves processed wafer area per bit unchanged. If a footprint-limited niche survives (HBM), fold a 50 nm SOI strip 8 times and measure metal continuity across the fold lines and transistor shift.
innovation.prior_art: Rolled-up/origami nanomembranes (Schmidt at IFW Dresden, X. Li at UIUC); Smart Cut layer transfer and CEA-Leti sequential 3D give c-Si tiers with nm alignment.

title: Four-pocket mirror-bit storage on both faces of channel sheets
idea: IFR: one gate crossing holds four bits. Each wordline crossing of a thin vertical oxide-semiconductor sheet stores charge in four spatially separate nitride-nanodot pockets (source-side and drain-side on front and back faces, with independent front and back gates), read by swapping source/drain direction as in mirror-bit NROM.

physics.key_insight: Mirror-bit NROM shows that spatially separate trapped-charge pockets with reverse read can store several bits per gate crossing.
physics.killer_doubt: Hot-carrier charge trapping endures ~1e5 cycles against a 3e8-7e13 need, and writes take us. N-type oxide channels have no holes, so NROM hot-hole erase is impossible.
physics.decisive_experiment: Fabricate an IGZO/SiN-nanodot front/back-gated transistor (~$150k); cycle program/erase at <=50 ns to 1e9 at 85 C. Kill if the window collapses before 1e8 or no erase works without holes.
physics.prior_art: Saifun/Spansion MirrorBit NROM (2-4 bits/cell), 3D charge-trap NAND; our N-10 direct-tunnel 3D AND is the better quasi-volatile version.

innovation.key_insight: Spatially separate trap pockets, read by swapping source and drain, give 4 bits per gate crossing: a real density lever if writes did not wear the dielectric.
innovation.killer_doubt: Hot-carrier and tunnel writes through nitride/oxide wear out at ~1e4-1e5 cycles. DRAM-class needs 3e8 (1 s refresh) to ~7e13 (hot rows), 1e4-1e9x more, and programming takes microseconds.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None worth funding as DRAM. A $50k cycling test of a double-gate IGZO/SONOS stack to 1e9 cycles at 85 C would confirm the charge-fluence rule.
innovation.prior_art: Saifun NROM and Spansion MirrorBit (including 4-bit/cell Quad); double-gate SONOS; Macronix 3D NOR/AND charge-trap flash.

title: Circulating drum memory: streaming access refreshes ultra-leaky cheap cells
idea: Capacitor size and leakage specs exist only to hold charge for 64 ms; if every row is read-and-restored every 100 us because data circulates through compute like a drum, retention can be 640x worse. That permits planar MIM capacitors on short bitlines and leaky access devices in fully depreciated 28-40 nm fabs, with no high-AR etch and no EUV, behind a controller that streams rows in fixed order.

physics.key_insight: Retention is set by the workload: data re-read every 100 us tolerates 640x leakier cells, which removes the high-aspect-ratio capacitor requirement.
physics.killer_doubt: Mature-node planar eDRAM is ~0.04-0.15 um2/bit versus ~0.001 um2 for DRAM (40-150x). Wafers ~3x cheaper leave $/bit 13-50x worse; 100 us revolutions aren't DRAM-class access.
physics.decisive_experiment: Paper cost model only: published 28 nm eDRAM bitcell areas times depreciated wafer price, against DDR5 $/GB. Revisit only if a mature-node cell <=0.01 um2 appears. ~$10k.
physics.prior_art: Delay-line and drum memories (1950s); logic eDRAM and gain-cell eDRAM (IBM deep-trench, Intel 22 nm eDRAM) (prior knowledge).

innovation.key_insight: Retention is a spec, not physics: if streaming restores every row every ~100 us, the capacitor and leakage requirements relax ~640x.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 28-40 nm planar-MIM cell is ~0.05-0.1 um2, 50-100x 1-beta's ~0.001 um2, and depreciated wafers are only ~2x cheaper, so cost/bit is ~25-50x worse. Circulating also costs ~1 W/GB.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A desk check of cell area and wafer cost at 28/40 nm against 1-beta, plus circulation power at 10-100 fJ/bit per restore. If cost/bit is above 1-beta, stop. Under $10k.
innovation.prior_art: Gain-cell eDRAM with microsecond retention (Teman, Giterman); Smart Refresh (MICRO 2007), where access acts as refresh; delay-line memory; Fiber Memory preprint (arXiv 2607.08407).

title: 77-kelvin DRAM: crude poly-Si transistors hold charge for hours
idea: Box: MIM charge x solid-phase-crystallized poly-Si TFT (leaky at 300 K) x voltage sense amp x 2D x glass or Si x PECVD a-Si plus furnace crystallization. At 77 K off-current falls by >1e6, so grain-boundary-limited TFTs from a low-mask university flow meet retention for liquid-nitrogen-cooled racks.

physics.key_insight: Temperature can substitute for process quality: thermally activated leakage with Ea ~0.3 eV falls ~1e14 from 300 to 77 K, so crude TFTs could hold charge.
physics.killer_doubt: Grain-boundary field-assisted tunnelling is nearly temperature-independent (expect ~1e2, not 1e6). IGZO already leaks <1e-18 A/um at 300 K, and 77 K costs 9.7-19.3 W per W.
physics.decisive_experiment: Cryoprobe Ioff distributions of 10^4 SPC poly-Si TFTs (to the 1e-6 tail) at 300/150/77 K and Vds 0.3-1.5 V, beside IGZO TFTs on the same glass. ~$60k.
physics.prior_art: Cryogenic DDR3 4,096 s at 77 K (JSTS 2022); IGZO 2T0C 8,000 s at 77 K (2025); Phase B N-94 cold oxide gain cells.

innovation.key_insight: Cold relaxes process quality: thermal SRH leakage essentially vanishes at 77 K, so crude low-mask poly-Si TFTs on glass could hold charge if their leakage were thermal.
innovation.killer_doubt: Grain-boundary leakage is trap-assisted and field-enhanced, so it likely falls ~1e2-1e3x, not 1e6. LN2 adds ~10-15 W at the wall per W, with no density gain.
innovation.decisive_experiment: In a university fab, build SPC poly-Si TFTs with 10 fF MIM caps. Measure off-current and retention from 300 K to 77 K at Vds 0.1-1.5 V on 200 devices. Under $50k.
innovation.prior_art: Rambus/Microsoft cryo-DRAM (2017); SNU CryoRAM (ISCA 2019); Phase B N-94 77 K oxide gain cell; R07 I-06479 150 K poly-Si (DROP).

title: Idle display fabs print stacked oxide-TFT memory panels
idea: Gen-8.5 LCD/OLED fabs (2.2 x 2.5 m glass, 1.5-2 um lithography, mature IGZO TFT know-how) sit in overcapacity. Retool them to build 4-8 BEOL-stacked oxide-TFT gain-cell memory layers on glass panels, dice panels into tiles, and attach them through a CXL controller as a ~100-300 ns capacity tier.

physics.key_insight: Display fabs are depreciated, EUV- and crucible-free, and know IGZO; a Gen-8.5 panel is ~78x a 300 mm wafer. B2-19 imprint at F~100 nm is the real revival.
physics.killer_doubt: At 2 um rules a ~30F2 cell is ~120 um2/bit: six layers give ~17 GB/panel versus 3,068 GB per 1b wafer, so ~$30-90/GB versus $1.48.
physics.decisive_experiment: One-week cost model with a panel maker's cash cost per mask-layer per m2; reaching $1.48/GB even at F=1 um needs under ~$0.6 per m2-mask. Expect failure.
physics.prior_art: ram-venture A1-03 killed display-glass IGZO memory at 2 um on density; memory-in-pixel LCDs (Sharp, JDI); SEL CAAC-IGZO memories.

innovation.key_insight: Depreciated Gen-8.5 lines are real idle capital with mature IGZO know-how, and one panel has ~78x the area of a 300 mm wafer.
innovation.killer_doubt: At 2 um rules a gain cell is ~80 um2, ~90,000x a 6F2 bit. Six layers give ~15-30 GB/panel, ~$30-100/GB against a $1.48/GB DRAM cost.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Spreadsheet only: cell area at the best panel-stepper rule (~1.2-1.5 um), tiers, array efficiency and per-mask panel cost. It survives only below $5/GB, which needs imprint-scale features (Phase B N-38).
innovation.prior_art: SEL/Sharp CAAC-IGZO DOSRAM/NOSRAM; ram-venture A1-03 killed display-glass memory at 2 um; Phase B N-38 imprinted panel-level 3D oxide.

title: Core-memory sense weaving cancels sneak current in selectorless 3D crosspoint
idea: Failure mined: core memory's sense wire zig-zagged through the cores so half-select noise cancelled, a trick lost in the move to semiconductors, while selectorless vertical crosspoints died on sneak current. Fix: pair each data pillar with a woven twin pillar that crosses the same word planes, with its half-selected cells biased in mirror image. A differential sense amp subtracts the matched sneak currents and leaves only the selected cell's current.

physics.key_insight: Differential sensing against a matched reference pillar is the right instinct for selectorless arrays. Core memory's sense-wire weaving is a genuinely lost trick.
physics.killer_doubt: Sneak current depends on data in ~31 half-selected cells per pillar, so at ON/OFF 10-100 twin mismatch exceeds the signal. RRAM/PCM endurance 1e6-1e9 vs 3e8-7e13 needed.
physics.decisive_experiment: Monte Carlo SPICE of a 32-plane vertical RRAM pillar pair with measured ON/OFF spread and random data. If sense margin is below 3 sigma, stop. ~$20k.
physics.prior_art: Vertical RRAM (Stanford Wong group, Samsung); complementary resistive switches (Linn et al., Nat. Mater. 2010); reference-column sneak cancellation schemes.

innovation.key_insight: Differential sensing against a matched twin is the right instinct for sneak currents, as core memory cancelled half-select noise by weaving its sense wire.
innovation.killer_doubt: Sneak current depends on data in ~N half-selected cells, so a twin cancels only with identical data (half the density); resistive elements endure ~1e6-1e9 cycles versus >=3e8 needed.
innovation.decisive_experiment: SPICE a 32-plane vertical crosspoint with measured self-rectifying RRAM I-V and random data in both pillars; report read margin versus array size. Stop unless margin survives 64x64 planes. ~$30k.
innovation.prior_art: Self-rectifying selectorless vertical RRAM and reference-line sneak-current subtraction, widely studied in crosspoint literature [training knowledge]; 1950s core-memory sense-wire weaving.

title: MLCC tape-stacking: hundred-layer horizontal capacitors contacted by one trench
idea: Copy multilayer ceramic capacitors. Sputter 20-50 alternating layers of electrode metal A (TiN) and metal B (W or Ru) separated by high-k. Etch one cell trench, then selectively recess A on one wall and B on the other so each fill touches only its own electrode set. The result is an interdigitated capacitor that scales with layer count, not aspect ratio.

physics.key_insight: A selective lateral recess, as in 3D NAND replacement gates, can contact alternating electrode sets from one trench without a high-AR hole etch.
physics.killer_doubt: Geometric equivalence: one layer at 864 nm2 is ~0.06 fF, not 0.5. 5.4 fF needs ~90 layers (~1.2 um); per-cell isolation is an AR ~90 metal etch.
physics.decisive_experiment: $80k nanofab: a 10-layer TiN/ZrO2/Ru stack, single trench, selective recess; measure C per layer, leakage per cell and recess uniformity. It shows the per-cell isolation etch is the wall.
physics.prior_art: Fujitsu fin-type stacked capacitor (IEDM 1988: multiple horizontal fins); stacked BEOL MIM; horizontal capacitors in 3D DRAM.

innovation.key_insight: Capacitance scaling with deposited layer count instead of etch aspect ratio is sound in MLCCs and IPDs, and selective lateral recess is proven 3D NAND processing.
innovation.killer_doubt: At a ~0.001 um2 cell, cuts and two contacts leave <~30% plate area: ~0.025 area-gain/nm of stack versus ~0.06/nm for a 20 nm pillar, so 2.5-5x taller.
innovation.decisive_experiment: In a university nanofab, deposit a 10-pair TiN/HfZrO/Ru stack, etch 100 nm trenches, test TiN-vs-Ru selective recess, and measure capacitance per footprint and edge leakage against a pillar benchmark.
innovation.prior_art: Fujitsu fin-type stacked capacitor (IEDM 1988, multi-fin storage node); TSMC multilayer SHDMIM in BEOL; MLCCs; 3D NAND lateral recess.

title: Another dimension: 512-tier vertical charge-coupled strings with one sense node
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: bits are charge packets in potential wells along a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel gated by 512 stacked wordline plates, a one-hole 3D-NAND-like process with no capacitor and no per-bit transistor. Reads clock the packets CCD-style down the pillar into one floating-diffusion sense node under the array, which regenerates them and re-injects them at the top, so refresh is just recirculation.

physics.key_insight: Recirculation through one regenerating node turns refresh into shifting; with IGZO's >200 s hold, one circulation every few seconds costs almost nothing.
physics.killer_doubt: 512 tiers x 4 phases is ~2,000 transfers per pass: CTE 0.9999 keeps 82%, imec's >98% keeps ~0. A ~25 um stack in 100 nm holes is AR ~250.
physics.decisive_experiment: Add 2,000-transfer recirculating loops to a planar IGZO CCD test chip (~$300k, shared with I-01064): measure cumulative loss and trailing charge; continue only if per-transfer loss is below 5e-5 at >=10 MHz.
physics.prior_art: imec IGZO 3D CCD buffer memory (IEDM 2024, IMW 2026); 1970s Si CCD bulk memories; Phase B N-08; I-00601 (same 200+-tier variant).

innovation.key_insight: Recirculating through a regenerating floating-diffusion node makes refresh a by-product of reading, and one sense node per 512 bits approaches NAND periphery economics.
innovation.killer_doubt: 512 packets x 3 phases is ~1,536 transfers. imec's >98% CTE leaves ~0% of the charge, and even 0.9999 leaves 86%. 10-50 us access is NAND-class, not DRAM-class.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Measure per-transfer CTE against clock frequency on a 32-tier IGZO vertical CCD test string, then extrapolate the maximum string length at 1e-15 BER. Shared with I-10793. ~$300k.
innovation.prior_art: imec IGZO 3D CCD (IMW 2026) and planar 142-bit device (IEDM 2024) (via search snippet, prior logs); 1970s recirculating CCD memories (Intel, Fairchild).

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers as one-dimensional memory substrates
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: replace the 2D wafer with a 1D substrate. A macroscopic preform of chalcogenide-glass semiconductor, polymer dielectric and metal electrodes is thermally drawn into kilometres of fiber whose cross-section is one memory column (bitline, storage electrodes, access channel); fibers are then woven or laminated with orthogonal wordline fibers into 3D blocks.

physics.key_insight: Draw towers make km of structured multimaterial fiber with no litho; a 1D substrate is a genuinely different capital model for passive or coarse electronics.
physics.killer_doubt: Woven crossings at >=10 um fiber pitch give ~1e6 bits/cm2 per layer versus DRAM ~1e10; amorphous chalcogenide mobility ~1e-3-1 cm2/Vs cannot drive ns access.
physics.decisive_experiment: Draw one chalcogenide/polymer/metal FET fiber (university draw tower, ~$150k); measure Ion/Ioff, switching time and minimum continuous feature; kill if Ion <1 uA at 1 V or features break up below 100 nm.
physics.prior_art: Fink lab (MIT) multimaterial fiber devices; Bayindir/Yaman iterative-draw chalcogenide nanowires; none found as DRAM-class memory.

innovation.key_insight: Thermal drawing replicates a multimaterial cross-section over kilometres per hour with no lithography. What carries over is litho-free cross-section replication, not woven memory fibres.
innovation.killer_doubt: Weavable fibres are >=10 um wide, so a woven crosspoint cell is ~100 um2 vs DRAM's 0.0017 um2: 1e4-1e5x less dense. Chalcogenide channels need in-fibre crystallisation even to work.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Not worth $1M. A <$100k check: draw a 50 um fibre with 16 crystallised-Se coaxial cells, weave a 16x16 mat, and measure access time and retention. The density ceiling follows from fibre pitch alone.
innovation.prior_art: Fink (MIT) and Sorin (EPFL) multimaterial fibres; Fink's 2010 metres-long in-fibre chalcogenide p-FET made by in-situ crystallisation (via search snippet).

title: Room-temperature single-electron electrometer at every vertical bitline foot
idea: Coulomb blockade: a sub-3 nm silicon island single-electron transistor, formed by self-limiting fin oxidation, sits at the base of each vertical bitline as a charge electrometer that can resolve ~10 electrons. Lateral 3D tier capacitors can then hold 0.2 fF instead of 5 fF, because the read no longer depends on charge-sharing against a large bitline capacitance.

physics.key_insight: RT Coulomb blockade needs E_c >~10 kT, which a ~2 nm Si island achieves. SETs are superb charge meters only for charge placed directly on their island or gate.
physics.killer_doubt: At the bitline foot the SET reads bitline voltage. A ~0.03 aF gate means a ~5 V period: a 33 mV signal moves ~0.006 e. Offset charge varies per device.
physics.decisive_experiment: Paper first: input-referred voltage noise of an RT SET versus a minimum MOSFET on a 3 fF node, including offset-charge drift. If you persist, put the SET inside the cell as gain (PADOX test chip, $200k).
physics.prior_art: NTT PADOX SETs (Takahashi 1995); Hitachi single-electron memory 128 Mb prototype (Yano, ISSCC 1998); RT Si SETs (~2 nm islands) [training knowledge].

innovation.key_insight: Counting electrons rather than volts is the right instinct. Electron resolution helps only at a tiny node, so the gain belongs to in-cell or per-segment gain, not the bitline foot.
innovation.killer_doubt: At the foot the cell shares charge with the bitline; kTC on 10 fF is ~40 e- rms, so 10-electron resolution is moot. Sub-3 nm islands drift with background charge.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Paper check (~$10k): noise budget for a 0.2 fF cell on a 5-20 fF vertical bitline, SET versus CDS or charge-transfer amp. Only if the SET wins, fabricate 100 PADOX SETs and map offset-charge spread at 300-360 K.
innovation.prior_art: NTT PADOX silicon SETs (Takahashi, 1990s); Hitachi room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano, 1994) and PLEDM; Phase B N-04 and in-study I-01381 (training knowledge).

title: Ultra-wide-gap amorphous Ga2O3 storage node holding 0.1 fF for hours
idea: Generation leakage scales as ni ~ exp(-Eg/2kT), so moving from IGZO (3.2 eV) to RT-sputtered a-Ga2O3 (4.8 eV) cuts intrinsic generation by ~1e13. A 0.1 fF planar MIM node behind an a-Ga2O3 access device then holds a 0.3 V signal for >1e4 s, read by a local gain transistor.

physics.key_insight: The arithmetic holds (1.6 eV more gap cuts intrinsic generation ~3e13x), and 187 electrons on 0.1 fF sit far above the ~4 e- kTC floor.
physics.killer_doubt: IGZO leakage is already defect- and gate-limited (<1 aA, 1e3-3e4 s retention), not intrinsic. a-Ga2O3 mobility <1-5 cm2/Vs slows writes; China supplies ~98% of gallium.
physics.decisive_experiment: Side-by-side 2T0C cells, IGZO versus ALD a-Ga2O3 write device, on one BEOL run (~$150k): retention distributions over 1e4 cells at 85-125 C and write time at 1 V.
physics.prior_art: IGZO 2T0C gain cells (imec, Kioxia OCTRAM); in-study I-03018 Ga2O3 coaxial cell (DROP); university Ga2O3 TFT work.

innovation.key_insight: The arithmetic holds: +1.6 eV of gap cuts intrinsic generation ~1e13x. But retention stopped being the scarce axis once oxide gain cells arrived.
innovation.killer_doubt: IGZO 2T0C is already defect- and gate-limited at <1 aA (1e3-1e4 s). a-Ga2O3 mobility ~0.1-1 cm2/Vs slows writes, and China supplies ~98% of gallium.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Only as a materials split: IGZO vs ALD a-Ga2O3 write device in one 2T0C BEOL run (~$150k); retention tails over 1e4 cells at 85-125 C and write time at 1 V.
innovation.prior_art: IGZO 2T0C gain cells (imec; Kioxia OCTRAM); in-study I-03018 Ga2O3 coaxial cell (DROP); university amorphous Ga2O3 TFT work.

title: Photomultiplier dynodes: electron-multiplying gain register on every bitline
idea: Forced connection to a photomultiplier/EMCCD dynode chain: between cell and sense amp insert a short serial register of 8-10 high-field transfer gates in the SA strip, each adding ~1.2x impact-ionization gain, so a 1 fF cell's ~3,000 signal electrons arrive at the latch as ~15,000-20,000. The register is clocked only during the sense phase.

physics.key_insight: Pre-latch charge gain is the right lever: ~5x gain before the latch would let Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~1 fF and shorten the pillar ~4x.
physics.killer_doubt: EMCCD stages give ~1-1.5% gain at ~40 V clocks. 1.2x per stage means near-breakdown fields, exponential V/T gain spread, hot-carrier aging, and +10-50 ns tRCD.
physics.decisive_experiment: 28-65 nm MPW: 10-stage high-field transfer-gate register. Measure gain per stage vs clock voltage, gain sigma across 1,000 registers, and gain decay after ~1e12 e- of throughput. ~$300k.
physics.prior_art: EMCCD (e2v L3Vision, TI Impactron); DRAM charge-transfer pre-sensing; short or segmented bitlines (Phase B N-40, N-04) get the same Cs cut at 1 V.

innovation.key_insight: Pre-latch charge gain would trade capacitor height for periphery, but the read side is already solved without gain by charge-transfer pre-sensing (N-04).
innovation.killer_doubt: EMCCD stages give only ~1-1.6% gain each at 40-50 V clocks; 1.2x per stage needs near-avalanche fields, excess noise (F~1.4) and gain spread far beyond 5 V periphery.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Not worth funding. If pursued: a 180 nm MPW with 10-gate high-field registers, measuring gain versus clock voltage and spread across 1,000 registers. Pass: 5x total at <=5 V with sigma <10%. ~$100k.
innovation.prior_art: EMCCD gain registers (TI Impactron, e2v L3Vision); Z-RAM impact ionisation; Mitsubishi charge-transfer presensing DRAM (JSSC 1997) [training knowledge]; study N-04; I-05065/I-02889 dropped.

title: Rotating nanostructured glass platter streams weights to batch inference
idea: In throughput-oriented batch inference the weight pass is a sequential scan of read-only data, which rotating media serve at the lowest cost per bit. A spinning fused-silica platter with laser-written multilevel nanostructures is read by a 10,000-element VCSEL/photodiode head array (~1 Gb/s each, ~10 Tb/s total), streaming a 70B FP8 model every ~60 ms, amortized over a batch of hundreds of sequences.

physics.key_insight: In batch inference the weight pass is a sequential read-only scan, so its storage medium need not be DRAM. That much is right.
physics.killer_doubt: At 60 m/s and 0.3 um voxels a track gives ~0.6 Gb/s, so 1.25 TB/s needs >10,000 heads each servoing <100 nm. Medium cost is moot: 70 GB NAND ~$5.
physics.decisive_experiment: Paper link budget: tracking tolerance, optical SNR and pJ/bit for a 100-head array against ~100 Gen5 SSDs or one HBF stack delivering 1.25 TB/s. Build nothing unless the head array costs less than SSDs.
physics.prior_art: Microsoft Project Silica (archival glass, slow read); SSD/HBF weight streaming (High Bandwidth Flash, GPUDirect Storage) does the job better.

innovation.key_insight: In batch inference the weight pass is a sequential, read-only scan, so its medium need not be DRAM. That part is right.
innovation.killer_doubt: Bandwidth is the cost: ~9 Tb/s at ~0.5 um voxels needs ~10,000 heads each tracking <100 nm; 70 GB of NAND costs ~$5, one HBF stack gives 1.6 TB/s.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Paper link budget: tracking tolerance, optical SNR and pJ/bit for a 100-head array versus ~100 Gen5 SSDs or one HBF stack at 1.25 TB/s. Build nothing unless heads cost less than SSDs.
innovation.prior_art: Microsoft Project Silica (archival glass, slow read); multi-beam optical pickups; SSD/HBF weight streaming (Apple 'LLM in a flash', HBF).

title: Core-rope weights: maskless via-programmed BEOL ROM frees HBM
idea: Revive Apollo's core-rope memory, where the wiring itself encoded the program: build generic base wafers with 8 stacked metal crossbar levels and encode a frozen model's weights only in the via layers, written maskless by multibeam e-beam, so each model ships as a ROM chiplet. Weights leave DRAM; HBM keeps only activations and KV cache.

physics.key_insight: Frozen weights need no writes or refresh, so a generic base wafer personalized only in its via layers puts model weights in read-only bits beside compute.
physics.killer_doubt: Diode-less via crosspoints short rows to columns, and sneak paths through ~50 ohm vias defeat reading. Multibeam writing ~2e13 vias per wafer per level takes tens to hundreds of hours.
physics.decisive_experiment: Tape out a 28-40 nm 2-deck via-ROM crossbar with and without per-via oxide diodes. Measure read margin against array size (64-1,024 lines). ~$300k MPW.
physics.prior_art: Logic mask/via ROM; Matrix poly-diode 3D OTP; our R16 I-03028 (ADVANCE, ArF via mask) and R18 I-02068 (DROP, sneak paths).

innovation.key_insight: Frozen weights need zero write endurance. A generic crossbar base wafer customised only in via layers turns each model into a ROM chiplet with no per-model mask set.
innovation.killer_doubt: Taalas HC1 already hardwires weights in N6 metal/via ROM. Multibeam e-beam writes one mask's area in ~10 h, so 8 via levels per 300 mm wafer take ~200-400 tool-hours.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Cost model (~$20k): multibeam write time per via level per wafer versus a ~$100k DUV via mask amortised over chips per model version, plus selector-less via-crosspoint sneak-path read margin.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1 mask-ROM weights, AMD acquiring (prior logs); Matrix 3D OTP; eASIC via-configurable ASICs; in-study I-02068 (same mechanism, DROP), I-02186 (ADVANCE).

title: Snack-bag web metallizers vacuum-coat 128-tier stacks by the kilometer
idea: Borrowed from roll-to-roll metallizers that coat packaging film at ~1,000 m/min: deposit 128 alternating Mo/SiOx wordline/insulator layers on a heat-tolerant web in multi-drum passes, laminate the stack onto a CMOS wafer, then one hole etch plus ALD finishes vertical-channel gain cells.

physics.key_insight: Decoupling tier-stack deposition from the wafer fab is a legitimate capital idea. Web coaters deposit area at ~100x lower cost.
physics.killer_doubt: Packaging coatings carry >=1 pinhole/cm2; 128 tiers need <0.01/cm2/layer or every die shorts. A 1 um particle voids ~mm2 on lamination. The stack is ~5% of wafer cost.
physics.decisive_experiment: Web-coat a 16-pair Mo/SiOx stack on polyimide, transfer it to a Si wafer, and measure pinhole shorts/cm2, bond-void density and thickness sigma per layer ($150k). Kill if shorts exceed 0.1/cm2/layer.
physics.prior_art: Roll-to-roll vacuum metallizing and barrier films; 3D NAND PECVD ON stacks; in-study I-10786 and I-07806 dropped laminated/wound stacks [training knowledge].

innovation.key_insight: Vacuum web coaters lay down multilayers at ~100x lower cost per m2. Decoupling the tier stack from the wafer would make tiers a laminated commodity film.
innovation.killer_doubt: Web-coated oxide barriers show ~1e2-1e3 pinholes/cm2 (estimate), while each of 127 interlayers needs <1e-3/cm2 for short-free tiers. Stack deposition is perhaps 10-20% of 3D wafer cost.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Coat a 16-pair Mo/SiOx stack on stainless or polyimide web in a pilot coater and laminate it onto 200 mm wafers. Map interlayer shorts per cm2 and voids by acoustic microscopy. Stop above 0.01 shorts/cm2. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: Vacuum web coaters for optical and barrier multilayers (Applied Materials SmartWeb, Buhler Leybold); 3M co-extruded multilayer optical film; 3D NAND PECVD tier stacks (training knowledge).

title: Roll a 2D array film into a multi-turn scroll
idea: Turn area into tiers by rolling instead of stacking: fabricate a thin-film oxide DRAM array on a strained bilayer membrane with the existing mask set, then use one added release mask so the film self-rolls into a 10-30 turn Swiss roll, with turns connected through contacts at the scroll edge.

physics.key_insight: Strain-driven self-rolling compacts a planar array 10-30x in footprint with one release etch. That could matter where footprint under an accelerator is scarce.
physics.killer_doubt: Rolling creates no bits: 20 turns need 20x the patterned area, so $/bit equals planar thin-film cost. R=5 um bends a 100 nm stack ~1%. Inner-turn contacts are unsolved.
physics.decisive_experiment: Roll a 1 mm2 IGZO TFT test array (5 turns) and measure Vt shift vs radius and edge-contact yield per turn ($100k). Note that a pass still leaves cost per bit unchanged.
physics.prior_art: Rolled-up nanomembranes (Prinz; Schmidt, IFW Dresden): rolled capacitors and microbatteries; duplicate of I-00027 (dropped elsewhere) [training knowledge].

innovation.key_insight: Self-rolling strained bilayers fold a patterned film into a compact multi-turn volume with one release mask. That helps only where footprint near logic, not cost, is the constraint.
innovation.killer_doubt: Rolling relocates film rather than multiplying it: a 20-turn roll uses 20x the processed wafer area, so cost/bit is unchanged. Inner-turn contacts and TFT bending strain add loss.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Spreadsheet first (~$5k): $/GB of rolled versus flat film from the same process. Only if footprint matters, roll a 64x64 IGZO TFT array on a strained SiNx bilayer and measure Vt shift and contact yield. ~$150k.
innovation.prior_art: O. G. Schmidt group (IFW Dresden, TU Chemnitz): rolled-up nanomembrane capacitors, inductors and micro-batteries; R27's laminated-sheet I-07806 dropped on the same cost logic (training knowledge).

title: Gigahertz CCD loops: one floating-diffusion amp per 64 bits
idea: Failure mined: 1970s CCD memories (Fairchild, Intel 2416) lost to DRAM on millisecond serial latency and charge-transfer loss. Fix: 64-stage buried-channel CCD loops with imaging-grade transfer efficiency (>99.9999%), 2-phase clocked at 4 GHz (worst-case 16 ns rotation), each sensed and re-injected by one floating-diffusion amplifier. Packets hold 2 bits (4 charge levels), and there are no per-bit contacts, capacitors or wordline drivers.

physics.key_insight: A nm-scale c-Si buried channel holds ~1e-7 bulk traps per stage and negligible dark charge. Regenerating each 64-stage loop relaxes the CTE need to ~0.9995.
physics.killer_doubt: A 2-phase stage is at least 4F^2 per packet, so at CIS F=45 nm a bit takes ~10x DRAM's area. One amp per 64 bits is 16x DRAM's amp count.
physics.decisive_experiment: 65 nm CIS MPW: 64-stage overlapping-gate buried-channel loop. Measure CTE from 10 MHz to 4 GHz, and 4-level packet error after 1e6 regenerated rotations. ~$250k.
physics.prior_art: Intel 2416 and Fairchild CCD memories (1970s); imec IGZO CCD buffer memory (IEDM 2024, 3D IMW 2026; logged in s2-innovation-R16).

innovation.key_insight: Circulating charge loops sensed by one floating-diffusion amp per 64 packets need no per-bit transistor, capacitor or wordline, and buried channels give seconds of retention.
innovation.killer_doubt: At CIS-fab F~45 nm a 2F2 packet is ~4,000 nm2, ~4.7x DRAM's 864 nm2 cell; clocking all gates at 4 GHz costs ~0.2 W per Mb at 0.05 fF/gate.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Fabricate 64-stage buried-channel CCD loops at minimum gate pitch on a CIS shuttle; measure transfer efficiency at 1-4 GHz, full well per um2 and clock power per bit. ~$300k.
innovation.prior_art: 1970s CCD memories (Fairchild, Intel 2416); imec IGZO CCD buffer memory, IEDM 2024 and 3D at IMW 2026 (via search snippet, R01 log).

title: Electron-beam-addressed charge film (EBAM) with field-emitter arrays
idea: Failure mined: 1970s EBAM/BEAMOS (GE, Control Data) stored bits as charge written and read by an electron beam on a MOS target, and died on vacuum, beam deflection and slow serial access. Fix: replace the deflected beam with a CMOS-driven Spindt field-emitter array in which each tip covers a 64x64 patch at 8 nm spot pitch through a small electrostatic microlens. Bits are charge in a nitride film, read by beam-induced current to a common backplate.

physics.key_insight: Moving addressing out of the array into a relaxed-pitch emitter array would remove per-bit transistors, wordlines and EUV, if beams could write reliably.
physics.killer_doubt: An 8x8 nm nitride spot holds ~1-6 trapped electrons (1e12-1e13 cm^-2). At ~1e15 e/cm2 per write, ~1 C/cm2 oxide damage arrives within ~1e3-1e4 cycles.
physics.decisive_experiment: In a commercial SEM, write and read 8 nm charge spots on an ONO film. Cycle 1e6 times, and measure retention, read disturb and signal per spot. ~$100k.
physics.prior_art: GE BEAMOS and Control Data EBAM (1970s); HP Atomic Resolution Storage, field emitters on phase-change media (~2000); IBM MEMS microcolumns.

innovation.key_insight: An unpatterned charge film addressed by a CMOS-driven field-emitter array removes per-bit transistors and lines; only a relaxed ~200 nm emitter grid needs patterning.
innovation.killer_doubt: Each tip needs its own 8 nm-focusing lens and 64x64 deflection, beyond multi-beam litho tools; beam writes through nitride are fluence-limited to ~1e2-1e5 cycles (C0-2) versus ~1e13.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Write and read 8-16 nm charge dots in a nitride film with an SEM, cycling one site 1e8 times to measure endurance and beam-induced read current. ~$80k.
innovation.prior_art: GE/Control Data EBAM/BEAMOS (1970s); HP Atomic Resolution Storage field-emitter storage (~2000); IBM Millipede probe storage [training knowledge].

title: Vinyl-record pressing: via-programmed mask ROM for frozen model weights
idea: Borrowed from record pressing, where one stamper makes millions of discs: frozen model weights are pressed into 1-transistor mask ROM by a single cheap via/metal mask on a commodity logic wafer (no EUV, no capacitor) stacked under the accelerator, so weights need zero DRAM and zero refresh; a new model version is a new via mask.

physics.key_insight: Frozen weights need no refresh or capacitor, and via-programmed ROM runs in mature U.S. logic fabs with one custom mask: a real capital and sourcing lever for small models.
physics.killer_doubt: Density. 28 nm via-ROM is ~0.01-0.03 Gb/mm2 against DRAM 1b's ~0.35, so 70 GB FP8 needs ~47,000 mm2 (~0.7 wafer, ~$20/GB). Not cheaper and cannot be co-packaged.
physics.decisive_experiment: Desk study first: price a ROM compiler macro at 28/22 nm (bits/mm2, 1-2 bit/cell) for 8B and 70B models against HBF/NAND and LPDDR $/GB and GB/s. A die only follows if ROM beats NAND.
physics.prior_art: Taalas hard-wired model chips (8B-class, per press); SanDisk/SK hynix High Bandwidth Flash for read-only weights at ~50x DRAM density.

innovation.key_insight: Frozen weights need no capacitor, refresh or EUV, and a via mask on a mature U.S. logic node is a real capital and sourcing lever for small, long-lived models.
innovation.killer_doubt: 28 nm via-ROM reaches ~0.05-0.13 Gb/mm2, so 70 GB FP8 needs ~4,300-11,000 mm2 (~$3-8/GB), scrapped when the model retires. HBF gives 8-16x HBM capacity at similar cost.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Desk study only: price a 28/22 nm ROM compiler macro (1-2 bit/cell) for 8B and 70B models against HBF, LPDDR and HBM in $/GB-year at 6, 12 and 24-month model lifetimes.
innovation.prior_art: Taalas HC1 hardwired Llama 8B in mask-ROM on N6 (AMD acquiring, 2026); YOLoC ROM-CiM; SanDisk/SK hynix HBF for read-only weights.

title: Photomultiplier read: avalanche gain junction under each pillar
idea: Like a photomultiplier or SPAD turning one photon into a pulse, place a quenched avalanche junction at the foot of each vertical bitline biased just below breakdown; a 0.1 fF cell's few hundred electrons trigger ~100x multiplication, then a passive quench resets it, so cells and lines stay tiny.

physics.key_insight: Pre-latch gain is the right lever: ~100x charge gain would let a 0.1 fF (~600 e-) cell drive a few-fF local line.
physics.killer_doubt: Si junctions avalanche at >=~6-10 V with ~10-20 mV/K Vbr drift, so gain spreads exponentially; 0.1 fF held 64 ms needs <=0.16 fA, ~80x below the 13 fA tail.
physics.decisive_experiment: Superseded by SPICE against N-04 charge-transfer sensing. If pursued: 65 nm MPW of vertical junctions at 30-100 nm pitch, measuring gain spread, dark counts and afterpulsing at 25-85 C.
physics.prior_art: SPAD and quanta image sensors; Z-RAM impact ionisation; EMCCD gain registers; siblings I-05065, I-02889 dropped; Phase B N-04 reaches 0.5 fF at 1 V.

innovation.key_insight: Gain before the latch could, in principle, read a few-hundred-electron node. Triage already solves the read side without gain: charge transfer (N-04) cuts Cs 10x.
innovation.killer_doubt: SPAD breakdown is ~10-25 V against a 3 V wordline floor. Guard rings need um pitch at 30-40 nm. A 0.1 fF node needs <0.5 fA, 26x below the tail.
innovation.decisive_experiment: No new experiment is justified. To revive it, run TCAD (~$30k) on a sub-100 nm pitch junction and show breakdown under 5 V, gain of at least 30 and no edge breakdown.
innovation.prior_art: Z-RAM impact-ionisation floating body; EMCCD gain registers; Fossum QIS jots. The same verdict was given on I-02889 and I-05065 in other batches (training knowledge).

title: Vertical plated-wire memory: NiFe-lined holes through word-plane stack
idea: Revive 1960s plated-wire memory (NiFe electroplated on beryllium-copper wire, non-destructive readout, flown in Apollo-era and Skylab systems): etch vertical holes through an epitaxial stack of heavily doped silicon word planes by metal-assisted chemical etching, electroplate a circumferentially magnetized NiFe film on each hole wall around a copper core, and store a bit where each word plane crosses a hole. A word current tilts the magnetization slightly and the core senses the induced voltage without destroying it.

physics.key_insight: A closed-flux circumferential NiFe bit around a vertical conductor is stray-field-free and non-destructively readable. One hole mask with aqueous MACE and plating avoids rare gases.
physics.killer_doubt: Inductive read collapses: a 10x50 nm NiFe ring links ~5e-16 Wb, so a 1 ns tilt gives ~0.1-0.25 uV against >=2 uV core-line thermal noise. TMR read makes it N-82.
physics.decisive_experiment: Plate 10 nm NiFe in 100 nm holes through 8 doped-Si planes. Pulse one plane and measure the core-line EMF with a low-noise amplifier against 4kTR noise. ~$150k; expect sub-uV.
physics.prior_art: 1960s-70s plated-wire memory (Univac; Apollo/Skylab-era systems); our R09 I-04150 and R21 I-08865 vertical magnetic tubes (both DROP).

innovation.key_insight: Closed-flux circumferential NiFe rings read non-destructively and write magnetically, so there is no charge-fluence wall; one hole mask with aqueous etch and plating builds the array.
innovation.killer_doubt: A 5 x 50 nm NiFe ring links ~2.5e-16 Wb; a 10% tilt in 1 ns induces ~25 nV. A 10 Oe word-plane field needs ~1.6 A per mm width.
innovation.decisive_experiment: None warranted at memory scale. If pursued, plate NiFe in 200 nm MacEtch holes through two doped-Si planes (~$80k) and measure inductive read signal and half-select disturb versus diameter.
innovation.prior_art: UNIVAC/Bell plated-wire memory (1960s); IBM racetrack; Phase B N-82 racetrack-in-hole; in-study I-08865, I-04287 (both DROP on signal).

title: Magnify throughput 100x: solar-style inline memory lines
idea: Borrow photovoltaic manufacturing (belt-fed inline PECVD, laser scribing, screen-print metallization at ~8,000 wafers/hour per line) to make vertical thin-film transistor-capacitor cells whose critical dimensions are set by film thickness and laser scribe, not lithography.

physics.key_insight: Vertical thin-film devices can take their channel length from film thickness, not litho, which is useful for tiered oxide cells, not PV lines.
physics.killer_doubt: Scribe/print pitch of 20-50 um gives ~1e3 um2/bit, ~4e5x below 1b, not 500x: ~6 MB per wafer, ~$30/GB. At 5 um laser pitch, serial scribing takes ~1e3 s per wafer-layer.
physics.decisive_experiment: Paper study ($10k): bits/wafer and $/GB versus scribe pitch and laser write speed, including periphery chips. This idea fails at every pitch reachable by PV tools.
physics.prior_art: Display-fab TFT ICs (PragmatIC flexible ICs); TFT memory on glass. A PV-line memory: none found.

innovation.key_insight: PV inline tools process a wafer for well under $1 at ~8,000 wafers/hour, and thickness-defined vertical channels can set one critical dimension without lithography.
innovation.killer_doubt: Laser-scribe and screen-print pitches are ~10-40 um, so each bit takes ~100-1,600 um2, ~1e5x less dense than 1b; NAND already serves slow tiers far cheaper.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Laser-scribe a PECVD a-Si or IGZO vertical TFT-capacitor array on glass at the finest PV scribe pitch; measure cell pitch, leakage and retention, then compute GB per M10 wafer.
innovation.prior_art: Thin-film/TFT memory work in display fabs; Phase B N-38 panel-level oxide memory at F~100 nm imprint is the stronger version.

title: Coaxial nested capacitor shells: four cells in one hole
idea: IFR: one hole holds many cells. Conformally deposit four concentric storage electrodes separated by high-k and plate shells in one deep hole, each ending at a different height so a ring-shaped oxide-TFT access device wraps each shell's exposed top edge at its own level; one etch plus depositions makes four cells per hole.

physics.key_insight: Nested shells use both faces of each electrode, and the wide holes needed would only be AR ~8-30, easing the HAR etch.
physics.killer_doubt: Each cell needs >=12-16 nm radial stack, so 4 shells need a >=100-140 nm hole: 18-45F2 per cell at F=12 nm, worse than 6F2.
physics.decisive_experiment: Free first: draw the radial stack with real film thicknesses. If pursued, a 3-shell coaxial MIM in a 200 nm hole tests selective staggered recess of concentric TiN shells.
physics.prior_art: Double-sided cylinder and fin/crown stacked DRAM capacitors (1990s); none found for staggered per-shell ring TFTs.

innovation.key_insight: Multi-electrode deposition inside one etched hole is the right instinct (one etch, many bits), but coaxial shells spend radial room the hole doesn't have.
innovation.killer_doubt: 4 storage and 3+ plate shells with ~5 nm dielectrics need ~50-85 nm radial build per side. Holes are ~40 nm today, so area grows 6-20x for 4 cells.
innovation.decisive_experiment: Do a geometry/TCAD study of radial build-up, per-shell Cs and a staggered-recess flow. Cross-section a 3-shell ALD stack in a 150 nm hole coupon. Under $100k.
innovation.prior_art: Double-sided cylinder capacitors (all DRAM makers); multi-plate container-capacitor patents; Phase B N-43 coaxial 2T0C uses the coax better.

title: Origami artist: roll one flat DRAM membrane into twenty tiers
idea: An origami artist turns a flat sheet into volume. Pattern one 2D cell array on a strained bilayer nanomembrane (e.g., SiN/SiGe) over a sacrificial layer; on release, built-in strain rolls it into a tight Swiss roll of ~20 turns, so one 2D lithography pass yields 20 tiers, with wordlines running along the roll and contacted at its edge.

physics.key_insight: Strain-driven self-rolling turns a planar array into ~20 windings with one release etch, converting area into volume without deep etch or stack deposition.
physics.killer_doubt: Rolling creates no bits: 20 turns need 20x the patterned flat area, so litho cost per bit is unchanged. A ~5 um radius bends a 100 nm stack ~1%.
physics.decisive_experiment: Roll a 20-turn SiN/SiGe membrane carrying 1k IGZO gain cells at a university fab. Measure the Ioff tail, Vt shift and edge-contact yield before and after rolling. ~$200k.
physics.prior_art: Schmidt group rolled-up nanomembrane electronics (IFW Dresden, from memory); our R08 I-00027 self-rolled array (DROP).

innovation.key_insight: Strain-driven rolling multiplies area per footprint by about the number of turns. That is a real volumetric density trick, useful only where footprint is the scarce axis.
innovation.killer_doubt: Rolling folds already-lithographed area: 20 turns need ~20x the patterned area, so litho cost per bit stays planar. Edge-contacting 20 turns at ~40 nm pitch is unsolved.
innovation.decisive_experiment: A spreadsheet of patterned area, wafers per GB and roll yield settles cost per bit. Only if footprint matters, roll a 5-turn IGZO TFT membrane (~$100k) and measure turn-to-turn registration.
innovation.prior_art: Rolled-up nanotechnology (O. G. Schmidt, IFW Dresden; X. Li, UIUC): rolled capacitors and TFTs; in-study I-00027, I-10175 (both DROP).
